Real streams (Twitter, news) are dominated by what a frozen web-scale embedding does NOT cover: brand-new hashtags, fresh named entities, breaking-event slang, misspellings, and drifting word meanings. These OOV/drifting terms are precisely the signal of emerging topics that online analytics cares about, yet a static embedding maps them to a wrong or diffuse region fixed before the event existed, silently violating the alignment precondition when a new topic appears. Embedding-free stream models (MStream/MStreamF, DP-BTM) handle drift in topic proportions but treat words as opaque discrete tokens over a fixed vocabulary, so they cannot use semantics for cold-start clusters or place unseen words. No model here lets word representations themselves adapt to the stream, leaving room for a model that keeps its semantic space in scope with the evolving data.
method: Propose SODA, an online nonparametric mixture model for short-text streams in which word representations are learned and continuously updated from the stream rather than frozen from an external corpus. Topic representation builds on NPMM: each topic is a Gaussian in embedding space plus a sparse discrete word distribution; a one-pass DP-mixture assignment decides per document whether it joins an existing topic or spawns a new one via Mahalanobis distance to topic Gaussians, removing the manual new-topic threshold. The key departure is adaptive embeddings: seed the table from pre-trained vectors only for covered words, and after each mini-batch run a lightweight online skip-gram update (directional skip-gram) on batch biterms so active words track drift, coupling embeddings to topics by regularizing each word toward the mean of its assigned topic Gaussian. OOV bootstrapping initializes an unseen word from subword n-gram vectors, within-batch context vectors, and the centroid of its host document's topic, then refines it online, keeping novel vocabulary in-scope. Drift detection tracks each word's embedding displacement across batches; large shifts flag meaning drift and can trigger a topic split, and a burst of mutually-close new/drifted words far from all topic Gaussians triggers an emerging-topic spawn, tying emergence detection to data-driven semantics. Bounded memory/forgetting (as in MStreamF) retires outdated topics and evicts inactive-word embeddings. Inference is one-pass collapsed Gibbs sampling interleaved with SGD embedding updates. Evaluate on streaming Twitter/news data with emerging events and novel vocabulary using clustering NMI/purity, topic coherence (NPMI), and emerging-topic recall and detection latency; baselines are MStream/MStreamF, DP-BTM, and NPMM with frozen GloVe; ablations isolate online vs frozen embeddings, OOV bootstrapping, and drift-triggered splitting. Expected gains concentrate exactly where the static-embedding assumption fails, closing the scope mismatch.

paper_title: Quantitative Performance Metrics for Mobile Robots Navigation
motivation: Reactive obstacle-avoidance methods in this corpus — potential fields (Khatib), VFH, the Dynamic Window Approach, elastic bands, and especially the Nearness Diagram (ND)/ORM family built on the situated-activity, "divide-and-conquer" paradigm — are the state of the art for moving robots through dense, cluttered, "troublesome" scenarios. But essentially all of them are formulated on an idealized sensing assumption: that at each control step the method receives an accurate, dense, geometrically clean snapshot of obstacle positions. ND makes this explicit: the authors state "We have not addressed the sensor noise in the ND method implementation. We believe that external modules should process the sensory information..." and only speculate that "increasing the security distance according to the sensor uncertainty could be designed." This offloading is fragile precisely where ND's power comes from: its behavior is chosen by a discrete, geometry-based classification of the situation (detecting gaps/discontinuities, free-walking areas, valleys, whether obstacles lie inside the security zone). Under real sensing — noisy or sparse ultrasonic rings, limited field-of-view depth sensors, specular dropouts, edge artifacts of the kind VFH documents for edge-detection — a single spurious or missing return can flip the detected situation, spuriously open/close a gap, or misplace the free-walking area, producing oscillation, unsafe near-misses, or traps. VFH partially addresses inaccurate sonar with a probabilistic certainty/histogram grid, but it lacks ND/ORM's situation-based competence in truly dense scenarios; conversely ND/ORM lack any explicit uncertainty model. Meanwhile the evaluation works in the corpus (the PerMIS metrics, the MoVeMA benchmark, and the navigation-evaluation paper) note that robustness is rarely quantified and there is no consensus protocol — and none of them stress-test reactive planners as a function of sensing quality. The gap: no reactive navigation method that retains ND-style competence in troublesome scenarios while functioning under weaker, more realistic sensing assumptions (noisy, sparse, intermittent, narrow-FOV), nor a benchmark axis that measures degradation with sensing quality.
method: Relax the clean-sensing assumption of the situated-activity/ND paradigm by re-deriving it on an explicit, distributional obstacle representation, yielding an Uncertainty-Aware Nearness Diagram (U-ND) that degrades gracefully under noisy/sparse sensing while preserving ND's divide-and-conquer competence. Concretely: (1) Probabilistic nearness representation — replace ND's deterministic per-sector nearness (PND/RND) with, for each angular sector, a short-horizon evidence-accumulated estimate of the distance-to-closest-obstacle together with its variance and an occupancy confidence, fusing consecutive scans (VFH certainty-grid style, but kept as per-sector distance distributions and decayed over time) so that dropouts and sparse rings do not erase known obstacles and outliers are down-weighted. (2) Confidence-gated gap/free-walking-area detection — a discontinuity is treated as a navigable gap only when the posterior probability that the opening is genuinely free (given estimated range noise and angular resolution) exceeds a threshold; this directly hardens the brittle geometric step that selects ND's behavior. (3) Direction- and time-varying, uncertainty-adaptive security zone — inflate the security distance per sector as a function of the local estimated variance/confidence (operationalizing ND's own speculative remark, but anisotropically and dynamically rather than as a global constant), so poorly-sensed directions are treated more conservatively. (4) Soft, probabilistic situation arbitration — instead of committing to one discrete ND situation (with only hysteresis), compute a posterior over the candidate situations near classification boundaries and blend their motion commands weighted by that posterior, suppressing chattering caused by noise-induced situation flips while collapsing to standard ND when confidence is high. This keeps ND's symbolic-level design intact (so ORM and other situated methods can adopt the same relaxation) but makes every geometric decision uncertainty-aware. Evaluation extends scope on the sensing axis: using a real/simulated dense-clutter, U-shape-trap, and narrow-corridor suite, systematically inject range noise, angular sparsity, random dropout, and limited FOV, and measure — with the PerMIS/MoVeMA-style metrics (success rate, minimum clearance/safety, path length, smoothness, and a new command-oscillation index) — performance as a function of sensing quality, comparing U-ND against baseline ND, VFH, and DWA. Success criterion: U-ND matches ND in clean high-quality sensing yet retains high success rate and safety where the baselines collapse, demonstrating that ND-class reactive navigation can be made to function under substantially weaker, more realistic sensing assumptions.

paper_title: Amazon.com Recommendations: Item-to-Item Collaborative Filtering
motivation:
The provided works collectively define the classical design space of collaborative filtering (CF), yet they interact only empirically. Memory-based user k-NN (GroupLens; Breese et al.'s "Empirical Analysis") offers high quality but O(n) online cost and acute sparsity sensitivity; item-based CF (Sarwar et al.; item-to-item similarity) is shown experimentally to give "dramatically better" quality and scalability, but the paper offers no principled explanation of *why* the item mode dominates the user mode. Model-based methods trade accuracy for speed by coarsening: clustering (Clustering Methods for CF; Scaling Clustering) partitions users, and dimensionality reduction (Eigentaste's PCA on a dense gauge set; SVD in Analysis of Recommendation Algorithms) projects to a low-dimensional subspace to achieve near-constant online time. Hybrid content injection (GroupLens filterbots; Content-Based Collaborative Recommendation) is used specifically to "bridge the gaps caused by sparsity." The Analysis paper even decomposes every CF system into three sub-processes (representation, neighborhood formation, recommendation generation) and the E-Commerce Applications survey frames the field's central tension as simultaneously meeting quality, throughput/latency, and coverage under "extreme sparsity."

Despite this shared structure, there is no unifying formal account that predicts, *a priori*, where a given design sits on the accuracy–scalability–coverage frontier as a function of a few structural parameters (choice of aggregation mode, its granularity/rank, and the observation density it implies). Every paper instead re-tunes knobs — neighborhood size k, number of clusters, number of principal components v, similarity metric — and reports measurements on MovieLens/EachMovie/Jester/Fingerhut. This leaves open a foundational gap: a derivation that explains, rather than merely observes, why item-based beats user-based, why clustering and low-rank projection sacrifice accuracy for online cost, why a dense "gauge set" is needed for constant-time methods, and by how much content filterbots relax sparsity. Such a theory matters because it would turn method selection and hyperparameter setting from empirical search into a computable design rule.
method:
Contribution type: a formal model, taxonomy, and a bias–variance–complexity bound that unifies all the surveyed CF families.

(1) Aggregation-Operator model. Represent the observed ratings as a sparse matrix A over users×items. Formalize *every* method in the corpus as a single parametric linear prediction operator: R̂ = W·Ã, where Ã is a mean-imputed/centered operand and W is a row-stochastic aggregation operator defined over a chosen *mode* and a chosen *granularity* r. Show, by explicit reduction, that user k-NN, item k-NN, cluster-average, and PCA/SVD projection are all instances differing only in (a) mode m ∈ {user, item, latent, content-augmented}, (b) effective rank/granularity r = number of free "prototypes" (r=n for full user-kNN, r=#clusters, r=v principal components, r=m for item-kNN), and (c) the support/sparsity pattern of W. This yields a taxonomy that places all ten works on three axes (mode × granularity × support).

(2) Structural parameters. Define per-parameter observation density d(m,r) = (number of observed ratings)/(number of free parameters the operator must estimate at granularity r in mode m), and online cost C ∝ r (lookup/inner-product count). Note item mode raises d because each item carries many ratings while W has m×m entries; latent mode raises d by shrinking parameters to O(r); a dense gauge set is precisely the device that guarantees high d for latent projection.

(3) Error decomposition and bound (the theorem). Under a generative low-rank-plus-noise model of Ã with rank ρ* and noise variance σ², derive the expected prediction error of R̂ as E[err] = B(r)² + V(r/d) + σ², where the bias term B(r) is monotonically decreasing in granularity r (coarser operators cannot resolve fine preference structure — quantifying clustering's accuracy loss), and the variance term V grows with r/d(m,r) (more prototypes estimated from the same sparse data inflate error — quantifying user-kNN's sparsity fragility). Prove that (i) for fixed observation budget there is an interior minimizer r*(sparsity) balancing bias and variance, and give its closed form under the low-rank model; (ii) the achievable error is a decreasing function of density d, so among modes the one maximizing d dominates the entire error–cost Pareto frontier — formally yielding "item mode ≻ user mode whenever ratings-per-item exceeds the user-count/item-count ratio," and "latent mode ≻ item mode when ρ* ≪ m"; (iii) content filterbots add pseudo-observations that increase d by a computable factor, shifting the frontier and lower-bounding the sparsity relief.

(4) Design corollary. From the bound, produce a computable rule: given only the observed sparsity, item/user counts, and estimated spectral decay of A, choose the mode that maximizes d, set granularity r=r* from the closed form, and pay online cost O(r*), achieving Pareto-optimal accuracy. Coverage is treated as a support-connectivity property of W and shown to improve monotonically as r decreases (transitivity via low rank), making the accuracy–coverage tension explicit.

(5) Validation. The derivation predicts numeric orderings and optimal r* that can be checked directly against the reported experiments in the corpus (item vs. user k-NN, choice of v in Eigentaste/SVD, number of clusters, filterbot sparsity gains) using the same MovieLens/EachMovie/Jester datasets, by measuring d and spectral decay and confirming the predicted error–cost frontier and r*. This turns the ten papers' scattered empirical comparisons into instances of one derived law.

paper_title: A Hierarchical Phrase-Based Model for Statistical Machine Translation
motivation: Log-linear SMT systems are tuned by Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) to maximize corpus BLEU on a small dev set. This tuning search has three weaknesses the listed works expose but do not resolve. First, it maximizes a single point estimate of BLEU, yet Koehn (2004) and Zhang et al. (2004) show via bootstrapping that BLEU on small sets has wide confidence intervals, so MERT can climb noise-driven peaks and overfit its own objective. Second, it is unstable: Och notes multiple random restarts are needed to escape local optima, and different restarts yield different weights with similar dev BLEU that diverge on test data. Third, it is expensive: it repeatedly re-decodes the whole dev set uniformly regardless of how much each sentence influences the objective. The bootstrap machinery these papers use only to report uncertainty is never folded into the tuning search itself, leaving an opportunity to make optimization variance-aware.
method: We propose Bootstrap-Robust MERT. Enabling fact: BLEU comes from per-sentence sufficient statistics, and Och's exact line search already yields, for each interval along a direction, the chosen hypothesis and its statistics per dev sentence, so evaluating BLEU on any bootstrap resample is near-free re-aggregation. Robust objective: pre-draw B resamples of dev indices; during the exact piecewise-linear line search, at each interval boundary aggregate statistics per resample to get a BLEU distribution and pick the interval maximizing a robust statistic such as a low percentile or mean minus lambda times standard deviation, rather than plain corpus BLEU. Bagging selection: run the robust search from many restarts and resample objectives, combine weight vectors by centroid averaging and by minimizing dispersion of robust BLEU, and report weight spread as a stability diagnostic. Adaptive candidate budget: score each sentence cross-resample contribution variance and proximity to interval switches, then allocate a fixed decoding budget preferentially to high-influence unstable sentences instead of uniform re-decoding. Evaluate on a phrase-based Pharaoh system against standard MERT on test BLEU, weight stability, and decoding cost, with significance by Koehn bootstrap test.

paper_title: Introductory Chapter: Swarm Intelligence and Particle Swarm Optimization
motivation: Adaptive PSO variants in this corpus such as ACEPSO adaptive inertia, ABeePSO diversity triggered rediversification with fuzzy switching, and chaos embedded PSO, and newer optimizers such as salp, grey wolf, moth flame, ant lion, and crow search, are validated only on deterministic static noise free benchmarks. They assume one evaluation gives the true objective so personal and global best memory is reliable and that measured diversity reflects true convergence. Searching all sources for noise, dynamic, and uncertainty finds almost nothing, and the salp paper flags noisy and dynamic objectives as unmet. Yet corpus applications are noisy, including economic dispatch, image thresholding, edge detection, denoising, robotic detection, UAV path planning, and load frequency control. Under noise an inflated sample installs a false global best and jitter corrupts the diversity trigger. The gap is that adaptive, diversity, and chaos PSO has never been made robust to noisy uncertain fitness.
method: Rebuild adaptive PSO for noisy fitness as an Uncertainty Aware Adaptive Swarm Optimizer with five parts. Statistical best memory accepts a personal or global best change only when improvement exceeds a confidence multiple of the pooled standard error over repeated evaluations. An uncertainty driven reevaluation budget concentrates resamples on the global best and on ambiguous particles with overlapping confidence intervals while sparing dominated ones. A noise corrected diversity trigger subtracts noise induced jitter from positional diversity before invoking the ABeePSO style diversity phase. Deterministic chaotic ergodic sequences drive rediversification coverage instead of randomizing parameters. Signal to noise aware inertia generalizes ACEPSO to respond to noise corrected significant improvement. Evaluate on benchmarks with additive Gaussian and multiplicative noise at several signal to noise levels against plain PSO, ACEPSO, CPSO, and ABeePSO run naively, plus a real noisy task such as image thresholding or edge detection on noisy images or economic dispatch under load uncertainty, with per component ablations.

paper_title: A Hierarchical Phrase-Based Model for Statistical Machine Translation
motivation:
Modern log-linear SMT systems (Och & Ney 2002, "Discriminative training and maximum entropy models") tune their feature weights with Minimum Error Rate Training (Och 2003), which directly maximizes a corpus-level automatic metric (BLEU; Papineni et al. 2002) on a single development set with a fixed set of references. MERT's efficient line search works by computing, along each search direction, a piecewise-linear error surface and accumulating corpus-level sufficient statistics (n-gram match counts, hypothesis/reference lengths) for BLEU. Crucially, MERT treats the dev-set metric as a single, exact point estimate of translation quality.

This assumption is fragile, and the same community that built MERT also produced the evidence against it. Bootstrap-based significance testing for MT (Koehn 2004, "Statistical significance tests for MT evaluation") and analyses of metric reliability ("Interpreting BLEU/NIST scores," 2004) show that corpus BLEU on a finite dev set has substantial sampling variance, that differences of a couple of points are often statistically meaningless, and that the estimate depends heavily on which sentences and which references happen to be in the set. Och himself notes that the MERT objective is unstable, has many local optima, and risks overfitting. As a result, standard MERT chases idiosyncrasies of one dev set / reference set, gives weights that vary widely across random restarts, and can "win" on a point-estimate metric without a real, generalizable gain. None of the prior works feeds this well-documented evaluation uncertainty back into the training objective: the significance machinery is used only *after* tuning to judge systems, never *during* tuning to choose weights. This leaves open a concrete opportunity to make MERT operate reliably under the noisier, more realistic conditions of small/single-reference dev sets that dominate real deployments.
method:
Proposed contribution: Confidence-Aware (distributionally robust) MERT — a strict generalization of Och's MERT that relaxes its core assumption from "optimize the dev-set metric point estimate" to "optimize a robust statistic of the metric's sampling distribution," making the tuning signal work under small, noisy, and single-reference dev sets.

Core idea and why it is feasible. Standard MERT reduces to a line search in which, for a search direction, each dev sentence contributes a set of interval boundaries where its argmax candidate switches; the boundaries and the selected candidate at each theta depend ONLY on that sentence's own feature scores, not on how sentences are aggregated into a corpus score. This is the key insight that makes robustness cheap: we can attach many *aggregation weightings* of the same per-sentence choices without recomputing the argmax structure. Concretely:
1. Pre-generate, once, B bootstrap resamples of the dev set (integer multiplicities per sentence), plus optional leave-one-reference-out replicates to also model reference-choice variance.
2. Run Och's exact interval-merging line search unchanged to get the ordered breakpoints along the direction. At each breakpoint, instead of accumulating one set of BLEU sufficient statistics, accumulate B parallel sets by scaling each sentence's n-gram/length statistics by its multiplicity in each resample. This yields, at every breakpoint, a vector of B corpus-BLEU values at essentially the cost of B fast counter updates (no extra decoding/argmax work).
3. Replace the scalar objective with a robust functional R over that B-vector, e.g. a lower-confidence bound such as the alpha-quantile (a CVaR-style worst-case average of the lower tail) or mean minus lambda*std. Pick the theta on the line maximizing R. Embed in Powell's coordinate descent with random restarts exactly as in MERT.

Extending scope further:
- Multi-metric robustness: compute per-breakpoint statistics for BLEU, NIST, and WER, normalize each, and let R be the worst-case normalized metric. This directly targets the "Interpreting BLEU/NIST" concern that a system can overfit one metric, producing weights that are good across metrics rather than metric-specific artifacts.
- Small/low-resource regime: because R rewards weights whose gains are stable across resamples, the method is expected to degrade gracefully exactly where point-estimate MERT overfits most — tiny dev sets and single references.

Experimental plan (using the same log-linear/phrase-based setup as Och 2003 and the alignment-template features):
(a) Stability: variance of chosen weights and of held-out test BLEU across many random restarts, vs. standard MERT.
(b) Generalization: dev-to-test gap and absolute test-set quality, with paired bootstrap significance tests (Koehn 2004) to verify improvements are real, not point-estimate noise.
(c) Regime sweep: vary dev-set size and number of references to show Confidence-Aware MERT's advantage grows as conditions get noisier/more realistic.
(d) Ablations over B, the robustness level alpha/lambda, reference-jackknife on/off, and single- vs. multi-metric R.

This addresses the gap by turning the community's post-hoc uncertainty quantification into the optimization objective itself: MERT becomes a special case (B=1, no reference resampling, R = identity), while the general method delivers weights that are provably tuned for robustness to the sampling and reference variability that Koehn (2004) and the BLEU-interpretation work showed to be pervasive.

paper_title: Using Filtering Agents to Improve Prediction Quality in the GroupLens Research Collaborative Filtering System
motivation: CF systems here passively use volunteered ratings. Avery and Zeckhauser prove this is inefficient: free-riding gives too few evaluations, volunteered ones are biased, and the order of who screens risky items first is wrong. They stop at economics with no elicitation algorithm. Gap: no adaptive incentive-aware optimization decides who evaluates what and in what order to maximize predictive gain per unit reading cost.
method: Adaptive Evaluation Allocation adds an optimization layer to a CF predictor giving prediction plus uncertainty per pair. It estimates value-of-information and personal reading cost per candidate request, then each round solves a budgeted assignment maximizing total value-of-information under per-user budgets via a greedy submodular knapsack, routing risky items to low-risk tasters and pricing incentive transfers. Replay evaluation uses Le and Lindgren paired ROC comparison against passive and random baselines.

paper_title: A Novel Objective Function for Improved Phoneme Recognition Using Time Delay Neural Networks
motivation: Scope-mismatch gap. The modular scaling program for phonemic Time-Delay Neural Networks (class-discriminatory learning, connectionist glue, selective/partial learning, all-net fine tuning) reaches 96 to 98.6 percent accuracy and is presented as the practical path to large-scale connectionist recognition. But every validation used an extremely narrow regime: the ATR database here was uttered in isolation by one male native Japanese speaker (MAU), recorded in a soundproof booth, giving clean, single-speaker, effectively pre-segmented tokens. The modular-composition premise silently assumes that phonemic subcategory modules (BDG, PTK, nasals, fricatives) are stable and separable and that only a small amount of glue is needed to join them. The authors name the true target, continuous speaker-independent recognition, yet never test whether modularity survives that transition. Two forces specific to the broadened regime attack the core assumption: speaker variability shifts the distribution of the frozen modules' hidden-unit features, and coarticulation across boundaries creates cross-module dependencies isolated-token training never exposed. The paper also rejects the obvious fallback, monolithic multi-speaker retraining, as computationally unmanageable. So the gap is real and unaddressed: can incremental modular construction transfer to speaker-independent connected speech without abandoning the efficiency that motivated modularity? This matters because the entire justification for glue and incremental growth is scalability toward real speech, and that claim has only been checked under boundary conditions that exclude the phenomena real speech is made of.
method: Extend modular TDNN construction into the speaker-independent, connected-speech regime with conditioned connectionist glue, preserving the frozen-module efficiency that is modularity's whole point. (1) Keep the trained phonemic subcategory TDNNs as frozen, reusable feature extractors, as in the original modular design. (2) Speaker-conditioned glue: add a small speaker-normalization sub-network mapping a short enrollment or context window to a low-dimensional speaker embedding; instead of fixed glue weights, let this embedding modulate glue units by multiplicative gating plus additive bias, so only the glue composition adapts per speaker while frozen modules serve many speakers untouched. (3) Boundary and coarticulation glue: train glue on connected-speech tokens with real coarticulated boundaries rather than isolated tokens, and widen the glue input receptive field with extra context frames straddling phoneme and word boundaries, turning the TDNN shift-invariance into tolerance of variable boundary conditions so glue units learn transition features the isolated-token modules never saw. (4) Selective low-cost training: apply the paper's own selective/partial learning, freezing subcategory modules and training only glue plus speaker sub-network across a multi-speaker connected corpus, then a short all-net fine-tune, keeping free parameters and cost bounded and directly answering the monolithic-retraining infeasibility objection. (5) Diagnostic glue allocation via exploratory data analysis: use Tukey-style EDA (box plots, stem-and-leaf, spread-versus-level, per-speaker and per-phoneme residual plots) on frozen modules' hidden-unit activations and per-class error, comparing the narrow single-speaker regime to the multi-speaker connected regime to pinpoint which modules and time frames suffer the largest distribution shift, so glue capacity and boundary-context frames are added there rather than uniformly. Evaluation: three conditions on multi-speaker connected data, (a) original single-speaker modular net applied cross-speaker as lower bound, (b) full monolithic multi-speaker retraining as accuracy and cost reference, (c) the proposed conditioned-glue net; report accuracy, training cost, and the fraction of narrow-to-broad degradation recovered by speaker conditioning versus boundary-context glue. Success is near-parity with monolithic retraining at a small fraction of its cost, showing incremental modularity, not just monolithic scaling, transfers out of its original narrow regime.

paper_title: A Novel Objective Function for Improved Phoneme Recognition Using Time Delay Neural Networks
motivation: The central obstacle identified across these works is *scaling*. Waibel et al. ("Modularity and Scaling in Large Phonemic Neural Networks", and the related "Consonant and Phoneme Recognition by Modular Construction" and "Phoneme Recognition Using TDNNs") show that simply enlarging and retraining a TDNN quickly "exceeds the capabilities of even the fastest and largest of today's supercomputers," and that "the complexity of searching a huge space of possible network configurations for good solutions quickly assumes unmanageable proportions." Their remedy — modular, incremental growth via class-discriminatory learning, connectionist glue, selective/partial learning, and all-net fine tuning — is powerful but almost entirely *hand-designed and heuristic*: (1) the decomposition into subcategory modules (BDG, PTK, nasals, fricatives...) is dictated by human phonetic prior knowledge rather than the data; (2) the number of glue units, the choice of which connections to freeze vs. free, the order in which modules are merged, and the amount of fine-tuning are all fixed by trial-and-error and reported as fixed constants (e.g., "4 glue units," "trained two days"). The "Scaling and Generalization" case study and the PDP/backpropagation foundations likewise treat architecture choices as given. This leaves a clear gap: no principled, budget-aware procedure decides *how* to decompose the task and *how much* incremental capacity and training to allocate at each growth step. Because the paper explicitly frames the bottleneck as an unmanageable search over configurations, and because the very "quick-and-dirty," data-first exploratory spirit of Tukey's Exploratory Data Analysis argues for letting the data reveal structure, there is room to turn the manual growth recipe into an explicit, resource-constrained optimization. Doing so matters because it would make modular scaling reproducible, remove reliance on phonetic expertise, and directly minimize the training time/data that the authors identify as the practical barrier to full-scale recognition systems.
method:
Cast the entire modular-growth process of Waibel-style TDNNs as a single resource-constrained search problem whose objective is to reach a target phoneme-recognition accuracy at minimum total training cost (measured as epochs × training tokens touched), or dually to maximize accuracy under a fixed compute budget. The framework has four coupled search/allocation stages that automate the paper's manual choices, all evaluated on the same excised-phoneme tasks (voiced/voiceless stops, nasals, fricatives, all-consonant task).

1. Data-driven decomposition discovery (replaces hand-picked phonetic modules). Train one cheap, small pilot TDNN on all target phonemes for a few epochs, compute its confusion matrix, and — in the exploratory, "let the data show the structure" spirit of Tukey — apply agglomerative clustering on confusability to propose candidate module groupings. This yields a hierarchy of easy-to-separate coarse classes and hard, confusable fine clusters, which become the leaf sub-networks to be trained first.

2. Beam search over the growth (merge) tree (replaces fixed merge order). Starting from the discovered leaf modules, maintain a beam of partial "growth trees." At each step, score every candidate merge of two existing modules by its estimated marginal accuracy gain per unit training cost, using a short low-fidelity trial merge as the estimator; keep the top-k trees and expand. This turns the unmanageable global architecture search into a guided greedy/beam search over a small number of high-value merges.

3. Adaptive capacity allocation for connectionist glue (replaces the fixed "4 glue units"). For each accepted merge, add glue units one small block at a time and continue only while validation-accuracy improvement per added compute exceeds a stopping threshold (a marginal-return / early-stopping criterion). This allocates more free capacity to hard merges and less to easy ones, spending the compute budget where it pays off.

4. Selective unfreezing as screening (replaces heuristic freeze/free and all-net fine tuning). Rather than freezing all sub-component connections or freeing all of them, rank pretrained connections by a cheap saliency signal (gradient magnitude / weight-change under a brief probe) and unfreeze only the top-scoring fraction, increasing that fraction only if marginal validation gains justify the extra optimization cost. Full all-net fine tuning becomes the limiting case chosen only when the budget allows.

Experiments: reproduce the BDG/PTK → BDGPTK and full-consonant constructions, then compare the automated framework against the hand-designed baseline on (a) final recognition accuracy and (b) total training cost, plotting accuracy-vs-compute tradeoff curves. Ablations isolate each stage (data-driven vs. phonetic decomposition; searched vs. fixed merge order; adaptive vs. fixed glue; selective vs. all-or-nothing unfreezing) to quantify how much of the savings each contributes. Success criterion: match or exceed the reported ~96–98.6% accuracies while measurably reducing training time/data and eliminating hand-tuned architecture constants.

paper_title: Hybrid Recommender Systems: Survey and Experiments
motivation: Prior recommenders here target a single solitary individual: GroupLens recommends to each user, PTV builds guides for individual users, the movie clique study targets individual target users for video-on-demand, and Pazzani scores per-user precision. But their flagship domains (living-room TV, video-on-demand, movies, restaurants) are shared decisions by a group whose members change each session. Treating one profile per device blends co-present people together, corrupts the model, optimizes an individual precision metric that is meaningless for a group, and ignores fairness across people and across repeated sessions. No provided work detects who is present, aggregates heterogeneous preferences, or measures group and fairness outcomes.
method: Reuse per-person models (content-based feature profiles from PTV and collaborative filtering from GroupLens) but re-target the co-present group. Infer who is present each session as a latent variable from explicit login or implicit access patterns (time-of-day, genre signatures, session length), crediting feedback only to present members to avoid profile corruption. Aggregate their scores with average, most-pleasure, and minimize-misery operators, plus a novel temporal fairness controller that tracks a per-member satisfaction ledger across sessions and upweights repeatedly overruled members, trading group utility against long-run equity. Evaluate by synthesizing groups from existing multi-user ratings (the 242-user movie set; GroupLens matrices) under varied compositions and repeated sessions, reporting mean satisfaction, worst-member satisfaction, within-session variance, and cross-session fairness versus single-profile and static-aggregation baselines.

paper_title: Author topic model for co-occurring normal documents and short texts to explore individual user preferences
motivation: Short-text stream clustering models (MStream, DP-BMM, NPMM) rely on hyperparameters (priors alpha and beta, new-cluster threshold, forgetting decay, batch size, embedding weight) tuned by offline grid search on labeled data then frozen. NPMM calls manual threshold setting a barrier yet only removes one heuristically; DP-BMM and MStream note the optimal topic number drifts over time, implying optimal thresholds and priors also drift, yet stay fixed; aggregated topic models tune a threshold offline on a sample. Streams have no online labels and per-batch sweeps are infeasible, so no method adapts the joint hyperparameter configuration online, label-free, under a compute budget as the stream drifts. Fixed configs are suboptimal under drift, fragmenting coherent topics or merging distinct events.
method: We propose STUNE, a model-agnostic online optimization wrapper self-tuning any short-text stream model's hyperparameters (alpha, beta, new-cluster threshold, forgetting decay, batch size, embedding weight) without labels under a per-batch compute budget. A label-free reward per batch from a maintained global word co-occurrence graph and word embeddings combines NPMI coherence of active clusters, embedding-space centroid separation, and held-out next-batch predictive likelihood, minus a duplicate-cluster penalty. Search uses resource allocation not sweeps: a small population of lightweight replicas share global statistics; each batch runs successive-halving over candidate configs (champion plus perturbations plus random draws), pruning low-reward ones, promoting survivors warm-started from champion statistics. A non-stationary discounted-UCB bandit steers perturbations; a Page-Hinkley test on champion reward triggers exploration and bandit reset on drift. Champion switches align clusters by bipartite topic-word matching. Evaluation on Google News, Tweets, and TweetSet uses NMI, NPMI, cluster count, and runtime versus offline grid-searched and oracle-tuned baselines, with injected drift for recovery time and ablations of reward terms and search strategy across budgets.

paper_title: Varying Naïve Bayes Models with Applications to Classification of Chinese Text Documents
motivation: High-dimensional classification uses marginal screening then a sparse classifier. Screening is non-robust: FAIR uses the two-sample t-statistic, SIS marginal correlation, sparse LDA class means and variances, all unbounded influence. A few feature outliers or mislabeled samples can push a discriminative gene below noise and screen it out. Robust classifiers here (truncated-hinge SVM, weighted DWD, LUM) act only after screening; discarded signal features cannot be recovered, so robustifying only the model gives false reliability. No robust classification screening exists with bounded influence to outliers and label noise plus a sure-screening guarantee under contamination.
method: Use one bounded truncated-hinge loss for both screening and classification. For each feature fit a univariate margin classifier with truncated hinge loss; importance is the bounded risk reduction versus the null, capping each observation and giving bounded influence. Keep top d features, with an iterative variant recomputing utilities on the robust margin. Prove a sure-screening property under an epsilon-contamination model with outliers and label flips, and a breakdown bound showing t-statistic ranking inverts under few outliers. Tune truncation and feature number via an upper bound on robust classification error. Couple to a sparse truncated-hinge or weighted-DWD classifier on retained features. Evaluate on leukemia microarray data with injected label noise and feature contamination, reporting gene retention, test error, and selection stability versus FAIR, SIS, and sparse LDA.

paper_title: A Novel Objective Function for Improved Phoneme Recognition Using Time Delay Neural Networks
motivation: Waibel et al.'s modular scaling of TDNNs grows large phonemic networks from small subcomponent nets via class-discriminatory learning, connectionist glue, class-distinctive features, selective/partial learning, and all-net fine tuning. Every technique is bootstrapped from a strong human-supplied assumption: the task is already decomposed into acoustically coherent linguistic subclasses (BDG, PTK, nasals, fricatives), and an expert names the cross-class distinctions to repair (e.g., a voiced/unvoiced net gluing BDG to PTK). Decomposition, growth order, and glue targets are all injected by phonetic expertise. This limits scope: it presupposes a known taxonomy, so it does not transfer to new languages, non-standard inventories, or sub-phonemic units; the chosen groupings may not match what the net actually confuses, so glue is spent on guessed features not true residual errors; and the taxonomy is fixed, whereas confusion structure shifts under noise and mis-segmentation (the paper uses only clean, hand-aligned excised tokens). The other sources supply the missing ingredient: Tukey's Exploratory Data Analysis offers resistant techniques for revealing structure in confusion/affinity data, and the PDP/backpropagation and scaling-and-generalization works show hidden-unit representations encode reusable structure. The gap: no method makes the modular-growth machinery function without a pre-given linguistic decomposition.
method: Make the decomposition, growth schedule, and glue targeting data-driven so modular TDNN scaling works on unknown inventories and noisier, mis-aligned data. (1) Seed: briefly train one small TDNN over the whole inventory with no linguistic grouping. (2) Build an acoustic affinity matrix combining the off-diagonal confusion matrix on held-out tokens with similarity of learned hidden-layer activation patterns per phoneme, reflecting what the net represents rather than labels. (3) Discover modules via exploratory data analysis: Tukey-style resistant reordering plus agglomerative clustering extracts subcategory groups and a hierarchy, replacing the hand-chosen split. (4) Grow modules: train a small well-generalizing TDNN per discovered cluster, exploiting the favorable size/data ratio motivating modularity. (5) Data-driven glue: freeze cluster modules' first-layer features, read out residual cross-cluster confusions, allocate targeted free glue units whose objective is exactly the still-confusable pairwise distinctions, then apply selective/partial learning and all-net fine tuning as in the original. (6) Recurse up the hierarchy until the full inventory is covered. Evaluation: verify the discovered decomposition recovers or improves on the linguistic taxonomy and matches or beats the original 95-96% accuracy on the same Japanese database at comparable cost with no phonetic knowledge; test the extend-scope claim on an inventory with no clean taxonomy and by re-deriving the decomposition under added noise and jittered segmentation, where a fixed linguistic grouping is sub-optimal but affinity-driven modules and glue adapt. Ablations compare data-driven vs. expert grouping and glue. This makes the same modular-growth machinery operate under weaker assumptions and broader, noisier regimes because the decomposition is learned from the network's own representations.

paper_title: Estimating Photometric Redshifts Using Support Vector Machines
motivation:
Two pillars of margin-based learning theory are represented here. Vapnik's Structural Risk Minimization (SRM) and Support Vector Machines choose a decision rule by controlling capacity (VC dimension / margin) while minimizing empirical risk, and he further notes (transductive inference) that when information is scarce one should exploit the actual test points rather than estimate the whole function. Tong Zhang's analysis of convex-risk-minimization classifiers (SVM, boosting, logistic) characterizes exactly which convex surrogate losses φ are "classification-calibrated," i.e., whose population minimizer f*_φ(η) has the sign of the Bayes rule and whose per-point optimal risk Q*(η) governs excess-risk bounds.

Both frameworks rest on the same load-bearing assumption: training and test examples are drawn i.i.d. from one fixed distribution D and the observed labels are clean. Under this assumption, minimizing the surrogate φ-risk on the training sample is (asymptotically) equivalent to targeting the Bayes rule, and SRM margin bounds control test error. But real deployments violate it in two coupled ways: (i) labels are corrupted (e.g., class-conditional label noise), and (ii) the test/target input distribution differs from the training one (covariate/target shift). In these regimes the population minimizer of the ordinary surrogate risk no longer aligns with the target Bayes rule — Zhang's calibration guarantee silently breaks — and SRM/SVM margin bounds no longer bound target error. Vapnik's transductive remark that unlabeled test points carry usable information is never formalized for shift or noise. There is thus an open, practically important gap: no unified theory tells us which surrogate losses remain calibrated, and how to control capacity, when labels are noisy and the target distribution has shifted, nor how to use transductive access to unlabeled target inputs to repair the mismatch.
method:
Extend both the surrogate-calibration theory of convex risk minimization and the SRM/SVM apparatus to the weaker, more realistic regime of noisy labels plus covariate/target shift, using transductive access to unlabeled target inputs. Four components:

1) Shift-and-noise calibration theory (relaxing Zhang's clean-i.i.d. assumption). Model the training distribution as the target distribution reweighted by a density ratio w(x)=p_target(x)/p_train(x), with labels passed through a class-conditional noise channel (flip rates ρ+, ρ-). Redo Zhang's pointwise argument: the training-population φ-risk at x is a distorted convex combination of the two label branches. Define a corrected surrogate risk — an importance-weighted, noise-corrected φ — and derive the modified per-point optimal function f̃*_φ(η) and optimal risk Q̃*(η). Prove conditions on φ under which the corrected population minimizer still has sign(2η_target−1), i.e., is "shift-and-noise calibrated," thereby generalizing "classification-calibrated" to weaker assumptions and identifying which of SVM/exponential/logistic/least-squares losses survive (and which need explicit correction).

2) Corrected, capacity-controlled algorithm (relaxing SVM/SRM). Instantiate the corrected risk as a weighted, noise-adjusted hinge/logistic objective and solve it in an RKHS. Retain SRM-style capacity control, but apply it to the corrected weighted empirical risk, so SVM keeps operating when labels are noisy and the target is shifted.

3) Transductive estimation of the correction (operationalizing Vapnik's transduction). Given the unlabeled target inputs available at prediction time, estimate w(x) by training a discriminative train-vs-target probe (or kernel mean matching), and estimate noise rates from high-confidence anchor points. Plug these into the corrected objective — using the test points to "get the best from restricted information" rather than estimating everything globally.

4) Finite-sample guarantee in the new regime. Extend Zhang's estimation-error / SRM margin bounds to the corrected weighted empirical risk, quantifying the extra variance from importance weights via an effective sample size, to yield excess-risk bounds relative to the target Bayes error. This bridges Zhang's consistency analysis and Vapnik's generalization bounds into the noisy-and-shifted regime.

Validation: on benchmarks with synthetic class-conditional noise and controlled covariate shift, compare corrected vs. standard SVM/boosting/logistic; verify empirically that only theoretically shift-and-noise-calibrated losses recover the target Bayes rule, and that transductive weight/noise estimation tightens both accuracy and the bounds — demonstrating that the classical margin theory extends to broader, noisier, distribution-shifted settings.

paper_title: A Systematic Comparison of Various Statistical Alignment Models
motivation: SMT decoding searches for the best target string and is intractable in general. Beam search is cheap but makes many search errors; A-star with admissible heuristics is optimal but far too costly for long sentences. Since only about 5 percent of errors are search errors (Candide), errors concentrate in a minority of sentences. No prior method certifies per-sentence whether a cheap decode is already optimal, nor allocates a fixed compute budget across a corpus to the sentences where extra search actually reduces errors. Admissible heuristics have been used only to guide A-star expansion, never as optimality certificates or as a basis for adaptive compute allocation, leaving room for a search method that gets A-star quality at beam cost.
method: Reframe decoding as corpus-level resource allocation with admissible heuristics as optimality certificates. A cheap beam pass gives each sentence a best score S (lower bound) and an admissible frontier upper bound U from the HTFLD rest-cost estimate; if S is at least U the output is certified optimal, else gap U minus S bounds improvement. A greedy knapsack ranks uncertified sentences by gap and escalates the highest-payoff ones to multi-pass A-star until a budget is spent, tightening the heuristic and certifying more as it goes. A learned predictor pre-allocates budget and per-sentence beam widths. Evaluate on Hansards and Verbmobil with IBM Model 4 and the HMM model versus pure beam and pure A-star at matched compute, reporting search-error rate, time, and fraction certified optimal.

paper_title: Least Squares Support Vector Machine Classifiers
motivation: These works repeatedly show that representationally equivalent learning machines generalize very differently, with no mechanistic explanation. Vapnik's SV method and the Schölkopf-style comparison note the SV machine contains polynomial, neural-net and RBF classifiers as special cases, yet an SVM with a Gaussian kernel beats a clustering-plus-backprop RBF on USPS digits. Ridella et al. prove the circular-backpropagation (CBP) network, an MLP with one extra input equal to the squared norm of x that interpolates a unit between a hyperplane and a hypersphere, can be made equivalent to a Gaussian RBF network, yet CBP outperforms both MLP and RBF. Saunders' dual ridge regression and Vapnik's SV function estimation are, in feature space, the same regularized linear model differing only in loss and regularizer, yet yield dense versus sparse solutions. The open question is explanatory: why, and under which conditions, do equivalent machines generalize differently, and why does the ranking vary with dataset and noise? Existing accounts use worst-case capacity (VC dimension, Cover capacity, SRM), which are loose and cannot explain why the single squared-norm term recovers most of a full RBF's benefit on some problems but not others, or how much of the SVM-RBF advantage is margin capacity control versus automatic center selection versus loss. A mechanistic, data-dependent causal account is missing.
method: Build one unifying regularized radial-augmented linear model containing CBP, classical RBF, SV-RBF, and dual kernel ridge regression as points on a continuum, then sweep it to causally decompose their generalization differences; this Relax/Extend-Scope generalizes CBP beyond classification, primal backprop, and a single squared-norm term. First, relax the augmentation: treat CBP's squared-norm term as the lowest-order term of a graded radial expansion with a continuous radial-order knob r (r=0 hyperplane, r=1 CBP, large r approaching full Gaussian RBF), making CBP's hyperplane-versus-hypersphere plasticity a smooth spectrum. Second, relax the estimator and task: move to dual/kernel and regression regimes via Saunders' ridge-regression-in-dual-variables and Vapnik's SV function estimation, adding independent knobs for loss (squared, epsilon-insensitive, hinge) and regularizer (weight decay versus margin), so each source machine is one triple trained by a single procedure under noiseless and noisy conditions. Third, replace worst-case capacity with data-dependent measures the model already yields: effective degrees of freedom from the Gram-matrix eigenspectrum (trace of the ridge hat matrix), the margin distribution, and support-vector counts. Fourth, decompose causally by ablation: sweep radial order, loss, and regularizer independently on USPS digits plus synthetic and noisy regression, using controlled interventions (fix capacity, vary r to isolate radial geometry; fix r, swap loss to isolate sparsity; match centers across CBP, RBF and SV-RBF to isolate center selection) and relate each error to measured effective capacity and margin. This explains when the cheap single-radial CBP term suffices, how much of SVM-RBF's edge is capacity control versus center selection versus loss, and why machine orderings flip with noise and geometry.

paper_title: Learning Quickly When Irrelevant Attributes Abound: A New Linear-threshold Algorithm
motivation: Passive PAC and Occam theory generalize from random samples but cannot control which examples they see; Angluin queries are more powerful but her algorithms are hand-crafted per class and her lower bounds rely on an adversary against whom each query removes at most one candidate; Mitchell version spaces give structure but no principle for selecting the next query. Gap: no general, class-agnostic adaptive query-selection strategy tied to the Occam-compression and VC quantities that govern generalization.
method: Frame active concept learning as adaptive search for the query that most evenly splits a description-length-weighted version space (an Occam potential), giving near-halving shrinkage that defeats the remove-one adversary. Approximate the split via an Occam near-minimum-hypothesis oracle plus screening of S/G boundary instances scored by disagreement among sampled consistent hypotheses, under a budget favoring cheap membership queries and invoking equivalence queries only when progress stalls. Prove query complexity scales as VC-dimension times log(1/target-weight) and the output is PAC-correct; evaluate on monomials, k-DNF, and linear separators.

paper_title: Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures
motivation: Resource bottleneck gap. Across these works, accuracy is improved by adding predictors: bagging aggregates bootstrap replicates, arcing/boosting stacks reweighted trees, the random subspace method grows forests over many feature subspaces, and Random Forests combine hundreds-to-thousands of randomized trees. This accuracy is bought with compute, memory, and prediction latency: a fixed large ensemble is costly to train, heavy to store, and slow to serve, a deployment/scalability bottleneck on constrained hardware and in real time. Two costs compound this. First, deciding how many predictors are enough and which to keep is normally settled with held-out data or cross-validation ("Cross-validatory choice...", "Computer intensive methods in statistics"), which is itself resource-costly and unreliable exactly where samples are scarce and expensive, e.g. high-dimensional few-sample tumor classification ("Comparison of discrimination methods for the classification of tumors"). Second, Random Forests already derive a generalization bound PE* <= rho(1-s^2)/s^2 (mean inter-tree correlation over squared strength) and supply these quantities for free via out-of-bag (OOB) estimates, which Breiman shows are as accurate as a same-size test set. Yet standard practice ignores this free signal: people fix a large tree count and a single subspace size m, though the random subspace work shows m trades individual strength against inter-tree correlation. No method uses the ensemble's own free, data-free internal estimates to build the minimal ensemble meeting an accuracy target under an explicit compute/memory/latency budget, eliminating both wasted predictors and costly separate validation.
method: Propose OOB-Budgeted Forests: a resource-aware, data-free procedure that grows and prunes a tree ensemble by optimizing the Random-Forest generalization bound per unit of resource cost, using only out-of-bag (OOB) estimates. First, online bound tracking: incrementally update OOB estimates of strength s, mean raw-margin correlation rho, and hence B = rho(1-s^2)/s^2 as each tree is added, reusing the bootstrap draws already made. Second, candidate-and-select growth: at each step generate a small batch of candidate trees, each with a randomly sampled subspace size m, and admit the one giving the largest decrease in the OOB bound per unit resource cost, where cost is a deployment proxy such as node count (memory) or expected traversal depth (latency); this favors diversity-adding low-correlation trees over redundant strong-but-correlated ones. Third, adaptive randomness: track via OOB how m shifts s and rho and bias sampling of m toward the region that most lowers B, self-tuning the strength/correlation tradeoff instead of fixing m. Fourth, budget-aware stopping: halt when marginal bound reduction per added tree (or per KB memory or per ms latency) drops below a user threshold, giving an explicit accuracy-versus-resource dial with no held-out data consumed. Fifth, optional deployment pruning: under a hard memory/latency budget, select the tree subset minimizing the OOB bound via greedy subset-selection, producing a compact model for constrained devices. Evaluation: on UCI benchmarks and high-dimensional small-sample gene-expression tumor datasets (where cross-validation is unstable and samples precious), compare ensemble size, memory, and latency against fixed-size Random Forests, bagging, and boosting at matched accuracy; verify the OOB bound tracks true test error and that budget-aware stopping recovers near-optimal accuracy with far fewer, smaller trees. This replaces grow-a-big-forest-plus-cross-validate with a single pass that spends compute only where it provably improves accuracy per the RF bound and stops when resource cost outweighs the gain.

paper_title: Toward the Next Generation of Recommender Systems: Applications and Research Challenges
motivation: Constraint-based recommenders and configurators (Falkner/Felfernig/Haag 2011) routinely reach a "no solution can be found" state when user requirements are inconsistent with the knowledge base. The standard remedy is model-based diagnosis: compute minimal sets of faulty requirements to relax. Reiter's hitting-set theory (1987) and FASTDIAG (Felfernig et al. 2012) make this efficient, and CoreDiag removes redundant constraints. Three gaps remain. (1) FASTDIAG returns the preferred diagnosis only relative to a predefined, static ordering of constraints (from importance/similarity metrics); this ordering is hard to author and does not reflect what a particular user will actually accept, because the algorithms optimize cardinality/structure, not acceptance. (2) The configuration-UX literature shows acceptance is governed by status-quo bias (Status Quo Bias in configuration systems 2011), anchoring (Recommender systems, consumer preferences, and anchoring effects 2011), and cognitive load (Empirical knowledge engineering 2010), yet these factors are not part of the diagnosis objective, so cardinality-minimal repairs are often rejected. (3) Group-based configuration and requirements negotiation are explicitly named open problems (configurable-products Issues for Future Research; Group decision support for requirements negotiation 2011; Group recommender systems: combining individual models 2011), but there is no principled search for repairs that fairly balance conflicting stakeholders. This matters because the no-solution dead-end is the most frustrating failure mode of interactive recommenders, and current diagnosis selects repairs by a fixed proxy ordering rather than minimizing real user effort or maximizing group consensus.
method: Recast conflict diagnosis/repair as an adaptive, acceptance-guided best-first search over minimal repairs, replacing FASTDIAG's static ordering with an online-learned utility model, and extend it to groups. Objective: attach to each requirement c a parametric relaxation-utility u(c;theta) capturing willingness to give it up, and to each candidate repair R (a minimal diagnosis plus concrete alternative value assignments) an expected-acceptance score A(R) combining learned utilities of the constraints touched, a status-quo/anchoring penalty proportional to distance from the user's current configuration, and a cognitive-load term penalizing large or hard-to-explain repairs; diagnosis then becomes finding the consistent repair that maximizes A(R) rather than minimizing cardinality. Search engine: keep FASTDIAG's divide-and-conquer consistency-check core but drive hitting-set/best-first expansion with the A(R) heuristic to produce anytime top-k leading repairs under a bounded consistency-check budget for interactive latency, and use CoreDiag-style redundancy elimination as a pre-screening step to prune never-active/redundant constraints and shrink the search space. Active/adaptive loop: instead of committing to one repair, present a small discriminating set of candidate repairs, or ask the single elicitation question that best separates competing hypotheses about theta, observe accept/reject/edit, and update theta via online Bayesian or gradient updates; the search goal is to minimize the number of interaction rounds needed to reach an accepted consistent repair, embedding active preference elicitation inside diagnosis. Group extension: learn per-stakeholder utility models and aggregate them into a group objective with an explicit fairness term, search for Pareto-minimal repairs, and label which stakeholder's requirement each repair relaxes, with a tunable knob between utilitarian (max total acceptance) and egalitarian (max-min) aggregation to support negotiation. Evaluation: on real and synthetic configuration knowledge bases and feature models, compare against breadth-first hitting sets and against FASTDIAG with static similarity ordering, measuring interaction cycles to an accepted repair, acceptance rate, repair cardinality, and consistency-check count under the anytime budget, and for groups adding consensus/fairness and time-to-agreement using simulated users from held-out preference profiles plus a small user study. Success criterion: fewer interaction rounds and higher acceptance at comparable or better computational cost than static-ordering FASTDIAG.

paper_title: Machine Learning in Automated Text Categorization
motivation: Hypertext categorization methods using linked neighbor labels assume one global regularity and reliable labels, but real Web graphs mix assortative and misleading links with noisy labels, so gains are fragile and need per domain tuning.
method: Learn a per link signed reliability gate from link features and neighbor label confidence, and fold it into a relaxation labeling loop that downweights misleading links, evaluated under injected label noise and sparse labels.

paper_title: Near-Optimal Reinforcement Learning in Polynomial Time
motivation: Existing exact learning curve theory for temporal difference methods applies only to tabular value estimates, offline updates, and absorbing reward processes, which excludes the function approximation regime where these methods are actually deployed in practice today.
method: We extend the exact mean squared error curve analysis from the tabular case to linear function approximation and state aggregation, deriving closed form recursions for the mean and covariance of the weight vector so that bias and variance can be tracked across trials under approximation.

paper_title: Markov Games as a Framework for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
motivation: TD self-play learning of evaluation functions is powerful but extremely sample- and compute-expensive: Tesauro reports 50,000-200,000 games and up to two weeks of computation per network, with cost scaling quadratically in network size. Tesauro noted that in high-volatility positions a look-ahead search process is the natural remedy, and that parameters need adaptive schedules, yet TD-Gammon used uniform shallow lookahead everywhere. Samuel's checkers program varied ply heuristically and memoized backed-up scores (rote learning) but with hand-crafted heuristics untethered from the learner's uncertainty. The dynamic-programming sources formalize that deeper backed-up values are lower-variance, more accurate targets, and the risk and undiscounted-reward works motivate treating value-estimate variance as first-class. No prior work frames the key bottleneck as spending a finite search and compute budget across self-play positions to maximize learning per unit computation. This is a resource-allocation gap: uniform shallow search wastes budget on well-evaluated positions while starving volatile, high-error positions where accurate deep targets would most accelerate learning.
method: Cast TD self-play target generation as adaptive budget allocation: given a fixed compute budget B of node expansions per batch, choose how much lookahead to invest in each position to maximize expected improvement of the evaluation function per expanded node. Step 1, Base learner: TD-lambda self-play training of a parametric value V, using linear features like Samuel or a small network like Tesauro, tested in a stochastic high-volatility domain and a deterministic one to test the volatility hypothesis. Step 2, Uncertainty estimator: a K-head ensemble or MC-dropout plus a variance head trained to predict squared TD error, giving per-state uncertainty and a volatility signal from successor-value spread. Step 3, Budget-constrained depth allocation: assign a search depth to each position by solving a knapsack-like problem that maximizes total estimated learning gain minus a cost times node count, where gain estimates target-error reduction from uncertainty, TD-error magnitude, volatility, and visit frequency; solve it greedily by repeatedly deepening the highest marginal-gain-per-node position via selective minimax or expectimax until B is spent, using the deeper backed-up value as the TD target only for selected positions. Step 4, Learned memoization: cache backed-up deep targets keyed by position with transposition and network generalization, reusing and propagating them to amplify the budget, generalizing Samuel's rote learning. Step 5, Annealed policy: spread budget broadly and shallowly early and concentrate on the high-uncertainty tail later, operationalizing Tesauro's call for adaptive lambda and learning-rate schedules. Step 6, Optional active data collection: bias self-play move and opening choice toward high-uncertainty regions, turning game generation into experimental design. Evaluation: games-to-strength and node-expansions-to-strength versus fixed-shallow TD-lambda, fixed-deep TD-lambda at equal compute, and Samuel-style heuristic adaptive ply, expecting fewer games and fewer expansions to reach target strength, with largest gains in the high-volatility domain, directly closing the sample-efficiency gap.

paper_title: Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures
motivation: Random forests come with an explanatory bound: generalization error is at most c over s squared, where c is the mean margin correlation between trees and s their strength; good forests keep trees strong while decorrelating them. Breiman shows s and correlation are estimable cheaply without held-out data via out-of-bag OOB aggregation, as accurate as an equal-sized test set. Yet randomization is set by one scalar F from a rule of thumb at one or two grid points with uniform feature sampling, and the random subspace method fixes subspace dimension a priori. Raising F increases both s and correlation, so a scalar cannot move the two bound terms separately, and OOB estimates are used only to monitor, never as an optimization target. Gap: no method uses the ensemble internal data-free strength and correlation estimates to actively search the randomization design minimizing c over s squared. This matters in high-dimensional small-n regimes like tumor microarray classification where uniform sampling wastes trees on noise features, while OOB is a stable near-free surrogate versus costly unstable external resampling tuning.
method: Frame forest growing as sequential optimization minimizing the OOB estimate of c over s squared, updated as trees are added; each tree has a config of F and a feature-sampling distribution p. First, after each batch compute OOB strength s and mean correlation from OOB margins, giving surrogate J. Second, treat candidate F values as bandit arms, grow trees in small batches, estimate each arm marginal change in J, and allocate the tree budget by UCB or successive-halving while pruning weak arms so F can drift. Third, search p by attributing to each feature its OOB contribution to strength versus pairwise margin correlation, then update p by multiplicative weights on the simplex to favor features adding strength with little shared correlation and suppress correlation-driving and noise features. Fourth, stop when the OOB J trajectory plateaus, a resource-allocation rule favoring the smallest adequate ensemble. Fifth, validate against Forest-RI, Forest-RC, and the random subspace method on UCI and tumor data, reporting test error and OOB diagnostics, ablating adaptive F versus feature reweighting, and extending to regression via the residual-correlation MSE bound.

paper_title: Introduction: The Challenge of Reinforcement Learning
motivation: Active deictic (look-and-mark) perception makes RL tractable by sensing a compact task-relevant slice of the world rather than an exponential propositional state (Whitehead and Ballard 1991; Mahadevan and Connell robots motivate it for hardware). But it causes perceptual aliasing: one internal representation confounds several world states, creating hidden state that destabilizes RL. The Lion algorithm fixes this by treating return variance as the fingerprint of aliasing and suppressing such states until representations are consistent. The contradiction: return variance is also exactly what a stochastic environment produces, so the method works only in deterministic worlds, yet active perception is most needed in noisy real robotic worlds. Where it is most valuable its founding assumption breaks. The authors concede they do not know how to handle stochastic worlds and that one anomalous outcome can chain-react and destroy an optimal policy; their fixes are ad-hoc variance thresholds that blur rather than separate the two variance sources. The gap: an agent cannot distinguish aliased perception from a noisy world, forcing a choice between compact active perception and robustness to stochasticity.
method: Core insight: aliasing variance is reducible by acquiring more perceptual information (adding a marker splits a confounded state into consistent low-variance sub-states) while true stochasticity is irreducible. The discriminating test is whether a state's outcome variance drops when more perception is added, a controllable experiment rather than an undecidable statistic. Approach: (1) Alongside action-values, learn a predictive world model that predicts the distribution of next percept and reward per internal state-action and tracks prediction error, following GOFER's model-based classifier system where learning triggers on model inadequacy, giving a per-state variance estimate decoupled from bootstrapping. (2) Flag high-variance states as Lion does, but instead of suppressing, run a disambiguation experiment: temporarily expand perception via perceptual actions, splitting the state into refined sub-states. (3) Use a variance-decomposition / information-gain test (in the spirit of stochastic learning-automata estimation under noise) over repeated visits: if refinement significantly reduces variance, declare aliasing, adopt the finer representation and reinforce the perceptual policy producing it (a noise-tolerant Lion); if variance persists across all refinements, declare irreducible stochasticity, freeze the representation and use expectation-based value learning (Q-learning) that averages over transitions instead of suppressing them. (4) This yields a per-state decision, refine perception vs accept stochasticity, giving a representation as fine as needed but no finer, stable in both regimes. (5) Use the model for Dyna-style asynchronous dynamic programming to accelerate learning and to run disambiguation as cheap mental trials. Evaluate on block-manipulation and navigation tasks with injected quasi-deterministic perturbations and noisy rewards; baselines are original Lion (should collapse under noise) and Q-learning with fixed rich perception (sample-inefficient or aliased); metrics are policy optimality and stability under increasing stochasticity, features recruited, and sample efficiency.

paper_title: Protein Secondary Structure Prediction Based on Position-specific Scoring Matrices
motivation: Secondary structure prediction has a Q3 accuracy near 72 to 78 percent as reported by Cuff and Barton in 1999, and it is mainly used as input to fold recognition. Russell and Barton in 1996 recognize folds by mapping predicted secondary structure, and Rost, Schneider and Sander in 1997 thread predicted secondary structure profiles, but both collapse sharply when moving from experimental to predicted secondary structure. Rost and Sander in 1994 argued that Q3 is the wrong target and proposed a segment overlap measure but never tested it against fold recognition success. Frishman and Argos in 1996 showed prediction errors concentrate on edge strands and non local hydrogen bonded residues. The field optimizes aggregate scores without knowing which error modes and residue locations actually break the downstream fold recognition step, and no source maps this.
method: Build a systematic diagnostic atlas linking secondary structure prediction error modes and locations to fold recognition failure. Take a low redundancy domain set with DSSP reference secondary structure and accessibility labeled by CATH class, architecture and topology, and annotate every residue with segment length, boundary versus core position, strand edge versus central status, non local hydrogen bond partners from beta bridge statistics, and solvent accessibility. For each domain build a graded set of profiles from the perfect DSSP assignment to outputs of established predictors and their consensus, plus synthetic perturbations that inject one calibrated error type at a time at controlled rates, including single residue flips, boundary shifts, and segment deletions, merges and splits, and errors aimed at strata such as only edge strands or only buried residues. Feed every profile into the two fold recognition paradigms from the sources, secondary structure mapping and prediction based threading, recording the rank of the correct fold, class accuracy and alignment accuracy. Regress fold recognition success on the injected error variables and residue covariates to produce a residue and segment level sensitivity map of which error modes and positions dominate failure across classes, and test whether segment errors predict loss better than per residue accuracy. Finally define a downstream weighted secondary structure score that reweights errors by measured impact and show it predicts fold recognition success better than Q3 or segment overlap, giving an evidence based target for future predictors.

paper_title: Varying Naïve Bayes Models with Applications to Classification of Chinese Text Documents
motivation: Large-margin classifiers form a continuum from soft (probability-estimating, e.g., LDA/logistic) to hard (decision-boundary, e.g., SVM), unified by the LUM knob c (hard-or-soft-classification-large-margin-unified-machines-20). But that work only shows empirically which is better, offering no mechanism. SVM data piling in high-dimension-low-sample-size (HDLSS) regimes motivated DWD (robust-truncated-hinge-loss-support-vector-machines-2007; weighted-distance-weighted-discrimination-and-its-asymptotic), for which Fisher consistency and HDLSS asymptotics exist; yet these show that methods work, not why the hard-versus-soft ranking reverses or why piling appears for some losses. The HDLSS geometric representation (Hall-Marron-Neeman) shows classes collapse to rigid simplices, and screening/sparse-LDA work (sure-independence-screening-for-ultra-high-dimensional-featu; sparse-linear-discriminant-analysis-by-thresholding-for-high) shows spurious correlation and noise grow with dimension. Missing is a causal account linking HDLSS geometry to the hard/soft continuum: why piling emerges as a function of loss shape, why hard wins in some dimension/separation/noise/imbalance regimes and soft in others, and what sets the optimal c. This matters because practitioners now pick among SVM, DWD, LDA and logistic classifiers by trial and error.
method: Build a geometry-driven theory of the hard-versus-soft reversal and data piling, then a selection rule. (1) Use the LUM loss family and the HDLSS simplex representation, modeling two classes with mean gap mu, noise sigma, dimension p, sample sizes and imbalance. (2) As p grows with n fixed, derive the limiting LUM normal direction and the distribution of training-point projections as a function of c, defining a piling index (variance of within-class projected scores) that shows why hard non-differentiable losses collapse projections while soft ones spread them. (3) From the same limits, express asymptotic misclassification error as a closed form in c and the model quantities, find its minimizer, and produce a phase diagram over signal-to-noise, p/n and imbalance showing where hard beats soft: hard wins when the probability surface is hard to estimate or SNR is high and piling is benign; soft wins when reliable probabilities suppress noise accumulation. (4) Map theory to estimable quantities (pairwise-distance concentration, empirical spurious correlation, mu and sigma after SIS-type screening) to form a plug-in estimator of optimal c, replacing cross-validation. (5) Validate via simulations sweeping p, n, SNR and imbalance to confirm the piling index, error curves and phase boundaries, and benchmark the adaptive rule against fixed-c LUM, SVM, DWD and sparse LDA on microarray, lung-cancer and Gisette-style data. Deliverable: theorems plus a phase diagram explaining why hard/soft performance varies and piling appears, and a principled c-selection procedure.

paper_title: Adaptive Control of Nonlinear Multivariable Systems Using Neural Networks
motivation: Narendra and Parthasarathy (1990, 1991) observe that neural identification using the series-parallel teacher-forced model reliably converges and stays stable, while the parallel fully recurrent model may diverge, and admit conditions for parallel-model convergence even in the linear case are unknown.
