The universal-approximation papers here (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1989; Hartman 1990; Barron 1993; Hornik derivatives 1990) only prove a network can match a static map and its Jacobian to bounded error, not what that error does inside a feedback loop. This is an explanation gap: no causal account exists for why teacher forcing works while free-running recurrence fails, why static approximation capacity fails to guarantee dynamic identification, and how the one-step versus multi-step gradient choice matters.
method: Develop and test a theory of how static approximation error propagates through feedback. Write the trained net as f plus epsilon, bounding epsilon via Barron's order one over root n rate and Hornik's Jacobian bound so it is tunable by network size. For the four SISO plant models, derive error dynamics: series-parallel uses true bounded signals giving one-step error of order epsilon, while parallel feeds back the model state giving recursion error approx J times error plus epsilon. Predict amplification gain one over one minus rho and stability edge at rho equals one, rho being the trajectory Jacobian spectral radius, via contraction analysis. Show dynamic back-propagation optimizes the true multi-step loss while series-parallel optimizes a one-step surrogate, explaining switching failure. Validate by reproducing the four examples, sweeping network size and plant parameters, confirming error scales as gain times epsilon, divergence onset at rho near one, and safe switching only when rho stays below one, for sigmoidal and Gaussian units.

paper_title: An Introduction to MCMC for Machine Learning
motivation: Rao Blackwellised particle filtering (RBPF; Murphy and Russell; Doucet and colleagues) reduces the variance of sequential Monte Carlo by partitioning the state into a sampled part and a conditionally tractable part that is marginalized exactly with a Kalman or HMM filter, but it assumes a fixed and known model structure with a fixed dimension for all time. Sequential Bayesian model selection (Andrieu, de Freitas and Doucet) relaxes the known model assumption by adding reversible jump moves to an online importance sampling and resampling scheme, yet it explicitly assumes the model index is fixed over time and that parameters only grow monotonically, it uses no variance reduction, and it is demonstrated only on a single autoregressive Gaussian family. Reversible jump variable dimension methods such as Green and the variable dimension radial basis function work of Holmes and Mallick, whose linear output weights are analytically marginalizable, are entirely batch. This leaves a clear gap for realistic streaming settings in which the model structure itself is non-stationary, such as a time varying number of tracked targets, a drifting signal order, regime switching systems, or online nonparametric regression where basis functions are born and killed. No method in this literature performs online trans dimensional filtering in which the dimension changes with time while simultaneously exploiting conditional analytic tractability to control the otherwise exploding importance weight variance of trans dimensional sequential Monte Carlo. Closing this gap matters because it would let principled online Bayesian inference operate under much weaker and more realistic assumptions.
method: Propose a Rao Blackwellised trans dimensional particle filter that relaxes the fixed structure assumption of RBPF and the fixed index assumption of sequential Bayesian model selection. Define a joint filtering target over an evolving structure variable together with continuous parameters and states, placing a Markov prior on structure transitions that permits birth, death, split and merge moves at every time step so that the state dimension varies with time rather than only growing. Each particle carries a sample of the discrete structure and the hard nonlinear parameters, plus a parametric Kalman or information filter representation of the conditionally tractable part, which is marginalized exactly to lower variance. The key new machinery is dimension matching updates for this analytic filter when the structure changes: a birth analytically initializes a new sub block from its prior, a death or merge marginalizes or collapses sub blocks in closed form, and a split allocates covariance, so that exact marginalization is preserved across trans dimensional moves. The sequential proposal is a reversible jump embedded inside sequential importance sampling, and the incremental importance weights include the reversible jump Jacobian and the marginal likelihood contributed by the analytic block. Adaptive resampling is triggered by effective sample size, and after resampling a few reversible jump MCMC rejuvenation moves that are invariant to the current time posterior diversify structures and combat the sample impoverishment and path degeneracy that trans dimensional filtering aggravates. When only part of the model is conditionally tractable the remainder stays in the particle set and the method degrades gracefully to ordinary trans dimensional sequential Monte Carlo, with effective sample size and structure entropy diagnostics and optional annealed weighting for large jumps. Evaluation covers online nonparametric regression with a time varying number of radial basis components, multi target tracking with an unknown and time varying number of objects, and sequential autoregressive order tracking with change points, comparing against the fixed index sequential model selector and a non Rao Blackwellised trans dimensional filter on estimation error, particle efficiency, and recovery of structure changes.

paper_title: Simultaneous Map Building and Localization for an Autonomous Mobile Robot
motivation: Sonar-based navigation in these works rests on interpretive assumptions: that specular environments produce regions of constant depth (Leonard & Durrant-Whyte's directed sonar sensing), that returns can be classified into planes/corners/edges/cylinders and tracked as geometric beacons via an EKF, that data association can be resolved (Cox's multiple-hypothesis approach), and that a heuristic credibility measure reflects whether a mapped feature is real (Leonard, Durrant-Whyte & Cox's dynamic map building). Yet the field has no way to observe or measure whether these assumptions hold. Evaluation is anecdotal: the dynamic-map-building paper validates against a single hand-measured room using 28 scans from precisely known positions, and admits the credibility update rule's functional form remains unclear. The phrase ground truth appears nowhere in the corpus, and there is no per-return record of what physically caused each echo. Kuc & Siegel's physically based acoustic simulator predicts such echoes in closed form and is verified against real sonar maps, but is used only for qualitative theory-vs-practice comparison, not as a measurement instrument. The result is an Evidence Gap: researchers cannot diagnose where in the pipeline errors originate, cannot condition failures on physical causes, cannot calibrate the credibility heuristic, and cannot compare algorithms on common labeled data. Progress rests on hand-picked scans rather than accumulated, comparable evidence.
method: Build a simulation-grounded benchmark and diagnostic framework that turns Kuc & Siegel's physically based acoustic model into a measurement oracle for the whole sonar perception pipeline. (1) Instrumented oracle: extend the closed-form simulator so every simulated time-of-flight return carries provenance labels — which target produced it and the echo mechanism (direct specular, corner/wall multi-bounce, edge diffraction, main-lobe vs side-lobe). Sweep environment layouts, transducer parameters, sampling density, and robot trajectories to generate large labeled scan corpora with ground-truth feature maps and poses. (2) Sim-to-real fidelity bound: quantitatively match simulated and real scans (range-vs-orientation profiles, RCD histograms) to establish per-regime confidence intervals so simulation evidence carries stated transfer validity to real Polaroid-style sonar. (3) Diagnostic metric suite: define per-return correct-association rate, RCD-extraction precision/recall against ground-truth constant-depth regions, a plane/corner/edge/cylinder classification confusion matrix, and false-feature and missed-feature rates. Condition every metric on physical provenance and geometry (incidence angle, range, sampling density, specularity) to produce failure-mode attribution rather than a single aggregate score. (4) Credibility calibration: treat the credibility measure as a probabilistic claim of feature validity and score it with reliability/calibration curves against known real-vs-artifact labels, quantifying how well and in which regimes credibility tracks truth — answering the open question the authors left unresolved. (5) Common leaderboard: run the corpus through the represented algorithm families — EKF geometric-beacon tracking, multiple-hypothesis data association, and stochastic-map map building — reporting the same conditioned metrics and, using the Kalman-filter computational-cost analysis, pairing accuracy with compute so trade-offs are comparable. This closes the observability gap: it makes each stage independently measurable, attributes errors to physical causes, calibrates the unvalidated credibility heuristic, and lets the community accumulate reproducible, comparable evidence instead of relying on hand-picked scans.

paper_title: Machine Learning in Automated Text Categorization
motivation: The hypertext-categorization literature shows an unexplained inconsistency in whether hyperlink information helps or hurts. Chakrabarti et al. (1998) report that naively adding neighbor terms increases error; Oh et al. (2000) report a large F1 drop from the same trick yet a gain when instead injecting neighbors' predicted class labels; Yang et al. (2002) find appending linked-neighborhood words helps all classifiers on one dataset but is more harmful than helpful on two others. Yang et al. reduce this to five qualitative hypertext regularities and conclude that identifying which holds is crucial but seldom obvious, and that automatically learning how to represent link information is an open question. Missing is a mechanistic, quantitative account of why link information helps or hurts, why it varies across datasets, and why injecting neighbors' class labels is more robust than injecting raw text. This is an explanation gap: the phenomenon is documented but has no predictive causal model. The corpus provides ingredients: class-conditional generative term models and naive-Bayes optimality analysis (Domingos and Pazzani 1997), feature-selection studies showing how vocabulary to training-set ratio governs noise (Yang and Pedersen), and the hypertext datasets used above.
method: Build and validate a generative signal-versus-dilution theory predicting the sign and magnitude of link information's effect on hypertext categorization. First, a model: local text is a bag of words drawn from a class-conditional term distribution; the neighborhood is a mixture where each neighbor's class is drawn from a per-class homophily matrix H and its text from the corresponding class distribution. This maps Yang's regularities to regions of H (encyclopedia near identity, co-referencing low-entropy off-diagonal, none uniform). Derive the expected change in a naive-Bayes or linear decision margin for three representations: local only, local plus neighbor text with volume proportional to neighbor count times length, and local plus neighbor labels. The closed form predicts text injection shifts the margin by a homophily term minus a dilution penalty growing with neighbor term volume relative to the local document and with vocabulary to training-size ratio, explaining the harm; and label injection lacks the term-dilution channel because it projects the neighborhood onto the low-dimensional class simplex, explaining the text versus label asymmetry. Second, a Link Utility Index: an estimable per-class, per-link-type scalar combining neighborhood label purity or entropy, divergence between the observed neighbor term distribution and the estimated true-class model, mean neighbor count times length ratio, and vocabulary to training-size ratio; text injection is predicted to help only when the index exceeds a derived threshold, label injection whenever purity exceeds chance. Third, causal validation: on prior-work corpora and representations such as patent citations, Reuters, and Web and encyclopedia sets with naive Bayes, kNN, and rule learners, test whether the index predicts the observed help or hurt sign and magnitude, and run interventions the theory says should flip the effect, such as varying neighbor volume by truncating or padding neighbor text, degrading homophily by rewiring a fraction of links, and varying feature-selection aggressiveness and training-set size, checking that accuracy moves as predicted. Fourth, payoff: convert the validated theory into an adaptive selector that estimates the index per class and weights local, neighbor-text, and neighbor-label features accordingly, and show it matches or beats the best fixed representation without manual tuning.

paper_title: Amazon.com Recommendations: Item-to-Item Collaborative Filtering
motivation: The provided works span the major collaborative-filtering families: user-based k-NN, item-based similarity, dimensionality-reduction and PCA/clustering (Eigentaste, SVD, scalable clustering), and content/hybrid methods. All cite the same pain points (quality, coverage under sparsity, scalability), yet each validates one algorithm on one dataset with one metric: Eigentaste uses NMAE on Jester, GroupLens coverage/ROC on netnews, item-based and the e-commerce Analysis paper MAE/F1 on MovieLens and retail data. Dataset, rating scale, density, and metric are confounded across papers, so claims are not comparable and sometimes conflict. The Analysis paper does only one density sweep on two datasets; E-Commerce Recommendation Applications only narrates sparsity, cold start, and scalability as open challenges. No work maps WHEN each family wins jointly across accuracy, coverage, and cost as the data regime varies. This matters because the best algorithm is regime-dependent, results do not transfer, and practitioners choose by folklore.
method: Build an empirical CF regime map: a controlled benchmark measuring how each algorithm family's accuracy, coverage, and cost vary as the data regime is perturbed, on shared datasets and metrics. Fix base datasets from the sources (MovieLens-style, Jester-style dense, and a sparse transaction set) and re-implement the corpus algorithms in one harness: popularity baseline, user-based k-NN, item-based CF, SVD, Eigentaste PCA-plus-clustering, scalable clustering CF, and a content/hybrid method. Define orthogonal perturbation axes: global density, per-user profile length (new-user cold start), per-item support (new-item cold start), catalog size, and rating granularity, sampled on a grid. For each algorithm-by-regime cell record a multi-objective profile: accuracy (normalized MAE and top-N F1/ROC), GroupLens usage-centric coverage, and cost (model-build time and online latency). Analyze the tensor into heat-maps and Pareto frontiers and detect crossover boundaries where one family overtakes another. Fit interpretable decision-tree surrogates mapping regime features to the winning algorithm and to accuracy-loss-per-latency-saved, giving an actionable selection guide. Deliverables: reproducible harness, perturbed benchmark suite, the maps, and crossover findings.

paper_title: Sentiment Classification using Machine Learning Techniques
motivation: Movie-review sentiment works optimize in-domain accuracy but ignore brittleness: naive single-not negation, reliance on spurious domain tokens, and untested reliability under perturbation and domain shift.
method: Create a stress-test suite (negation, entity-masking, domain-shift) to measure flip-rate and cross-domain retention of PMI, Naive Bayes and SVM, then recalibrate via negation-scope handling, POS/WordNet opinion-word filtering, and a Turney PMI backoff prior.

paper_title: Neocognitron: A Self-Organizing Neural Network Model for a Mechanism of Visual Pattern Recognition
motivation: Neocognitron self organization is brittle: small changes in parameters or presentation order critically change recognition, and it cannot reject unfamiliar inputs, causing overconfident misclassification.
method: Add consensus training over randomized presentation orders to keep only stable feature templates, redundant multi seed reinforcement with adaptive plane growth to remove the single winner point of failure, and an abstention readout using top layer response sharpness versus inhibitory signal to reject unfamiliar inputs. Evaluate on the paper digit and letter stimuli for reproducibility, robustness, and rejection.

paper_title: Bayesian CART Model Search: Rejoinder
motivation: All eight prior works ultimately produce a collection of simple structural pieces combined into a flexible regression function: MARS (1991) assembles tensor-product spline basis functions of varying interaction order; Generalized Additive Models (1990) assemble univariate smooth main effects; CART and Bayesian CART (1998), Bayesian MARS (1998), and simulation-based Bayesian nonparametric regression (1997) assemble trees or basis functions with posterior weights; and the model-combination methods boosting/AdaBoost (1996), stacked generalization (1992), and the MLE strategy for combining CART models (1997) assemble weighted ensembles of base learners. Bayesian MARS even notes its posterior sample reveals the relative importance of predictors and can favour main effects over interaction terms when interpretation matters more than prediction. Yet the evidence these papers accumulate is almost entirely predictive accuracy on a few datasets. There is no shared way to observe and measure what these schemes actually recover about the data-generating structure: which variables truly matter, whether an effect is additive or a genuine interaction, the order of interactions, and whether structural conclusions carry calibrated uncertainty. This matters because these methods are routinely used for interpretation and variable screening, yet we lack any common benchmark or diagnostic to compare, audit, and validate their structural fidelity on equal footing. The Bayesian methods emit structural uncertainty via posterior inclusion probabilities, while boosting, stacking, and MLE-combined CART emit no comparable structural readout, so their structural claims cannot even in principle be audited against the Bayesian ones. EVIDENCE GAP: the field lacks a way to observe, measure, benchmark, and compare how faithfully, and with what calibrated uncertainty, flexible-regression and model-combination methods recover the underlying functional structure, rather than only how accurately they predict.
method: Build a structural-fidelity evidence framework that makes MARS, GAM, CART, Bayesian CART, Bayesian MARS, simulation-based Bayesian regression, boosting, stacked generalization, and MLE-combined CART directly comparable on what they infer about structure, not just prediction error. Step 1, common structural readout: represent every fitted method through a functional ANOVA decomposition of its prediction surface into an intercept, univariate main effects, pairwise interactions, and higher-order terms. Because all methods deliver a callable predictor, estimate these components model-agnostically by Monte Carlo projection of the fitted surface onto orthogonal main-effect and low-order interaction subspaces over the predictor distribution, using held-out design points. This maps disparate representations (spline bases, trees, additive smooths, weighted ensembles) onto shared coordinates: per-variable main-effect energy, per-pair interaction energy, and an effective interaction-order spectrum. Step 2, ground-truth benchmark: construct synthetic regression functions with known ANOVA structure, systematically varying pure additivity versus controlled two- and three-way interactions (reusing the interaction and radial test functions from the MARS and Bayesian MARS papers as anchors), number of irrelevant variables, predictor correlation, dimensionality, and noise, giving exact targets for variable relevance, interaction presence and order, and component shapes. Step 3, fidelity metrics: beyond test RMSE, score each method on variable-selection ROC/AUC (relevant versus noise variables), interaction-detection precision/recall and order accuracy, and component-recovery error measured as L2 distance between estimated and true ANOVA components, converting interpretability claims into measurable evidence. Step 4, common uncertainty audit: for the Bayesian methods use the posterior sample of models directly to obtain distributions of each component energy and of variable inclusion; for the frequentist combiners (boosting, stacking, MLE-combined CART) generate a matched ensemble by nonparametric bootstrap of the training data and recompute the ANOVA readout per replicate; then measure calibration of structural claims via empirical coverage of nominal intervals for component energies and false-discovery rates of declared variables and interactions across the benchmark. Step 5, analysis: aggregate into a leaderboard that separates predictive skill from structural fidelity and from uncertainty calibration, revealing trade-offs such as whether accuracy-driven boosting over-attributes spurious interactions, whether Bayesian model averaging yields better-calibrated structural uncertainty, and whether stacking's meta-combination distorts the decomposition, and validate on a few real datasets from the source papers by checking cross-method agreement of recovered structure. The approach is feasible using the base algorithms described in the sources plus standard Monte Carlo integration and bootstrap, and directly fills the evidence gap by providing an observable, benchmarked, auditable basis for comparing what these combination methods learn about structure and how trustworthy those conclusions are.

paper_title: A Simple Rule-Based Part of Speech Tagger
motivation:
Across the provided works, three research communities independently attacked the same core problem — resolving the grammatical category (part of speech) of words in running text — yet they developed in near-isolation and were never placed on common ground.

(1) A linguistic/rule community built symbolic disambiguators grounded in morphology and hand or acquired rules: Klein & Simmons' 1963 computational grammar coder that classifies words by suffix "batteries" and small exception lists without a large dictionary; Greene & Rubin's automated tagging; and Hindle's 1989 acquisition of disambiguation rules from a deterministic parser (Fidditch).

(2) A statistical-NLP tagging community treated the task as decoding a hidden Markov model: Church (1988), DeRose (1988), Kupiec (1989) and Cutting et al. (1992), the last reporting >96% accuracy from only a lexicon and unlabeled text, using ambiguity/equivalence classes and suffix guessing for unknown words.

(3) A speech / information-theory community used the very same Markov-source machinery for a different downstream goal: Jelinek's 1985 Markov source modeling annotates POS as a by-product of a 40-tag language model built by Forward–Backward for continuous speech recognition, and the phoneme-to-text transcription work fuses statistical Markov decoding with an explicit grammar to pick transcriptions.

These literatures share almost identical mathematics (n-gram/HMM scoring, Viterbi, equivalence classes) and even cite common corpora (Francis & Kučera's Brown Corpus), but they are disconnected in three consequential ways. First, they are evaluated on incompatible tagsets (Brown's fine tags vs. Fidditch's collapsed PRO; ad hoc speech alphabets) and disjoint texts, so their headline numbers (90% on scientific text, <2%/5% training error, "96%") are not comparable and no one knows which paradigm actually wins where. Second, they make radically different resource assumptions (hand-tagged corpus vs. lexicon-only vs. parser vs. morphology rules), yet no study controls for supervision, lexicon coverage, or morphological knowledge to isolate what each ingredient buys. Third, the "tagging as a tool" and "tagging as a by-product of a language model for transcription" framings have never been cross-evaluated, even though they are the same noisy-channel model. This bridge gap matters because the paradigms appear complementary — morphology-based rules should excel exactly on the low-frequency/unknown words where HMM lexicon statistics are weakest (the Zipf tail Church highlights), and parser-derived rules encode long-distance agreement that fixed HMM windows miss (the very errors the phoneme-to-text grammar was added to fix). Without a common empirical map, the field cannot see these complementarities or justify principled hybrids.
method:
We propose an empirical mapping study: a unified diagnostic benchmark and comparative analysis that places the rule/morphology, statistical-HMM, and speech-oriented Markov paradigms on identical footing, then charts where each succeeds, fails, and complements the others.

1. Common substrate. Anchor everything on the Tagged Brown Corpus (Francis & Kučera). Define a canonical tagset plus an explicit, documented many-to-one mapping to each paradigm's native tagset (fine Brown tags; Fidditch-style collapsed tags; the 40-tag speech alphabet), so all systems are scored under one normalized label space via the mapping, and separately under their own granularity.

2. Re-implemented, normalized systems. Build faithful, minimal reimplementations of one representative per paradigm, sharing I/O and lexicon interfaces: (a) a morphology/rule coder in the Klein–Simmons style (suffix tests + small exception list, no large dictionary); (b) an HMM tagger with ambiguity/equivalence classes and suffix-based unknown-word guessing (Cutting/Kupiec/Church); (c) a Jelinek-style Markov-source model trained by Forward–Backward that emits POS as a Viterbi by-product; and (d) a parser-rule disambiguator approximated by Hindle-style acquired context patterns. Each is trained/tuned only with resources native to its paradigm, all recorded.

3. Diagnostics (the map). Rather than a single accuracy number, produce a multi-axis empirical map: (i) per-category accuracy and full confusion matrices; (ii) stratification by word-frequency band and known-vs-OOV status, to test the hypothesis that morphology dominates in the Zipf tail while HMM statistics dominate on frequent words; (iii) genre robustness across Brown's sub-corpora; (iv) resource curves that sweep amount of labeled data, unlabeled data, lexicon coverage, and presence/absence of morphology rules, isolating each ingredient's marginal contribution; (v) context-window sensitivity, contrasting fixed HMM windows with parser/state-chain long-distance dependencies on hand-selected agreement cases; and (vi) inter-system agreement/complementarity analysis (pairwise disagreement, oracle-combination ceiling) to quantify how much each paradigm could gain from the others.

4. Cross-community bridge task. Reconnect tagging with the transcription line by evaluating every model both as a tagger and as the language model in a controlled noisy-channel decoder over deliberately ambiguated input (e.g., devoweled or homophone-confused text mimicking the phoneme-to-text/stenotypy setting). We measure whether design choices that help tagging accuracy also reduce transcription word-error, and vice versa, mapping transfer between the two objectives that the sources treated separately.

5. Deliverables. (i) A reusable, open evaluation harness with the tagset-mapping layer, resource-controlled protocols, and OOV/frequency stratification; (ii) an empirical map of the design space (linguistic features vs. statistics vs. supervision vs. context length) with confusion and complementarity findings; and (iii) a data-driven specification for a hybrid — e.g., morphology-first backoff for the OOV tail feeding HMM decoding, with parser-derived long-distance corrections — whose predicted gains are read directly off the oracle-combination ceiling.

This addresses the bridge gap by making the three literatures directly comparable for the first time, attributing performance to specific mechanisms rather than to incomparable corpora/tagsets, and empirically demonstrating (or refuting) their complementarity across both the tagging and transcription tasks.

paper_title: Unsupervised Learning of Action Classes with Continuous Temporal Embedding
motivation: Weakly-supervised action segmentation aligns a long video (T frames) to a short ordered transcript (N actions, N far smaller than T). Kuehne's HMM, NeuralNetwork-Viterbi (visual, Poisson-length, grammar), ECTC (alignment-sum with visual similarity), RNN fine-to-coarse, and ISBA all suffer the same degenerate-alignment collapse, where one action swallows most frames, and each fixes it with a different hand-tuned device. No work formally explains why collapse happens, what minimal prior prevents it, how the fixes relate, or when segmentation is identifiable across supervision levels (transcript vs action set vs none).
method: A formal-derivation contribution. (1) Define a canonical segmental likelihood: sum over monotone alignments of products of emission, length, and context factors; prove Kuehne, ECTC, NN-Viterbi, ISBA are special cases differing only in sum-vs-max and the length/consistency factor (a taxonomy of three biases: emission separability, length concentration, ordering). (2) Degeneracy theorem via a boundary-shift lemma: with independent emissions and a flat length prior, shifting a frame across a boundary changes log-likelihood by the emission log-prob difference alone, independent of lengths, so the objective is length-scale-free and collapses to one action. (3) Regularizer-equivalence theorem: any length prior with strictly convex negative log-likelihood (Poisson, Gaussian) equals, up to constants, an entropy regularizer on segment lengths that bounds collapse, and ECTC's similarity factor does the same by forbidding boundaries in smooth runs, placing both in one anti-collapse class. (4) Error bound and identifiability theorem: bound boundary error by emission margin, length-prior concentration, and ordering constraints; give conditions for a unique MAP as T grows; extend to action sets, where identifiability holds only up to grammar-consistent orderings, quantifying the transcript-vs-set information gap. (5) Derive a length-normalized, entropy-regularized objective that is provably scale-invariant and collapse-free without a tuned rate, drops into existing Viterbi/forward-backward decoders, and is testable on Breakfast and Hollywood-Extended.

paper_title: Freeman Code Based Online Handwritten Character Recognition for Malayalam Using Backpropagation Neural Networks
motivation: In all six prior recognizers, the main failure mode is confusion among visually similar characters. The Tamil system manually groups confused pairs and hand-codes cues; the Malayalam positional-analyzer paper calls shape similarity the main factor hindering accuracy; the Kohonen and kNN papers design features to separate similar characters. Yet all report only top-1 accuracy with no confidence, calibration, or abstention, so on confusable classes they are silently and confidently wrong, a reliability risk for text entry. Reported accuracies also come from tiny writer-limited corpora (Arabic: 4 train, 5 test writers, 336 samples; Malayalam: 40 writers), overstating real reliability. The only remedy, manual per-script cues, does not scale and gives no coverage guarantee.
method: A calibrated, confusion-aware recognizer with selective prediction wrapping any prior backbone (kNN, SOM, 2DPCA-NN, chain-code, matching). (1) Calibration: map raw outputs (kNN distances, SOM quantization error, match scores) to calibrated posteriors via temperature/Platt scaling. (2) Automatic confusion-graph discovery: threshold the leave-one-out confusion matrix into a graph whose connected components are confusion clusters, replacing manual grouping. (3) Learned disambiguators: per cluster, train a lightweight discriminator on existing direction/curvature and context-bitmap features, invoked only inside clusters. (4) Conformal selective prediction: output candidate sets with coverage guarantees; commit on singletons, arbitrate inside clusters, abstain/defer (prompt rewrite or offer candidates) when uncertain. Evaluate with writer-independent splits, risk-coverage curves, selective accuracy, calibration error, and conformal coverage under writer shift, across two scripts.

paper_title: Author topic model for co-occurring normal documents and short texts to explore individual user preferences
motivation: Streaming short-text cluster models (MStream/MStreamF, DP-BMM/DP-BMM-FP, and embedding-based NPMM) use a Dirichlet-Process Multinomial Mixture that makes an irreversible one-pass choice per document: join an existing cluster or spawn a new one. On noisy social streams this is brittle: spam and off-topic posts with unusual words get high new-cluster probability and spawn spurious topics or trigger false concept drift, while outliers forced into real clusters corrupt topic-word distributions, and one-pass inference makes these errors permanent. Existing remedies do not cover this streaming short-text setting: GSDPMM detects outliers only in static batch corpora, COTM flags spam only given co-occurring long documents and a manual threshold, NPMM uses embeddings for the new-topic decision but never quarantines noisy documents, and MStream deliberately drops any threshold and thus cannot separate genuine novelty from noise. No streaming short-text model robustly distinguishes an emerging topic from isolated noise or protects topic-word distributions from low-quality inputs, so downstream tasks like event detection and popularity prediction inherit corrupted, over-fragmented topics.
method: Propose R-Stream, a robust extension of the streaming DPMM framework (as in MStream and DP-BMM) with three mechanisms that reduce brittleness to noise. First, a background noise component whose word distribution is the corpus background; each incoming document also gets a probability of coming from this background, and documents best explained by it are quarantined and never update topical cluster counts, preventing topic-word corruption. Second, embedding-based reliability gating that scores each document by internal semantic coherence (compactness of its content-word embeddings) and distance to the candidate cluster centroid, combined into a reliability weight that softly scales its contribution to cluster counts and biases the noise-versus-new-cluster decision toward quarantine for incoherent posts. Third, corroboration-based drift confirmation, where a document choosing a new cluster enters a short-lived provisional buffer and becomes a real topic only after enough mutually-coherent documents corroborate it within a time window, while uncorroborated provisional clusters expire as noise, separating genuine concept drift from isolated spam and curbing spurious-topic explosion. Inference keeps one-pass online Gibbs sampling with forgetting rules for scalability. Evaluate by injecting controlled contamination (random-word documents, off-topic tweets, near-duplicate boilerplate, keyword-stuffed spam) at varying rates into standard short-text stream benchmarks and comparing NMI-versus-noise curves, spurious-cluster count, false concept-drift rate, quarantine precision/recall, and topic coherence against MStream/MStreamF, DP-BMM/DP-BMM-FP and NPMM.

paper_title: An Experiment in Linguistic Synthesis with a Fuzzy Logic Controller
motivation: The six works split into two traditions never formally joined. Teaching as CONTROL: Pask (1971) treats an adaptive teaching machine B as a controller sensing the learner's uncertainty reduction and raising difficulty, removing cooperative assistance as proficiency rises; Gaines (1973) frames training as control in the state-space of the trainee's adaption-automaton, showing men and machines both fail on the final task alone but succeed under an ascending-difficulty schedule; the 1966 learning-machine paper supplies the same control paradigm. Instruction as LINGUISTIC: Luria (1961) holds that speech regulates behavior and is internalized as self-instruction; Winograd (1972) shows natural-language commands understood as executable, domain-grounded procedures; Zadeh (1973) shows fuzzy conditional statements over linguistic variables can communicate control know-how. Gaines even cites Zadeh's adaptive control and Winograd as the same control situation, yet none formalizes the teaching signal AS natural-language instruction: the control papers use only scalar difficulty; Zadeh describes fuzzy control for a designer of a static system, not a teacher steering a learner over time; Winograd gives procedural meaning without learning dynamics; Luria gives internalization without formalism. The gap: no model treats verbal instruction as a fuzzy control law over a learner's state-space trajectory, explains why an ascending schedule is optimal, and formalizes external-to-internalized regulation. This matters for teaching machines, curriculum scheduling, and instructable agents.
method: Develop a formal model, Verbal Regulatory Control (VRC), with a central theorem. Constructs: a task is a controlled system with state space X (Gaines's adaption-automaton); the learner holds a discrimination partition Pi_p of X whose resolution grows with proficiency p. An instruction is a Zadeh fuzzy algorithm IF (fuzzy state) THEN (fuzzy action) over linguistic variables with granularity g. A grounding map M (Winograd procedural semantics) sends each instruction to a fuzzy control relation R on X, applied via Zadeh's compositional rule of inference; the learner uses only the projection of R onto Pi_p. Derivations: (1) Representation theorem: the scalar difficulty of Pask/Gaines is recovered as the coarseness of the projected relation, making the classic teaching loop a one-dimensional special case of VRC. (2) Uncertainty bound: with a fuzzy entropy H over the learner's policy, prove per-instruction gain DeltaH is bounded by min(information content of R, resolution of Pi_p): too-fuzzy instruction carries little information, too-precise instruction delivers unresolvable variety and induces error, formalizing Pask's overloaded novice. (3) Optimal-granularity theorem: DeltaH is maximized when g matches current discrimination resolution; since Pi_p refines as p rises, optimal g refines monotonically, deriving the ascending-difficulty schedule Gaines/Pask imposed heuristically and predicting Pask's null-point steady state as granularity tracking resolution. (4) Internalization taxonomy (Luria): model learning as the internal policy converging to R, distinguishing external regulation (R in teacher B) from internalized regulation (R transferred into A as self-instruction), and prove Pask's removal of assistance is the optimal policy of withdrawing the external controller when the internal policy matches R within Pi_p tolerance. Validation: instantiate VRC in a Winograd-style blocks-world and Gaines's tracking task; simulate an adaptive controller as learner and test that matching linguistic granularity to discrimination resolution beats fixed-granularity and scalar-difficulty instruction, reproducing Gaines's men-and-machines equivalence.

paper_title: Additive Logistic Regression: A Statistical View of Boosting
motivation: Bagging reduces variance by bootstrap aggregation (Breiman 1996), gradient boosting reduces bias via stagewise additive expansions in function space (Friedman 1999), GAMs (Hastie and Tibshirani 1990) offer an explicit complexity knob, and Practical Optimization (Gill 1981) frames the optimization view. Breiman says instability is the vital element deciding whether bagging helps and notes a crossover where bagging hurts stable procedures, but instability stays qualitative and the crossover is shown via one simulation. No prior work gives an operational pre-training measurement of instability or a systematic map of where the crossover lies versus measurable dataset and base-learner properties. Practitioners thus lack a diagnostic to choose bagging versus boosting before spending compute; the GAM complexity knob is an unused way to move learners between regimes.
method: Build an empirical instability-bias map and diagnostic. Define two cheap coordinates per dataset and base-learner from a few bootstrap replicates: an instability index (mean bootstrap prediction variance across test points) and a bias index (error of the bootstrap-averaged predictor versus a strong reference). Benchmark on Breiman's UCI datasets plus simulations with known truth (waveform, 30-variable regression) so bias and variance are exact. Sweep a complexity knob (tree depth, subset size m, GAM degrees of freedom, k-NN k) to trace trajectories. For each configuration measure single, bagged, and gradient-boosted errors across squared, LAD, and logistic losses, decomposing gains into bias and variance. Plot bagging and boosting improvement as surfaces over the two coordinates to locate the crossover contour and dominance regions. Fit and validate a diagnostic that predicts the winning strategy and expected gain from the measured indices, tested on held-out datasets and trajectories.

paper_title: Hybrid Recommender Systems: Survey and Experiments
motivation: Recommenders rest on one premise: similarity to the past predicts value (content-based recommends similar content; collaborative recommends what similar users liked; see Pazzani and GroupLens). Yet the sources reveal a paradox: optimizing this objective can make the system worse for the user. Balabanovic (Exploring versus Exploiting) shows pure exploitation causes over-specialization, freezing the user model and flooding one topic; exploration fixes this and tracks changing interests but only by delivering suboptimal items now. He also notes novelty is the relevance criterion second only to topical relevance, yet excludes it because it conflicts with similarity. CoFIND independently finds similarity-to-the-past founders for evolving learning needs, because usefulness is multi-dimensional and context-dependent (their qualities). So similarity and novelty are in tension, and current fixes disappoint: Balabanovic's exploration is blind and offloaded to a manual slider, while CoFIND's value dimensions require heavy manual collaborative curation and struggled in the pilot. The gap: nobody makes exploration itself value-bearing, aimed at items that are simultaneously informative to the model and novel and useful, nor discovers value dimensions automatically. Dissolving rather than tuning this tradeoff would let recommenders stay accurate now while remaining adaptive over time.
method: Propose value-directed exploration to dissolve the explore-exploit tradeoff. First, two-space items: a topical content space (vector-space or LSI factors) and a latent value space discovered automatically by factoring the residual of the feedback matrix after removing the topical component, yielding axes for why items are valued beyond topic (an automatic analogue of CoFIND qualities). Second, an uncertainty-aware user model: a probabilistic profile over both spaces recording which topical regions and value dimensions have not yet been probed, extending Balabanovic's vector model with explicit uncertainty. Third, a value-bearing objective: score a candidate by predicted preference plus marginal novelty versus already-consumed items (the factor Balabanovic excluded, made central) plus expected information gain about under-probed value dimensions, but restrict exploratory candidates to items collaborative neighbors rate high along those under-probed dimensions. This makes exploration warm: uncertainty-reducing picks are also community-validated and novel, so they tend to be useful even while exploratory. Fourth, drift handling: sustained mismatch signals interest drift and triggers targeted re-exploration of relevant-but-new regions; a single adventurousness control tunes the weight but the exploration is directed, not random. Fifth, evaluation: extend Balabanovic's simulation with drifting users and a multi-criteria utility (topical plus novelty plus value match); compare pure exploitation, blind exploration, value-directed exploration, and manual-slider on immediate quality versus cumulative usefulness and learning speed. Hypothesis: value-directed exploration Pareto-dominates, matching exploitation's immediate quality while keeping exploration's learning speed and drift tracking. Validate on real feedback data (Syskill and Webert ratings and a news set) against content-based, collaborative, and random-exploration baselines.

paper_title: Adaptive Signal Processing for Adaptive Control
motivation: Two traditions dominate these sources. Widrow's LMS line (Stationary/Nonstationary Learning Characteristics 1976; Adaptive Noise Cancelling 1975; On Adaptive Inverse Control 1981) adapts a filter by descending a quadratic error surface with a step-size mu (speed of adaptation). The 1976 paper proves that steady-state misadjustment decomposes additively into a gradient-noise term growing with mu and a lag term growing with nonstationarity and shrinking with mu, so an optimal mu* balances them; but it admits mu* is found by trial and error, assumes nonstationarity statistics are known, and uses one global mu. The self-tuning/stochastic tradition (On Self-tuning Regulators 1973; Self-Tuning via Pole-Zero Placement 1980; MRAS survey 1974; Unbiased Recursive Identification 1976; Adaptive Stochastic Control 1972; Learning Dual Control 1973) recursively estimates plant parameters under certainty-equivalence, and the dual-control work names the estimation-vs-control conflict: gains depend on parameter-error covariance and energy should be split between identification and control. The gap: in all these works the adaptation resource itself (per-parameter learning gain/forgetting factor and identification excitation energy) is fixed or hand-tuned, though the misadjustment optimum depends on unknown, time-varying quantities (per-parameter drift rate, input eigenstructure, estimation covariance). No source treats adaptation speed and probing excitation as an online optimization, nor allocates it per-parameter. This matters because adaptive inverse control, noise cancelling, and self-tuning regulators inherit a single scalar rate that is provably suboptimal when parameters drift at different rates or the input is ill-conditioned, forcing trial-and-error and leaving performance off the noise-vs-tracking frontier.
method: Propose a self-optimizing adaptive filter/controller: an online meta-optimization layer that treats adaptation as a resource-allocation problem and searches for the allocation minimizing the tracking-lag-vs-estimation-noise objective, replacing the hand-tuned scalar step-size in LMS, adaptive inverse control, and self-tuning regulators. (1) Objective: use the 1976 additive misadjustment decomposition per parameter k, M = sum_k [ a_k*mu_k + b_k*NS_k/mu_k ], with a_k the gradient/estimation-noise weight (input power in direction k) and b_k*NS_k the lag weight (parameter drift variance NS_k); decision variables are per-parameter gains mu_k (diagonal gain matrix in LMS/RLS, or per-parameter forgetting factors). (2) Certainty-equivalence estimation: following the self-tuning-regulator philosophy, a fast inner estimator on residual dynamics estimates online the input eigenstructure (a_k), the estimation-noise covariance, and each drift rate NS_k, extracted from the low-frequency lag component of the weight-error autocovariance separated from high-frequency gradient noise via a two-timescale filter; plug into the analytic minimizer mu_k* = sqrt(b_k*NS_k/a_k), a coordinate-wise closed-form optimizer recomputed recursively, i.e. self-tuning the learning rate rather than the controller. (3) Active excitation design (dual-control layer): add an input-power budget P and solve a water-filling-style allocation distributing probing energy to parameters with largest product of uncertainty-covariance and drift-rate (the estimation-vs-control conflict from the dual-control source), re-solved online and shaped to least degrade output in inverse-control/noise-cancelling settings. (4) Robustness wrapper: wrap the analytic optimum in a bandit-style bracketing search over a small candidate set of gains, using measured excess mean-square error to correct a_k, b_k so the allocation tracks the true frontier even when white-input/first-order-Markov assumptions fail. Evaluation: reproduce the 1976 nonstationary Markov-drift benchmark and adaptive-inverse-control/noise-cancelling setups and show the method finds mu* without trial and error, beats any fixed scalar mu under heterogeneous drift and disparate eigenvalues, and via active excitation converges the least-certain parameters faster, driving misadjustment toward the theoretical efficiency limit of the 1976 analysis. This is an optimization/search contribution: adaptive allocation of adaptation-speed and probing-energy unifying LMS misadjustment theory with self-tuning and dual-control principles.

paper_title: Best Practices for Convolutional Neural Networks Applied to Visual Document Analysis
motivation: Segmentation-based NN–HMM hybrid word recognizers (as in the offline cursive system) are only as reliable as the neural character classifier that supplies observation probabilities to the HMM. That system uses softmax MLP outputs divided by class priors, P(letter|segment)/P(letter), directly as HMM emission likelihoods, with a single "junk" class meant to reject non-letter segments. This design has three brittleness sources that the prior works leave unaddressed together: (1) Transformation variability — handwriting varies in slant, scale, stroke width, baseline position, and ligature stretch; the classifier only sees whatever variety happens to be in the labeled corpus. The invariant-SVM work demonstrates that explicitly injecting transformation invariance (virtual support vectors, tangent distance) substantially lowers isolated-digit error, and LeNet's document-recognition work relies on input distortions, yet these invariance techniques have never been brought inside the in-graph character classifier of a word recognizer. (2) Mis-segmentation shift — the sliding-window segmentation graph generates many frames that are letter fragments, merged letters, or over-splits; on these out-of-distribution inputs a softmax classifier tends to be overconfident, corrupting the word likelihood, and a single junk class trained only on incidental non-letters is a weak defense. (3) Miscalibration — raw posteriors treated as likelihoods are not calibrated, so the HMM integrates untrustworthy scores. The paucity-of-data study shows classifier performance depends strongly on corpus size, so for the limited IRONOFF/SRTP handwriting corpora, principled augmentation and invariance are especially valuable. Finally, the Hornik–Stinchcombe–White result that feedforward networks can approximate a mapping and its derivatives provides the missing theoretical justification for training a network to have prescribed derivatives, i.e. to be locally invariant. There is thus a clear gap: robustifying the observation-probability estimator of a word recognizer against transformation and segmentation-induced distribution shift, and making its emitted likelihoods trustworthy, rather than only optimizing isolated-character accuracy.
method:
Robustify the in-graph neural character classifier so that the observation probabilities fed to the HMM are invariant to nuisance handwriting transformations, reliable on mis-segmented frames, and calibrated. Four coordinated components, all trainable with the existing bootstrap pipeline:

1) Invariance-consistency (tangent-prop) regularization. In addition to the standard cross-entropy on the 140-dimensional frame features, add a penalty on the directional derivative of the network's log-posterior along known handwriting transformation directions (slant shear, horizontal/vertical scale, stroke-width dilation/erosion, baseline shift, ligature stretch). The transformation tangents are computed on the frame/feature representation; the penalty forces small transformations to leave the posterior nearly unchanged. This is exactly the "approximate the function AND its derivatives" regime the universal-approximation-of-derivatives paper guarantees is feasible, and it operationalizes the tangent-distance idea from the invariant-SVM review inside a neural classifier.

2) Targeted virtual-example augmentation. Rather than blanket distortion, mimic the virtual-support-vector philosophy: identify the hard/boundary frames (low-margin correct frames and frames near the junk boundary) via the bootstrap HMM alignment, and generate transformed virtual copies concentrated on those examples. This adds information where the decision surface is fragile while controlling cost, directly targeting the paucity-of-data limitation for small handwriting corpora.

3) Structured junk/rejection robustification. Systematically synthesize the frames the segmentation graph actually produces — letter fragments, merged pairs, and over-split slices — from the alignment, and use them to train the junk class and an auxiliary out-of-distribution score. This gives spurious graph paths reliably low emission probability instead of accidental overconfident letter scores.

4) Calibrated likelihood conversion. Before dividing by class priors, calibrate posteriors (temperature scaling fitted on held-out aligned frames) and fold the OOD score into an uncertainty-aware emission that down-weights frames the classifier flags as off-manifold, so the HMM's Viterbi/forward-backward decoding integrates trustworthy likelihoods.

Evaluation: on IRONOFF-196, IRONOFF-Cheque, and SRTP-Cheque, compare the robustified hybrid against the baseline NN–HMM and discrete-HMM systems on (a) clean word recognition rate, (b) robustness under injected slant/scale/stroke distortions and segmentation jitter, (c) calibration of emission probabilities (reliability diagrams, negative log-likelihood), and (d) accuracy as training-corpus size is reduced, to test the paucity-of-data benefit. Ablate each component to isolate the contribution of invariance regularization, targeted augmentation, junk synthesis, and calibration. Success criterion: reduced word-error rate and improved calibration under distribution shift with no clean-accuracy loss.

paper_title: Additive Logistic Regression: A Statistical View of Boosting
motivation: Breiman's bagging analysis (1996) establishes that bootstrap aggregation only helps when the base procedure is unstable and is neutral or harmful for stable procedures. He identifies a qualitative cross-over point between stability and instability, and in classification distinguishes order-correct inputs, where aggregation drives the predictor toward Bayes-optimal, from inputs where a poor predictor becomes worse. Friedman's gradient boosting and Hastie-Tibshirani generalized additive models attack the complementary systematic-bias side of error via stagewise additive structure. The evidence gap: the field has no operational instrument that, before committing to an ensembling strategy, observes and quantifies how unstable a base-learner and dataset pairing actually is, where in input space that instability lives, how much error is aggregation-removable versus systematic, and on which side of the cross-over point the pairing sits. Breiman diagnoses these only qualitatively and post hoc; Friedman and Hastie-Tibshirani give no diagnostic for when bias-reduction is the right lever. Practitioners thus cannot audit, predict, or accumulate comparable evidence about when an ensemble helps or backfires. This matters because bagging can degrade stable or near-optimal predictors, and the choice between variance-reduction and bias-reduction is made blindly. Crucially, Breiman supplies an unexploited lever: since a bootstrap replicate approximates the data distribution, the learning set can serve as a test set for models grown on bootstrap samples, so instability can be measured directly from training data with no held-out set.
method: Develop Instability Spectroscopy, an out-of-bag bootstrap diagnostic that measures a predictor sampling behavior and predicts, ahead of time, the sign, magnitude, and location of bagging's effect, and flags when bias-reduction is the better lever. Step 1, instability signature: fit the base learner on B bootstrap replicates; for each training point x use only replicates where x was out-of-bag to estimate the empirical prediction distribution at x, namely regression prediction variance or the classification class-vote distribution, with no separate test set. Step 2, diagnostics: a per-point and global instability index from OOB variance or vote entropy; an empirical order-correctness map using OOB votes to estimate where the aggregated majority class differs from the single-model prediction and the vote margin, separating regions where aggregation helps from regions where a biased learner is pushed further from optimal; and a decomposition of OOB error into an aggregation-removable component and a systematic component. Step 3, cross-over prediction: combine the removable-variance and systematic-error estimates to predict expected bagging gain and locate the cross-over point as a function of complexity knobs such as tree size or number of retained variables, emitting a bag or do-not-bag verdict and expected error change before any bagged test evaluation. Step 4, bias-versus-variance routing: where error is attributed to systematic bias, recommend and quantify expected benefit of stagewise boosting or additive-model fitting via an analogous OOB residual decomposition, yielding an auditable decision rule and a spatially adaptive hybrid that bags high-instability regions and boosts high-bias regions. Step 5, validation: benchmark predictions against actual outcomes on Breiman's procedures such as CART trees, forward subset-selection regression, and k-NN as a stable control, across his datasets and simulations plus modern learners; verify the predicted cross-over point matches where measured bagged test error stops improving, predicted per-region gains correlate with realized gains, and the order-correctness map predicts where classification is helped versus degraded; report calibration curves and sensitivity to B.

paper_title: A Bit of Progress in Language Modeling (Extended Version)
motivation: Large-span and adaptive language models, including LSA pseudodocument models, dynamic caches, word triggers, and topic mixtures, share one architecture: during recognition they maintain a running representation of the history and update it in an unsupervised loop from the recognizer's own hypothesized words. This loop is a documented but unaddressed source of brittleness. First, error feedback: Bellegarda notes recognition errors affect the LSA context well into the future through a flawed pseudodocument representation, and caches and triggers reinforce erroneous words similarly. Second, error-blind uniform updates: every hypothesized word is folded in at full weight even though errors concentrate on short confusable function words that carry little semantic signal. Third, a single hand-tuned static forgetting constant chosen offline by expected session heterogeneity, which cannot react to within-session topic drift. Fourth, no hedging under uncertainty: the interpolation weight between the large-span prior and the local n-gram is fixed regardless of whether the representation was built from clean or corrupted evidence. Jelinek's review argues for a Bayesian treatment carrying uncertainty into model integration, yet no available work makes the history update uncertainty-aware. This leaves room to robustify adaptive language models against their dominant failure mode of unsupervised context corruption.
method: We propose a confidence-weighted, drift-adaptive history representation that robustifies large-span and adaptive language models against unsupervised context corruption, as a drop-in modification of the history-update step demonstrated on the LSA pseudodocument model and transferable to caches and triggers. Part one, confidence-weighted context construction: replace the hard one-best update with a soft update in which each recognized token contributes in proportion to a reliability score derived from recognizer word posteriors from lattices or N-best lists, reusing existing lattice and N-best rescoring machinery. The context vector becomes a confidence-and-saliency-weighted sum in which the existing entropy weight further down-weights function words. Part two, uncertainty-marginalized update: rather than committing to the single best word, compute the expected context contribution under the posterior over competing lattice hypotheses. Part three, adaptive forgetting driven by measured drift: replace the global forgetting constant with a per-step decay computed online from the semantic movement of the running vector, forgetting faster on strong drift and retaining longer when homogeneous. Part four, reliability-gated interpolation: make the weight on the large-span prior increase with the aggregate reliability of the evidence that built it, so after a burst of low-confidence words the model defers to the well-estimated local n-gram and re-expands as reliable evidence accumulates. For evaluation we measure perplexity and word error rate on WSJ or NAB and Switchboard in unsupervised adaptation mode, run a brittleness stress test injecting controlled recognition errors with success defined as the robustified advantage widening as conditions worsen, test heterogeneous topic-shifting sessions, and ablate the four parts. All changes touch only history-update and interpolation-weight computation, so the added cost is a few operations per word.

paper_title: Markov Games as a Framework for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
motivation: Why does self-play TD learning succeed in backgammon (TD-Gammon) yet self-play is fragile in deterministic games? No source explains the causal role of stochastic dice.
method: Vary environmental stochasticity in a fixed game, train identical self-play TD nets, and measure state coverage, local optima, and error decomposition to isolate exploration versus target-smoothing mechanisms.

paper_title: The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain
motivation: Von Neumann reliable-organism synthesis achieves reliability from unreliable elements by uniform multiplexing, using the same bundle size of about twenty thousand lines everywhere and a restoring organ after every organ, ignoring how much each organ contributes to output error. Culbertson uneconomical robots share this brute-force spirit. Minsky universal elements show automata use heterogeneous parts with unequal fan-out, path multiplicity, and logical masking, so errors do not propagate equally. Thus classical reliable synthesis is uneconomical, and neither von Neumann, Culbertson, nor the reliability-agnostic adaptive schemes of Uttley, Rosenblatt, and Hebb allocate a scarce redundancy budget where it most reduces output error. Closing this gap yields an economical budget-aware synthesis principle for resource-limited realizations.
method: Cast reliable-automaton synthesis as constrained resource allocation solved by sensitivity-guided search. Given an automaton for a function from Minsky and McCulloch and Pitts elements, per-element failure probabilities, and a target output error epsilon, choose per-element bundle sizes and binary restoring-organ insertions that minimize total component cost subject to output reliability at least one minus epsilon. Evaluate candidates by propagating von Neumann excitation-level and dispersion recursions along the circuit graph, cross-checked with Monte Carlo simulation. Screen each element by its marginal output-error reduction per added line and per restorer using an influence and logical-masking pass, and prune elements in the stable contracting regime. Search greedily by adding redundancy to the element with the best error-reduction per cost, with local swaps and minimum-cost cut-set placement of restorers that keep every path accumulated error below threshold, re-estimating sensitivities after each move as an adaptive design loop. Evaluate on Sheffer-stroke adders, majority organs, and Minsky-element compositions, comparing component count against uniform multiplexing at equal reliability and reporting the reliability versus cost Pareto frontier.

paper_title: Least Squares Support Vector Machine Classifiers
motivation: Prior work shows SVM-RBF beats k-means RBF but does not explain why: is it boundary-anchored centers, margin-based capacity control, or the prototype-versus-surface paradigm? An explanatory account is missing.
method: Use circular backpropagation's quadratic coefficient as a dial between surface and prototype units to factorially separate paradigm, center placement, and weight objective, and link them to VC and Cover capacity to explain the generalization gap.

paper_title: Least Squares Support Vector Machine Classifiers
motivation:
A recurring but untested claim runs through this literature: that seemingly different learning machines are secretly the same family living on a continuum between "surface-based" (global hyperplane/discriminant) and "prototype-based" (local, center/radius) representations. Schölkopf et al. and the SV function-estimation work assert that the SV machine "contains polynomial classifiers, neural networks, and RBF networks as special cases," with the paradigm fixed a priori by the kernel choice. Ridella et al.'s circular backpropagation (CBP) network claims a "paradigm plasticity" in which a single quadratic input lets each unit slide between the perceptron (surface) and hypersphere (prototype) forms, and it proves the endpoint capacities exactly (VC = d+1 for the affine perceptron, d+2 for the circular unit). Kernel ridge regression in dual variables and Gaussian-kernel RBF machines are yet more members of the same broad club. Vapnik's statistical learning theory supplies capacity control (SRM) and the margin/radius VC bound h ≤ [R²/margin²].

Yet the field has no way to OBSERVE, MEASURE, or COMPARE where a *trained* machine actually sits on this surface↔prototype axis. "Plasticity" and "contains as special cases" are stated but never quantified: there is no model-agnostic coordinate on which an MLP, a CBP net, an RBF net, a linear/polynomial/Gaussian-kernel SVM, and a kernel-ridge machine can be placed side by side; no way to audit whether a deployed model is relying on local prototypes or global surfaces; and no capacity account that varies *continuously* along the axis rather than only at the two endpoints. Capacity theory treats the paradigm (architecture/kernel) as a designer's fixed choice, not as a learned, measurable property. This is an evidence gap: we cannot accumulate comparable evidence linking a model's representational regime to its capacity and generalization.
method:
Contribution is a formal derivation that turns "paradigm plasticity" and "special-case" folklore into a measurable, comparable, and capacity-linked quantity.

1) Canonical form and representation theorem. Take the CBP stimulus as the canonical generalized-quadratic decision form g(x) = a·‖x‖² + wᵀx + b. Prove an embedding theorem: (i) the affine perceptron (a=0) and CBP circular unit are the endpoints; (ii) a degree-2 polynomial-kernel SVM decision function is exactly of this form; (iii) each term of a Gaussian-kernel RBF/SVM and of a dual-variable kernel-ridge machine, expanded to second order about its center, is a local instance of this form. This gives one shared coordinate system for machines that are otherwise incomparable.

2) Paradigm (locality) index. Define a scale-invariant scalar ρ ∈ [0,1], ρ = |a|R / (|a|R + ‖w‖), where R is the data radius, and show it is invariant to input rescaling and to the CBP linear→circular parameter change (center/radius/gain of the equivalent hypersphere). ρ→0 ≡ pure surface (hyperplane); ρ→1 ≡ pure prototype (hypersphere). For multi-unit/multi-support-vector models, define the machine's "paradigm spectrum" as the distribution of ρ over units/support vectors, with audit statistics (mean locality, spectrum entropy).

3) Interpolating capacity bound (core theorem). Derive an ρ-parameterized effective-capacity bound that (a) reduces to Cover/VC endpoints d+1 and d+2 from the CBP analysis, and (b) reduces to Vapnik's margin/radius bound h ≤ [R²/margin²] in the appropriate limit, by treating the quadratic term as lifting to an augmented feature space whose effective radius grows with ρ. This yields a continuous complexity coordinate: capacity as a monotone function of the paradigm spectrum, closing the gap between the two known regimes.

4) Taxonomy and diagnostic protocol. Classify machine families by their induced ρ-spectra, and provide a post-hoc, retraining-free procedure to compute ρ-spectra directly from trained parameters of MLP, CBP, RBF, linear/polynomial/Gaussian SVM, and kernel-ridge models.

5) Validation. On the USPS handwritten-digit benchmark used by the SVM-vs-RBF comparison and CBP experiments, empirically test that (i) the measured ρ-spectrum distinguishes the model families as predicted (e.g., linear SVM ≈ 0, Gaussian SVM/RBF near 1, CBP intermediate and data-dependent), and (ii) the derived ρ-capacity bound tracks the ranking of measured test error across models. Success criterion: the bound orders generalization consistently and the index exposes cases where nominally "surface" models have drifted local, and vice versa — providing the missing, comparable evidence linking representational paradigm to capacity.

paper_title: Best Practices for Convolutional Neural Networks Applied to Visual Document Analysis
motivation: Handwriting pipelines feed a character classifier into a graph or HMM word decoder, as in the LeCun GTN cheque reader and the Tay et al cursive system where a net emits per letter observation probabilities to an HMM. Invariance methods such as Training Invariant SVMs with virtual support vectors and tangent distance maximize accuracy on clean isolated glyphs, but segmentation graphs produce distorted partial and non character junk sub images. The cursive system uses only an ad hoc junk softmax class and none of these works offer calibration or rejection, so one overconfident wrong letter score can dominate an HMM path and silently corrupt a decoded word, a real risk when reading millions of cheques. Invariance is also enforced only as accuracy never as confidence stability, though Hornik Stinchcombe White prove nets can approximate derivatives, licensing derivative constraints for reliability. This is the failure and risk gap: no method gives calibrated transformation stable confidence with a built in out of manifold rejection signal propagated into the word decoder.
method: Train a character classifier with a tangent consistency penalty that keeps predictions and confidence invariant under known transformations such as rotation slant scale stroke thickness and window shift. Derive an uncertainty score from how much predictions vary under those transformations plus distance to class tangent subspaces, replacing the ad hoc junk class. Calibrate outputs and turn the score into a reject option and a per hypothesis reliability weight. Feed the calibrated reliability weighted scores as observation probabilities into the HMM or GTN word decoder, pruning off manifold segments. Evaluate on MNIST USPS and IRONOFF reporting word accuracy calibration error robustness under distortion error rejection curves and junk detection against softmax plus junk augmentation and virtual support vector baselines.

paper_title: Quantitative Performance Metrics for Mobile Robots Navigation
motivation: Reactive obstacle-avoidance methods are the workhorses for moving robots safely in unknown, cluttered, dynamic environments. The most capable in troublesome scenarios—the Nearness Diagram (ND) family and its global variant (GND), and behavior/situation-based schemes—make DISCRETE decisions directly from raw geometry: they detect gaps as discontinuities in a proximity diagram (a gap exists when the distance difference between adjacent sectors exceeds the robot diameter), classify the instantaneous scan into one of a small set of mutually exclusive situations (situated-activity / divide-and-conquer paradigm), and execute the single action law bound to the argmax situation. This discrete decision structure is a hidden source of brittleness: a single spurious range reading, misreading, partial occlusion, or a moving obstacle can create or destroy a gap and flip the selected situation from one cycle to the next. Because each situation triggers a qualitatively different action law, such flips produce discontinuous motion commands, causing command chattering, oscillation in narrow passages, and elevated collision risk. The ND paper reports observing oscillations, resorts to an ad hoc hysteresis to smooth transitions, and explicitly states it has not addressed sensor noise (suggesting external modules should process the data), while merely conjecturing that increasing the security distance according to sensor uncertainty could be designed. Potential-field analyses independently catalog oscillation near obstacles and in narrow passages as inherent failure modes, and VFH handles noise only at the low level of a certainty grid, never at the level of the discrete gap/situation decision that drives the robot. The evaluation/benchmarking literature (security, smoothness/bending-energy, dimensional metrics; MoVeMA; the Good Experimental Methodology SIG) supplies instruments to measure these failures but has not been used to characterize robustness of reactive methods under controlled perceptual degradation. The gap: no reactive-navigation work robustifies the discrete decision layer against sensor noise and transient clutter in a principled way. It matters because these methods run daily as the innermost safety-critical control loop, where chattering and situation flip-flop cause oscillation, wasted energy, and near-collisions.
method: Propose a drop-in robustification layer that wraps any gap/situation-based reactive navigator (ND, GND, behavior-fusion) and converts its brittle hard decisions into uncertainty-aware, temporally consistent ones, without altering the underlying action laws that give these methods their competence. Four components: (1) Uncertainty-aware perception front end: maintain a short recursive estimate of the proximity diagram per angular sector with an explicit per-sector confidence (generalizing VFH certainty values to ND's sector representation), filtering single-cycle misreadings and yielding a distance estimate with variance per sector. (2) Probabilistic gap detection and situation posterior: replace the deterministic threshold (gap iff adjacent-sector distance difference exceeds robot diameter) with the probability that a gap exists given sector distance variances, and track gaps across cycles via simple data association so persistent gaps (real openings) are distinguished from flickering ones (noise/dynamic occlusion); propagate these into a posterior over the small set of ND situations rather than an argmax label. (3) Hysteresis-as-inference command generation: formalize ND's ad hoc hysteresis as principled switching with a confidence-dependent dwell/switching cost, committing to a new situation only when its posterior sufficiently and persistently dominates; near decision boundaries produce a soft mixture-of-actions command—each situation's action law weighted by its posterior probability—so the motor command varies continuously as belief shifts, eliminating the discontinuous jumps that cause chattering and oscillation. (4) Uncertainty-adaptive safety margin: implement the security-distance idea the ND authors only conjectured by inflating the effective robot radius/clearance requirement as a monotone function of current perceptual uncertainty (aggregate sector variance) and estimated obstacle motion, so safety is preserved exactly when sensing is least trustworthy. Evaluation: instantiate on ND/GND and a behavior-fusion baseline and evaluate with the published metrics—security (mean/min clearance), smoothness (bending energy, command-variation as a chattering proxy), and dimensional (path length, control periods, time)—following a fixed benchmark protocol (MoVeMA / GEM best practices). Run the ND troublesome-scenario suite (U-shaped traps, narrow corridors, doorways, dense clutter) in simulation and on a real laser/sonar platform while sweeping controlled levels of injected sensor noise, misreadings, and dynamic obstacles. Hypotheses: the layer (a) sharply reduces command chattering, situation flip-flop rate, and oscillation and improves smoothness; (b) lowers near-collision incidence and raises minimum clearance under noise via the adaptive margin; and (c) preserves the baseline's success rate with only marginal path-length/time increase in clean conditions—demonstrating reduced brittleness with negligible competence loss. Ablations isolate the contribution of each component.

paper_title: Black Box Optimization, Machine Learning, and No-Free Lunch Theorems
motivation: NFL theorems and their refinements converge on one claim: an algorithm beats random search only insofar as its implicit prior aligns with structure in the actual distribution of problems, and departure from closure-under-permutation enables superiority. The algorithmic-information-theory literature argues real problems are compressible, so a universal Occam-style bias should reap free lunches. Yet the field lacks a systematic empirical bridge: nobody has measured, across a broad controlled corpus, how far practical problem distributions depart from the NFL null, how much realized advantage concrete optimizers extract, and whether that advantage is predicted by compressibility. The alignment condition stays abstract. The community-detection NFL paper shows feasibility by pairing an NFL proof with concrete structure statistics. The gap is a domain-general empirical map tying NFL's alignment condition, Occam/Kolmogorov structure, and real optimizer behavior into a diagnostic for algorithm selection.
method: Build an Empirical Atlas of Free Lunches. (1) Problem corpus spanning a controllable structure axis: synthetic landscapes interpolating from the NFL null (uniform-random tables) to highly structured ones (tunable-ruggedness NK-landscapes); real tasks (TSP, MAX-SAT); and permutation-shuffled versions as the null-model orbit. (2) Measurable structure descriptors: compressibility via general-purpose compressors and MDL codelength (a Kolmogorov-complexity proxy testing the Occam claim); landscape autocorrelation/ruggedness; cost-value entropy; and a deviation-from-c.u.p. statistic.
