(3) Algorithm panel with diverse priors: random search, hill-climbing, simulated annealing, a GA, and estimation-of-distribution optimizers (Cross-Entropy method, MIMIC, parametric-learning black-box optimizer). (4) A Realized Free Lunch metric: for each algorithm-problem pair, run under a fixed budget using the Macready-Wolpert hardness measure and also over a Monte Carlo sample of the permutation orbit; since NFL makes the orbit-mean algorithm-independent, RFL equals true-problem performance minus orbit-mean, isolating structure exploitation. (5) Empirical maps: regress RFL on descriptors to test whether compressibility predicts free-lunch magnitude; compute per-algorithm alignment fingerprints; produce comparative heatmaps of advantage over the structure space. (6) A meta-model predicting, from cheap descriptors, which algorithm family realizes the largest free lunch, validated on held-out real problems. This operationalizes NFL's alignment condition and the Occam/Kolmogorov argument as measurable quantities.

paper_title: Introductory Chapter: Swarm Intelligence and Particle Swarm Optimization
motivation: Corpus swarm optimizers such as PSO, chaos PSO, GWO, MFO, ALO, SSA and ABC all suffer premature convergence and are validated only by many-run statistics on benchmarks with known optima. In real deployments like real-time UAV path planning and economic dispatch the optimum is unknown and restarts are unaffordable, so a user cannot tell if one run succeeded or confidently failed. No source gives an online ground-truth-free failure probability or calibrated confidence, leaving deployment brittle and untrustworthy.
method: Wrap any optimizer in a reliability layer running a heterogeneous portfolio of constriction PSO, chaos PSO, GWO and ABC-diversity. From internal signals such as diversity, improvement rate and stagnation length, an extreme-value tail fit to best-so-far values, and cross-member agreement, compute a calibrated failure probability and a confidence interval on the optimum. Calibrate on benchmarks with known optima using reliability diagrams. Use the failure probability to reallocate evaluations and inject escape mechanisms only when flagged. Output a reliability certificate, and evaluate calibration, one-shot success versus single-run baselines, and UAV and dispatch case studies.

paper_title: An Experiment in Linguistic Synthesis with a Fuzzy Logic Controller
motivation:
Across this body of work, learning and skill acquisition in both men and machines are studied through the lens of control. Gaines ("The learning of perceptual-motor skills by men and machines") models a trainee as an "adaption-automaton" whose state is defined purely by input-output satisfactoriness (inputs = tasks, output = whether performance is satisfactory) and argues that human and machine learning phenomena are similar because both are governed by the same "epistemological problems" of the dual control problem. Pask ("A cybernetic experimental method") drives adaptive teaching by a single scalar time-averaged proficiency measure P and reaches a "null point/steady state." A related learning-machine/general-control-problem framing rounds this out.

The Evidence Gap: in all of these, the only observable of a learner's state is behavioral scalar performance (tracking satisfactoriness, proficiency P). There is no instrument to observe, describe, diagnose, or compare the CONTENT and STRUCTURE of what a learner has actually internalized — the hypotheses and control rules constituting its adaption-automaton — in a representation common to men and machines. This blocks the field's central claims from being evidenced: two learners with identical proficiency curves may hold entirely different internal models; "epistemological failures" of learning cannot be located (is a rule missing, mis-generalized, or mis-conditioned?); and man-vs-machine similarity can only be asserted from the shape of aggregate learning curves, not from rule-level correspondence. Consequently evidence about what is learned, and why learning fails, cannot be accumulated or audited.

The remaining sources supply exactly the missing representational and elicitation machinery but were never joined to this measurement problem. Zadeh ("Outline of a new approach...") argues that ill-defined, humanistic systems are best characterized approximately by linguistic variables and fuzzy IF-THEN algorithms — a natural language for internal models too fuzzy for precise equations. Winograd ("Understanding Natural Language") shows natural-language utterances can be parsed into structured, procedural representations grounded in a task micro-world. The speech-regulation-of-behaviour work supplies the premise that verbalization is coupled to, and regulates, action — so a learner's talk is a genuine window onto its control state. Together these leave open, and make feasible, an instrument for measuring learning-state content that Gaines and Pask lacked.
method:
Build a "linguistic learning-state instrument" that represents a learner's internal model of a control skill as a fuzzy-linguistic algorithm — a set of IF-THEN fuzzy conditional rules over linguistic variables describing the task state (e.g., IF error is large-and-growing THEN correction is strong) in Zadeh's formalism — and use it to observe, diagnose, and compare learning in both humans and learning machines.

Setup (reusing Gaines' paradigm). Use a high-order tracking task and run it identically on (i) human subjects and (ii) computer-simulated learning-machine controllers, logging trial-by-trial state-action data, and periodically eliciting short natural-language self-descriptions of the learner's current strategy (for machines, the analogous internal policy is dumped).

Two independent estimators of the same representation:
1. Behavioral estimator: fit, over the task state-space, the fuzzy rule-set (membership functions for the linguistic variables plus IF-THEN rules) whose compositional-rule-of-inference output best reproduces the learner's observed control actions on held-out trials.
2. Verbal estimator: parse the natural-language self-reports into the SAME fuzzy-rule representation using a Winograd-style grounded procedural parser whose vocabulary is the task's linguistic variables.

Measurements and diagnostics this enables:
- Content trajectory: track the rule-set as it evolves across training, replacing Pask's scalar proficiency with a structured state description.
- Coherence/validation: quantify agreement between the behavioral and verbal estimates (a within-subject validity check on both the instrument and the speech-regulation premise).
- Epistemological-failure taxonomy: locate specific defects — missing rules, over-broad fuzzy sets (over-generalization), mis-conditioned antecedents — and test Gaines' claim that failures are task-intrinsic by checking whether the same defects appear in machines.
- Man-machine comparison benchmark: define a rule-level similarity metric so that similarity is evidenced by correspondence of internal models, not merely by learning-curve shape; report where humans and machines converge and diverge.
- Diagnostic adaptive training: close Pask's loop on the diagnosed rule-set rather than on scalar P — select next tasks that target the specific missing/faulty rule, and test whether rule-targeted training beats proficiency-driven difficulty adaptation.

Evaluation. Cross-validate the fitted rule-sets on held-out trials; test whether behavioral and verbal estimates agree above chance; test whether identified defects predict subsequent errors and whether rule-targeted adaptation accelerates learning; and report the man-vs-machine rule-similarity distribution. Deliverable: a shared, auditable, accumulable evidence base of learning states — a standard instrument for measuring and comparing what men and machines actually learn, not just how well they perform.

paper_title: On the momentum term in gradient descent learning algorithms
motivation: Qian and Sejnowski's protein secondary-structure network shows an unexplained pattern: networks with zero to eighty hidden units all plateau near 62 to 64 percent test accuracy, a second-order conjunctive input coding also fails to help real proteins, and continued training raises training accuracy while test accuracy falls. They interpret this as a local-information limit, but that is an indirect hypothesis rather than a mechanistic account. Three causes remain unresolved: a genuine information limit, a capacity-utilization failure where the nonlinear net collapses onto an effectively linear solution, or an optimization and overfitting artifact. The prior works supply instruments never applied to this question: backprop trains the models, Optimal Brain Damage gives a saliency measure of which weights a trained network relies on, and Jacobs' delta-bar-delta adaptive learning rates let optimization quality vary with architecture fixed. Explaining why hidden units and higher-order codings fail, and why the ceiling appears, dictates whether to pursue richer local models or non-local information, and it is a prototype for capacity-invariant ceilings in local-window sequence learning.
method: Decompose the ceiling into information, capacity, and optimization causes. Reproduce the windowed network, train models with varying hidden-unit counts by backprop, then use Optimal Brain Damage saliency to prune weights and record test accuracy versus fraction retained; unused capacity predicts that effective parameters saturate at the same small value for every hidden size and match the linear model, with surplus weights carrying negligible generalization saliency that explains the train-test gap. Also inspect per-position and per-order saliency for genuine second-order interactions. Retrain with delta-bar-delta and momentum versus plain steepest descent to rule out optimization if ceilings and saliency profiles are unchanged. Regenerate first- and second-order artificial structures with tunable higher-order content to calibrate a curve linking true local information to achievable accuracy and measured salient higher-order weight, then place real-protein networks on it to attribute the ceiling to available information rather than unused capacity, testing the prediction that hidden units grow the train-test gap in proportion to parameters while salient generalizable weights stay fixed.

paper_title: Toward the Next Generation of Recommender Systems: Applications and Research Challenges
motivation: Matrix-factorization recommenders lump much rating variation into user and item bias and temporal terms that absorb variance without explaining it. Separately, studies show the same user rates the same item differently due to mood, interface framing, anchoring, and defaults, each studied in isolation. The gap is that there is no mechanistic causal account of why feedback is unstable, how much of a rating is stable preference versus transient affect versus presentation artifact, and why this varies across users, items, and domains. It matters because if the dominant bias terms are confounds of mood and framing, optimizing accuracy on contaminated ratings entrenches artifacts and cannot explain when a recommendation is accepted.
method: Model feedback as a stable preference term plus context-conditioned deviation terms for affect, framing and anchoring, and defaults, reinterpreting opaque bias and temporal terms as identifiable causes. Identify them via a within-subjects study reusing corpus paradigms such as induced mood, manipulated anchors, and manipulated defaults, where users rate the same items across contexts and sessions. Fit a hierarchical constrained factorization model, quantify variance per source, and predict each user susceptibility from covariates like domain complexity and expertise. Validate by predicting held-out accept or reject choices versus an MF-with-biases baseline and testing whether context-removed preferences yield more consistently accepted recommendations.

paper_title: Learning to Predict by the Methods of Temporal Differences
motivation: Evidence gap. These sources form a lineage of real-time models of classical conditioning: Rescorla-Wagner, the Sutton-Barto element (1981), its temporal-difference extension (1987), the nictitating-membrane variant of Moore et al. (1986), and Klopf's drive-reinforcement model (1987). Each claims to reproduce a long but different, overlapping list of phenomena (ISI functions, blocking, conditioned inhibition, second-order conditioning, extinction, serial-compound temporal primacy, CR topography). But the supporting evidence is ad hoc: each uses its own stimulus coding (Moore et al. invoke unspecified coding processes), time-step convention, and hand-set parameters, and comparisons are qualitative (Klopf's Figure 5 claims Sutton-Barto predicts inhibition where data show excitation). There is no common quantitative benchmark to evaluate these competing models on the same empirical data with the same fitting discipline. So the field cannot audit which claimed successes survive controlled comparison, cannot separate the contribution of learning rule versus stimulus representation, cannot identify which phenomena actually discriminate the models, and cannot accumulate evidence as new models appear. This matters because the lineage's credibility rests on a claim of broad empirical coverage never measured on common ground.
method: Build a standardized benchmark and shared simulation harness for real-time conditioning models. (1) Curate a conditioning battery: empirical phenomena from the sources encoded as quantitative targets with tolerances rather than yes/no claims - the ISI curve peaking near 250-500 ms and CR topography from Moore et al.; serial-compound temporal-primacy dynamics from Kehoe, Schreurs and Graham; plus blocking, conditioned inhibition, second-order, extinction/reacquisition, and partial reinforcement. (2) Fix a shared harness: common 10 ms time step, common US channel, and an explicit swappable CS-to-internal-trace representation module so each model's hidden coding becomes a controlled component. (3) Reimplement each learning rule (Rescorla-Wagner baseline, Sutton-Barto 1981, TD 1987, Klopf drive-reinforcement) in the harness and run a factorial cross of rules by representations. (4) Apply one unified fitting protocol: fit small parameter sets on a training subset by grid/coordinate search, evaluate on held-out phenomena, report per-phenomenon discrepancy scores and an aggregate leaderboard. (5) Run diagnostics the harness enables: parameter identifiability/sensitivity, representation-versus-rule attribution, and automatic detection of discriminating phenomena where model predictions diverge maximally (formalizing Klopf's excitation-versus-inhibition case) to prioritize future experiments. Deliverable: an extensible open benchmark plus a report of which successes replicate under controlled fitting, which phenomena no model captures, and which experiments best separate the models.

paper_title: Recognizing Action at a Distance
motivation: Silhouette and template based human recognition methods in this corpus (Collins gait identification via normalized-correlation nearest neighbor on periodic key frames; Bobick-Davis temporal templates; Mori-Malik shape-context pose) always output a nearest-neighbor decision. They are view-dependent and rely on noisy background-subtraction silhouettes, yet none estimate when they are wrong. This is a Failure and Risk gap: a degraded silhouette or an unseen viewpoint still yields a confident label, and because gait is a biometric a false accept is a security event with no defense against impostors or replayed gait. Reliability, calibration, out-of-competence detection, and spoof resistance are absent, while the literature reports only average recognition rate on clean in-view data.
method: Add a reliability and security wrapper that converts forced nearest-neighbor outputs into calibrated accept, reject, or abstain decisions with a bounded false-accept rate. First, exploit gait periodicity: silhouettes at the same phase across cycles must match after alignment and dynamic time warping, so the residual to a phase-averaged silhouette scores input quality and flags segmentation failures from shadows or occlusion. Second, a viewpoint competence check from the periodic width and height signature decides whether the probe viewpoint lies within the gallery range, otherwise abstain. Third, model per-view and per-phase impostor score distributions and combine the top-two match margin with quality and competence scores into a calibrated confidence thresholded for a target false-accept rate. Fourth, an anti-spoof plausibility test flags unstable periodicity, implausible stride frequency, or asymmetric left-right phase as replayed or imitated gait. Evaluate on multi-view gait datasets such as CMU Mobo, reporting risk-coverage curves, recognition under injected silhouette degradation, cross-view generalization with the competence gate on and off, and false-accept rates against impostor and spoof sequences.

paper_title: Object Identification by 3D LIDAR Using Nested Infinite Gaussian Mixture Model
motivation:
Multimodal recognition systems in these works improve accuracy by fusing cues: RGB-D pipelines merge 2D, 3D local and semi-global descriptors via hypothesis verification that enhances strengths and diminishes weaknesses; camera and laser fusion aids vehicle recognition; LIDAR pedestrian work adds reflection-intensity and slice features because plain geometry degrades. Yet all report strong, unexplained variation: the HD-LIDAR paper states detection was very sensitive to distance, intensity helps because NIR reflectance is material-specific, texture favors 2D while geometry favors shape descriptors, and verification boosts accuracy. These are facts without a causal account. Missing is a mechanistic explanation of why and when each cue is informative versus misleading, why fusion helps or hurts, and which failure modes hypothesis verification repairs. This matters for safety-critical vehicle perception: without knowing which condition makes a modality unreliable, a fused system cannot justify confidence, anticipate breakdowns, or decide when an object is genuinely unknown versus mis-seen. Prior work optimizes accuracy but leaves the causal structure of multimodal reliability unexplained.
throwaway slot to absorb the dropped second parameter
method: Build a framework that decomposes and causally tests why multimodal recognition succeeds or fails. Reassemble source-validated pipelines, namely a 2D RGB local recognizer, a 3D shape and semi-global recognizer, and a LIDAR recognizer using geometric, intensity, and slice features, run in parallel to yield per-instance hypotheses as in the hypothesis-verification system. For each detection compute conditioning variables the sources implicate but never jointly model: range, point-cloud density, occlusion fraction, texture richness, reflectivity, and segment size. Fit a condition-conditioned reliability model predicting each modality's correctness from these variables using a nonparametric Bayesian regime-discovery model in the spirit of the nested infinite Gaussian mixture, which clusters detections into an unbounded set of operating regimes and estimates per regime each modality's reliability and the marginal gain of a second cue, mapping when each cue is trustworthy and why fusion helps. Produce an attribution ledger for hypothesis verification: for each corrected error, trace which conditioning variable caused the failure and which cue rescued it, turning the black-box boost into enumerated failure-to-repair mechanisms. Validate causally via a predictive test that forecasts on held-out scenes which modality will fail before seeing labels, and an interventional test that ablates or degrades a cue, such as stripping intensity, subsampling points to emulate longer range, or synthetically occluding, then confirms accuracy drops only in regimes predicted cue-dependent, verifying that distance sensitivity is mediated by density and that intensity helps low-texture distinctive-material targets. Extend to open set by testing which modality first signals unknown via novel-regime assignment. The result is a validated causal theory of multimodal fusion and verification for confidence-aware perception.

paper_title: A Survey of Industrial Model Predictive Control Technology
motivation: MPC two-tier robust design assumes a perfect handoff between the steady state economic target and the dynamic controller, so targets certified feasible at steady state may be dynamically unreachable under model uncertainty.
method: Use one identification derived ellipsoid across both tiers and add a robust dynamic reachability second order cone constraint to the steady state target calculation so chosen targets are both feasible and reachable.

paper_title: Adaptive Pattern Classification and Universal Recoding: II. Feedback, Expectation, Olfaction, Illusions
motivation:
Grossberg's family of neural theories in this corpus (operant conditioning dynamics; the qualitative and quantitative theory of punishment and avoidance; the attention/reinforcement/discrimination model) makes bold but strictly qualitative bridges between internal model variables and observable physiology. The attention model explicitly asserts that its "conditionable nonspecific late slow potential shift," which encodes arousal, drive, reinforcement and motivation, is the in-vivo contingent negative variation (CNV) reported by Walter (1964); the operant-conditioning paper repeats this CNV analogy and ties slow negativity to release of motor activity; and the reinforcement circuitry is claimed to ride on catecholamine reward pathways (norepinephrine reward receptors; 6-hydroxydopa/monoamine-mapping sources) with serotonergic punishment channels, driving antagonistic "fear-to-relief" rebounds when events are unexpected.

Meanwhile, a parallel empirical corpus already quantifies exactly the phenomena the theory claims to explain: CNV amplitude scaling with expectancy (Walter), with motivational variables (Irwin), and with voluntary "conation" (McAdam's W-shaped think-high/think-low curve), increases in CNS excitability during negative cortical slow potentials (McAdam), and monoamine reward/punishment pharmacology and anatomy.

The evidence gap is that these two bodies of work have never been placed on a common measurement footing. The "CNV = model feedback" and "reward = catecholamine gate" statements are asserted as analogies; there is no shared observable, no reproducible protocol, and no quantitative benchmark that converts the theory's physiological claims into falsifiable, comparable predictions about measured slow-potential waveforms and their pharmacological modulation. As a result the field cannot audit, validate, or accumulate evidence for or against the mechanistic identity claims, nor compare competing model variants (e.g., passive-decay vs recurrent-reverberation short-term memory, single- vs dual-transmitter gating) on the physiological data they invoke.
method:
Build an explicit, reusable "model-to-slow-potential" validation benchmark that forces Grossberg's reinforcement/arousal theory to make quantitative, falsifiable predictions about the CNV and its pharmacology.

1) Minimal mechanism. Instantiate as ODEs the smallest opponent-processing ("gated dipole") reinforcement/arousal subcircuit that the quantitative punishment/avoidance theory and the attention model share: drive input, conditioned-reinforcer input, slowly accumulating/depleting transmitter gates on the two opponent channels, a nonspecific arousal source whose level is set by the degree of unexpectedness, and the conditionable nonspecific feedback signal that the theory names as the CNV generator. Keep both short-term-memory variants (slow passive decay vs recurrent reverberation) as swappable modules.

2) Observation model. Define an explicit, fixed linear readout that maps the summed nonspecific slow-potential feedback to a scalar "vertex negativity" observable matching the standard warning/imperative CNV recording convention, plus a coupling term making evoked-response gain increase with ongoing negativity (to model CNS excitability during negative shifts).

3) Paradigm encoding. Drive the circuit with canonical S1(warning)->S2(imperative) foreperiod inputs and parametrically manipulate expectancy/probability, incentive magnitude and drive (motivation), a top-down "conation" bias, unexpected omission of S2/nonreward, and reward vs punishment contingencies.

4) Prediction battery. Derive ordinal/quantitative, falsifiable predictions: CNV onset tied to S1-evoked reverberation; amplitude monotonic in drive x incentive (motivation) and controllable by the conation bias (reproducing or failing to reproduce the W-curve); resolution at S2/response; a predicted positive overshoot (antagonistic rebound) after unexpected omission; and heightened evoked excitability during negativity.

5) Pharmacological arm. Because reward is modeled as catecholamine transmitter gating, predict dose-response-shaped effects: catecholamine depletion (6-hydroxydopa) or alpha-noradrenergic blockade should reduce reward-related negativity and abolish the rebound, while serotonergic manipulation should selectively alter punishment-driven dipole dynamics.

6) Benchmarking and evidence accumulation. Digitize the summary statistics/waveform features reported in the corpus (Walter expectancy; Irwin motivation; McAdam conation and CNS-excitability notes; Cohen conditioning; monoamine reward/punishment pharmacology) into a structured target set, and score each model prediction against them on timing, parametric monotonicity, sign of rebound, and pharmacological direction. Report a transparent match/mismatch table, and re-run it across the swappable STM and single- vs dual-transmitter variants so alternative theoretical commitments can be compared head-to-head. This turns the currently untested CNV/catecholamine analogies into an auditable, extensible testbed that both validates existing claims and yields concrete, quantitative predictions for new CNV and pharmacological experiments.

paper_title: Extracting Refined Rules from Knowledge-Based Neural Networks
motivation: KBANN, in the Shavlik, Mooney and Towell comparison and related insertion, refinement, extraction and gene-recognition works, compiles an approximately correct propositional domain theory into a fixed network topology, refines it with backpropagation, and extracts rules. Its flagship result is 92 percent on E. coli promoter recognition versus 82 percent for ID3. But compilation assumes each antecedent binds to a single absolute input position, for example a base at fixed offset minus 35, which only works if all sequences are pre-aligned to a common reference and motif geometry is rigid. The biology contradicts both. Promoter compilations by Harley and Reynolds and by Hawley and McClure show variable minus 35 to minus 10 spacing of 16 to 18 base pairs, range 15 to 21, and Stormo stresses that alignment is itself a hard separate problem. On raw unaligned genomic sequence with insertions and deletions, a KBANN net that hard wires fixed positions and gaps cannot represent that the minus 10 hexamer occurs 15 to 21 base pairs downstream of the minus 35 hexamer wherever it is. Thus KBANN success lives in an idealized pre-aligned fixed spacing regime. The corpus has ingredients to relax this, namely weight sharing from Nowlan and Hinton and Rumelhart et al, M of N and X of N concepts from ID2-of-3 and the promoter analysis, and pruning via skeletonization and soft weight sharing, but none combine them to remove the positional invariance and rigid spacing assumptions.
method: Extend KBANN rule-to-network compilation to work under weaker assumptions: relative positions, variable spacing, and unaligned input with insertions or deletions. Change the mapping in three ways. First, motif rules become scanning weight-shared detectors. A motif rule such as the minus 35 or minus 10 consensus compiles into position-replicated units that share one weight vector and are slid across candidate offsets, with a soft-OR or soft-max aggregator that fires if the motif matches at any allowed position. Detector weights are initialized from the domain theory consensus base preferences, as KBANN initializes rule weights. Second, rigid gaps become learnable relative-offset relations. Connect the minus 10 detector group to the minus 35 group through a bank of gated gap units spanning the permitted range of 15 to 21 base pairs, each unit representing one displacement, so backpropagation learns the empirical spacing distribution rather than a single fixed gap. This encodes relational rules that a KBANN propositional topology cannot express. Third, add top-level M of N aggregation over the position-invariant motif and compatible-spacing evidence, initialized from the theory and refined, following the X of N insight and ID2-of-3. The training regime is the actual relaxation: slide the network over unaligned raw sequence windows with no pre-alignment to a start point, tolerating small indels, so the model localizes motifs and infers spacing jointly. After refinement, prune redundant position copies with skeletonization or soft weight sharing so the shared detectors and surviving gap units collapse into compact position-relative refined rules of the form minus 35 motif, then a 15 to 21 base-pair gap, then minus 10 motif, with at least K constraints satisfied. Evaluation: reproduce standard KBANN on aligned promoter data as a control; test on deliberately mis-aligned and variable-spacing versions and on longer unaligned genomic windows; compare accuracy against KBANN and Staden-style weight-matrix methods; measure robustness as alignment noise grows; and check whether the network recovers the true 16 to 18 base-pair spacing distribution and correct motif localizations. Success means retaining the KBANN prior-knowledge advantage while functioning in the unaligned, variable-spacing, indel-noisy regime where the fixed-position formulation fails.

paper_title: An Introduction to MCMC for Machine Learning
motivation: Particle filters and sequential Monte Carlo are central to online Bayesian inference in this corpus (tracking and guidance, robot localization, dynamic Bayesian networks via Rao-Blackwellised PF, communications demodulation, noisy-sinusoid detection). Yet they are brittle to outliers and transient measurement-model misspecification: one anomalous observation makes the likelihood peak away from the particle cloud, a single particle seizes nearly all the weight, effective sample size (ESS) collapses, and the filter diverges. Pitt and Shephard (auxiliary particle filters) note the particle filter is not robust to outliers for two reasons (simulator design and discrete support) and tackle only the first, leaving the observation-model and weighting side open. The robustness tools in the corpus are static and pre-specified: Carter and Kohn and the SMC demodulation model use fixed variance mixtures with known variances and fixed outlier probabilities; Meinhold and Singpurwalla use a fixed t-distribution; the RBPF via data augmentation uses a fixed sampling/selection swap. These require the contamination model known a priori and always on, sacrificing efficiency on clean data and staying brittle under mismatch, and none use the filter's own ESS or weight-variance signal to decide when and how much to robustify. Adaptive MCMC through regeneration shows online adaptation can be made safe with the invariant target preserved, but no analogous safe online robustification exists for SMC. The gap is a self-diagnosing, adaptively robust particle filter that activates protection only when reliability degrades and corrects for its effect so clean-data inference stays exact.
method: Propose a Self-Diagnosing Adaptively Robust Rao-Blackwellised Particle Filter whose robustification is triggered and calibrated by the filter's own reliability signal instead of a fixed contamination model. An online failure detector computes effective sample size from the normalized weights each step; a sharp drop below a target fraction of the particle count flags measurement conflict, turning the ESS diagnostic into an anomaly alarm. An adaptive robust likelihood models observations as a scale mixture of Gaussians with a latent per-observation scale and outlier probability (the Carter-Kohn and SMC-demodulation structure), but infers these online under a hyperprior and couples tail-heaviness to the detector through a data-driven tempering exponent between zero and one applied to the likelihood and driven by the ESS gap: the exponent equals one when data are clean and shrinks toward zero when ESS collapses, locally down-weighting anomalous observations instead of annihilating the particle set. A guided robust proposal uses an auxiliary-particle-filter lookahead with the robustified likelihood so surviving particles are consistent with the down-weighted observation. Rao-Blackwellisation analytically marginalizes the conditionally linear-Gaussian substate with a Kalman or HMM filter, lowering weight variance and stabilizing the ESS signal and tempering decision. A consistency safeguard records the applied tempering and scale variables and corrects via a delayed importance-weight adjustment so that on clean data the filter is asymptotically unbiased for the true posterior and reduces exactly to a standard RBPF; robustification is opt-in, activated only under detected conflict. Evaluation on tracking, robot localization, and communications demodulation with injected glitches, heavy-tailed and misspecified noise, and clutter measures track-loss and divergence rate, RMSE under contamination, ESS stability, and clean-data efficiency versus a standard PF, an auxiliary PF, and fixed-t robust PFs, expecting reduced catastrophic failure at no accuracy cost on clean data.

paper_title: Markov Random Field Modeling in Image Analysis
motivation: Line processes, weak string, outlier processes, robust M-estimators, and discontinuity-adaptive priors are one family, yet no theory explains when a break forms during annealing.
method: Model a break as a bifurcation of the local subsystem, derive its critical annealing value from contrast and noise, and validate against Blake's exact weak-string benchmark.

paper_title: Q-Learning
motivation: Dyna imagines hypothetical experience by sampling state-action pairs uniformly at random, wasting most planning backups on values that do not change. This leaves open the question raised by On the computational economics of reinforcement learning: under a fixed compute budget per action, how to maximize learning per unit computation. No provided work decides where and how much model-based planning to do based on where a backup is valuable.
method: Add a priority queue to Dyna keyed by one-step error magnitude; after a real transition with large error, enqueue model predecessors weighted by transition probability, pop the top pair each planning step, back it up, and enqueue its predecessors when the change is large, so value sweeps backward from informative transitions. Use a budget controller that stops planning when top priority falls below a cost-benefit threshold, and add an exploration bonus to priorities. Evaluate on the Dyna maze, blocking and shortcut tasks, and the box-pushing robot versus uniform Dyna and Q-learning, measuring learning per unit computation.

paper_title: Parametric shape recognition using a probabilistic inverse theory
motivation: These works share one active-vision paradigm: fit a volumetric primitive to range data, quantify uncertainty as a Gaussian ellipsoid of confidence, and plan the next view to shrink the covariance determinant. Yet Uncertain views reports that sometimes extra data makes things worse and the mean prediction error does not detect these cases, that model variation spikes chaotically in mid-latitudes, and that there are inherent degeneracies in certain data configurations, offering only a qualitative convexity conjecture. The merit function is blind to its own failure. This is an explanation gap: why does uncertainty-driven exploration sometimes raise rather than lower true uncertainty, and why can the metric not see it? It is not model inadequacy (Knowing when we are wrong handles a wrong model class via residual tests); these failures occur with the correct model class and are failures of the uncertainty quantification itself, which rests on an unexamined local linear-Gaussian approximation of a highly non-linear fit that Autonomous exploration admits breaks down for non-linear models. Without a causal account, an explorer cannot know when to trust its next-best-view decisions.
method: Build a mechanistic theory of why uncertainty-driven exploration of superquadric models sometimes increases rather than decreases true uncertainty, tracing it to breakdown of the local linear-Gaussian approximation behind the covariance merit. Cast superquadric fitting as a non-linear inverse problem and compute both the Jacobian-based linearized covariance and the second-derivative curvature of its solution manifold. Define a trust index from three drivers: manifold curvature relative to confidence-region size, Jacobian ill-conditioning, and proximity to a shape symmetry. Establish a Monte Carlo ground truth for true uncertainty by resampling noisy scans and refitting, reproducing the extra-data-makes-things-worse effect. Replicate the Uncertain views latitude sweep across shapes from near-degenerate to generic and test whether the trust index predicts, a priori, where variation spikes and where covariance-minimizing view selection raises true variance. Ablate the convex constraint and parametrization to separate intrinsic from parameter-effects curvature. Finally derive a curvature- and identifiability-aware next-view criterion that trusts the linearized covariance only where the trust index is low.

paper_title: Best Practices for Convolutional Neural Networks Applied to Visual Document Analysis
motivation:
A recurring theme across these works is that incorporating prior knowledge about *invariances* is the most reliable route to top accuracy on handwriting recognition. The Training Invariant SVM paper (2002) formalizes three routes—invariant kernels built from the tangent vectors ∂/∂t Lt x of a known Lie group, "virtual examples/virtual support vectors," and their combination—and shows they yield record MNIST/USPS results. LeCun et al. (1998) similarly rely on hand-designed affine and elastic distortions to augment data, and Simard's tangent distance uses analytically specified transformations. Crucially, all of these methods make two strong assumptions: (1) the class-preserving transformations are *known a priori and specified analytically* (translation, rotation, scaling, line thickness, elastic warps), and (2) training operates on *isolated, pre-segmented characters* (MNIST/USPS).

Both assumptions break in the more realistic regime of the offline cursive word recognition system (Tay et al., 2001). There, the dominant within-class variation is writer-specific: slant, ligature/connection shapes, and idiosyncratic stroke styles that are not well described by any known Lie group; and there are no isolated character labels—only word-level lexicon labels exist, with character boundaries hidden inside an ambiguous segmentation graph. The paucity-of-data study (2001) shows classifier accuracy keeps improving with more labeled data, but real character-level handwriting data is exactly what is scarce and unsegmented. Hence the powerful invariance machinery is stranded on clean, segmented digits and cannot be applied where it is most needed. The Hornik–Stinchcombe–White result (1990) that feedforward networks can approximate a mapping *and its derivatives* suggests the missing piece—the transformation tangents—can itself be learned rather than assumed.

The gap: no method incorporates invariances when the transformations are unknown and only weak (word-level) supervision is available. This matters because it is the actual condition of deployed handwriting/document systems.
method:
We propose Data-Driven Invariance Learning (DDIL): a pipeline that *discovers* the relevant class-preserving transformations from weakly labeled cursive words and injects them as virtual examples and tangent regularization, thereby relaxing the two core assumptions (known analytic transformations; segmented character labels) of prior invariance methods.

Step 1 — Weak-supervision alignment. Starting from the NN-HMM word recognizer (Tay et al., 2001), use forced alignment / EM over the segmentation graph with only word-level lexicon labels to obtain soft character-level assignments. This produces, for each character class, many aligned instances spanning writers—without ever requiring hand-segmented character ground truth.

Step 2 — Learn the deformation manifold (replacing the known Lie group). For each class, register aligned instances to a reference and estimate a low-dimensional set of empirical "tangent directions." Concretely, fit warp/displacement fields between instances and extract the principal deformation modes (e.g., PCA on displacement fields, or a small network trained to output the warp field, justified by Hornik et al.'s guarantee that networks can approximate a mapping and its derivatives). These learned tangents are the data-driven analogue of the analytic ∂/∂t Lt x used in tangent distance and invariant kernels.

Step 3 — Inject invariances two ways. (a) Virtual examples: extend the Virtual SV / distortion approach by generating synthetic characters that move along the *learned* deformation directions (including discrete, non-Lie transformations such as ligature substitutions), augmenting the scarce weak-labeled data. (b) Tangent regularization: penalize the character classifier's output change along the learned tangents, giving local invariance without an analytic transformation group.

Step 4 — Self-training loop. Retrain the classifier on the augmented/regularized data → better character posteriors → sharper graph alignment → refined, less noisy invariance estimates. Iterate until convergence.

Evaluation. On IRONOFF and cheque databases, compare word/character recognition rate against: the plain NN-HMM baseline, hand-designed affine/elastic distortions (LeNet-style), and Virtual SV/tangent distance with analytic transforms. Ablate the amount of word-level supervision to test the "extended scope" claim (works under weak labels), and vary training-set size to quantify the paucity-of-data benefit. As a controlled sanity check, run DDIL on MNIST by *hiding* the known transformations and verifying it rediscovers translation/rotation/thickness-like tangents and approaches the accuracy of methods that were given those transformations explicitly.

This makes invariance-based training function under weaker assumptions (unknown transformations, writer-dependent deformations) and broader scope (segmentation-free, word-level supervision, multi-writer cursive script)—precisely the noisier, realistic setting the prior works do not cover.

paper_title: A Bit of Progress in Language Modeling (Extended Version)
motivation: Whole-sentence maximum entropy (WSME) language models encode arbitrary global sentence properties as a bag of features without per-history normalization (Rosenfeld et al., Whole-sentence exponential language models; Chen and Rosenfeld, Efficient sampling and feature selection). Two bottlenecks, both left open in these sources, keep them impractical. First, static redundancy-blind feature selection: the recipe generates one artificial corpus from a fixed baseline trigram, computes a per-candidate chi-square discrepancy against the training corpus, thresholds it, adds all surviving features at once, and trains once. The discrepancy is never re-estimated after the model changes; near-duplicate co-linear features are admitted together because variants share the same top chi-square; and chi-square is not the training objective of expected log-likelihood gain, so WER gains were small even at 52k features. Second, fixed undifferentiated sampling effort: training uses Monte-Carlo expectations with a fixed 100k-sentence sample and fixed iteration counts. The authors explicitly list but never implement three efficiency ideas: small samples early when only sign and rough magnitude of updates matter, enlarged near convergence; sample size set dynamically from per-feature observation counts; and gradual feature addition. They also note importance sampling degrades as the model drifts from the generating distribution, forcing expensive Metropolis regeneration. Because both the feature set and the sampling budget are chosen by fixed heuristics rather than optimized, WSME models train inefficiently and become over-parameterized, undermining the framework promise that a modeler can add any computable property.
method: Recast WSME construction as one budget-constrained optimization that jointly searches for a compact feature set maximizing held-out likelihood while allocating a fixed Monte-Carlo sampling budget across candidate evaluation, parameter updates, and sample regeneration. Gain-guided greedy feature induction replaces one-shot chi-square: an outer loop draws a sample from the current model via importance sampling from the trigram base, then for every candidate computes its single-parameter maximum log-likelihood gain in closed form from sample statistics, re-targeting selection to what the model still gets wrong after each update. Redundancy-aware batch selection via submodular maximization picks a batch maximizing summed marginal gain minus a correlation penalty from feature co-activation counts, blocking near-duplicate cliques; the candidate space is shrunk by class-based factoring from Classes for fast maximum entropy training, searching class-level generalized n-grams first and refining to words only where gain warrants. An adaptive sampling-budget controller treats sample size as the scarce resource: it maintains per-feature confidence intervals on the expectation gap from variance across sub-samples, uses few samples early and enlarges as gaps shrink, gives more samples to features whose gain interval straddles the threshold and fewer to clear cases in a sequential UCB-style allocation, and stops when the best marginal gain falls below a noise floor set by interval widths. Effective-sample-size-triggered resampling monitors importance-weight ESS and pays for Metropolis regeneration only when ESS drops below threshold, otherwise reusing the reweighted sample. Parameters are regularized with a Gaussian prior following A Gaussian prior for smoothing maximum entropy models. Evaluation reproduces the Switchboard and Broadcast News setups, reporting perplexity and N-best rescoring WER against number of selected features and against total sampling cost, versus the static chi-square-threshold fixed-sample baseline, with ablations isolating adaptive budgeting, gain-based versus chi-square selection, and the redundancy penalty. Success is matching or beating the baseline with far fewer features and lower total sampling cost.

paper_title: Connectionist Learning Procedures
motivation: Discovering transformation invariant representations, such as recognizing a shape regardless of position, is done in this literature only with supervision or hand wiring: supervised back propagation on labeled instances at many positions, clamped Boltzmann learning, or fixed pooling in the Neocognitron. Unsupervised principles such as competitive learning, Linsker Hebbian variance maximizing cells, and the Pearlmutter and Hinton G maximization procedure act on a single input window and detect structure at a fixed location. They have no notion that two views can share a common cause, so they cannot yield invariant features. Hinton observes that back propagation can be made unsupervised by predicting one input part from nearby parts, but reconstructing the raw signal forces the code to keep nuisance detail such as exact position, noise, and texture rather than the shared invariant property. The gap is that no unsupervised principle uses the natural coherence of the world, such as adjacent patches, successive frames, or the two eyes, as a free teaching signal to extract only the invariant common cause and to discard view specific nuisances. This matters because a general learner must build invariant internal representations from unlabeled sensory data.
method: Propose Coherence Maximization, an unsupervised method that learns invariant feature detectors by maximizing the statistical agreement between the low dimensional codes of two modules that receive coherent views of the same scene element, such as adjacent image patches, the two eyes, or successive speech frames. Each module is a small network with a local receptive field mapping its window to a code A or B. Instead of reconstructing the input, maximize the mutual information between A and B over coherent pairs, equal to the entropy of A plus the entropy of B minus their joint entropy. The joint term forces the codes to agree, so each module can only encode what is common to both views, namely the invariant cause. The marginal entropy terms prevent the trivial constant solution and play the anti collapse role that the G maximization difference from independence measure plays. For continuous Gaussian codes this reduces to maximizing the log ratio of the variance of A to the variance of A minus B. For stochastic binary units, estimate the joint and marginal statistics online in the same way G maximization tracks running averages, keeping learning local, and ascend the gradient. Reuse the G maximization decorrelation and mutual inhibition idea so that neighboring module pairs extract different invariant features. Evaluate on translating shapes for position invariant features compared against supervised back propagation and the Neocognitron, on two eye random dot scenes for disparity tuned units learned without depth labels, and on adjacent speech frames for time invariant phonetic front end codes usable by the corpus speech recognizers. The central claim is that agreement across coherent views preserves the invariant common cause and discards nuisance variation.

paper_title: Building a Large Annotated Corpus of English: The Penn Treebank
motivation: Pereira and Schabes (1992) extend the inside-outside algorithm to train stochastic context-free grammars on partially bracketed corpora, achieving faster convergence and far more linguistically faithful structure than raw-text training. But they assume brackets are hand-annotated (Penn Treebank), which is costly and existed only for tiny samples, and they treat brackets as hard constraints: a zero-or-one indicator forbids any derivation span that crosses a human bracket, so every bracket must be perfectly correct. This blocks the use of the cheap, abundant but noisy automatic constituent cues in this collection: Church's (1988) stochastic NP parser, Hindle's Fidditch and partial parsers, Magerman-Marcus mutual-information boundaries, and prosodic phrase breaks. No method lets inside-outside grammar induction exploit automatically obtained, uncertain, partial brackets, so the demonstrated benefits stay locked to small gold treebanks rather than scaling to unrestricted text.
method: Relax the hard-bracket assumption into a soft, confidence-weighted, multi-source scheme so inside-outside runs on unannotated corpora. Replace the zero-or-one bracket indicator with a per-span weight equal to the product, over all brackets that the span crosses, of one minus that bracket's confidence: crossing a confident bracket is penalized but never forbidden; confidence one recovers the original hard constraint and confidence zero recovers raw-text inside-outside, so the method strictly generalizes both. Substitute this weight into the inside and outside recurrences and the reestimation formulae at unchanged complexity. Generate brackets automatically with calibrated confidences from Church's NP parser (path-score margin), Fidditch (rule certainty), mutual-information valleys (MI-drop magnitude), and prosodic breaks (break probability), fusing them as independent soft constraints whose penalties multiply. Add self-correcting confidence reestimation that each EM pass down-weights brackets systematically crossed by high-probability parses. Evaluate on the palindrome and ATIS tasks using automatic noisy brackets in place of gold, measuring convergence speed and constituent compatibility with held-out Treebank structure, and plot robustness under injected bracket errors comparing hard versus soft weighting.

paper_title: The Strength of Weak Learnability
motivation: Composition frameworks such as Helmbold, Sloan and Warmuth's learn rich concept classes—arbitrary-depth nested differences DIFF(C) and DIFF(C,B), capturing rules-with-exceptions like staircases, unions of intervals and rectangles, and nested differences of monomials that generalize Rivest's decision lists—by repeatedly invoking a single Closure subroutine (the smallest concept in an intersection-closed class containing all positive examples), and they attain provably optimal PAC sample complexity (via the Blumer et al. VC-dimension bound) and mistake bounds. Crucially, however, these results assume perfectly consistent labels. The construction is catastrophically brittle under noise: a single negative example whose label is flipped to positive forces the Closure to expand irreversibly, and the Total-Recall master algorithm iteratively closes and flips labels until its hypothesis is exactly consistent with the sample. Under classification noise no consistent nested difference exists, so the master keeps peeling off spurious exception layers, fitting the noise and producing arbitrarily deep over-fit hypotheses. This matters because the motivating applications are noisy—the paper itself points to Salzberg's empirical medical (breast-cancer) prediction using nested differences of rectangles—and the field (Angluin–Laird, Sloan's types of noise) had flagged noise tolerance as central. Yet no composition-based, closure-driven learner is known to tolerate noise; the elegant optimality guarantees exist only in the pristine noise-free regime. This leaves a clear gap: relax the exact-consistency assumption so the composition framework survives realistic, noisy, and agnostic conditions while keeping its structural subroutine-reuse elegance.
method: Relax the noise-free consistency assumption to random classification noise at rate eta below one half, and more broadly to an agnostic regime where the target is only approximately a nested difference. First, introduce a Statistical Closure subroutine that replaces the exact closure: given noisy examples and a cross-validated estimate of eta, it returns the minimal concept in the intersection-closed class C whose enclosed region is statistically justified—meaning the empirical fraction of positive labels among examples inside a candidate concept significantly exceeds the noise floor eta by a Hoeffding-based margin at confidence delta—rather than requiring zero enclosed negatives. This prevents a single flipped label from irreversibly expanding the closure, and it remains efficiently implementable for the paper's concrete classes (orthogonal rectangles, monomials, submodules) by admitting only boundary expansions that pass the significance test. Second, replace the iterate-until-exactly-consistent master with a disagreement-minimizing, depth-adaptive peeling procedure: it builds nested layers by alternately applying the statistical closure to the currently-positive and label-flipped populations, and stops adding a layer once the extra layer fails to reduce empirical disagreement by a Hoeffding-significant amount, so the nested-difference depth is chosen from data and noise-driven overfitting is blocked. Third, analyze the excess error by combining Occam/compression and VC-dimension sample-complexity tools (Blumer et al.) with a noise-rescaling factor of one over the square of one minus two eta, showing the sample size and running time stay polynomial in the accuracy, confidence, depth, VC dimension, and one over one minus two eta, so optimality degrades gracefully rather than breaking. Fourth, extend scope with both a batch PAC version and a noise-tolerant space-efficient online variant that accumulates per-region label statistics instead of retaining raw examples, plus extensions to DIFF(C,B) with an arbitrary noisy innermost learner and to approximately intersection-closed classes whose statistical closure tolerates a controlled fraction of interior negatives. Validate empirically on the paper's own testbeds—unions of intervals and rectangles, nested differences of monomials—with injected classification noise, comparing hypothesis depth and generalization error against the original brittle Closure/Total-Recall algorithms.

paper_title: Machine Learning in Automated Text Categorization
motivation: Prior link-based hypertext categorization methods each assume a single fixed structure. Chakrabarti et al. (enhanced-hypertext-categorization-using-hyperlinks-1998) reinforce with neighbor classes assuming homophily; Oh et al. (a-practical-hypertext-categorization-method-using-links-and) filter links by similarity; Fuernkranz uses only anchor text. Yang, Slattery and Ghani (a-study-of-approaches-to-hypertext-categorization-2002) show the best representation depends on which of five regularities holds (none, encyclopedia homophily, co-referencing heterophily, preclassified hub, meta-data), that adding neighbor words helped one corpus but hurt two others, and that this identification is crucial but seldom obvious, with partial co-referencing especially hard to exploit. The gap: no method automatically diagnoses which regularity holds per class and adapts the classifier accordingly, handles heterophily, discovers latent shared neighbor topics, and safely reverts to local text when no regularity exists. This matters because current systems require manual per-domain trial-and-error and discard heterophilic and latent structure.
method: We propose a self-configuring framework over base classifiers such as Naive Bayes, kNN, and SVM. First, diagnostics from training labels and the link graph estimate, per class and link direction, a class-to-class link transition matrix where diagonal dominance signals homophily and off-diagonal mass signals co-referencing, plus a hub score for preclassified structure, and by clustering unlabeled-neighbor words and testing information gain a latent-topic co-occurrence measure for partial co-referencing; each yields a per-class regularity confidence with a no-regularity default. Second, a relational feature generator builds a bank of neighbor views: transition-weighted neighbor class-probabilities that generalize Chakrabarti reinforcement to heterophily, tagged neighbor words, latent-cluster memberships, hub features, and meta-data from tags; because neighbor labels are unknown at test time these use a short relaxation-labeling loop initialized by the local classifier. Third, confidence-gated stacking fuses the local-text prediction with each view weighted by its diagnostic confidence, so absent regularities are suppressed and the system degrades to the local baseline. We evaluate on WebKB, IBM patent citations, an encyclopedia corpus, and a non-linked Reuters set, reporting micro and macro F1, with ablations on learned transitions versus fixed homophily, latent-cluster features, and gating.

paper_title: A Simple Neural Network Generating an Interactive Memory
motivation: Across these works one idea recurs: a category, whether a biological species, a sensory quality, a perceived object, or a machine-recognized pattern, is a region in a multidimensional space separated from others by discontinuities. Mayr's Animal Species and Evolution frames species as clusters of populations in a multidimensional space, contrasting typological imposed boundaries with population thinking that must handle within-group variability, and concedes that objective delimitation in a multidimensional system is an impossibility. Sensory Communication treats perception as re-representing stimuli in a neural coding space via efficient redundancy-reducing transformations, autocorrelation, and adaptation. Pattern Recognition and Minsky's Computation build and bound machines that carve decision boundaries. Sommerville's Geometry of N-Dimensions supplies the formal apparatus of distances, angles, and volumes, and The Uncertain Nervous System insists neural noise is intrinsic. The evidence gap is that each community measures category structure in incommensurable terms: taxonomists by expert-judged gaps, physiologists by tuning curves, psychophysicists by thresholds, machine builders by classification error. There is no shared, geometry-grounded way to observe and measure where category boundaries fall, how sharp they are relative to within-category variability, and whether boundaries drawn by a taxonomist, a nervous system, and a machine coincide. So the field cannot benchmark machines against biological discrimination, cannot audit whether a category is natural versus imposed, and cannot accumulate comparable cross-modal, cross-species evidence for unifying principles such as efficient coding.
method: Develop a single modality-independent measurement framework, noise-normalized representational geometry of categories, that makes taxonomic, neural, perceptual, and machine category structure directly comparable. Embed instances as point clouds in an n-dimensional metric space following Sommerville: organisms in character space, stimuli in physical-parameter space, neural populations in firing-rate space, behavioral responses as psychophysical dissimilarity spaces, and machine activations as feature-space points. Following The Uncertain Nervous System, estimate each system's within-category variability ellipsoid from repeated or trial-to-trial data and use it to define the metric, so all measures are in units of intrinsic noise and comparable across modalities. Compute three statistics: a Gap Statistic that is noise-normalized between-cluster separation minus within-cluster spread, operationalizing Mayr's discontinuity as a discriminability index like d-prime; a Redundancy measure of how much a representation decorrelates and reduces effective dimensionality relative to the raw stimulus space, testing Barlow-style efficient coding; and a Boundary Complexity measure of the order or curvature of the separating surface, connecting to Minsky perceptron limits. Apply the identical pipeline to taxonomic character matrices, sensory neural recordings across modalities, psychophysical discrimination data, and trained pattern-recognition machines, asking one common question: given each system's noise scale, where are the gaps and how sharp are they? Because every result is a comparable noise-normalized statistic, findings across labs, modalities, and species can be pooled to test that natural categories show larger Gap Statistics than randomly imposed partitions, that neural and perceptual coding increase gaps and reduce redundancy relative to the stimulus space, and that machines recovering high-gap structure better match biological boundaries. This turns the assumption of categories as regions in hyperspace into an observable, auditable quantity and provides a missing common instrument to accumulate evidence for or against unifying principles of categorization and sensory coding.

paper_title: A Simple Rule-Based Part of Speech Tagger
motivation: A striking fact recurs across these taggers but is never explained. The unsupervised HMM family (Jelinek 1985; Kupiec 1989; Cutting et al. 1992) collapses tens of thousands of words into a few hundred part-of-speech ambiguity classes, discarding each word's individual tag bias. Kupiec asserts word context provides significant constraint so the trade-off is remarkably favorable, and Cutting et al. say the collapse comes without significant accuracy loss, yet neither explains why it is favorable, when it fails, or how much context replaces the lost lexical prior. The word-specific-emission family (Church 1988; DeRose 1988) keeps per-word probabilities and reaches nearly the same 96 percent, and Merialdo bootstrapping (Derouault and Merialdo 1986) reaches it from another regime, a convergence with no causal account. The field patched this with heuristics: Kupiec modeled the top-100 frequent words individually, zeroed specific to-infinitive transitions, and hand-designed state chains from manual error analysis. These are symptoms of a missing theory. Without a causal account we cannot predict which words need individual modeling, which classes need richer context, or when the class-based trade-off breaks on a new corpus or language.
method: Build a mechanistic, information-theoretic explanation of why and when context substitutes for per-word lexical priors, using resources these papers assume (Brown corpus as gold reference, a lexicon, standard HMM Viterbi and Baum-Welch). First, factorize each ambiguous token's decision into three predictors of the true tag: per-word prior, class prior, and context posterior given class plus neighbors; build taggers toggling word-specific versus class-based emissions crossed with zeroth, first, and second-order context so accuracy differences isolate each factor. Second, quantify the trade-off per class via conditional entropy of the true tag given word alone, class alone, and class plus context: the class-minus-word gap measures information destroyed by collapsing, the class-minus-context gap measures what context recovers, and the trade-off is favorable exactly when recovery exceeds discarded word information. Third, adjudicate token by token where per-word prior and context posterior disagree, measuring which wins against gold. Fourth, explain the frequency heuristic by testing whether residual per-word information concentrates in high-frequency function words deviating most from their class average, deriving Kupiec's top-100 rule from a principled entropy-deviation criterion. Fifth, explain systematic errors as low-context-information cases where target class and neighbor have low mutual information, and show the manual state chain works by raising it. Sixth, explain supervised versus unsupervised convergence by comparing Baum-Welch and supervised estimates against the entropy diagnostics. Deliverable: a predictive score forecasting which words need individual modeling, which classes need augmented context, and cross-corpus robustness.

paper_title: Efficient Graph-Based Image Segmentation via Speeded-Up Turbo Pixels
motivation: The provided works span fundamentally different segmentation paradigms evaluated on incompatible terms. Region-based Ncuts (2008) uses MSE on custom mosaics; TurboPixels (2009) uses boundary recall and undersegmentation error on Berkeley at matched segment counts; JSEG (2001) uses its own J-value plus subjective inspection; Normalized Cuts (1997), multiscale graph decomposition (2005), Mean Shift (2002), mean-shift+Ncuts (2007), GSEG (2009), and supervised perceptual grouping (2000) each report on different data with different scores, several only qualitatively. Each also exposes a different, uncontrolled granularity knob (number of cuts, bandwidth, superpixel density, merge threshold) that TurboPixels shows dominates the accuracy numbers. This is an Evidence Gap: the field has no way to fairly compare these paradigms and no way to observe and attribute WHERE and WHY each fails. A single scalar cannot reveal whether error comes from leaking across weak boundaries, hallucinating splits inside textured or smoothly graded regions (failures JSEG and mean-shift papers flag), or losing thin/small structures (handled differently by compactness-constrained Ncuts/TurboPixels vs. mean-shift). Because errors are neither localized nor conditioned on local image structure, and granularity is not held constant, the community cannot accumulate reusable evidence about which method suits which conditions, nor quantify the headroom that motivated hybrid designs.
method: Build a structure-conditioned diagnostic benchmark and error-attribution protocol that turns evaluation from a single scalar into localized, condition-stratified evidence, then use it to profile the corpus paradigms. (1) Corpus with exact ground truth: combine natural images with human boundaries (Berkeley, as in TurboPixels) and controllable synthetic mosaics of homogeneous color patches and texture swatches (as in region-based Ncuts and JSEG), giving pixel-exact masks and dial-able structure. (2) Per-pixel condition maps: derive interpretable local descriptors — true-boundary contrast (gradient across ground-truth edges), texturedness (local feature variance / JSEG-style J value), region scale via medial-axis distance (reusing TurboPixels skeleton machinery), and within-region smooth color gradient. (3) Confound control: sweep each algorithm's native granularity knob to matched segment counts and report error-vs-granularity curves, generalizing TurboPixels' matched-count protocol to all methods. (4) Localized error taxonomy: match output regions to ground truth and classify each error into boundary leakage, interior splitting/boundary hallucination, thin-structure loss, and small-region omission, tagging each with the local condition value where it occurred. (5) Condition-stratified scorecards: aggregate into curves (leakage vs. boundary contrast, splitting vs. texturedness, recall vs. region scale) with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests across methods, yielding a reusable diagnostic fingerprint per paradigm. (6) Oracle headroom analysis: compute an oracle that picks the best method per local condition, quantifying how much a condition-aware hybrid could gain over any single method — measured justification for combinations like mean-shift+Ncuts. Deliverables: the annotated benchmark, an open attribution tool, and paradigm fingerprints, letting the field observe, localize, and compare failure modes under matched granularity and known image conditions.

paper_title: A Bit of Progress in Language Modeling (Extended Version)
motivation: These works combine heterogeneous LM knowledge sources (n-grams, classes/POS, cache, triggers, LSA, topic mixtures), but the fusion rule is chosen by convention: linear interpolation vs log-linear/maximum-entropy (whole-sentence exponential models; maxent). The LSA paper uses an ad hoc independence assumption; the Two-decades survey names principled integration as the open problem. Two gaps: no theory says which rule fits a given source pair; and none accounts for redundancy, since cache, trigger, LSA, and topic models all estimate the same latent document/topic state. So log-linear combination double-counts shared evidence while interpolation caps gains at the best component. Since most gains come from adding the most mutually redundant long-span sources, practice and evaluation rest on an untreated confound.
method: An information-geometric framework for source combination. (1) Ontology: cast each model as an exponential-family object classified on two axes, feature scope and normalization scope (word-conditional vs whole-sentence vs document). (2) Duality theorem: prove linear interpolation is the M-projection and log-linear/maxent is the I-projection onto the intersection of marginal-constraint sets, coinciding iff sources are conditionally independent given the base. (3) Redundancy bound: define redundancy as conditional mutual information between sources given the base; via the MI chain rule prove maximal perplexity reduction equals I(word; all sources|base), so marginal-constraint maxent over-counts by exactly the total redundancy. (4) Main derivation: add joint co-occurrence constraints between correlated sources, yielding interaction features (Lagrange multipliers) that give the true joint I-projection; prove this removes double-counting and recovers log-linear and interpolation as independent/redundant limits, trainable by GIS with a Gaussian prior. (5) Corollary: estimate redundancy from corpus co-occurrence to rank sources a priori. Validate on WSJ/NAB, Broadcast News, and Switchboard, combining n-gram, class, cache, trigger, and LSA models, checking gains match the bound and beat interpolation and standard maxent.

paper_title: On the Statistical Analysis of Dirty Pictures
motivation: Contextual MRF classifiers for LANDSAT-type data beat per-pixel classification by combining a spatially correlated label field with a spatially correlated spectral field. But Kiiveri and Campbell found, surprisingly, that once label correlation is modeled, adding a CAR model on the spectral data yields only marginal accuracy gains, worsens optimization by creating extra local maxima, and does not fix boundary errors, offering only an informal double-dipping intuition. Kittler and Foglein report boundary failures and Kent, Mardia and Switzer highlight mixed pixels. No mechanistic theory explains when the data-correlation channel is redundant, why it adds local maxima, and why it cannot fix boundary error, so model choice is trial-and-error with unpredictable payoff.
method: Formalize a generative model with a Potts label field (interaction beta) and, given labels, spectral data equal to class means plus noise (white or CAR with parameter rho), plus a sensor mixing operator that blends neighbor means at boundaries. Decompose the neighbor information for a label into a label-prior channel and a data-correlation channel; derive an expected error-reduction formula in beta, rho, class separability, and patch size, predicting redundancy of the CAR term as beta and separability grow. Use mean-field and ICM analysis to show CAR coupling makes the posterior multimodal, explaining extra local maxima. Show boundary error stems from mean contamination that a noise-correlation CAR cannot correct. Validate with Monte Carlo scenes sweeping these parameters, comparing per-pixel ML, label-only MRF, and label-plus-CAR classifiers. Deliver a phase diagram and a cheap diagnostic from estimable quantities predicting whether modeling spectral correlation helps.

paper_title: Unsupervised Learning of Action Classes with Continuous Temporal Embedding
motivation: Weakly supervised action segmentation aligns video frames to a per-video transcript assumed clean and complete, as in ECTC, HMM/HTK, the fine-to-coarse RNN, ISBA/TCFPN, and NeuralNetwork-Viterbi. Real transcripts from narration, ASR, or crowdsourcing omit silent steps, mention steps never shown, and reorder steps, so rigid transcript-constrained aligners corrupt the pseudo-ground-truth used for training. Unsupervised methods avoid transcripts but discard the cheap ordering signal. This noisy-transcript regime is unaddressed.
method: Relax the clean-transcript assumption with a noise-tolerant alignment graph that augments the transcript path with penalized drop, insert, and swap edits (clean alignment is the large-penalty limit). A generalized Viterbi, reusing per-action length and context models, jointly infers a frame alignment and a corrected transcript used as pseudo-ground-truth for iterative retraining. Edit penalties form an EM-learned noise model, and a cross-video consensus ordering prior favors insertions seen across videos and deletion of idiosyncratic steps. It degrades gracefully to action-set and unsupervised regimes. Evaluate on Breakfast and Hollywood-Extended with injected transcript noise versus NN-Viterbi, ISBA, HMM, and CTC, and on real ASR/narration transcripts.

paper_title: A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets
motivation: Transformation invariance is a resource bottleneck: invariant SVMs multiply data via virtual support vectors, distortion CNNs need long training on augmented labels, and hierarchical PoE trains one deep model per class, while cheap contrastive-divergence feature learners never amortize invariance to cut downstream label and compute cost.
method: Learn one shared class-agnostic invariant feature model via transformation-augmented contrastive divergence on unlabeled images, pooling expert responses over an orbit of small transformations so invariance is learned once, stacking layers greedily, then training a cheap classifier with few labels, and benchmarking label and compute savings versus invariant SVMs, distortion CNNs, and per-class PoE on MNIST and embryo phenotyping.

paper_title: Recognizing Action at a Distance
motivation: A family of 2D appearance-based representations succeeds at recognizing human movement, actions, object classes, and identity: Bobick and Davis temporal templates (MEI/MHI), Collins et al. silhouette gait templates, Cutler and Davis self-similarity matrices, Seitz and Dyer period traces, and Polana and Nelson periodic-motion templates. Several claim or exhibit view-invariance, yet no mechanistic account explains WHY they work despite discarding 3D structure, and WHEN view-invariance holds or breaks. Each conflates two intertwined sources: static body shape/appearance and motion dynamics/temporal recurrence. MEI (where motion occurred, the shape of motion) versus MHI (recency, the temporal ordering) is an unexamined instance. Tellingly, Collins et al. report their silhouette matcher still identifies people when gait TYPE differs between training and test, hinting identity rides on static shape more than dynamics, even though gait is framed as a dynamic biometric. Explaining which component carries action-class versus identity information, and which drives view-invariance versus its breakdown, matters for robustness, for understanding what a gait biometric actually measures, and for building genuinely view-invariant recognizers.
method: Provide a causal decomposition attributing discriminative power and view-(in)variance to static shape versus dynamics. First, recast each representation into a Static-shape channel S and a Dynamics/recurrence channel D: MEI approximates S, MHI approximates D; silhouette key-frames are S; self-similarity matrices and period traces are pure-D, discarding absolute shape and keeping only temporal recurrence. Second, run causal interventions on real silhouette/periodic sequences from Collins's multi-view multi-gait databases and Cutler and Davis and Polana and Nelson periodic sequences: shape-preserving dynamics-altering edits (temporal rewarping, tempo swaps, phase randomization, frame reordering); dynamics-preserving shape-altering edits (warp frames to a canonical body template, dilate silhouettes to erase anthropometry while preserving recurrence); and viewpoint change across angles. Third, for each channel and edit, use the originals' matchers (normalized-correlation nearest neighbor; time-frequency/lattice analysis) to quantify identity- and action-discriminability, attributing each signal to S or D. Fourth, derive theory from Seitz and Dyer affine-invariance conditions and Cutler and Davis symmetry/lattice analysis, predicting that the self-similarity recurrence/period lattice is viewpoint-invariant and encodes action structure, whereas similarity magnitudes are viewpoint- and shape-dependent and encode identity.
