Falsifiable predictions: P1 action-class info lives in the view-invariant recurrence structure; P2 identity lives in view-dependent static shape and survives dynamics-altering edits, explaining Collins's cross-gait-type robustness; P3 invariance breaks when viewpoint perturbs similarity magnitudes rather than the lattice. Finally, test P1-P3 against the intervention results to yield an explanatory model reconciling the dynamic-gait-biometric narrative with the dominance of static shape, and predicting which representations transfer across viewpoint.

paper_title: Adaptive Pattern Classification and Universal Recoding: II. Feedback, Expectation, Olfaction, Illusions
motivation: The corpus shares one primitive never unified into a working artifact: shunting on-center off-surround networks plus opponent gated dipole channels whose rebound is driven by slowly accumulating and depleting transmitter gates. Grossberg's punishment and avoidance theory derives affective fear-to-relief rebound from transmitter accumulation and depletion and ties it to catecholamine reward pathways studied by Fuxe, Ungerstedt, and Stein; the attention and reinforcement model links the same gating to the CNV slow potential documented by Walter and McAdam. Separately, perceptual aftereffects use near-identical machinery: Levine and Grossberg derive tilt aftereffect and angle expansion, Wilson models spatial-frequency adaptation, and classical afterimage work by Fechner and Helmholtz describes complementary-color rebounds analogous to the dipole off-response. The gap is that sensory aftereffects, affective rebounds, and slow cortical potentials are each modeled by separate bespoke equations even though all plausibly express the same transmitter-gated opponent primitive whose parameters should map to catecholaminergic pharmacology. No shared executable artifact instantiates this primitive, fits multiple domains with one gate module, or yields falsifiable cross-domain predictions such as a 6-OHDA-like depletion co-varying aftereffect duration, affective rebound, and CNV amplitude.
method: Build DipoleNet, an open modular simulation platform. Core engine integrates shunting on-center off-surround cells and gated dipole opponent channels using a two-variable transmitter scheme, where a gate slowly accumulates and depletes with throughput so input offset or phasic arousal produces a rebound. One shared Gate module exposes named parameters for tonic arousal, accumulation, depletion, and opponent coupling, each annotated to a catecholaminergic correlate. Assemblies built from the same primitives: a Vision assembly with a tuned feature-detector field and generalization-gradient inhibition for tilt aftereffect and angle expansion, usage-dependent inhibition for spatial-frequency threshold elevation and long recovery, and an opponent-color dipole for afterimages; an Affect assembly with a drive dipole for fear-to-relief rebound; and an Electrophysiology assembly whose summed slow gate activity is read as a CNV-like slow potential. A fitting harness calibrates each assembly to canonical source curves such as angle expansion peaking near ten degrees, spatial-frequency aftereffects saturating while recovery lengthens, afterimage decay, rebound latency, and CNV build-up, while constraining the shared Gate parameters to be identical across assemblies so one gate physiology must span domains. Prediction experiments perturb a single Gate parameter to emulate transmitter depletion or arousal change, yielding quantitative co-varying predictions across vision, affect, and EEG. Deliverables are the engine, a primitive and assembly library with gate-to-pharmacology annotation, reproducible notebooks regenerating each phenomenon, and pre-registered cross-domain predictions.

paper_title: Prioritized Sweeping: Reinforcement Learning With Less Data and Less Time
motivation: Tesauro's "Practical Issues in Temporal Difference Learning" reports a result its own author flags as unexplained: a nonlinear network trained by TD(lambda) purely on the outcome of self-play, with zero built-in knowledge, learns to play backgammon at tournament level, which he calls "so far beyond what one would have expected beforehand that it seems worthwhile to devote some further effort to understanding exactly how this is possible." Yet the available theory, Sutton's TD(lambda) convergence proof and Dayan's extension to general lambda, covers only linear approximators and pure prediction, and offers no guarantee for nonlinear prediction-plus-control, which is exactly the regime that succeeds here. Several concrete phenomena in the paper resist explanation and appear only as informal conjectures: move-selection quality is far better than the roughly 10 percent absolute value error should permit, attributed to "systematic error that cancels out" but never measured; self-play bootstraps from random weights to strong play with no explicit exploration mechanism, whereas Sato et al. show that learning control of finite Markov chains generally requires an explicit estimation-control trade-off, and Samuel's deterministic checkers program needed hand-crafted features and an imposed intermediate goal (material advantage); training time scales far better with sequence length and task complexity than temporal-credit-assignment intuition predicts; lambda has "almost no effect" on maximum performance; and low-volatility late-game (racing) play is worse than early engaged play, the opposite of the intuition that states near the reward are easiest. These anomalies plausibly share a single cause the literature never isolates: the environmental stochasticity of the dice, the salient difference between backgammon and Samuel's deterministic checkers. It could simultaneously supply, for free, the exploration that control learning is thought to require and smooth the value function so that residual approximation error becomes common-mode across sibling moves. The gap is therefore a missing causal and mechanistic account of why model-free nonlinear TD self-play works so well and what role environmental stochasticity plays; closing it matters because it would let practitioners predict when the recipe should work rather than leaving its success as folklore about one game.
method: The central hypothesis is that environmental (dice) stochasticity is the causal driver of TD self-play success, operating through two channels, free exploration and value-function smoothing, and it can be tested with a formal error decomposition and a controlled-stochasticity testbed. First, for every self-play decision state, decompose the network's value-prediction error over the legal successor moves into a common-mode component (the mean error shared by all successors of that state) and a differential-mode component (the residual that varies across successors and alone determines which move is chosen by argmax). Track both quantities over training against exactly solvable bearoff and racing endgames, which provide ground-truth win probabilities and optimal moves; this operationalizes and tests Tesauro's unproven "systematic error cancels out" conjecture, predicting that move-selection quality tracks the small differential-mode error while the large absolute error is dominated by benign common-mode error. Second, build a testbed with a single scalar knob that interpolates transition randomness from fully deterministic (checkers-like) to fully stochastic (dice-like), including a matched-branching deterministic game, holding the learner, input representation, lambda, and network capacity fixed so stochasticity is the sole manipulated cause. Third, sweep stochasticity, lambda, and hidden-unit count and measure state coverage and revisitation as an exploration proxy tied to Sato et al.'s estimation-control trade-off, whether self-play converges or collapses into degenerate cycles or poor local optima, the common-versus-differential error split, the gap between absolute and move-selection accuracy, sensitivity to lambda, and the early-versus-late phase performance profile. The predictions are that increasing stochasticity raises coverage and eliminates the need for any explicit exploration mechanism, shrinks differential-mode error and local-optima trapping, and flattens lambda-sensitivity as bootstrapping-target variance comes to dominate the bias-variance trade-off, whereas the deterministic limit should stall or require the hand-crafted features and imposed intermediate goal that Samuel's checkers needed. Fourth, to explain the counterintuitive late-game weakness, replace the fixed network with a variable-resolution or memory-based function approximator that adaptively refines resolution near terminal states while holding stochasticity fixed; if selective repair of late-game play results, the deficit is attributable to representational inductive bias rather than to temporal distance from the reward. Fifth, derive from the measured decomposition a sufficient condition for correct move selection despite large absolute error, namely that differential-mode error is smaller than the value gap between the optimal and next-best moves, and argue that stochastic smoothing shrinks differential-mode error, yielding a bound that explains the accuracy gap and connects the empirically successful nonlinear TD control back to the linear TD convergence theory it currently sits outside. The deliverables are a falsifiable causal chain (stochasticity, then exploration plus smoothing, then common-mode-dominated error, then robust control) and a practitioner-facing predictor of when TD self-play should be expected to succeed or fail.

paper_title: Forecasting of Electric Peak Load Using ANN-Cascaded, ANN-NARX and GPR Techniques
motivation: Across the provided load-forecasting literature, three patterns recur but are never explained mechanistically. First, a local-minima and solution-uniqueness narrative drives method choice: the genetic-fuzzy-NN paper cites the local-minima problem and unguaranteed convergence, and the ANN-GA/ANN-PSO paper argues backpropagation reduces convergence and the uniqueness of the final solution because of the local minima problem, supposedly fixed by global metaheuristics. Yet no paper verifies this: no one shows backprop solutions are truly non-unique in function space, that metaheuristics reach flatter basins, or that uniqueness is what improves forecasts. Second, metaheuristics rank differently with no account of why: the sine-cosine paper reports GA still outperforms SCA under the same test conditions, and the peak-demand paper contrasts ANN-GA vs ANN-PSO; the field just publishes another optimizer, treating optimizer novelty as the cause of accuracy. Third, simple beats complex under specific regimes: the robust-methods paper finds a simple robust method outperforms all others for normal days and notes load curves fall into distinct regimes, implying complex-model advantage is regime-dependent, yet nobody ties model class to the underlying load dynamics. The gap is explanatory and causal, not another predictor: there is no account of why accuracy varies across optimizers, model classes, and load regimes. This matters because practitioners choose methods by trial and error, trust is undermined, and an unverified folk-explanation propagates unchecked.
method: A diagnostic, hypothesis-testing study reusing the model families in these sources (multiple linear regression, exponential smoothing/SARIMA-RME, ARMAX, and single-hidden-layer ANNs trained by backprop vs GA/PSO/SCA) on common load and weather series with labeled normal vs anomalous, holiday, and weather-extreme days. Architecture and data are held fixed while the studied factor varies. Step 1: Test the local-minima and uniqueness claim by training the identical ANN with backprop and each metaheuristic across many seeds and measuring dispersion of weights vs dispersion of the realized input-output function, final loss and basin geometry (Hessian spectrum, sharpness under weight perturbation), and whether flatter minima actually yield lower test error, confirming or falsifying whether escaping local minima is the operative mechanism or the real driver is exploration breadth or basin flatness. Step 2: Characterize the true load structure using NARMAX error-reduction-ratio structure detection to select significant lagged-load and weather terms, yielding a per-window nonlinearity index and minimal sufficient complexity. Step 3: Add an uncertainty lens by fitting a Gaussian Process for calibrated per-day predictive variance as a measure of local hardness. Step 4: Attribute error by regime, computing per-method per-regime error and fitting an interpretable meta-regression predicting each method's per-day error from NARMAX nonlinearity, GP variance, weather volatility, day-type, outlier presence, and the landscape metrics from Step 1; coefficients quantify why each method wins and which mechanism dominates. Deliverables: a verdict on the local-minima and uniqueness folklore, a mechanistic explanation of why metaheuristics differ, and a causal decision rule mapping regime characteristics to the expected best model class.

paper_title: Building a Large Annotated Corpus of English: The Penn Treebank
motivation:
Across this literature there is a striking, unexplained asymmetry in what corpus statistics can and cannot recover. The SAME local co-occurrence machinery that reliably recovers *lexical categories* fails to recover *hierarchical constituency* from raw text. Brill (1991) shows that a plain bigram Markov model clusters words into clean substitution classes (pronouns, prepositions, modals, count nouns) purely from adjacency statistics; Church (1988) and the POST work (1991) show local n-gram statistics tag parts of speech at high accuracy; Hindle (1989) shows disambiguation rules can be induced from tagged text and beat hand-written ones. Yet Pereira & Schabes (1992) show that when the identical statistical estimation logic (inside-outside) is turned on hierarchical structure, only 35% of induced constituents from raw text are correct, versus 88% with bracketing — and the errors are systematic and repeatable: the learner groups subject pronoun with verb, "(is the)", "(about the)", and noun with sentence-final punctuation. Magerman & Marcus's mutual-information parser (1990) hits the identical failure mode.

The field's response has been to *patch* the symptom rather than explain it: Magerman & Marcus stipulate a hand-listed set of "never embraced" pairs (verb-preposition, pronoun-verb); Pereira & Schabes inject constituent brackets. Both authors explicitly note these constraints are supplied in advance, not derived, and neither offers a mechanistic account of WHY raw-text induction fails, WHY it fails on exactly these pairs, or WHY bracketing repairs it. This missing causal account matters: without it, the choice of which/how many brackets to supply, or which pairs to forbid, is ad hoc, and we cannot predict when unsupervised structure induction will work. The explanation gap is: what property of the statistics makes categories learnable but constituency not, and does that property predict the specific errors?
method:
Propose and test a single mechanistic hypothesis: the "collocation–constituency conflict." Unsupervised objectives here (inside-outside likelihood; MI-greedy parsing) are driven by adjacent-pair association strength, so they merge the most strongly associated adjacent tokens first. Constituency succeeds only when association strength aligns with true boundaries; it fails precisely where high adjacent mutual information straddles a constituent boundary (function word + head, pronoun+verb, noun+punctuation) or where a true internal boundary sits between a low-association pair. This reframes the categories-vs-constituency asymmetry: distributional statistics identify *substitutability* (equivalence classes — categories) robustly, but *constituency* requires association to track nesting, which it systematically does not.

Steps, all feasible with the sources' own data and tools:
1. Operationalize the mechanism. Using Church-style estimation on Brown/WSJ and the ATIS POS strings, compute pointwise mutual information for adjacent tag pairs (and word pairs). For every gold Penn Treebank constituent, define a per-boundary "conflict score": e.g., whether the maximum-MI adjacency within a span crosses a gold boundary, and the gap between cross-boundary and within-boundary MI.
2. Test the explanation. Reproduce the raw-text inside-outside grammar (GR) and MI-greedy parses, and log which constituents are mislearned. Test the falsifiable prediction that the conflict score predicts induction error at the boundary/constituent level (rank correlation, precision of "high-conflict ⇒ mislearned"). Show that the hand-stipulated forbidden pairs of Magerman & Marcus are exactly the top-conflict pairs — i.e., derive their list from the theory.
3. Establish causality with controlled grammars. Build synthetic corpora (as in the paper's palindrome experiment) where MI–constituency alignment is dialed continuously, plus tag-remapping manipulations that raise/lower cross-boundary MI without changing the grammar. Predict and verify that induction error tracks the conflict score, isolating collocation strength as the causal driver rather than grammar size or nonterminal count.
4. Convert the explanation into prediction and a recipe. The theory predicts that brackets placed at the highest-conflict boundaries should yield the largest accuracy/convergence gains per bracket. Test this in the partially-bracketed inside-outside framework: compare targeted "high-conflict" bracketing against random and uniform bracketing at matched bracket budgets. A win both validates the mechanism and yields a principled minimal-supervision recipe, explaining WHY Pereira & Schabes's bracketing helps and quantifying how little, and where, is needed.

The outcome is a causal, measurable account of when distributional statistics recover linguistic structure — explaining the category/constituency asymmetry, predicting the specific systematic errors documented across these papers, and unifying the two ad hoc fixes (forbidden pairs; bracketing) under one derivable quantity.

paper_title: Snakes: Active Contour Models
motivation: Prior works propose competing theories of how the visual system interpolates missing contours: Ullman's filling-in-the-gaps model (biarcs of two tangent circles minimizing total curvature), regularization and controlled-continuity interpolation minimizing tension energy with discontinuities (Terzopoulos), and relaxation-labeling curve enhancement (Zucker, Hummel, Rosenfeld). Each is validated only qualitatively on a few Kanizsa-style figures. Evidence gap: there is no common quantitative measurement of the actual shape of perceived interpolated contours across a varied stimulus space, and no shared metric or protocol to compare these models, diagnose where each diverges from perception, and accumulate evidence about which interpolation principle the brain implements. Competing models are thus non-comparable and hard to falsify. This matters because contour completion is a fundamental early-vision operation shared with stereo interpolation, motion filling, and surface reconstruction.
method: Build an open perceptual benchmark with three parts. First, a parametric stimulus generator varying gap length, edge orientation difference, corner presence, terminator curvature, and contrast polarity. Second, a measurement instrument: a psychophysical nulling protocol where observers adjust a probe dot to lie on the perceived contour at several positions across the gap, yielding an empirical contour locus with confidence bands and an inter-observer variability envelope. Third, model reimplementation and scoring: instantiate each theory (Ullman biarc network; controlled-continuity tension-spline regularization with a free smoothness weight; relaxation-labeling enhancement; straight-line null baseline) on identical geometry, extract curves and check multi-scale stability with scale-space filtering, and score agreement using a deformation-based shape distance from elastic matching of line drawings, normalized by the inter-observer envelope. Outputs include region-of-validity maps, an audit of failure modes and whether one fitted parameter rescues a model per observer, and a test of whether residuals grow where the contour is perceptually weaker. Release the generator, dataset, and metric as a reusable benchmark.

paper_title: Fuzzy Logic, Neural Networks, and Soft Computing
motivation:
Two research lines in this corpus solve complementary halves of the adaptive fuzzy control problem, but each rests on a narrow boundary condition that mismatches the scope of real deployment.

(1) Stable adaptive fuzzy control of nonlinear systems obtains rigorous Lyapunov stability, but only under strong, static assumptions: the fuzzy approximator of the unknown plant nonlinearity f(x) is a "universal approximator" and the derived bounds are valid *only on a predefined compact set S_x*. The text itself concedes that "if in reality the models and/or bounds are only valid when x ∈ S_x ... there may be cases when the stability analysis is invalid," e.g. when the state "travels too far away from the nominal operating point." The rule-base structure (number of rules and the membership functions that tile S_x) is fixed a priori and never changes. This assumes the operating envelope is known in advance and that the trajectory never leaves it — unrealistic under disturbances, faults, set-point changes, or nonstationary/ill-defined plants (precisely the plants fuzzy control is advertised for).

(2) Neuro-fuzzy structure/parameter learners can *build* the rule base from data: ANFIS tunes membership functions but "partitions the input space" on a fixed grid whose rule count explodes with dimension and must be chosen up front; Jang's temporal back-propagation and the Lin–Lee connectionist model even allocate rules by self-organized clustering. Yet all of these operate offline/batch on given training data and provide no closed-loop stability guarantee — the self-organizing structure is untethered from any Lyapunov argument, and structural changes during operation could destabilize a controller.

The scope mismatch — and the open gap — is that no method makes the *region of validity itself* an online, discovered quantity while keeping stability guarantees: stable control assumes a fixed, known coverage region and structure; structure learners give up guarantees and assume offline data. Nothing grows fuzzy coverage as the state ventures into previously unseen regions and simultaneously certifies boundedness across those structural changes.
method:
Propose a coverage-aware, self-structuring stable adaptive fuzzy controller for feedback-linearizable nonlinear systems that discovers its own region of validity online while retaining a Lyapunov guarantee.

Components:
1. Approximator: represent the unknown nonlinearity f(x) by a Takagi–Sugeno / fuzzy-basis-function network with local (Gaussian) receptive fields, as in the stable-adaptive-control setting — but with a *variable* rule set R(t) rather than a fixed grid.
2. Coverage monitor: at each step compute a coverage/novelty statistic from rule firing strengths (e.g., the maximum normalized activation, i.e. distance of the current state to the nearest rule center). This measures whether the state lies inside the union of active receptive fields.
3. Online rule allocation (borrowing the self-organized clustering idea from Lin–Lee, made incremental): when coverage drops below a threshold as the trajectory enters an uncovered region, instantiate a new rule centered at the current state, initialized with zero consequent contribution so it does not perturb the current control output at the insertion instant. Optionally merge/prune redundant rules to bound complexity — allocating rules only along the visited trajectory (a lazy, local partition) rather than a full grid, directly sidestepping ANFIS's exponential grid growth.
4. Parameter adaptation: update consequent (and, gradient-style à la ANFIS/temporal back-propagation, premise) parameters via a Lyapunov-derived adaptation law with projection.
5. Robustifying term: add a nonlinear-damping/sliding term (from the stable-adaptive-control framework) that guarantees uniform ultimate boundedness even where approximation is currently poor — i.e., during the transient when the state has just entered an as-yet-uncovered region before a new rule is trained. This makes venturing outside the current coverage safe rather than fatal.
6. Stability across structural change: prove a switched/composite-Lyapunov result. Because each new rule is inserted with zero output contribution and its adaptable weights enter the same Lyapunov function, V does not jump at insertion events; pruning is admitted only when a rule's contribution is below a certified bound. Thus the guarantee holds across a growing/shrinking rule base, replacing the assumption of a fixed known compact set S_x with an online-expanded certified region.

Evaluation: benchmark on the inverted pendulum (as in the temporal-back-propagation paper) and single-input feedback-linearizable systems (as in the stable-adaptive-control examples), under scenarios that deliberately push the state outside any initially covered region — large initial conditions, step disturbances, moving set-points, and slowly drifting (nonstationary) dynamics. Compare tracking error, transient boundedness, and final rule count against (a) fixed-grid ANFIS-style approximators, (b) fixed-structure stable adaptive fuzzy control with an a-priori S_x, and (c) offline self-organized neuro-fuzzy controllers, demonstrating that the proposed method maintains stability while automatically matching its structure to the realized, not assumed, operating envelope.

paper_title: Adaptive Signal Processing for Adaptive Control
motivation: Scope-mismatch gap. LMS adaptive filtering is the shared engine behind adaptive noise cancelling (Widrow 1975) and adaptive inverse and model-reference control of nonminimum-phase plants (On Adaptive Inverse Control 1981; Convergence Results for Widrow's Adaptive Controller 1981). All depend on the step size mu, yet the only principled rules for choosing it come from Stationary and Nonstationary Learning Characteristics of the LMS Adaptive Filter (1976), which assume a narrow regime: a stationary first-order Markov random-walk drift of the optimal weights with known variance, a constant input correlation matrix R, a stationary input, and near-equal eigenvalues of R. The optimal mu balancing gradient-noise misadjustment (grows with mu) against lag misadjustment (grows with 1/mu) then requires drift statistics known in advance. Real settings violate this: ECG, speech, and interference cancelling, and inverse control of time-varying plants, exhibit abrupt, non-Markov, unknown drift with correlated large-eigenvalue-spread inputs. A fixed mu is mismatched, too slow for fast drift and too noisy when quiescent. The self-tuning regulator line (On Self-Tuning Regulators 1973; Self-Tuning Controllers Based on Pole-Zero Placement 1980) tunes plant parameters but never its own adaptation gain, and assumes known order, delay, and minimum phase. No work adapts the learning rate itself to unknown general nonstationarity.
method: Regulate the LMS step size mu online as a self-tuning gain balancing gradient-noise misadjustment against lag misadjustment without knowing drift statistics or eigenvalues. Lag dominates when the optimum drifts persistently, making successive instantaneous gradients g (error times input) stay aligned; gradient noise is zero-mean and white. Track an exponential moving average of g and gradient power, and update mu multiplicatively toward the point where estimated lag and noise excess-MSE are equal (the misadjustment minimizer): raise mu when gradients stay aligned (fast drift), lower it when they fluctuate. This senses drift rate directly and handles abrupt, non-Markov change. Handle eigenvalue spread by replacing scalar mu with a diagonal preconditioner normalizing each tap by its running input power (cheap Newton whitening), applying the rule per whitened mode. Insert this self-tuned LMS into the adaptive noise canceller and the adaptive inverse and model-reference controller including a nonminimum-phase plant. Evaluate against fixed mu from the 1976 formulas and an oracle knowing true drift statistics, on assumption-violating scenarios: abruptly switching and non-Markov optima, correlated high-spread inputs, and nonstationary reference statistics. Measure lag error, steady-state misadjustment, output SNR, and command-tracking error. Success is approaching oracle-mu performance where any fixed mu fails.

paper_title: Building a Large Annotated Corpus of English: The Penn Treebank
motivation: SCFG induction by the inside-outside algorithm is brittle: hierarchical structure is undetermined by raw text, the search has poor local maxima, and convergence worsens as nonterminals grow, so grammars from raw text rarely match linguistic constituency. Pereira and Schabes fix this by reestimating from a partially bracketed corpus, but they treat hand-parsed brackets as HARD constraints (their filter is zero whenever a candidate span overlaps a given bracket). Hand bracketing is expensive and scarce. Yet the literature offers cheap but UNRELIABLE partial-structure sources: Church's stochastic NP parser, mutual-information-based bracketing, partial parsers like Fidditch, and prosodic parse-scoring of phrase boundaries. None is trustworthy enough to be gold. The gap: there is no robust way to exploit abundant-but-noisy heterogeneous partial structure. Feeding noisy brackets into the hard-constraint algorithm is dangerous because one wrong bracket forbids the correct analysis, so errors propagate and induction can fail. This forces reliance on scarce hand-parsed data exactly where robustness to imperfect supervision would most cut cost and failure risk.
method: A robustified inside-outside reestimation that consumes multiple noisy partial-bracketing sources via soft, confidence-weighted, reliability-learned constraints. (1) Soft compatibility: replace the hard 0/1 indicator with a graded weight w(i,j) in [0,1] in the inside/outside recurrences; a span violating a bracket is down-weighted, not forbidden, with cost scaling as one minus source reliability, so contradicting an unreliable bracket stays reachable. (2) Multi-source aggregation: each source (Church NP brackets, MI brackets, Fidditch fragments, prosodic boundaries) emits candidate brackets with optional confidence, combined as a product of per-source soft penalties, so agreement sharpens constraints and conflict softens them. (3) Joint reliability estimation via noisy-channel EM: treat true bracketing as latent in an outer loop alternating soft inside-outside reestimation and updating each source's reliability and bias from how often its brackets match the model's most-likely parses, so consistently wrong sources are automatically discounted. (4) Local-maximum robustification: multiple random restarts, model selection by cross-source bracket consistency on held-out data rather than likelihood, per-constituent uncertainty from posterior variance across restarts, and rule smoothing to avoid degenerate collapse. (5) Evaluation on ATIS/Brown POS strings comparing raw-text inside-outside, hard-constraint bracketing on the SAME noisy brackets, the soft multi-source method, and a hand-bracket upper bound, measuring crossing-bracket compatibility, convergence speed, and degradation curves under injected bracket noise, expecting graceful degradation versus catastrophic failure of the hard-constraint baseline.

paper_title: An Automated ECG Beat Classification System Using Convolutional Neural Networks
motivation: SVEB detection is consistently far worse than VEB across HMM, SVM, fuzzy, PSO-ANN, and CNN/SDAE methods here. The 1990 HMM paper said SVEB needs P-wave analysis, which most systems omit. Explanation gap: why does SVEB fail everywhere? Tangled untested causes: imbalance, missing P-wave features, S/N overlap, atrial interpatient variability.
method: Attribution study over wavelet+RR+PCA, SDAE, and 1-D CNN under one AAMI protocol on MIT-BIH/INCART/SVDB: decompose S errors (S-vs-N vs S-vs-V) and measure N/S/V geometry; ablate P-wave/QRS/T/RR segments with saliency to see if models use the P-wave; fix class prior then add P-wave features to measure S recovery; compare within- vs between-patient variance of S- vs V-features. Yields a quantified cause attribution and a fix.

paper_title: Sentiment Classification using Machine Learning Techniques
motivation: Prior movie-review sentiment work (Pang NB/SVM, feature-selection n-gram pipeline, document-level opinion mining) aggregates all opinion words over the whole document, assuming every sentiment word reflects the reviewer's verdict. This product-domain assumption fails for movies: Turney notes movies mix elements (events, actors) with the whole (the film as art), so an evil character does not make a bad movie, giving movies the worst accuracy (66 vs 84 percent) and an open problem none of the six works address.
method: Separate whole-evaluative from element-descriptive sentences, then classify. Tag each sentence WHOLE, ELEMENT, or NEUTRAL via film-craft lexicons, narrative markers (NER character subjects, story verbs, tense via POS), and discourse position, using a small self-trained logistic model. Build scope-partitioned unigram/bigram/trigram features (token-at-WHOLE vs token-at-ELEMENT) with information-gain selection; train SVM and Naive Bayes up-weighting WHOLE evidence so element sentiment is decoupled from the film rating. Evaluate on Cornell polarity v2.0 versus unscoped baselines with ablations, and test transfer on Turney's multi-domain reviews.

paper_title: A Machine Learning Approach to Coreference Resolution of Noun Phrases
motivation: 1990s trainable coreference systems recast coreference as classification over pairs of noun phrases plus ad-hoc decoding into chains, yet coreference is an equivalence relation and MUC scores the partition, not pairs. Aone and Bennett report inconsistent non-transitive classifications, batch-mode failure to percolate links, and no principled antecedent choice; UMass RESOLVE finds prepruning positive pairs sharply shifts recall versus precision; CogNIAC trades recall for precision by abstaining. None formally link pairwise training loss to chain-level scoring, so high pairwise accuracy need not yield good chains and decoders and significance tests are chosen ad hoc. This gap motivates a formal partition-level theory.
method: Formal theory of coreference as partitioning. Ontology separating three conflated objects: the directed resolution graph G where each anaphor links to one antecedent, the coreference relation R that is the transitive closure of G, and the entity partition P that MUC scores; transitive-closure positives and easiest positives are shown to be different uncalibrated samplers of R. Model: from any pairwise classifier take log-odds weights and prove that Bayes-optimal decoding under pair independence plus hard transitivity is the max-agreement equivalence relation maximizing summed weights over coreferent pairs, a correlation-clustering objective, with closest-first, best-first, threshold-plus-closure, and clustering as greedy special cases. Theorem 1: a thresholded independent classifier generically violates transitivity, shown by a three-mention counterexample and a lower bound on violating triples in pairwise error. Theorem 2: express MUC and B-cubed metrics via the pairwise confusion matrix and cluster-size distribution, proving pairwise error bounds chain error neither above nor below since one cross-cluster false positive destroys a times b separations. Corollary: derive size-dependent per-pair loss reweighting aligning training loss with the partition metric, explaining UMass prepruning. Corollary: cast CogNIAC abstention as thresholding weight magnitude and derive the F-maximizing threshold from the cluster-size prior. Validation on MUC-6 data compares greedy versus max-agreement decoding and proves pairwise significance tests invalid because transitivity induces dependence, requiring document-level resampling.

paper_title: Introduction: The Challenge of Reinforcement Learning
motivation: RL control architectures using active/deictic perception suffer perceptual aliasing: an internal representation confounds several world states, destabilizing value-based learning (Whitehead and Ballard, 1991). Their Lion algorithm detects an aliased (inconsistent) state because its greedy value chronically overestimates the true one-step return, and suppresses any state whose value overestimates (reset to zero) so consistent representations win. The explicit weakness is brittleness to non-determinism: the trigger is a hard threshold (if the one-step error is negative, suppress to zero). The authors note it works only in deterministic worlds; in stochastic worlds consistent states also gain return variance and would be wrongly weeded out; and a single anomalous transition or reward can catastrophically suppress a good state and cascade, destroying an otherwise perfect policy. Their proposed fixes (fixed thresholds, partial 95 percent suppression) are speculative and untested, and their earlier SAMUEL-style variance-subtraction failed because return-variance estimates are unreliable under unequal state visitation. This matters because real embedded and behavior-based agents (e.g., Mahadevan and Connell's OBELIX box-pushing robot; stochastic settings motivating the learning-automata literature) violate the deterministic assumption. The field thus has a mechanism that removes hidden-state aliasing only in noise-free worlds and no principled way to tell genuine aliasing from benign stochasticity, a clear robustification gap.
method: Robustify aliasing detection by replacing the Lion algorithm's brittle hard-threshold suppression with a statistically robust, self-correcting consistency detector. Core insight, grounded in the prior work: perceptual aliasing produces a systematic, persistent bias in an internal state's one-step TD error (the greedy operator repeatedly picks the optimistic world-state, so the target sits chronically below the inflated Q), whereas environmental stochasticity produces zero-mean symmetric fluctuations. The method exploits bias-versus-variance, not magnitude. Components: (1) Per-state error statistics: for each internal state-action, maintain online exponentially weighted estimates of the mean and dispersion of the TD error plus counts of over- versus under-estimation, turning the single-sample test into an accumulated-evidence statistic. (2) Sequential bias test instead of a threshold: suppress only when a one-sided sequential test (a CUSUM or sign-test accumulator on the error stream) shows statistically significant persistent overestimation beyond the state's own noise level, so occasional anomalous overestimates no longer trigger suppression, eliminating the single-perturbation cascade. (3) Graded, noise-scaled suppression: when firing, reduce the action-value toward the robust lower estimate by an amount proportional to detection confidence and inversely to noise variance, so consistent-but-noisy states settle near their true average while truly aliased states are driven down. (4) Pooled variance estimation via spatial clustering: fix the unequal-visitation problem that sank variance-subtraction by pooling error samples across internal states similar under a feature/Hamming metric (statistical-clustering idea from Mahadevan and Connell), yielding reliable per-state noise baselines even for rarely visited states. (5) Recovery/hysteresis: keep the evidence accumulator after suppression so a wrongly suppressed state can regain lionhood once evidence shows consistency, guaranteeing recovery from transient errors and preventing permanent policy collapse. Evaluation: reproduce the block-manipulation (pick-up-green-block) and missile-evasion tasks and inject controlled stochasticity (quasi-deterministic perturbations, reward noise, fully stochastic transitions). Compare against the original Lion algorithm, plain Q-learning, and SAMUEL-style variance-subtraction, measuring frequency of catastrophic policy collapse, greedy-policy stability over time, asymptotic success rate, and detector precision/recall in flagging truly aliased versus consistent-noisy states. Success means retaining removal of hidden-state aliasing while eliminating catastrophic suppression and extending reliable operation from deterministic to stochastic environments.

paper_title: Learning in feedforward layered networks: the tiling algorithm
motivation:
Two 1980s explanations of generalization in these works are never connected. Carnevali and Patarnello (Exhaustive thermodynamical analysis of Boolean learning networks, 1987) show that zero-error training samples networks in proportion to how many implement each function, so generalization follows from the second law: the most-implemented function (largest statistical weight H(P)) wins, and problem complexity is AS = log2(N/H(P)). This requires exhaustive enumeration, and they explicitly ask for an a priori estimate of AS. Krauth and Mezard (Learning algorithms with optimal stability, 1987), via Gardner, instead use the stability margin Delta and compute the volume of coupling space with stability at least Delta, but only for associative-memory recall, never generalization, and never link margin to function complexity.

Gap: both compute the same object, the volume of parameter space solving a task, one combinatorially (H(P)) and one geometrically (margin Delta), yet no formal object unifies them. They are in tension: entropy favors the most-implemented, small-margin solution; optimal stability favors a unique large-margin one. Unifying them would give one account of generalization and supply the analytic AS estimate Carnevali and Patarnello requested, spanning perceptrons (Rosenblatt; Minsky-Papert; Optimal linear discriminants) and backprop internal representations (Rumelhart et al.).
method:
A formal margin-resolved solution-volume theory of generalization.

Object: for parameter space of measure N, target P, training set S, define V(P,Delta) as the measure of parameters implementing P on all of S with per-example stability at least Delta; margin density rho(Delta) is minus its derivative. V(P,0) is Carnevali-Patarnello's weight H(P), so AS(P)=log2(N/V(P,0)); the largest Delta with V positive is Krauth-Mezard/Gardner optimal stability. Define margin-resolved complexity AS(P,Delta)=log2(N/V(P,Delta)).

Learner: model any zero-error trainer as returning f with probability proportional to V(f,0)*exp(beta*Delta(f)). beta=0 is the entropic learner (typical most-implemented function); beta to infinity is the optimal-stability learner. This gives a taxonomy: combinatorial Occam simplicity versus geometric robustness simplicity as two poles of one family.

Bound: a fresh labeled input multiplies surviving volume by the fraction of solutions already consistent with it, so expected generalization error is at most one minus the average ratio V(after)/V(before), governed via rho by the mass near Delta zero. Theorem: error falls as the margin distribution shifts from zero and as volume grows, factorizing into a prior term (large H(P)) and a robustness term (large Delta), predicting an optimal intermediate beta.

Open problem: since V(P,Delta) is the Gardner-type volume computable by replica/annealed methods, AS can be estimated analytically instead of by enumeration. For layered nets, extend V by counting internal representations (hidden-code volume times readout volume), linking to Rumelhart et al. and linear discriminants.

Validation: on the enumerable Boolean networks with known H(P), check the decomposition reproduces the learning curves and AS and test the intermediate-beta optimum; on random-pattern perceptrons, check V(Delta) matches Gardner's optimal-stability curve and that the generalization term tracks learning curves; sweep beta to exhibit the predicted minimum.

paper_title: Sentiment Classification using Machine Learning Techniques
motivation:
All six prior works reduce document sentiment to a flat aggregation of word/phrase polarities. Turney (thumbs-up source) predicts a review's class from the *average* semantic orientation of adjective/adverb phrases; the document-level opinion-mining paper takes a *majority count* of positive vs. negative opinion words (with negation reduced to "flip polarity if preceded by not"); and the feature-selection and ML papers (NB/SVM with feature-selection schemes and n-grams up to 4-grams) use *bag-of-words* linear scoring. These are three surface variants of the same operation: an order-insensitive, shifter-blind sum/vote over token polarities.

The papers' own evidence shows this is the systematic source of error. Turney's misclassified examples are all composition failures: negation scope ("the very talented Laurence Fishbourne is not so good either"), discourse contrast ("nothing special, but…"), context-reversed valence ("I loved it! It made him seem… more evil"), non-evaluative descriptive phrases scored as sentiment ("blue skies"), and the explicit part-whole problem ("good beaches do not necessarily add up to a good vacation"). The same crude negation flip appears in the doc-level paper, and the feature-selection paper's move to higher-order n-grams is an implicit, unprincipled attempt to capture local composition. Tellingly, Turney reports 66% accuracy on movies vs. 84% on automobiles — a domain gap plausibly driven by the density of contrast/irony/negation in movie reviews, which the flat aggregators cannot represent.

The gap: there is no formal, unified account of *how* phrase-level polarity composes into document-level polarity through valence shifters (negation, intensifiers, diminishers), discourse contrast, a subjectivity gate separating evaluative from descriptive predicates, and part-whole aggregation. Each paper re-invents an ad hoc fix. A formal model would explain why the existing methods fail, unify them as special cases, and predict where and how much they err — which matters because it converts scattered engineering patches into a principled, testable theory.
method:
Contribution type: a formal derivation — a "sentiment composition algebra" that unifies and corrects the aggregation methods in the six sources.

1. Objects. Assign each token/phrase a pair (s, w): sentiment value s ∈ [-1,1] and subjectivity weight w ∈ [0,1] (w≈0 for descriptive, non-evaluative predicates such as "blue skies"). Composition is a fold over the syntactic/discourse parse rather than a flat sum.

2. Operators and taxonomy. Define a taxonomy of valence shifters as operators on [-1,1]: negation N, intensification/attenuation I_c (scaling by degree words), contrastive discourse ⊕_but (asymmetric reweighting favoring the post-connective clause), and neutral conjunction ⊕ (a subjectivity-weighted mean). Document polarity D is the value at the root of the fold.

3. Reduction theorem. Prove that Turney's average-SO rule, the doc-level majority count, and a linear bag-of-words classifier are all the SAME degenerate instance of the algebra: obtained when every shifter operator is the identity, subjectivity weights are uniform (w≡1), and composition is order-insensitive unweighted mean/sign. This formally locates the three methods as corners of one model.

4. Negation lemma. Show the naive sign-flip N(s)=−s is inconsistent with the bounded semantics of negation: "not excellent" (s≈0.9) should not map to "terrible" (s≈−0.9). Derive the correct form N(s) = −λs (0<λ<1, an attenuation-toward-mild-opposite) from two desiderata — neutrality preservation (N(0)=0) and non-overshoot — and characterize the admissible λ range; the sign-flip used by the sources is the boundary case λ=1 shown to violate non-overshoot.

5. Error bound. Prove that the polarity error of any shifter-blind aggregator (i.e., the existing methods) relative to the compositional value is bounded by (fraction of tokens under a non-identity shifter scope) × (mean shift magnitude). This yields a testable prediction: domains/reviews with denser negation and contrast (e.g., movies) incur larger error — quantitatively rationalizing Turney's 66% vs. 84% gap.

6. Expressiveness theorem. Prove the algebra strictly subsumes k-gram features: order-k n-grams realize only compositions inside a fixed window k, whereas the parse-based fold represents unbounded negation scope and cross-sentence contrast; hence the feature-selection paper's higher-order n-grams are a bounded, incomplete approximation of the algebra.

7. Subjectivity gate and part-whole aggregation. Formalize the evaluative/descriptive distinction as the weight w (gating out "blue skies"), and model the "elements vs. wholes" problem as a two-level fold where aspect-level polarities aggregate to a whole-object polarity through a learned (or domain-tagged) part-whole operator rather than a plain average.

8. Instantiation and validation. Give a concrete instantiation (lexicon/PMI seeds from Turney and WordNet as in the doc-level paper for base (s,w); dependency+discourse parse for the fold) and an evaluation protocol on the standard movie-review polarity dataset used by the feature-selection paper, comparing the compositional aggregator against the three baselines it generalizes (average-SO, majority-count, NB/SVM BoW/n-gram). The empirical test is whether measured accuracy gains match the per-review error-bound predictions of step 5, confirming the derivation.

paper_title: Efficient Graph-Based Image Segmentation via Speeded-Up Turbo Pixels
motivation: The ten provided works span the dominant classic image-segmentation paradigms: pixel-affinity normalized cuts (Shi-Malik 1997), simple min-cut (1994), multiscale spectral graph decomposition (Cour 2005), region-graph cuts (Cigla 2008), feature-space mode-seeking via mean shift (Comaniciu 2002), superpixels via geometric flow (TurboPixels 2009), unsupervised color-texture region growing (JSEG 2001), a hybrid mean-shift+Ncut pipeline (Tao 2007), supervised learned perceptual grouping (Sarkar 2000), and gradient multiresolution merging (MAPGSEG 2009). Evaluation across them is fragmented and self-favorable: papers use different data and different metrics (qualitative displays, Normalized Probabilistic Rand in MAPGSEG, undersegmentation-error vs superpixel density in TurboPixels), so superiority claims are neither comparable nor causally explained. Moreover, results are reported at a single hand-tuned parameter setting even though the decisive knobs are unresolved and consequential: mean-shift bandwidth selection is explicitly open, Ncut/spectral methods require a preset segment count and affinity scale, superpixels a target density, JSEG a scale/threshold, and MAPGSEG a threshold ladder. The works articulate mutually conflicting quality axes (undersegmentation vs boundary adherence vs compactness in TurboPixels; spatial coherence vs feature separability motivating mean-shift+Ncut; faint boundaries amid textured clutter in multiscale spectral), yet no source isolates which image properties trigger which failure, or how the trade-offs move as parameters vary. Practitioners therefore cannot know which family to deploy under which conditions, and improvement claims rest on incommensurable evidence. The works leave this room because each optimizes and reports for its own method rather than mapping the shared design space.
method: Construct an Empirical Mapping of classic segmentation paradigms: a controlled, factor-isolating benchmark plus a decomposed diagnostic. (1) Factor-controlled dataset with exact ground truth: synthesize composite images varying five difficulty factors independently while holding all else fixed (boundary contrast strong-to-faint, texture-clutter density, region-scale mixture, additive noise, number of regions), and create semi-synthetic Berkeley variants that preserve human ground truth while dialing a single factor (attenuate contrast only across annotated boundaries, inject texture inside regions, add noise, downscale). (2) Decomposed error taxonomy instead of one aggregate: split each method's error into boundary-localization error, merging (undersegmentation) error, splitting (oversegmentation) error, spatial-incoherence error (fraction of a predicted segment lying in disconnected image components, a direct diagnostic for feature-space grouping), region-count deviation, and compactness; also recompute all three legacy metrics used in these papers (Rand/NPR, undersegmentation error, boundary F-measure) to quantify metric disagreement and reveal when rankings flip with the metric. (3) Parameter-surface characterization: for every algorithm sweep its principal controls (mean-shift bandwidth; spectral/Ncut segment count and affinity sigma; superpixel density; JSEG scale/threshold; region-graph merge count; MAPGSEG threshold ladder) and report full performance surfaces rather than single points, including the achievable Pareto frontier between undersegmentation and boundary adherence and a stability measure (width of the parameter range yielding a stable region count, formalizing the bandwidth-stability heuristic noted for mean shift). (4) Scaling map: measure runtime and memory versus image size and versus target region count for each family, capturing the global-optimization cost that motivates region-based and multiscale variants. (5) Synthesis into an operating-regime map: fit an interpretable model (decision tree/regression) predicting from difficulty factors and parameter regime which paradigm dominates and which error mode appears, and correlate outcomes with structural predictors (spatial-constraint use, compactness enforcement, texture modeling, global vs greedy, pixel- vs region-node graph). Deliverables are a practitioner decision guide, a quantified account of when reported wins are metric artifacts, and identification of unfilled regions of the difficulty space where no existing paradigm performs well, replacing incommensurable single-setting comparisons with a reproducible empirical map that ties failures to specific image properties and parameter regimes.

paper_title: Adaptive Signal Processing for Adaptive Control
motivation:
Across these works two distinct research communities pursue "adaptive control" with essentially incompatible evidence bases. Widrow's signal-processing school (LMS adaptive filter, adaptive noise cancelling, adaptive inverse control) reports performance as excess mean-square error relative to the optimal Wiener solution, captured by the clean, decomposable "misadjustment" metric (gradient-noise term + tracking-lag term). The control-theory school (Åström–Wittenmark self-tuning regulators, MRAC and unbiased MRAS identification, pole–zero-placement self-tuners, OLFO/dual and predictive adaptive control) instead reports asymptotic optimality (e.g., convergence to the minimum-variance or known-parameter controller), hyperstability, or convergence conditions, and separately hints that active learning carries a "probing" cost (the OLFO gain depends on future parameter uncertainty; the separation theorem fails).

The result is an Evidence Gap: there is no common yardstick to observe, quantify and compare how much any of these schemes actually pays for adapting, nor to compare a self-tuning regulator, an MRAC/adaptive-inverse controller, and a dual controller on the same plant under the same conditions. Misadjustment exists only for feedforward, single-minimum MSE surfaces; the control side offers only asymptotic (parameters-converged) statements that are silent on transient cost, on tracking lag when the true plant drifts, and on the price of probing. Consequently the field cannot answer basic comparative questions — which paradigm loses least to adaptation on a nonminimum-phase plant with slowly drifting parameters? — and evidence cannot accumulate across the two literatures because it is reported in non-comparable units.

Why it matters: several sources explicitly address time-varying parameters (adaptive stochastic control, "A New Solution to Adaptive Control"), nonminimum-phase plants (self-tuning for nonminimum-phase systems), and the caution-vs-probing tension (dual/OLFO control), yet none provides a shared measurement framework to weigh these effects against one another.
method:
Develop a paradigm-agnostic "cost-of-adaptation" (generalized misadjustment / excess-loss) framework and an accompanying benchmark suite that lets any adaptive controller in these works be measured and compared on identical footing.

1) Common reference and metric. Fix a task loss J (e.g., steady-state output/tracking-error variance). For each experiment define the oracle loss J* achievable by the optimal controller that knows the (possibly time-varying) plant parameters at every instant. Define the generalized misadjustment M = (E[J_adaptive] − J*)/J*, directly extending Widrow's dimensionless excess-MSE ratio from the feedforward LMS setting to closed-loop adaptive controllers.

2) Additive decomposition. Building on the LMS analysis (which splits misadjustment into a gradient-noise term proportional to adaptation speed and a lag term inversely proportional to it), derive a three-way decomposition of M for closed-loop schemes under a slow-adaptation / small parameter-error approximation: (a) an estimation-variance term from noisy parameter/weight estimates (linked to the estimator covariance in self-tuning and MRAS identification), (b) a tracking-lag term from the estimate trailing drifting true parameters (modelled, as in the LMS paper, by a first-order Markov drift of the optimal parameters), and (c) a probing term equal to the deliberate excess loss injected to gain information, read off from the dual/OLFO characterization where the adaptive gain depends on future parameter uncertainty. For non-dual schemes (self-tuning, MRAC, adaptive inverse) term (c) is zero, exposing exactly what dual control buys and costs.

3) Predicted trade-off law. The framework predicts a speed-vs-accuracy law: total M is minimized when the estimation-variance and lag terms balance (generalizing the LMS optimal-adaptation-rate result to closed loop), yielding an optimal adaptation-gain/forgetting-factor for each paradigm as a function of drift rate and noise level.

4) Benchmark suite. Assemble a small, well-specified library of discrete-time SISO/MIMO plants spanning the conditions these papers care about: minimum vs nonminimum phase, stationary vs Markov-drifting parameters, and low/high input-correlation eigenvalue spread (which the LMS paper shows governs conditioning). Specify standardized inputs, noise, and horizons.

5) Comparative evaluation. Implement representative controllers from the sources — least-squares self-tuning minimum-variance regulator, pole–zero-placement self-tuner, MRAC/adaptive-inverse and hyperstable series inverse controller, and an OLFO/dual controller — and measure their empirical M and its three components on every benchmark case via Monte Carlo, checking the additivity and the trade-off law against the analytical predictions.

This addresses the gap by turning heterogeneous, asymptotics-only claims into a single measurable, decomposable quantity, giving the field a reproducible way to audit each scheme's true adaptation cost, benchmark paradigms head-to-head, and accumulate comparable evidence about when feedforward adaptive-inverse, self-tuning feedback, or dual control is preferable.

paper_title: Intelligent switching control of a pneumatic muscle robot arm using learning vector quantization neural network
motivation: Pneumatic muscle actuators (PMA: McKibben/braided/Rubbertuator) are praised across the corpus for high power-to-weight ratio and inherent compliance, but every paper agrees they are dominated by hard-to-model effects: friction-induced hysteresis, temperature-dependent and time-varying rubber properties, and strong force-length-pressure nonlinearity (adaptive-position-control, analysis-and-control-of-a-rubber-actuator-arm, modeling-of-braided-pneumatic-actuators, fuzzy-logic-linearizing, fuzzy-PD+I). In response the field produced many controllers (PID, adaptive pole-placement, neural network, fuzzy PD+I learning, fuzzy linearizing, sliding/variable-structure, H-infinity), each validated on its own bespoke actuator, rig, valve, and payload and reported with idiosyncratic metrics (roughly 2 degrees accuracy in one paper, up to 10 degrees in another). Modeling is equally fragmented: Colbrunn's model explicitly does not predict hysteresis and patches it with an empirical effectiveness factor, while van der Smagt derives hysteresis from structure, yet no model is validated on a common dataset and none links model fidelity to closed-loop control performance. This is an evidence gap: there is no way to observe, measure, and fairly compare how controllers and models handle the specific PMA nonlinearities, nor to accumulate reproducible evidence about which approach wins under which operating condition (load, frequency, temperature, hysteresis direction). Claims of superior tracking cannot be audited or reproduced because the actuator characterization, task, and disturbance profile differ every time. This matters because PMAs target safety-critical, human-adjacent uses (exoskeletons, nuclear-waste manipulators) where control robustness must be trustworthy and comparable, and because scattered private results prevent the community from diagnosing the true error sources.
method: Build a standardized benchmarking and diagnostic framework for PMA control with three coordinated components. (1) Common characterization protocol and open dataset: a fixed procedure that sweeps each actuator over the full pressure and length range in both loading directions to capture the force-length-pressure surface, hysteresis loops (with loop area as a scalar hysteresis index), valve air-flow dynamics following Colbrunn's solenoid-modulated flow model, and temperature drift over sustained cycling; publish the curves as a shared reference so any lab can report where its actuator sits relative to the benchmark. (2) Calibrated open simulation model with graded fidelity: assemble one parameterized PMA-plus-valve model from corpus building blocks (Chou-Hannaford/Colbrunn static geometry with the effectiveness correction, Colbrunn dynamic air-flow, and a van der Smagt-style structural hysteresis term), fit it to the reference dataset, and provide ablated versions (static-only, plus-dynamics, plus-hysteresis, plus-temperature) so each nonlinearity's contribution is explicit and model fidelity is itself measurable against real data. (3) Task battery, unified metrics, and controller re-implementation: specify fixed tasks (step response, multi-frequency sinusoidal tracking, variable-payload positioning, antagonistic-joint control, injected disturbances) with a single reporting sheet of comparable metrics (RMS and peak tracking error in consistent units, settling time, bandwidth, steady-state accuracy, and robustness deltas as load and temperature change), then re-implement the representative controllers from the sources (PID baseline, adaptive pole-placement, neural network, fuzzy PD+I, fuzzy linearizing, sliding-mode, H-infinity) and run all of them on both the shared simulation model and a physical rig under identical conditions to produce a head-to-head leaderboard. Add a diagnostic decomposition layer that uses the ablated models as controlled ground truth to attribute each controller's residual tracking error to specific causes (hysteresis direction, temperature drift, valve lag, or unmodeled nonlinearity) by comparing performance across ablations and operating regimes. This yields auditable evidence not only of which controller is best overall but of which nonlinearity each method actually conquers and where it fails. The framework is feasible with the equations, hardware, and controllers already described in the sources, and its output is a reusable benchmark that lets future PMA control claims be validated, audited, compared, and accumulated rather than merely asserted.

paper_title: Short Term Load Forecasting Using Artificial Neural Network
motivation: Prior STLF works forecast load from calendar and weather with no operational feedback to demand. The 2001 market paper adds spot price as an ANN input and acknowledges load and price are bidirectionally related, yet treats price as exogenous. Gap: price and load are simultaneously determined in equilibrium, so regressing load on realized price learns an equilibrium conditional expectation, not the structural demand response, and future price must itself be forecast, coupling price-forecast error into load error. No source formalizes when price helps versus injects endogeneity bias. This bias has operational cost, leaving room for a formal theory of price endogeneity in market-based STLF.
method: A formal structural theory of price-conditioned STLF. Model the market as two simultaneous equations: demand and price with mutual feedback. Prove a bias theorem, decompose error into irreducible variance, endogeneity bias, and a price-propagation term, and derive a break-even inequality for when price helps. Define three regimes: exogenous, predetermined day-ahead, and simultaneous real-time price. For estimation, reinterpret the neighboring-system price as an instrument and give a two-stage control-function estimator with a cost-weighted loss and a Hausman-style test. Validate on Ontario-style load and price data.

paper_title: A Trainable System for Object Detection
motivation: Two strands in this corpus never meet. One builds detectors by assembling parts under geometric configuration constraints: the human-nudes grouper that fires only if skin regions form a spine/limb/girdle group, body plans as grouping hints, detection by components, and articulated pedestrian/walking models. These are justified only empirically: the nudes paper reports recall and an ad hoc response ratio, noting the grouper alone has response ratio 1.4 but composed with a skin filter reaches 7-10, and that precision depends on positive density in the test stream. There is no theory for why composing weak part detectors with a geometric constraint controls false alarms, how many parts to require, or how tight the constraint should be. The other strand, statistical learning theory and SVMs, gives rigorous VC/margin bounds, but only for a single monolithic classifier on a fixed feature vector, ignoring part structure, occlusion, articulation, and accidental grouping. The gap: no formal model derives the generalization behavior of a configuration-based detector from its component classifiers and its grouping constraint, hence no principled objective for allocating capacity between parts and configuration.
method: Develop a formal theory of configural detection that decomposes a part-based detector into k component classifiers and a configuration predicate C over the spatial arrangement of accepted parts. Define two capacity resources: discriminative capacity (per-component detection rate d and false-accept rate p) and configural selectivity (accidental-grouping probability a, the chance a background tuple satisfies C). Prove a decomposition theorem bounding expected false alarms per image by the number of candidate tuples times the product of the p values times a, while detection probability equals the product of the d values times b, where b is the chance a true object satisfies C; this formalizes the response ratio as the multiplicative selectivity gain from adding a grouper. Define a VC-style accidentalness dimension for the class of admissible predicates C, bounding how small a can be while C still admits real articulated instances. Insert empirical component rates into Vapnik distribution-independent bounds so the quantities transfer to deployment with confidence terms, yielding a precision bound as an explicit function of positive-example density. Combine everything into one risk objective, derive first-order conditions for the optimal number of parts k and constraint tightness, and prove a complementarity result that at fixed risk capacity shifts along an iso-risk curve between discrimination and selectivity. This gives a conceptual distinction and a taxonomy placing corpus detectors by where capacity sits. Validate from the corpus alone by estimating the rates for skin and limb components and spine or girdle constraints and checking the predicted recall-vs-response-ratio curve and optimal k against reported grouper configurations.

paper_title: A Computer Aided Diagnosis System in Mammography Using Artificial Neural Networks
motivation: Across the provided works, CAD systems for microcalcifications and lung nodules use different algorithm families: fuzzy-logic enhancement, wavelet subband decomposition, shape-factor classification, and neural networks. Each reports strong performance, yet the lung-disease review documents CAD sensitivity varying from 38 to 95 percent with varying false-positive rates, attributed to algorithm differences and case selection. The CAD editorial blames structure noise that camouflages anatomy, and the mammography papers note lesion-to-dense-tissue contrast may fall below detectability. This is an explanation gap: the literature reports THAT performance varies and THAT dense tissue hurts detection, but gives no causal, mechanistic account of WHY a detector family succeeds or fails on a given image, or why families disagree. Performance is reported as aggregate ROC numbers, not a theory linking measurable image properties to per-lesion outcomes. Without such an account, scores cannot be trusted to generalize and one cannot know which algorithm to deploy for which image.
method: Build a controlled explanatory study treating the source algorithms as objects of mechanistic inquiry. First, re-implement three representative detectors on a common image set: fuzzy brightness enhancement with iterative thresholding, wavelet subband reconstruction, and region-growing with shape-factor classification, plus a neural-network baseline. Second, for each lesion compute image covariates drawn from the papers' hypothesized failure causes: background density, local lesion-to-background contrast, a structure-noise texture measure, calcification size, contour roughness, cluster spacing, and spectral overlap between lesion and background. Third, fit explanatory models predicting per-lesion outcome of hit, miss, or false positive for each detector from these covariates, quantifying which factors dominate each family's failures. Fourth, run controlled perturbation experiments as the causal core: synthetically insert calcifications with varied contrast, size, and roughness onto backgrounds with varied density and structure-noise, changing one covariate at a time, to isolate whether wavelet detection collapses under spectral overlap with dense tissue, whether fuzzy enhancement fails below a contrast threshold, and whether shape classification fails because low contrast degrades segmentation. Fifth, synthesize a mechanistic account of the field's variance and inter-family disagreement, plus operating-envelope maps showing where each detector is reliable, enabling image-conditioned method selection or fusion. This is feasible using digitized mammogram sets used in these papers plus synthetic lesion insertion.

paper_title: A Survey of Industrial Model Predictive Control Technology
motivation: Industrial MPC achieves robustness to model error almost entirely through one heuristic knob, move suppression (a penalty on input increments), plus short control horizons. The sources treat it empirically: QDMC (Garcia and Morshedi) says only that larger input penalties reduce controller gain and improve stability under model inaccuracies, and that the weight must be tuned as a function of the actual model mismatch; Qin and Badgwell merely list it among detuning knobs. This is an explanation gap: there is no mechanistic account of why move suppression confers robustness, why it trades off against performance as it does, and why it fails to robustify some multivariable plants (e.g. high-purity distillation and other ill-conditioned units) no matter how large it is set, while succeeding on thousands of other loops. Corpus theory does not close this: formal robust MPC (Kothare LMIs; min-max feedback MPC; robust QDMC with an end condition deriving move-suppression inequalities under FIR uncertainty) gives sufficient guarantees but is admittedly conservative and unused in practice, while the state-space interpretation (Lee, Morari, Garcia) shows move suppression and the disturbance model form an implicit observer/filter but stops at nominal equivalences. Practice (works but we cannot say why or when it fails) and theory (guarantees too conservative to explain practice) both point to a missing causal account. This matters because commissioning is dominated by trial-and-error tuning, and knowing when detuning cannot help would redirect effort to the right remedy.
method: Build and test a mechanistic, directional explanation of the move-suppression robustness mechanism for step-response (DMC/QDMC/IDCOM) MPC. First, from the unconstrained active-set closed form and the step-response/state-space model, express the closed-loop input-output and sensitivity maps as explicit functions of the move-suppression weight Lambda, horizons, and the output-bias disturbance model, nominally and under multiplicative/FIR-coefficient error, yielding the effective loop gain and implicit robustness filter. Second, propose the directional explanation: SVD the dynamic gain matrix into strong and weak input directions; a scalar/diagonal Lambda detunes directions nearly isotropically, while performance loads the strong direction and model error plus inversion of near-singular gains amplify the weak direction. Hypothesis: well-conditioned plants have comparable directions so one Lambda robustifies with little loss (explaining ubiquitous success), whereas ill-conditioned plants need opposite treatment per direction so no single Lambda can robustify the weak direction without destroying strong-direction performance (explaining categorical failure regardless of magnitude). Formalize this as a direction-resolved robustness margin and per-direction performance/robustness Pareto front. Third, reconcile with theory by showing robust-QDMC/LMI conditions are the isotropic worst-direction projection of the directional margin, quantifying the conservatism from ignoring directionality and the disturbance filter. Fourth, validate by ablation and intervention on corpus benchmarks (the distillation column and the Shell control problem) plus a well-conditioned counterexample: map the true stability/robustness boundary under gain, time-constant, and delay errors and compare to predicted margins; ablate Lambda, control horizon, and disturbance model to attribute robustness; then run the falsifiable test of replacing scalar/diagonal Lambda with an anisotropic weight aligned with input singular directions and the uncertainty structure. If the account holds, direction-aware detuning robustifies the weak direction while preserving strong-direction performance on the ill-conditioned plant and is unnecessary on the well-conditioned one. Deliverable: a causal explanation plus an a priori diagnostic telling an engineer whether detuning can work for a given plant and, if not, which remedy (re-identifying the weak direction or direction-aware weighting) is needed.

paper_title: Unsupervised Learning of Action Classes with Continuous Temporal Embedding
motivation: Weakly supervised action segmentation from transcripts assumes each training transcript is exactly correct. Real transcripts from movie scripts, speech recognition of narration, and crowd annotation often contain missing steps, spurious steps, and swapped orderings. Because leading methods such as NeuralNetwork Viterbi, Extended CTC, iterative soft boundary assignment, and HMM based recurrent models align every frame to the given transcript with a strict monotonic decoder, one wrong token misroutes the whole alignment and corrupts the learned appearance, length, and context models, and these errors grow across iterative retraining. No prior work in this literature detects, discounts, or corrects transcript errors, so making transcript based weak supervision robust to noisy transcripts is an open and important problem for scaling weak supervision.
method: Treat every transcript as a noisy observation of a latent true action sequence rather than as ground truth. First, extend the transcript constrained decoder with sparsely regularized edit operations, namely deleting a spurious token, inserting a background segment absent from the transcript, and substituting or locally swapping tokens, each carrying a learned penalty, so the decoder defaults to the transcript and repairs it only where visual evidence strongly disagrees, using frame to frame visual similarity to separate genuine boundaries from noise. Second, add a confidence weighted robust loss that down weights videos and tokens whose transcript constrained alignment score is far below the best unconstrained alignment, so a few corrupted transcripts cannot dominate learning. Third, iterate noise aware alignment, confidence weighted model updates, and committing only high confidence edits to produce cleaned transcripts and per token reliability estimates. Evaluate on Breakfast and Hollywood Extended, plus controlled synthetic corruption at increasing rates, comparing against NeuralNetwork Viterbi, iterative soft boundary assignment, Extended CTC, and HMM recurrent baselines, and report accuracy retention curves and transcript recovery, with success defined as graceful degradation where baselines collapse and no loss when transcripts are clean.

paper_title: Pseudo Conditional Random Fields: Joint Training Approach to Segmenting and Labeling Sequence Data
motivation: Cascaded NLP pipelines suffer error propagation, and prior fixes that preserve uncertainty between stages assume each stage emits a trustworthy distribution, which fails because discriminative models are miscalibrated under domain shift, leaving a robustness gap.
method: Recalibrate each stage before propagating uncertainty using a learned coverage-driven temperature, then decode by minimum-Bayes-risk over calibrated samples.

paper_title: Bayesian CART Model Search: Rejoinder
motivation: Nonparametric regression from adaptive basis functions (MARS, CART, additive models) is powerful but a single fitted structure is high-variance. The provided works give two independent traditions for combining many such models. (1) Bayesian model averaging: Bayesian MARS (bayesian-mars-1998), Bayesian CART (a-bayesian-cart-algorithm-1998), and Simulation-Based Bayesian Nonparametric Regression place a prior over structures (a Poisson prior on the number of MARS basis functions controls overfitting) and average predictions with posterior weights p(M|y) proportional to prior times likelihood via reversible-jump MCMC, yielding interpretable posterior inclusion probabilities.
