(2) Frequentist combination: Stacked Generalization (stacked-generalization-1992) learns weights from out-of-sample CV performance; An MLE Strategy for Combining CART Models uses in-sample maximum-likelihood mixture weights; boosting (experiments-with-a-new-boosting-algorithm-1996) builds a weighted vote stagewise with margin bounds. Gap: these weighting rules are derived in isolation, with no common formal account. Posterior (BMA) weights are optimal only when the true model lies in the class; but in nonparametric regression misspecification is the norm and in-sample scoring is optimistically biased toward complex models, so posterior/MLE averaging can concentrate on overfit structures, while stacking targets predictive risk but discards Bayesian interpretability. A unifying formal framework placing BMA, stacking, MLE-combination, and boosting on common axes, explaining BMA's misspecification failure, and yielding a principled tunable combiner is missing.
method: Formal Derivation unifying model averaging and ensembling of adaptive-basis regressors. (1) Objects: M is the space of adaptive-basis models (MARS term sets, CART trees), each giving predictor f_M; the combined predictor is f_q(x)=E_{M~q}[f_M(x)] for distribution q over M with prior pi. (2) Objective: J_eta(q)=E_{M~q}[n R_hat(M)] + KL(q||pi), with scoring functional R_hat and temperature eta>0. Theorem 1 (Gibbs optimality via Donsker-Varadhan duality): the minimizer is the tempered posterior q*(M) proportional to pi(M) exp(-eta n R_hat(M)). (3) Taxonomy theorem on two axes (scoring in-sample vs out-of-sample; temperature/prior). Instantiating (R_hat,eta,pi) recovers each prior work: in-sample negative log-likelihood, eta=1, Poisson prior gives Bayesian MARS/CART model averaging; in-sample loss with eta to infinity gives MLE-combination (point mass on max-likelihood model); K-fold/LOO CV loss with uniform pi on a finite candidate set and q on the simplex gives stacked generalization; stagewise coordinate descent with exponential loss gives boosting. (4) Optimism lemma plus PAC-Bayes bound (Theorem 2): true risk of f_{q*} is bounded by empirical/CV risk plus a KL(q*||pi)/(eta n) term, optimized over eta (recovering boosting's margin bound). Lemma: expected in-sample score differs from predictive risk by an optimism term increasing in model complexity, so in-sample (BMA/MLE) weights are systematically biased toward overfit structures under misspecification while CV scoring is asymptotically unbiased, formally explaining why Bayesian and frequentist combiners disagree. (5) Derived algorithm: the bound identifies an interior optimum, a cross-validatory tempered posterior over adaptive-basis models. Run the existing Bayesian MARS/CART reversible-jump MCMC but replace the likelihood in the target with exp(-eta n CV-predictive-loss), choosing eta to minimize the Theorem-2 bound; predict by the posterior-weighted average and retain inclusion probabilities. It interpolates between and dominates both endpoints (posterior averaging and stacking). (6) Validation on the simulated surfaces used in the sources (Friedman 1991; Hwang examples in bayesian-mars-1998): recovered special cases reproduce reported results, and the tuned interior combiner lowers fraction-of-variance-unexplained. Feasible with existing RJMCMC and CV machinery.

paper_title: Natural Actor-Critic
motivation: Robot motor-primitive learning with episodic Natural Actor-Critic wastes scarce, dangerous trials because exploration, rollout count, and step size are unmanaged.
method: ACTIVE-eNAC adds a search layer to episodic Natural Actor-Critic: using the Fisher matrix and gradient variances it already maintains, it allocates a per-parameter exploration covariance maximizing expected improvement per trial under a trust region and safety box, stops rollouts by a sequential rule, and sets step size by trust-region line search with off-policy reuse.

paper_title: Comparison of Vector Stacking, Multi-SVMs Fuzzy Output, and Multi-SVMs Voting Methods for Multiscale VHR Urban Mapping
motivation: Nearly every advance in this collection injects spatial information into a spectral classifier: extended morphological profiles, KPCA-based EMP, morphological feature fusion with SVM, watershed plus majority voting, clustering plus majority voting, mean-shift objects, multilevel context, and decision fusion. Yet validation has not advanced: each method is judged by aggregate scores on the same one or two ROSIS Pavia or DC Mall scenes against a pixel-wise baseline. This is an evidence gap: aggregate accuracy raises OA chiefly by homogenizing large regions, while the same papers warn it erases small structures and blurs edges. No shared instrument exists to observe where and why spatial information helps or hurts, to audit the homogeneity-versus-detail trade-off, to compare methods like-for-like, or to test whether gains are statistically real per condition.
method: Build a diagnostic benchmark. Common backbone: reimplement representative spatial mechanisms on one pixel-wise SVM base with pairwise-coupling probabilities so differences reflect the spatial mechanism. Spatially stratified metrics instead of a single OA: boundary-band accuracy versus distance to reference edges; object-size survival via morphological area operators; interior-region homogeneity gain; separability-conditional gain by Jeffries-Matusita; and training-size curves. A gain-budget decomposition attributes net OA change into interior gain minus boundary loss minus small-object loss. A confidence audit builds reliability maps and evaluates calibration per stratum. McNemar tests overall and per stratum make claims condition-specific, and semi-synthetic morphological scenes with controlled object size and spectral contrast isolate when each mechanism helps or hurts. Deliverable: an evidence table ranking methods by stratified profiles and gain budgets, not a single OA.

paper_title: Reinforcement learning of dialogue strategies with hierarchical abstract machines
motivation: RL of dialogue-management policies depends on a trained user simulator (Schatzmann survey; Cuayahuitl HMM simulation; hybrid RL/SL on COMMUNICATOR), since real corpora are too small to explore the state/policy space (NJFun, multi-goal HRL). The field documents an unexplained phenomenon: a simulator's accuracy does not predict the utility of the policy learned against it. Cross-model tests show policies learned with a poor simulator look excellent on that same simulator but collapse on a better one, and succeed only by exploiting simulator deficiencies such as asking for all slots at once because cooperativeness and action-conditioned errors are unmodelled. Accuracy metrics such as precision/recall, symmetrized-KL HMM distance, perplexity, and statistical matching rank simulators but do not guarantee sensible behaviour in the unseen situations a new RL strategy induces. This is an explanation gap: there is no causal or mechanistic account of why accuracy and utility decouple, nor of which simulator properties cause RL to produce brittle, non-transferring policies. Such an account would tell practitioners what a simulator must get right for transferable RL, and explain why train-and-test-on-the-same-model evaluation misleads.
method: Build a family of intention-level simulators over COMMUNICATOR (bigram, standard and Input-Output HMMs of Cuayahuitl, richer conditional), each with causal knobs isolating candidate mechanisms: cooperativeness for multi-slot requests, action-conditioned error rate, goal drift, and response variety. Run a full cross-model matrix: train an RL policy (state-action reduction from the multi-goal HRL work; linear function approximation from the hybrid paper) against each variant, then test every policy against every variant plus a held-out corpus proxy, giving paired accuracy-metric and transfer-utility measurements. Treat each knob as an intervention to estimate its causal effect on policy behaviour and cross-model utility, and add a policy-exploitation probe over the learned Q-values that flags actions whose value depends on simulator regions with little real-data support. Test two hypotheses: H1, accuracy metrics are dominated by frequent easy states while policy value is dominated by rare decision-critical states, decoupling accuracy from utility; H2, missing action-conditioned constraints leave free reward RL exploits. Test H1 by decomposing accuracy metrics by state frequency and correlating only the decision-critical part with utility; test H2 by showing the constraint knobs alone remove exploitation without improving overall realism. Deliver a decision-critical, action-conditioned constraint diagnostic that predicts simulator utility better than KL/HMM-distance and perplexity, providing a causal account of why realistic-looking simulators yield brittle policies.

paper_title: Improving Generalization with Active Learning
motivation: Cohn & Tesauro (1992) report an unexplained phenomenon: two problems with identical VC dimension and architecture learn at qualitatively different rates. Discrete symmetric Boolean targets (majority, majority-XOR) show error decaying EXPONENTIALLY in the number of random examples m, while their real-valued analogues (threshold, threshold-XOR) obey the worst-case ~1/m VC behavior. The authors state they "have been unable to identify the causes." They ruled out a representation gap and a weight-space gap, leaving three unresolved explanations: (1) an inductive gap where backprop dynamics avoid near-perfect solutions; (2) an effect inherent to discrete problem structure; (3) a statistical-mechanics gap/dip in the generalization spectrum they could not find. This is a real explanation gap with high stakes: whether the exponential regime is caused by the algorithm or by problem geometry decides whether to invest in better algorithms or better representations. Query-by-committee (Seung/Opper/Sompolinsky, 1992) shows finite per-example information gain yields exponential decay, but only for a Gibbs learner sampling the version space (Mitchell's Generalization as search) under active querying. MacKay's information objectives assume a correct hypothesis space. Baum & Haussler's VC counting and Blumer et al.'s theory are blind to which same-VC problem is easy. Critically, Cohn & Tesauro's weight-space test perturbed one fixed solution rather than the version space conditioned on m random examples, so it could not detect the effect. A mechanistic account linking version-space geometry, information gain, and algorithmic bias is missing.
method: Provide and test a version-space explanation that separates algorithm-induced bias from problem geometry. Step 1: Reproduce Cohn & Tesauro's four matched tasks (majority vs. real threshold; majority-XOR vs. threshold-XOR) with the same architecture and VC dimension, confirming exponential vs. ~1/m curves. Step 2: For each m, instead of perturbing one solution, probe the version space V(m) of weight vectors consistent with m random examples by sampling with a flat prior via MCMC/Langevin or rejection (the Gibbs learner of query-by-committee), and estimate the distribution of generalization error over V(m) versus m, the object the statistical theories actually predict. Step 3: From sampled version-space volumes estimate per-example information gain (log-volume shrinkage) for binary vs. real inputs, testing the hypothesis that discreteness keeps information gain asymptotically finite (exponential) while a continuum of examples near a real decision boundary makes it vanish (power law); formalize via the density of examples near the boundary (margin distribution). Step 4: For each m, compare backprop solutions' generalization to the mean and spectrum of Gibbs samples from the SAME V(m). If backprop is systematically better than typical consistent hypotheses, the inductive gap is confirmed and quantified; if they coincide, the effect is problem-inherent, resolving the open question. Repeat with weight decay and varied initializations as a further discriminator. Step 5: Turn the account into a falsifiable law: from a target and input distribution compute the boundary/margin statistic and predict exponential vs. ~1/m; validate on synthetic families that quantize inputs to k levels, predicting a smooth crossover from exponential to power-law as k grows, unifying random-example and active-query learning via the finite-information-gain principle.

paper_title: A Tutorial on Hidden Markov Models and Selected Applications in Speech Recognition
motivation: HMM recognizers decide by MAP classification, structurally identical to decoding a codeword over a noisy channel, yet the corpus keeps these worlds apart. Viterbi's Error Bounds for Convolutional Codes (1967) bounds decoding error via union bounds over pairwise Chernoff/Bhattacharyya distances. On the speech side three estimation criteria coexist with no common error-theoretic footing: ML/Baum-Welch is provably non-discriminative; MMI (Bahl et al. 1986) is discriminative but purely empirical with no link to error rate; and MDI/cross-entropy (Ephraim, Dembo, Rabiner 1987) is a proven descent algorithm but a fit criterion, not an error bound. The only tool comparing two whole HMMs, the Juang-Rabiner distance (1985), is an asymmetric KL rate computed by Monte-Carlo simulation with no closed form, never connected to the probability of confusing two words. So there is no computable quantity predicting word confusability and no training criterion with an error guarantee, though recognizers succeed exactly according to how separable competing models are, the regime coding theory captures with pairwise distances and union bounds.
method: Deliver a formal error-exponent theory of HMM recognition. (1) Cast word recognition as soft channel decoding with a codebook of word models and priors and MAP decoding. (2) Core theorem: define the Chernoff overlap Z_s(T) as the sum over O of P(O|i)^(1-s) P(O|j)^s; prove its decay rate Delta_s equals minus the log of the Perron eigenvalue of an explicit product operator M_s of size Ni times Nj with entries a_ab(i) a_cd(j) kappa_s(b,d), where kappa_s is the emission overlap integral, closed form for discrete, Gaussian and LPC-autoregressive densities. This gives a spectral simulation-free divergence, unlike Juang-Rabiner. (3) Union bound: P_error at most sum_i pi_i sum_{j not i} exp(-T Delta*_ij) with Delta*_ij the max over s of Delta_s, the HMM analogue of Viterbi's bound; the minimum pairwise exponent governs error. (4) Taxonomy: prove s to 0 recovers the Juang-Rabiner KL rate, ML optimizes only the diagonal self-term, MMI is a first-order relaxation of the union-bound exponent, MDI is its fit term, unifying all four. (5) Training with descent proof: maximize the minimum Delta*_ij subject to a likelihood-fidelity constraint via a soft-min surrogate; use Perron eigenvalue perturbation for gradients and derive Baum-style growth-transformation reestimation with a monotone-improvement proof; a corollary quantifies how geometric duration inflates confusability. (6) Validate on connected-digit and isolated-word tasks in the corpus: check the predicted exponent versus measured error, match Juang-Rabiner values cheaply, and reduce confusions beyond ML and MMI.

paper_title: Parametric shape recognition using a probabilistic inverse theory
motivation: Whaite and Ferrie's active exploration (1991-1994) plans gaze to reduce a superquadric model's parameter covariance, but the optimization is myopic (greedy gradient on the covariance determinant, one step), single-model, cost-blind, and uses an ad-hoc size/gradient heuristic to allocate scans across multi-part scenes. Model-class discrimination (Subrahmonia/Cooper/Keren 1992, isolated objects only) and model-adequacy testing (knowing-when-we-are-wrong chi-squared residual statistics) are separate machineries never jointly optimized, and detected misfit is never used to actively search for a better model class such as higher-degree implicit polynomials. No unified, budget-aware, non-myopic planner jointly reduces class uncertainty, parameter uncertainty, and model-inadequacy while allocating limited scanning across a whole multi-part scene, which matters for autonomous systems with finite time and energy facing multiple, possibly mis-modeled parts.
method: Cast next-view selection as budget-constrained, non-myopic search maximizing expected reduction of one unified uncertainty. Segment range data into parts; give each part a hypothesis set spanning superquadric to higher-degree implicit polynomials, a Bayesian class posterior, a parameter covariance, and a residual misfit statistic. Per-part uncertainty is a weighted sum of class-posterior entropy, log-determinant of the covariance, and expected misfit; scene uncertainty sums over parts. For each candidate view on the view sphere, predict revealed surfaces and expected samples, then estimate the drop in scene uncertainty using the closed-form prediction-variance term for the covariance component and an asymptotic Bayesian Mahalanobis update for the class component. Replace one-step gradient descent with receding-horizon rollout or beam search over the view sphere maximizing summed expected gain minus weighted travel-and-acquisition cost under a total budget; since gains are near-submodular, greedily allocate each scan to the part-view pair with highest marginal gain per unit cost (knapsack-style), replacing the size/gradient heuristic. When a part's misfit statistic exceeds its chi-squared threshold, expand its hypothesis set with the next higher-complexity model and re-value views for discriminating that enlarged set, turning misfit detection into active model search. Stop at a target uncertainty or budget exhaustion. Evaluate on laser-rangefinder scans of single and multi-part, occluded, and deliberately mis-modeled objects against the greedy covariance-determinant planner, random and uniform views, and a discrimination-only Bayesian planner, measuring views and path-cost to reach target certainty, recognition accuracy, and robustness to model inadequacy.

paper_title: The Recognition of Human Movement Using Temporal Templates
motivation: View-based motion recognizers (MEI/MHI Hu moments, orientation histograms, SHOSLIF, gesture HMMs) and 3D model-based trackers all commit to a class even when inputs fall outside competence: untrained viewpoint, novel gesture, failed segmentation, or occlusion. The only reliability tool in the corpus is one global confidence threshold (SHOSLIF), conflating causes and yielding confident errors in deployed systems (ALIVE, KidsRoom). No source lets a recognizer know when it does not know.
method: Add a competence-aware layer with four calibrated detectors: input-quality (flow-outlier fraction plus silhouette stability for segmentation/occlusion), viewpoint-competence (MEI Hu-moment aspect bank flags out-of-range views), novelty (per-class density gives open-set out-of-vocabulary detection), and cross-representation consistency (shape vs phase-space disagreement). Fuse into a calibrated reliability plus attributed cause via risk-coverage tuning, then accept, back off, abstain, or request a new view. Evaluate under untrained angles, occlusion, and novel gestures via risk-coverage and confident-error versus forced-choice and single-threshold baselines.

paper_title: Accurate Unlexicalized Parsing
motivation: Statistical parsing progress is tracked mainly by one aggregate PARSEVAL score on WSJ, yet the parsers in these sources reach similar accuracy through very different mechanisms, and the field lacks a shared way to observe which linguistic dependency types each parser recovers and which internal components such as bilexical head words versus distance, subcategorization, or structural priors are responsible. Collins reports a per-dependency-type breakdown for only one model on one WSJ section, others report incomparable metrics, and the corpus-variation study shows accuracy drops off-WSJ without saying which components fail. This is an evidence gap: there is no benchmark or attribution methodology to accumulate comparable, phenomenon-level, cross-corpus evidence about what statistical parsers have actually learned.
method: Build a reusable parser-autopsy benchmark. A shared harness converts gold and each parser output into normalized head-dependency triples and reports precision and recall per dependency type and per hard construction such as PP attachment, coordination, adjuncts, NP modification, and long distance. Controlled ablation disables one conditioning source at a time and reruns the harness to attribute each component contribution per phenomenon. Minimal-pair probing compares model probabilities of two candidate parses to isolate learned lexical preference from search errors. Everything is rerun on WSJ and a second genre such as Brown to measure per-component generalization, yielding an attribution report indexed by component, phenomenon, and corpus.

paper_title: Freeman Code Based Online Handwritten Character Recognition for Malayalam Using Backpropagation Neural Networks
motivation: The six works all recognize handwritten characters of scripts dense with visually similar shapes, but each uses ad hoc, script-specific engineering: chain-code histograms, a vertical/horizontal positional analyzer, a Kohonen context bitmap, and k-NN direction+curvature for Malayalam; 2DPCA+nearest-neighbor plus a hand-grouped confusion table with interest-point/Fourier rules for Tamil; and dot count/placement for Arabic. A common pattern recurs: a global-shape first-stage classifier saturates, then a script-specific post-processing stage is added to resolve residual confusions among similar characters. Gaps: (1) no principled, script-independent way to say why two characters are confusable or to predict confusion pairs/accuracy before training (pairs are found empirically via LOOCV confusion matrices and grouped by hand); (2) the choice and number of disambiguating cues is guessed per pair, so nothing transfers across scripts though the same feature channels (position, direction, curvature, topology, diacritic/dot) recur everywhere; (3) no formal account of when and how much a two-stage scheme can help. This matters because manual cue-engineering is the dominant cost and blocks generalization across scripts.
method:
A formal, script-agnostic theory of character confusability that derives the observed two-stage strategies.

1) Channel ontology and a conceptual distinction: model each class as a joint distribution over orthogonal structural channels abstracting the corpus features (positional/zone, directional/chain-code, curvature, topological/stroke-order, differential/diacritic, spatial-context bitmap). Distinguish global-shape channels (high mutual information with identity across the alphabet; first-stage) from local-differential channels (low global but high within-clique conditional information; disambiguation). This formalizes the first-stage/post-processing split.

2) Confusability functional and error-decomposition theorem: for a channel subset S with class-conditional densities, define pairwise confusability C_S(a,b) via the Bhattacharyya coefficient (an upper bound on two-class Bayes error) and a weighted confusion graph. Prove that minimum error under S equals a separable term plus a residual confusion mass concentrated on heavy edges (the object the LOOCV confusion matrix estimates). Corollary: post-processing removes at most this residual mass, and the value of adding channels S2 to first-stage S1 equals the residual mass on edges whose overlap drops below target error under S1 union S2, bounding the Tamil paper's reported gains.

3) Minimal-disambiguating-channel objective: per confusion clique, choose the smallest channel subset pushing every pairwise overlap below tolerance epsilon. Show this is weighted set cover (channels cover pairs they separate); via additivity of Bhattacharyya exponents across conditionally independent channels, obtain a submodular surrogate, so greedy selection has a (1+ln n) guarantee. The manual Tamil interest-point rule and Arabic dot rule are special cases.

4) Derived taxonomy: label each heavy edge by the channel that most reduces its overlap (positional, directional, curvature, topological, differential). This yields falsifiable predictions of which pairs a given feature set must confuse.

5) Validation: instantiate channels using the six papers' features/datasets, estimate distributions, build the confusion graph, and compare predicted heavy edges to reported empirical confusions; test whether predicted accuracy tracks measured accuracy and whether greedy channel sets recover the hand-chosen cues.

paper_title: A Simple Rule-Based Part of Speech Tagger
motivation: Bridge opportunity across three streams never joined. The probabilistic HMM tagging line (Church 1988; Kupiec 1989; Cutting 1992) reaches about 96 percent but assumes a reliable lexicon listing each word's possible tags; unknown words are patched by a suffix heuristic and a default open-class ambiguity class. The lexicon-free morphological-coding line (Klein and Simmons 1963) predicts word class at about 90 percent with no dictionary using affix tests plus context-frame rules, but is hand-built and non-probabilistic. The speech language-modeling line (Markov source modeling 1985; phoneme-to-text 1986) decodes noisy uncertain word streams and speculated that grammatical or POS equivalence classes could sharpen decoding, but had no trainable morphological tagger to plug in. Why it matters: leaving clean in-domain text for new genres, ASR or phoneme output, OCR, or historical text breaks both assumptions at once, since the lexicon is absent or wrong and OOV soars, and tokens are uncertain. No work connects the morphological-generative and probabilistic-HMM traditions into one trainable model that also tolerates a noisy channel.
method: Relax the two assumptions of statistical taggers, a complete lexicon and clean tokens. Keep the HMM tag-transition structure, optionally with Kupiec selective state chains, but replace the lexicon plus ambiguity-class plus default-class scaffolding with a generative morphological emission model for word given tag: a per-tag character or morpheme sub-model that decomposes a token into stem plus affixes and scores it with a within-tag character n-gram generator in a trie. Any token, seen or unseen, gets a nonzero form-informed probability, subsuming the ambiguity-class trick and suffix heuristic into one process, with Klein and Simmons affixes seeding the priors. Train by Baum-Welch EM on unlabeled text with no lexicon, or with only a small seed affix list as priors, giving an open-vocabulary tagger whose parameters do not grow with vocabulary. Extend to noisy input by composing with a channel model for observation given word, such as phoneme-confusion or OCR errors, so decoding jointly recovers tags and words in one Viterbi pass, with POS transitions acting as the grammatical equivalence-class constraint the IBM work called for. Evaluate tagging accuracy versus rising OOV and domain shift against lexicon-dependent baselines, joint tag and transcription accuracy on pseudophonetic input versus a word n-gram source, and ablations against suffix-heuristic, default-open-class, and hand-rule Klein and Simmons baselines.

paper_title: Learning to Predict by the Methods of Temporal Differences
motivation: Real-time associative-learning models built from neuron-like adaptive elements — the Sutton–Barto element ("Toward a Modern Theory of Adaptive Networks," 1981), its TD-based successor ("A Temporal-Difference Model of Classical Conditioning," 1987), and the nictitating-membrane simulation (Moore et al., 1986) — are celebrated for reproducing a wide range of conditioning phenomena: ISI dependency curves, blocking, conditioned inhibition, higher-order conditioning, CR topography, and even the temporal-primacy-vs-prior-training result of Kehoe, Schreurs & Graham (1987). However, these successes conceal a serious reliability/brittleness risk. The models' most important empirical predictions are not produced by the learning rule itself but are essentially inherited from a hand-chosen, "unspecified coding process" that converts each CS into a temporally extended stimulus trace x_i(t). The 1981 paper states outright that if the UCS leaves no trace "one can obtain an ISI dependency curve whose shape resembles that of the stimulus trace function"; the 1986 simulation concedes CS inputs "are instead shaped by unspecified coding processes so as to produce outputs that conform with the real-time properties of NM conditioning." In other words, the trace shape, duration, delay, and eligibility decay are free knobs tuned per paradigm to match data, making the fits partly circular, non-reproducible across modelers, and fragile: different but equally plausible trace choices yield qualitatively different (and sometimes contradictory) predictions about ISI optima, primacy, and topography. This is precisely the "escaping brittleness" concern raised in the 1986 rule-system work, but at the level of temporal representation rather than symbolic rules. None of the provided works learns the temporal representation; they assume it and then evaluate the learning rule on top of it. This leaves open a concrete gap: can the temporal representation be derived rather than stipulated, and how much of the models' explanatory power survives once we remove the tuned trace?
method: Turn the assumed stimulus trace into a learned internal representation and then stress-test reliability. (1) Build a two-stage real-time network: a hidden bank of temporal-basis units (tapped-delay lines / leaky integrators whose delays, time-constants, and eligibility-decay parameters are adjustable) feeding a Sutton–Barto/TD output element that predicts imminent reinforcement. Train the hidden parameters by propagating the TD prediction error (s(t)-s(t-1) target) back into the basis units using the error-propagation machinery of "Learning Internal Representations by Error Propagation," so the temporal code that produces CRs is discovered from the CS–US timing statistics rather than hand-set. (2) Quantify the brittleness of the incumbent fixed-trace models: sweep a family of plausible trace functions (exponential, gamma, delayed-onset, variable duration) through the 1981/1986/1987 models and measure how much core predictions — ISI-optimum location, blocking magnitude, and the primacy-vs-prior-training outcome — move as a function of arbitrary trace choices, producing a sensitivity/brittleness map that makes the hidden degrees of freedom explicit. (3) Evaluate the learned-representation model against the same battery (acquisition, extinction, ISI curves peaking near 250 ms, blocking, conditioned inhibition, CR topography, and Kehoe et al.'s serial-compound CSA-CSB-US primacy result) under a single fixed set of learning-rate parameters with no per-experiment retuning, testing whether one model reproduces all phenomena simultaneously. (4) Test generalization/robustness: train on a subset of ISIs and serial arrangements and check zero-shot prediction of held-out ISIs and novel compound orderings, and check stability under input noise and time-step granularity. Success criteria are: predictions become far less sensitive to representational assumptions (flatter brittleness map), the same parameters fit multiple paradigms, and held-out timing phenomena are predicted — converting an assumption-laden, tuned account into a reproducible, self-contained one and isolating which conditioning phenomena are genuinely explained by TD learning versus smuggled in through the trace.

paper_title: Learning Distributed Representations of Concepts Using Linear Relational Embedding
motivation: Nets are charged with lacking systematicity, yet Elman's SRN shows John1:John2::Mary1:Mary2 and RAAM builds all 16 LOVED-X-Y frames from 4 trained; the role-by-filler geometry proving this is exactly what tree-clustering, the field's main tool, cannot express, so it was averaged away.
method: Tag SRN and RAAM hidden vectors by role and filler, fit a bilinear style-content model via truncated SVD, and score systematicity by a factorization index versus clustering plus held-out extrapolation to unseen role-filler combinations.

paper_title: Near-Optimal Reinforcement Learning in Polynomial Time
motivation: Singh and Dayan (1998) derive exact finite-trial bias/variance MSE curves for TD(lambda) and explain why learning behavior varies with alpha, lambda, mixing, determinism, and cyclicity, concluding no algorithm dominates. That account holds only for lookup tables; the authors note the effect of relaxing this is unknown. Function-approximation theory (Gordon 1995; Tsitsiklis and Van Roy) gives only worst-case asymptotic max-norm fixed-point bounds and ignores eligibility traces. Yet the key empirical fact (Singh and Sutton 1996) is that trace type and lambda strongly change performance under coarse coding on Mountain-Car. So the phenomenon that optimal lambda and the replacing-vs-accumulating advantage shift once states are aggregated has no mechanistic explanation. Explaining it would make trace and step-size choices predictable from representation and problem structure.
method: Extend Singh and Dayan's exact-MSE framework from lookup tables to soft state aggregation (Singh, Jaakkola, Jordan 1995). Since aggregation is a linear averager (Gordon 1995), offline TD(lambda) keeps a linear update, so bias-vector and covariance recurrences can be re-derived in cluster space and mapped to per-state predictions. Decompose MSE into representational bias (fixed-point gap, shrinking as lambda approaches 1), bootstrapping bias (from lambda below 1, decaying with mixing and determinism), and sampling variance (growing with lambda and within-trial revisitation, separating replacing from accumulating traces), all as functions of the aggregation map and chain structure. Build a tool that outputs exact MSE curves and the MSE-minimizing lambda given the chain and aggregation. Validate against Monte-Carlo-averaged curves on chains varying mixing, determinism, cyclicity, and coarseness, and check that predictions reproduce the Mountain-Car coarse-coding results of Singh and Sutton. Predicted mechanism: aggregation adds a bias floor higher lambda reduces at a variance cost amplified by revisitation and slow mixing, so optimal lambda rises with coarser aggregation and falls for cyclic or slow-mixing chains.

paper_title: Fuzzy Logic, Neural Networks, and Soft Computing
motivation: The provided works established many competing ways to build a fuzzy inference system but never a common way to compare them. Expert linguistic synthesis (Mamdani), Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy identification, ANFIS hybrid learning, temporal back-propagation, connectionist self-organizing fuzzy systems, genetic-algorithm design, and stable adaptive fuzzy control each report success on a different toy problem. Two gaps follow. First, there is no shared benchmark or apples-to-apples comparison; ANFIS notes no standard methods exist for building rule bases, and the connectionist paper states there is no systematic procedure for designing fuzzy logic systems. Second, the founding premise (Zadeh's linguistic variable, where each fuzzy set carries human-readable meaning like SMALL/LARGE) is quietly abandoned by the learning methods that improve accuracy: the genetic-algorithm paper reports that overlap restrictions were not placed on the sets and complete overlap could occur, and ANFIS relabels tuned sets as SMALL/LARGE even after gradient descent moves them arbitrarily. No work in this corpus measures whether automatically tuned membership functions and rule bases stay linguistically meaningful, nor quantifies the accuracy or rule-count price of keeping them interpretable. This matters because the practical appeal of fuzzy systems is transparency; if learning destroys it silently, practitioners choose methods blind to a core trade-off.
method: Build an empirical map placing the corpus design methods on a common performance-interpretability plane. Assemble a shared benchmark from tasks already used in these papers: inverted-pendulum control, Mackey-Glass prediction, nonlinear function approximation, a Takagi-Sugeno modeling task, and an expert-crafted Mamdani control task, with identical inputs, ranges, splits, and evaluation. Reimplement representative methods spanning manual to automatic: expert rule crafting, Takagi-Sugeno least-squares identification, ANFIS hybrid learning, temporal back-propagation, connectionist self-organizing learning, and genetic-algorithm design with and without its rule-count penalty. Define interpretability diagnostics grounded in linguistic-variable theory: membership-function distinguishability and overlap, input coverage and completeness, normality and convexity of learned sets, rule-base compactness, rule consistency, and consequent locality for TSK models, aggregated into a transparent index reported beside accuracy. Produce the map by scattering each method-task run in the performance-interpretability plane, tracing the Pareto frontier, and analyzing patterns such as interpretability lost per unit accuracy gained, which methods drift off the linguistic-meaning manifold as they optimize, and how the rule-count penalty or regularization shifts the frontier. As a controlled diagnostic, sweep interpretability-preserving constraints (overlap bounds, fixed anchors, monotonicity) on each learner to measure the causal cost of enforcing linguistic integrity. Deliverables are a reusable benchmark, a diagnostic toolkit, and a comparative map showing which method occupies which region of the accuracy-interpretability trade-off per task.

paper_title: Tests on a Cell Assembly Theory of the Action of the Brain, Using a Large Digital Computer
motivation: Evidence gap. These foundational works establish what neural nets can represent in principle but give no way to measure what a functioning network realizes. McCulloch and Pitts prove nerve nets realize propositional-logic expressions and that distinct neurophysiological assumptions can be behaviorally equivalent. Kleene sharpens this into an exact equivalence in which a nerve net or finite automaton represents all and only the regular events, grading behavior from definite events with bounded memory to full regular events requiring reverberating cycles for unbounded memory. Craik adds that the nervous system models external events. Yet none provides a way to observe, in an actual recording or trained recurrent network, which automaton the system realizes, how much theoretical capacity is used, or where the idealizations fail. Kleene himself flags that the theory assumes no errors in neuron functioning, unrealistic given the graded, refractory, partly analog behavior in the excitation, conduction, and synaptic-mechanism literature, and leaves the minimal-representation problem open. The field thus has deep existence theorems but no instruments to accumulate evidence about them: no benchmark grading tasks by regular-event complexity, no procedure to extract and validate the automaton a network implements, no audit of when the all-or-none idealization breaks down, and no empirical test of the equivalence or internal-model claims. This matters because modern claims that neural systems compute, have states, and model the world rest on this untested scaffolding.
method: Build an empirical automaton-auditing framework that turns the McCulloch-Pitts and Kleene existence theorems into measurable quantities, applied first to fully observable trained recurrent networks and then to neural recordings. A benchmark ladder provides stimulus-to-response tasks graded along Kleene's hierarchy, from definite events with fixed memory windows to full regular events needing reverberating-cycle memory. Automaton extraction treats input and output firing streams as event streams and inverts Kleene's state construction, clustering input histories into equivalence classes that yield distinguishable future responses to recover the minimal finite automaton consistent with observed behavior and its state count, operationalizing Kleene's open minimal-tables problem. A regularity score validates the automaton by held-out prediction on novel sequences and localizes where regularity breaks. An idealization audit uses temporal summation, refractoriness, synaptic delay, and inhibition timing to quantify deviations from the discrete error-free all-or-none model and measures how graded responses, jitter, and firing errors degrade the extracted automaton. An equivalence audit instantiates networks differing only in microscale assumptions McCulloch and Pitts claimed equivalent, such as inhibition by threshold-raising versus local opposition, and checks whether they yield the same automaton. A Craik internal-model test compares the extracted state-transition graph to the statistical and temporal structure of the stimulus environment. Reported per system, these metrics form a reusable benchmark for accumulating comparable evidence across biological and artificial networks.

paper_title: The Upstart Algorithm: A Method for Constructing and Training Feedforward Neural Networks
motivation: Evidence gap: the constructive network-growth algorithms (tiling, growth, three constructive algorithms) and their swappable inner linear-discriminant subroutines (perceptron, pocket, optimal linear discriminants, thermal perceptron, Minover) were never benchmarked on common ground. There is no controlled way to observe which yields smaller or better-generalizing networks, or whether gains come from the growth rule versus the discriminant. The tiling paper claim that fewer hidden units improve generalization rests on an informal phase-space-volume argument and is never measured, and no diagnostic tracks how internal representations, unit margins, or faithfulness efficiency evolve. This leaves room to build the missing measurement and benchmarking infrastructure.
method: Build a modular benchmark decoupling the growth strategy from the inner linear-discriminant learner: implement tiling, growth, and constructive algorithms behind one interface whose fit-a-unit call swaps among perceptron, pocket, optimal discriminants, thermal perceptron, and Minover, giving a strategy-by-discriminant grid. Evaluate on random Boolean functions, parity and symmetry, and the domain-wall-count task, varying input correlation and training-set size. Per cell, log network size, per-layer error decrement, held-out generalization error, faithfulness efficiency, and unit-stability distributions with confidence intervals. Test the size-to-generalization conjecture by correlating unit count with generalization within fixed tasks and controlled discriminant. Make the phase-space-volume argument measurable via Monte Carlo importance sampling over weight space to estimate each architecture solution-space volume ratio, testing whether larger ratios and smaller networks predict better generalization. Deliver a public benchmark, per-method diagnostics, and an evidence-based ranking.

paper_title: Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers
motivation: The sources split early machine intelligence into learners that generalize from experience (Rosenblatt's perceptron; Farley and Clark's self-organizing system; Rochester et al.'s cell-assembly net) and search systems (Shannon's chess program; the chess-complexity papers; Strachey). Shared unresolved question: where does generalization beyond training data come from? Rosenblatt says the perceptron generalizes only in a differentiated environment of similar correlated stimuli, treating similarity as given by the stimulus and random A-unit wiring, and admits statistical separability cannot capture relational concepts. Goodman's Fact, Fiction and Forecast argues similarity and projectibility are not given by data (the grue riddle): generalization is silently fixed by a learner's predicates and representation. No source connects these; Farley and Clark even concede they did no systematic evaluation of their parameters. Gap: no controlled empirical map of how much these founding machines' generalization is set by built-in predicates and wiring versus data, and where each paradigm's bias succeeds or fails.
method: Build an empirical atlas of inductive bias for 1950s architectures, testing Goodman's projectibility riddle against Rosenblatt's differentiated-environment claim. Reimplement the perceptron and the Farley-Clark self-organizing net, with Shannon's minimax-plus-evaluation chess system as a search baseline. Generate parametric environments varying three axes: differentiation (random-overlapping to disjoint correlated classes); predicate ambiguity (paired labelings agreeing on all training data but diverging on held-out data, one natural stable-feature concept and one grue-like concept keyed to presentation order or region); and concept type (absolute versus relational like left-of). Sweep representation as an explicit variable: A-unit connectivity, feature detectors, or evaluation terms and lookahead depth. Measure Rosenblatt's probability of correct generalization on held-out data, split by natural-versus-grue convergence, plus sample efficiency, chance-collapse boundaries, and a projectibility index (fraction of representations under which the natural concept is learned). Output a comparative phase map showing where reliable generalization occurs, where it collapses to chance, and where a machine confidently learns the wrong grue projection, quantifying how much bias comes from wiring versus data.

paper_title: The Nonstochastic Multiarmed Bandit Problem
motivation: Evidence gap on equilibrium selection under no-regret dynamics. Regret-matching, Hedge, smooth fictitious play, calibrated-forecast play, and approachability procedures all guarantee only that empirical play converges to the SET of correlated equilibria, a high-dimensional polytope whose points differ in welfare, fairness, entropy, and actual correlation. The listed works never measure or benchmark which point is selected, how fast, or under which feedback and hyperparameters. The field lacks a standardized instrument to observe and compare selection behavior across these algorithms.
method: Build CE-Scope, an empirical benchmark. Assemble games whose CE polytopes are computed exactly by LP: Chicken, Battle-of-Sexes, Shapley cycling games, congestion games, zero-sum controls, and random games. Implement regret-matching, Hedge, smooth fictitious play, calibrated-forecast play, approachability play, and bandit variants under one interface, varying internal vs external regret, inertia, and step-size. Measure distance of empirical joint play to the polytope over time and its decay exponent, which face is selected, welfare relative to best and worst CE, joint entropy, mutual information capturing genuine correlation, and cycling. Over many seeds produce selection maps and test claims such as internal-regret reaching higher mutual information than external-regret and inertia shifting selection toward higher-entropy CE.

paper_title: Additive Logistic Regression: A Statistical View of Boosting
motivation: Resource bottleneck. Bagging (Breiman 1996) cuts the variance of unstable predictors (trees, neural nets, subset-selection regression) only by training and storing many models: many bootstrap re-fits at training and many evaluations plus large memory at deployment. Breiman notes this is compute-hungry (for neural nets, replications may need many days of computing) and that one loses a simple, interpretable structure. Gradient boosting (Friedman 1999) has the complementary cost: its stagewise additive expansion is sequential and yields hundreds of trees to store and evaluate. For real-time, edge, embedded, or large-scale deployment, and for interpretability-critical settings, these training, storage, and latency costs plus the loss of a single readable model are a real deployment and scalability bottleneck. Explaining bagging (Buhlmann and Yu 2000) argues bagging's benefit is essentially deterministic smoothing of hard-threshold indicator decisions precisely where the base learner is discontinuous and high-variance; Breiman agrees that instability lives in split points and variables competing for inclusion. If the gain is fundamentally smoothing of a few thresholds, paying for hundreds of re-trainings and storing an ensemble is wasteful. None of the five works asks whether bagging's smoothing can be produced directly from one fitted model, without the bootstrap, leaving room to remove the resource bottleneck while keeping accuracy and recovering interpretability comparable to a Generalized Additive Model (Hastie and Tibshirani 1990).
method: Analytic Bagging reproduces bagging's variance reduction from one fitted model by smoothing its hard-threshold decisions, with bandwidths estimated cheaply rather than by resampling. Fit one base learner on the full data (a CART tree, or a forward subset-selection linear model). Extract its decision atoms: each split indicator and each variable-inclusion indicator. For each threshold, estimate the sampling spread sigma that bagging would average over, without many re-fits, via an analytic delta-method or influence-function estimate using the local gradient and curvature of the split criterion (the perturbation machinery of Practical Optimization, Gill, Murray and Wright 1981), or a small calibration set of subsamples used only to fit sigma. Replace each hard split indicator by a smooth sigmoid transition scaled by sigma, the closed form Buhlmann and Yu give as the population limit of the bagged indicator, composing the smoothed atoms into one compact model: soft split gates for trees, or a shrinkage weight per selected variable, yielding a GAM-style representation (Hastie and Tibshirani 1990). Extend to boosting by smoothing every split across the stagewise expansion so the additive function-space model (Friedman 1999) becomes differentiable and can be lightly re-tuned with line-search or Newton methods, instead of adding trees for variance control. Evaluate on Breiman's benchmarks (waveform, heart, breast cancer, ionosphere, diabetes, glass, subset-selection simulation), claiming full-bagging accuracy while measuring wins in training compute, model size, and inference latency versus ensembles of 25 to 100, with ablations on analytic versus small-sample sigma, sensitivity to sigma, and interpretability. This decouples bagging's statistical benefit from its costly resampling and ensemble-storage mechanism, giving bagging or boosting-level accuracy at single-model cost, memory, and latency in an interpretable form.

paper_title: Learning Distributed Representations of Concepts Using Linear Relational Embedding
motivation:
Resource bottleneck: constructing an empirical similarity space with multidimensional scaling (MDS) requires human pairwise (dis)similarity judgments, whose number grows as O(N^2) in the number of items. Kruskal's nonmetric MDS and the broader MDS enterprise (Young) therefore confine psychological similarity studies to small item sets (typically tens of objects); building large, corpus-scale semantic maps from human data is experimentally infeasible because of the judgment-collection burden and the fatigue/quality decay of collecting thousands of ratings from each participant.

At the same time, Latent Semantic Analysis (Landauer & Dumais) shows that a fully automatic method can induce a usable similarity structure over an essentially unlimited vocabulary directly from text, with no human judgments at all. But LSA has two limitations relevant here: (1) its core singular value decomposition of the word-by-document matrix is compute-heavy and static — adding items forces recomputation — and (2) its cosine similarities are not calibrated to the specific human judgment space an experimenter cares about and are known to diverge from it in systematic ways (e.g., polysemy, low co-occurrence). The "indexing by LSA" work already shows that Random Mapping gives an inexpensive, incrementally-updatable approximation to LSA vectors, sidestepping SVD, and Kruskal's method critically depends only on the RANK ORDER (monotone relationship) of dissimilarities, not their exact values.

The gap: no method exploits cheap, scalable corpus-derived similarity to drastically cut the amount of expensive human judgment needed to recover a VALID MDS configuration. Bridging the scalable-but-uncalibrated corpus signal with the valid-but-unscalable human signal would remove the dominant cost that keeps empirical similarity spaces small.
method:
Propose "corpus-seeded active MDS": a pipeline that recovers a human-valid MDS configuration for large item sets while collecting only a small, actively chosen subset of human judgments.

1. Cheap full prior matrix. For N items, build an initial N x N dissimilarity matrix from corpus co-occurrence using the Random Mapping approximation to LSA (no SVD; supports incrementally adding items later). This gives, for free, an ordering of all pairs.

2. Rank-order seeding. Because Kruskal's nonmetric MDS uses only the monotone (rank) relationship between dissimilarities and distances, feed the corpus rank order into nonmetric MDS to obtain an initial low-dimensional configuration at zero human cost.

3. Active sampling of human judgments. Iteratively select a small budget (target O(N) to O(N log N) pairs instead of O(N^2)) of the most informative pairs to send to human raters, choosing pairs that (a) contribute the largest local stress, (b) show the largest disagreement between the current MDS distances and the corpus rank, or (c) have unreliable corpus signal (low co-occurrence counts / high polysemy). These are the pairs where corpus similarity is most likely to mislead.

4. Learned calibration transform. From the sampled human judgments, fit a monotone transform (and optionally a low-rank/bilinear correction, in the spirit of separating a shared "content" axis from a domain-specific "style" distortion) that maps corpus dissimilarities onto human dissimilarities. Apply it to the full matrix so that the small human sample is generalized to all N^2 pairs.

5. Refit and iterate. Re-run nonmetric MDS on the calibrated matrix, recompute stress, re-select the next batch of informative pairs, and repeat until stress stabilizes.

Evaluation. On item sets for which a full human dissimilarity matrix already exists (e.g., classic MDS/similarity datasets), measure how few human judgments are needed for the corpus-seeded active procedure to reproduce the gold-standard full-human configuration (via Procrustes alignment and stress), compared with (i) random pair sampling and (ii) corpus-only MDS with no human input. Sweep item-set size N to show that per-item human cost grows sublinearly, enabling MDS spaces one to two orders of magnitude larger than current practice. The Random Mapping backbone additionally lets new items be folded in and re-calibrated without recomputing an SVD, addressing both the human-data and compute bottlenecks.

This directly targets the resource bottleneck: it converts the O(N^2) human experimental burden of MDS into a small actively chosen sample, uses an SVD-free incremental corpus model for scalability, and exploits MDS's rank-only requirement so that a coarse but cheap similarity signal is sufficient to seed and be corrected toward a valid human space.

paper_title: Solving the Multiple Instance Problem with Axis-Parallel Rectangles
motivation: Compass and dynamic reposing outperform fixed pose 3D QSAR like CoMFA, and ablations show the gain comes almost entirely from automatic pose selection, yet no work explains why. Geometric recovery says the objective finds the true bioactive pose; invariance says any self consistent alignment would do. This matters because recovered poses are read mechanistically to guide synthesis, yet no source shows when a pose is identifiable or why dynamic reposing beats tangent distance.
method: Build semi synthetic benchmarks with a known receptor template so the true pose is known, plus steroid, musk, and 5HT1A sets with reference poses. Measure pose recovery and prediction accuracy separately and correlate. Intervene with oracle, model selected, wrong but consistent, random, and adversarial poses, crossed with nonlinear net versus PLS and reposing versus tangent distance. Accuracy tracking correctness supports recovery; a wrong consistent alignment matching accuracy supports invariance. Derive an identifiability condition for a unique consensus shape optimum as a function of chemotype diversity and actives, and validate by titrating diversity, yielding a causal account and a diagnostic for when mechanistic conclusions are unwarranted.

paper_title: Learning to Predict by the Methods of Temporal Differences
motivation: The sources contain a proliferation of real-time neural models of classical conditioning, all descendants of Rescorla-Wagner built around a prediction-error signal plus a stimulus-eligibility trace: the Sutton-Barto element, its nictitating-membrane variant by Moore et al., the temporal-difference model, and Klopf's drive-reinforcement model. Each is claimed by its own authors to reproduce a large overlapping battery of phenomena such as acquisition, extinction, ISI functions, CR topography, blocking, overshadowing, conditioned inhibition, second-order conditioning, partial reinforcement, backward conditioning, and serial-compound effects, and the neuronal model asserts it eliminates inconsistencies of earlier models. But these validations were done in isolation, with different time steps, different and often unspecified CS representations, different parameters, and largely qualitative comparison to hand-picked data. The Kehoe, Schreurs and Graham temporal-primacy experiment shows how one carefully designed protocol can discriminate among models, favoring real-time over trial-level accounts and revealing that Sutton-Barto derives temporal primacy from the same mechanism as second-order conditioning. Yet no common quantitative benchmark exists, so one cannot tell whether a model's success reflects its core mechanism, meaning the form of the error term, the eligibility-trace shape, or the CS representation, or merely a fortunate encoding and parameter choice. This matters because the same ingredients are exported to engineering reinforcement learning and adaptive control, including the neuronal model's claimed relevance to adaptive control and signal processing and the TD prediction idea underlying Learning to Predict Sequences, the checkers work, and the discrete-time Markov controller. A factorized empirical understanding of which ingredient is necessary or sufficient for which phenomenon would clarify both the biology and the transferable computational principles.
method: An Empirical Mapping contribution building a standardized benchmark, unified simulation harness, and diagnostic phenomenon-by-mechanism map for the family of prediction-error conditioning models. Step one is a test battery encoding the canonical conditioning paradigms as machine-readable real-time CS and US event timelines at fixed 10 ms resolution following Moore et al., covering acquisition, extinction, forward-delay and trace ISI series, within-trial CR topography, blocking, overshadowing, conditioned inhibition with summation and retardation tests, second-order conditioning and its inter-stimulus decay, partial reinforcement, backward conditioning, and the discriminating serial-compound temporal-primacy versus prior-training protocol from Kehoe et al. Step two curates quantitative empirical targets from the cited rabbit nictitating-membrane literature as scoring metrics, including the roughly 250 ms ISI optimum with tail-off, the decreasing-latency and growing-amplitude topography peaking at the US, the primacy-overrides-blocking asymmetry, and the decay of second-order conditioning over 0 to 2000 ms, each with a continuous fit metric and a pass or fail qualitative-signature test. Step three builds a factorized harness that re-implements all candidate models within one interface separating four interchangeable components, namely CS representation, eligibility and trace dynamics, the prediction-error term, and the response mapping, so that the published models are specific component settings and novel hybrids occupy unused combinations. Step four runs a systematic factorial sweep evaluating every model and component combination on every phenomenon across principled parameter grids, recording fit, pass or fail, and the sensitivity of each success to parameters and representation choice. Step five delivers the empirical map, a phenomenon-by-mechanism matrix identifying which ingredient is necessary and sufficient for each phenomenon, and flagging phenomena whose reported successes are fragile to encoding or parameters, released together with recommended discriminating protocols and implications for prediction-based reinforcement learning and adaptive control.

paper_title: PAC-Bayesian Model Averaging
motivation:
A powerful line of work efficiently maintains a mixture over the exponentially many prunings of a template tree and predicts online, provably competitive with the single best pruning in hindsight. Helmbold & Schapire ("Predicting nearly as well as the best pruning of a decision tree") synthesize expert-advice bounds with Buntine/Willems-style recursions to get updates costing only O(path length); Pereira & Singer extend this to the richer class of edge-based prunings and to any bounded loss under the Freund–Schapire framework; Oliver & Hand show empirically that averaging over prunings beats single pruned trees. Complexity-regularization / MDL and PAC-Bayesian analyses (Barron; McAllester; Kearns et al.) explain the size/complexity penalty these mixtures pay as a prior over models.

All of these guarantees, however, are anchored to a *single, fixed* comparator: the best pruning (and, implicitly, fixed node predictors estimated once) for the entire data stream. This assumes stationarity. In the very applications these methods target — statistical language modeling of streaming text whose topic/vocabulary shifts, and streaming classification with concept drift — the pruning that predicts best early in the stream is often not the one that predicts best later, and rarely-visited node statistics go stale. Against a drifting environment, the best fixed pruning can be arbitrarily worse than the best *sequence* of prunings, so the existing regret bounds become vacuous. None of the provided sources address non-stationarity, tracking, or a shifting comparator (searches for "tracking"/"nonstationary" return nothing), and the naive fix — running a shifting-experts weight-share across the exponentially many prunings each round — destroys the product/recursion structure that made these methods efficient. This leaves open a concrete gap: can the elegant O(depth) tree-mixture machinery be made to work under the weaker, more realistic assumption of a drifting best pruning?
method:
We propose Drifting Tree Mixtures (DTM), a relaxation of the tree-mixture prediction framework from the stationary "best fixed pruning" regime to the non-stationary regime where the comparator is the best *sequence* of prunings with a bounded number of switches, while preserving per-example cost linear in the path depth.

Core idea — localize the switch/share. The static algorithms exploit that a pruning's mixture weight factorizes into a product over nodes of a local "stop (be a leaf) vs. continue (recurse into subtree)" decision, enabling a bottom-up recurrence. Instead of applying a global fixed-share step over all prunings (infeasible), DTM injects a per-node switching kernel with a small parameter alpha into exactly this recurrence: after each Bayesian-style multiplicative update, each node mixes a fraction alpha of its accumulated stop/continue weight back toward the node's prior (a convex combination of "keep current local decision" and "revert to prior"). Because the global pruning weight is a product of local factors, a convex mix applied factor-by-factor still yields a valid, computable sum over prunings — now a sum over *time-indexed pruning sequences*, with each local switch contributing a log(1/alpha) penalty. This keeps the recurrence intact and the per-round update O(depth), for both node-based (Helmbold–Schapire) and edge-based (Pereira–Singer) pruning classes and any bounded/logarithmic loss via the Freund–Schapire weight-allocation framework.

Two relaxations combined: (1) drifting structure — the switching kernel lets the effective pruning move over time; (2) drifting leaf statistics — replace the once-estimated node predictors with discounted/sliding-window count estimators (Krichevsky–Trofimov with decay), so stale, rarely-visited nodes adapt, directly addressing the poor-estimate problem Pereira & Singer raised.

Analysis. We prove a shifting-regret bound: cumulative loss of DTM <= loss of the best pruning sequence with m switches + O(complexity(prunings)*log|Sigma| + m*log(1/alpha) + T*alpha*C), and optimize alpha ~ m/T. This reinterprets the classical MDL/PAC-Bayesian complexity penalty (Barron; McAllester) as a *two-part temporal codelength*: a spatial term for pruning size plus a temporal term for the number of switches — a strict generalization that recovers the existing single-pruning bounds when m=0. We also give a PAC-Bayesian reading of alpha as a prior over switch times.

Evaluation. (a) Streaming language modeling with induced drift: extend Pereira & Singer's next-word prediction by concatenating text from shifting domains/topics; measure per-symbol log-loss/perplexity vs. static node- and edge-based mixtures and back-off models. (b) Synthetic and real concept-drift classification streams (abrupt and gradual drift) built on C4.5-style template trees; compare against static tree mixtures, a periodically-retrained C4.5, and a fixed-share-over-experts baseline. Success criteria: DTM matches static mixtures in stationary segments and substantially reduces loss across drift points, at the same asymptotic time/space cost, with empirical regret tracking the theoretical bound in m and alpha.

paper_title: A Survey of Industrial Model Predictive Control Technology
motivation: Industrial MPC uses two-stage optimization: an economic steady-state target calculation plus a dynamic control QP. The robust steady-state target calculation shows this target is acutely sensitive to steady-state gain uncertainty and recasts the robust target as a second-order cone program whose back-off shifts the economic optimum and governs feasibility. Gains and their uncertainty come from plant testing and identification, which the field study of industrial modeling and the NMPC overview identify as the dominant cost of MPC projects. The gap is that identification minimizes generic prediction error, agnostic to what the controller economically needs, so budget is spent on gains that never affect the operating point while economically critical gain directions stay uncertain. No corpus work allocates limited plant-test resources to reduce the gain-uncertainty directions that matter for the economics and feasibility of the MPC target.
method: Close the loop between the robust MPC target program and plant testing via economics-aware adaptive experiment design. Solve the robust target program with an ellipsoidal gain-uncertainty set from the identification covariance, and use its dual to rank which gain directions most degrade economics or inflate constraint-violation risk. Because the identification information matrix is affine in input power spectrum, cast experiment design as a convex program choosing test-signal spectra, per-input excitation energy, perturbation directions, and duration to minimize economic back-off from residual uncertainty, subject to a plant-test budget and output-excursion limits. Iterate greedily: run a test segment, re-estimate gains and covariance by subspace identification, re-solve the target program to find newly binding constraints, re-optimize the next segment, and stop when the marginal economic value of further excitation falls below marginal test cost. Validate on the heavy-oil-fractionator benchmark against broadband and D-optimal designs.

paper_title: Off-line Path Integral Reinforcement Learning Using Stochastic Robot Dynamics Approximated By Sparse Pseudo-input Gaussian Processes: Application to Humanoid Robot Motor Learning in the Real Environment
motivation:
Path-integral policy improvement (PI², "A generalized path integral control approach to reinforcement learning") has become a workhorse for learning high-dimensional robot behaviors such as the whole-body center-of-mass movements studied on the CB humanoid and, in model-based form, biped stepping via a GP-approximated Poincaré map. In every case the two knobs that most affect success — the magnitude/structure of exploration noise and the temperature/action-cost weighting (λ, R) — are set by heuristic. This is not a minor tuning nuisance: Doya's continuous-time RL study reports that performance was "very unstable" and depended strongly on the exploration noise size σ0 and the action cost c, and Morimoto & Atkeson rely on GP model uncertainty as an implicit, state-dependent noise source. Strikingly, Kappen's path-integral optimal-control theory — the very transformation of the nonlinear HJB equation into a linear/partition-function form that underlies PI² — predicts that the noise level ν produces qualitatively different optimal controls: above a critical value the optimal control is the *average* of competing deterministic solutions, while below it the control *commits* to one solution (symmetry breaking at a critical ν). 

The explanation gap: no work connects this symmetry-breaking mechanism to the observed, poorly-understood variability of robot RL — why a given task sometimes converges to one gait versus another, why learning oscillates or blends conflicting solutions into a failing controller, and why exploration-noise magnitude and action cost so sharply govern outcomes. Practitioners treat these phenomena as empirical quirks; the field lacks a causal, theoretical account linking exploration/cost parameters to which solution is learned and to convergence robustness. Closing this gap would convert exploration and cost tuning from black art into a predictable design principle.
method: Provide a mechanistic account of robot RL variability by reinterpreting path-integral policy improvement as a statistical-mechanics partition sum and testing Kappen's symmetry-breaking prediction directly on the sources' robot tasks. (1) Cast the whole-body CoM dynamic-balancing task and the GP-Poincaré-map biped stepping task in PI² form, where each iteration's update is a weighting of noisy rollouts by w ∝ exp(−S/λ). (2) Define per-iteration diagnostics computable from the sampled rollouts: the free energy F = −λ log Σ exp(−S/λ), the participation ratio / effective number of dominant trajectories, and the multimodality of the update (cluster elite rollouts in policy-parameter space). These operationalize "averaging" (many comparable modes) versus "committing" (one dominant mode). (3) Using Kappen's Laplace approximation around competing local minima of the cost/action, derive a predicted critical temperature/noise λ_c(x) as a function of the local curvature and the gap between competing solutions, yielding a falsifiable boundary between the averaging and symmetry-broken regimes. (4) Empirically sweep the exploration covariance Σ_ε and temperature/action cost (λ, R) across both tasks in the SL simulator with the CB humanoid dynamics, plus the low-dimensional cart-pole/pendulum benchmarks from Doya to reproduce his instability findings; check whether the transition from converged single-gait behavior to oscillating or blended-and-failing controllers coincides with the predicted crossing of λ_c and with a drop/jump in the participation-ratio and free-energy diagnostics. (5) Test the model-based case: treat the GP posterior variance of the Poincaré map as a state-dependent noise term and evaluate the hypothesis that uncertainty-modulated exploration keeps the learner on the "committing" side of the critical point in well-sampled regions while averaging in unexplored regions — offering a mechanistic explanation for why model-based RL converges in far fewer real-robot trials. (6) Deliver (a) an explanation of the observed phenomena as proximity to a symmetry-breaking critical point and (b) a predictive design rule that sets exploration covariance and cost weighting from the measured cost-landscape curvature to target a chosen regime, validated by out-of-sample prediction of which gait/solution is learned. Feasibility rests entirely on artifacts in the sources: the PI² weighting scheme, Kappen's linearized-HJB/Laplace theory, the SL/CB simulation platform, the GP (and sparse-GP) Poincaré-map machinery, and Doya's continuous-time benchmarks.

paper_title: The Strength of Weak Learnability
motivation: A recurring theme in this corpus is that PAC-learnability equals data compression. Occam's Razor: a consistent hypothesis of description length sublinear in sample size suffices for learnability. Board-Pitt: the converse holds for classes closed under exception lists. Kearns-Valiant crypto hardness is the contrapositive: Boolean formulae and DFAs are hard because compressing a pseudorandom sample would break a cryptosystem, so hardness is incompressibility. Gaps: length-based and dimension-based compression use separate machinery with no unifying measure (Board-Pitt note infinite domains need a different notion); compression amount is treated as binary though Sloan (slight, insufficient) versus Occam (sublinear, sufficient) imply a spectrum with an unformalized threshold; and improper versus proper compression is only anecdotal. A unified formal account would turn scattered theorems into one framework and clarify what boosting buys.
method: Build one theory of learning-as-compression. For any poly-time consistent compressor A, define its Effective Compression Dimension as the VC dimension of A's effective hypothesis space; prove it reduces to bit-length on finite domains and to VC dimension on infinite domains. Prove a master bound err below c times (ECD log m + log(1/delta))/m, with Occam and VC bounds as corollaries. Threshold theorem: define compression rate rho as the infimum over poly-time A of ECD; prove efficient PAC-learnability iff rho is sublinear in m, separating incompressible, slight-linear (Sloan), and sublinear (Occam), formalizing the compression gap. Give a two-axis taxonomy (strength and properness) with placement theorems for Occam, Board-Pitt, and Kearns-Valiant as an incompressibility lower bound. Recast Schapire boosting as amplification lifting slight to sublinear compression, giving weak-learnability equals sublinear compressibility.

paper_title: Neural Networks and Principal Component Analysis: Learning from Examples Without Local Minima
motivation: Scope-mismatch gap. Unsupervised feature learning here rests on narrow boundary conditions under which methods collapse to extracting second-order (covariance) structure, i.e. PCA. Oja's neuron extracts the first principal component of a static i.i.d. stream. Linsker's self-adaptive Hebbian network produces feature cells whose emergent structure is governed entirely by the input covariance function under static spontaneous activity. Bourlard and Kamp give the sharpest version: for auto-association with linear output and MSE, hidden nonlinearities are useless and the optimum is exactly SVD/Karhunen-Loeve (PCA); the decisive, unexamined boundary condition is that the target equals the input. Yet natural signals are temporally correlated, nonstationary, and dominated by higher-order structure. Elman and Zipser feed speech to backprop as static arrays of about 20 FFT frames and find rich features (vowel/consonant units plus novel nonstandard ones), but with no principled unsupervised objective explaining what should be captured, treating each token as static, and unexplained by the PCA-equivalence results. Gap: no principled unsupervised principle designed for the temporal/nonstationary regime that provably requires nonlinearity rather than making it useless.
method: Predictive-bottleneck learning: replace the auto-association target (reconstruct current input) with prediction of temporally adjacent frames (past/future context) through a low-dimensional bottleneck, and characterize how this escapes the PCA-equivalence regime. (1) Theory: show the Bourlard-Kamp nonlinearity-is-useless result is an artifact of the identity-target condition; for a bottleneck mapping context window x_t to a shifted target x_t+tau with nonlinear lagged dependencies, linear hidden units are strictly suboptimal, so nonlinearity becomes necessary. Prove the linear version of the predictive objective equals reduced-rank regression / canonical-correlation analysis between context and future (grounding in the Multivariate Analysis source), and that at zero lag it reduces exactly to the SVD/PCA autoencoder, so predictive coding strictly generalizes PCA-autoencoding with lagged cross-covariance replacing static covariance. (2) Local rule: derive a lagged-Hebbian rule correlating current presynaptic with future postsynaptic activity (Oja-style normalization on cross-covariance), and predict Linsker-type layered self-organization under this rule yields cells tuned to temporal/dynamic features rather than only static spatial-opponent patterns. (3) Experiments on the Elman-Zipser speech setup (Hamming-windowed FFT frames): a 2x2 comparison of {reconstruction target (PCA baseline), predictive target} by {linear, nonlinear hidden units}. Falsifiable predictions: nonlinearity gives no error reduction for reconstruction (confirming Bourlard-Kamp) but strict reduction for prediction; predictive bottlenecks capture phonetic distinctions and temporal dynamics better than equal-width reconstruction bottlenecks; downstream phoneme labeling improves; emergent hidden units show tuning to dynamic/transition features (consonant releases, formant transitions) rather than static spectral energy.

paper_title: An Adaptive Version of the Boost by Majority Algorithm
motivation:
Resource bottleneck at deployment. The voting methods studied in these works — bagging (Breiman 1996), AdaBoost (Freund & Schapire 1997), and randomized ensembles (Dietterich 2000) — obtain their accuracy by combining large numbers of base classifiers. The margins paper (Schapire, Freund, Bartlett & Lee 1998) explicitly documents ensembles of up to 1000 trees, and observes that test error keeps improving as the ensemble grows very large, so practitioners are pushed toward big ensembles. But every one of those T base learners (often a full decision tree) must be evaluated for every prediction, so inference cost, latency, memory, and energy scale linearly with T. This is a severe deployment/scalability friction for real-time and edge settings, and it is precisely the regime the theory rewards (large T => better margins).

Crucially, the same body of theory says the full ensemble is usually unnecessary per example. The margins result establishes that a prediction is just the sign of a weighted vote and that generalization is governed by the *distribution of margins*: most examples end up with large margins, i.e. their label is over-determined.
