The drifting-games framework (Schapire 2001; continuous drifting games 2000) provides potential functions that tightly bound how much a running weighted vote can still move given the remaining rounds and the permitted per-round movement set B (including multiclass and abstaining hypotheses). These two facts together imply that for the majority of test examples the final prediction can be certified long before all T classifiers are evaluated — yet no work here exploits margin/potential structure to cut *inference* cost. Existing size-reduction is limited to training-time tricks (e.g., outlier removal in Freund 1999 / additive-logistic-regression 1998) or blunt truncation to a fixed prefix, which sacrifices accuracy uniformly. The gap: a principled, per-example, accuracy-preserving way to spend base-learner evaluations only where they are needed.
method:
Propose "potential-certified anytime voting": a post-hoc, per-example early-exit rule for any trained voting ensemble (bagged, boosted, or randomized) that provably reproduces (or ε-approximates) the full ensemble's prediction while evaluating far fewer base classifiers on average.

1. Setup. Given base classifiers h_1..h_T with nonnegative weights alpha_t (alpha_t equal for bagging; the AdaBoost coefficients for boosting). For a test x, define the partial score after t evaluations s_t(x) = sum_{i<=t} alpha_i h_i(x) and the remaining budget R_t = sum_{i>t} alpha_i.

2. Exact (lossless) certification. Stop and output sign(s_t) as soon as |s_t| > R_t, because no assignment of the remaining votes can flip the sign — this yields exactly the full-ensemble label. Use the drifting-games potential (OS algorithm potentials over R^n with permitted movement set B) to generalize this test to multiclass and abstaining/graded hypotheses, where "R_t" becomes the max potential movement of the current-best label's lead.

3. Evaluation ordering. Because the exit rule triggers earlier when large-magnitude, high-agreement classifiers come first, learn a fixed evaluation order that minimizes expected evaluations: start from descending alpha_t, then greedily reorder on a validation set to maximize the fraction of examples certified early. This is a training-free reordering of an existing model.

4. Tunable approximate certification. Using the empirical margin distribution on a validation set, calibrate per-round thresholds tau_t so that stopping when |s_t| > tau_t disagrees with the full ensemble on at most epsilon of examples; drifting-games potentials bound this disagreement probability from the margin distribution, giving a certified cost-accuracy dial that degrades gracefully (in contrast to fixed-prefix truncation).

5. Cost-aware retraining (optional extension). Modify boosting's per-round loss/potential to reward ensembles whose margins concentrate early in the evaluation order (a cost-aware analogue of directly optimizing margins), producing models explicitly built to exit early.

6. Evaluation. On the datasets used in these papers (e.g., letter and the UCI suite) and on bagged, boosted, and randomized C4.5 ensembles, measure average number of base classifiers evaluated per example vs. accuracy, at multiple epsilon, comparing against fixed truncation and against evaluating the full ensemble. Report inference-time/energy savings and verify the lossless mode reproduces full-ensemble accuracy exactly, quantifying how the margin distribution (skewed for boosting, flatter under label noise per Dietterich 2000) predicts achievable savings.

This directly attacks the deployment resource bottleneck: it converts the theory's own margin/potential machinery into a per-example compute budget, spending many base-learner calls only on the few genuinely hard, small-margin examples while cheaply certifying the confident majority — all without retraining and with a provable accuracy guarantee.

paper_title: The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain
motivation: Von Neumann's "Probabilistic Logics and the Synthesis of Reliable Organisms from Unreliable Components" is the foundational result that reliable computation can be built from unreliable elements via majority-restoring "multiplexing." But its guarantee rests on assumptions von Neumann himself flags as unrealistic and adopts only for simplicity: (1) each component "has, statistically independently of all else, exactly the probability epsilon of misfiring" — he notes the "more realistic" dependent case but declines to treat it; (2) epsilon is a single, fixed, KNOWN constant below a hard threshold (epsilon<1/6 for the three-input majority organ); (3) redundancy is static and uniform (his estimates give N about 20,000 lines per bundle everywhere, regardless of local need); (4) stage-to-stage independence is restored by an unspecified "randomizing permutation" U that "will not be considered here"; (5) the single-line analysis covers only circle-free (acyclic) automata. This leaves a large gap. Culbertson notes real brains achieve reliability with few, plastic, only partially reliable cells — the opposite of blind 20,000-fold redundancy. Uttley's conditional-probability machines show simple units can estimate probabilities online, log-scale and time-weighted. Hebb's cell-assembly Mark II shows adaptive redundancy via recruitment. Minsky's universal elements show functionally equivalent modules can be built in structurally diverse ways. Yet no work extends von Neumann's synthesis to unknown, heterogeneous, correlated, and time-varying component error, nor gives a constructive replacement for his hand-waved decorrelating permutation. This matters because every physical or biological substrate has exactly these properties (aging, burst noise, shared-mode/correlated failures, per-component variation), precisely where von Neumann's static independence-based bound gives no guarantee or demands absurd redundancy.
method: We propose "adaptive multiplexing": an extension of von Neumann's reliability synthesis that operates under weaker, realistic assumptions — unknown, heterogeneous, correlated, time-varying error in cyclic as well as acyclic networks — while using far fewer components than static multiplexing. Setup: keep von Neumann's blocks (Sheffer/McCulloch-Pitts neurons, majority-restoring organs, bundles of N lines per message). Replace fixed known epsilon with an unknown per-component, state-dependent, time-varying process epsilon_i(t) with unknown pairwise correlation. Goal unchanged: hold each bundle's post-restoration malfunction probability below fiduciary level Delta, but without knowing epsilon and at minimum cost. (1) Reliability made observable: a multiplexed bundle already exposes its reliability — the empirical dissent count D/N (fraction of lines disagreeing with the majority) is an observable, unbiased running signal of local error, needing no external knowledge of epsilon. Attach to each restoring organ an Uttley-style logarithmic counter maintaining an exponentially time-weighted estimate of malfunction probability from D; the time-weighting tracks drifting, nonstationary epsilon(t). (2) Adaptive redundancy: a local rule adjusts N per bundle — recruit extra parallel copies (Hebb-style recruitment) when estimated post-restoration error exceeds Delta, prune lines when comfortably below. Analyze as a stochastic-approximation loop and derive an adaptive analog of von Neumann's static bound: the estimate tracks true drifting error within a bound and N self-adjusts to the smallest value meeting Delta. Static uniform multiplexing is the special case (stationary, independent, known epsilon); we predict adaptive N collapses far below von Neumann's worst case because redundancy is spent only where local error is high. (3) Constructive decorrelation replacing U: each bundle measures within-bundle pairwise agreement/covariance. When correlation is detected (breaking voting's independence), we (a) diversify — route redundant copies through structurally distinct sub-networks assembled from Minsky's universal elements so copies share no common-mode failure path; and (b) learn an interleaving/permutation minimizing measured covariance, a data-driven realization of von Neumann's "randomizing permutation." We give a modified majority-organ error-propagation inequality using measured correlations, generalizing his e* = epsilon + (1-2epsilon)theta which assumed independence, so the reliability certificate stays valid under dependence. (4) Beyond acyclic networks: since estimation/control are local and online, the scheme applies to recurrent/cyclic automata von Neumann excluded — the running dissent estimator stabilizes loops by triggering recruitment when a cycle's error grows. Evaluation: simulate Sheffer/majority-organ networks computing fixed logical functions under four regimes: (i) stationary independent epsilon (recover von Neumann; show adaptive N much less than static N for the same Delta); (ii) heterogeneous epsilon_i; (iii) nonstationary drifting/bursty epsilon(t); (iv) spatially correlated failures. Metrics: achieved reliability vs target Delta, total components vs static-multiplexing baseline, estimator tracking error, and robustness of the correlation-aware bound. This makes von Neumann's guarantee hold when epsilon is unknown, uneven, correlated, and changing — the conditions of any real substrate — turning his fixed, blind, astronomically large redundancy into adaptive, minimal, self-monitoring redundancy.

paper_title: Simultaneous Map Building and Localization for an Autonomous Mobile Robot
motivation: Sonar navigation systems in these sources share one cycle: predict returns from a map, match with an EKF over a stochastic map, update. Two coupled problems stay unsolved. Kuc and Siegel show naive time-of-flight interpretation omits real obstacles and inserts artifactual ones, because corners, edges and multi-bounce paths produce echoes not on the transducer axis; their physics simulator predicts which surfaces and reflections cause each return, but it is used only offline. Leonard, Durrant-Whyte and Cox's dynamic map building collapses every mismatch into one ad hoc credibility count whose functional form they admit remains unclear; a missed detection, a specular phantom, and a moving object look identical to it, so maps fill with phantoms or drop real features. Directed-sonar work notes the sonar time problem of deciding where to point, and Smith and Cheeseman give the stochastic-map uncertainty machinery. Missing is an artifact closing the loop: no system uses a high-fidelity physics model online to explain each individual return, so data association, feature validity, moving-object segmentation, and where-to-look are decided without knowing whether an echo is physically consistent with the current map, causing phantom obstacles, corrupted maps, and wasted sensing time in specular indoor spaces.
method: Build PHASE, a deployable perception and mapping system on a wheeled robot with a Polaroid time-of-flight transducer on a servo steerable mount, whose core is an embedded real-time acoustic simulator wired into the EKF stochastic-map loop as a per-return explanation engine. A prediction engine re-implements the Kuc and Siegel closed-form reflection model for walls, corners, edges and cylinders as an incremental online predictor over the current stochastic map and pose belief, emitting predicted regions of constant depth plus the causal chain for each return, namely which surfaces and whether first-order or multi-bounce; real-time speed comes from Kuc and Siegel per-cell contributing-element encoding and cached visibility, with the filter budget sized from the discrete Kalman filter cost analysis. Explanation-based association tests each observed return against the map under pose covariance: direct matches feed the EKF, returns explainable only as specular or multi-bounce artifacts are suppressed as phantoms, and unexplainable ones become candidates, replacing the ad hoc credibility counter with a physics-grounded validity likelihood that penalizes a feature only when it should be directly observable yet is absent. Static and dynamic segmentation routes persistent returns unexplainable by any static-map-plus-specular hypothesis to a multi-target tracker forming a moving-object layer separate from static geometry. Active directed sensing simulates candidate aim angles and steers the servo to the angle that most disambiguates competing hypotheses such as real object versus corner multi-bounce. Evaluate on a real robot in a specular room with moving obstacles against the credibility-only baseline on phantoms inserted, real features omitted, localization accuracy, return classification, and sensing time, and validate explanation accuracy first against the Kuc and Siegel simulator's known causal labels.

paper_title: Factorial Hidden Markov Models
motivation: HMMs, Boltzmann chains, Neal belief nets, and Williams-Hinton mean-field nets classify sequences like protein families (Baldi) and words (Rabiner), yet the sources never quantify score reliability, a failure and risk gap. Mean-field and tractable-substructure bounds (Saul-Jordan) have unknown per-input tightness so classifiers are silently wrong; exact HMMs are overconfident on out-of-family or distorted inputs; Gibbs sampling gives irreproducible scores. The machinery to detect these risks exists but is never made into a reliability signal.
method: A self-diagnosing scorer. First, a two-sided gap: pair a variational lower bound (mean-field or tractable-substructure) with a cheap upper estimate from a tractable HMM backbone; gap Delta flags per-input inference unreliability and structural surprise versus a background model. Second, codelength calibration: score equals negative variational free energy (Helmholtz and MDL), and excess codelength over a background code is a calibrated out-of-distribution score. Third, abstention: decide only when Delta is small and codelength margin exceeds residual uncertainty; for Gibbs belief nets add inter-chain free-energy variance to Delta for reproducibility. Evaluate on protein-family classification, distorted strings, and a toy HMM via reliability diagrams, selective-risk curves, OOD AUC, and whether Delta predicts error.

paper_title: Tests on a Cell Assembly Theory of the Action of the Brain, Using a Large Digital Computer
motivation: The foundational results in these sources are existence proofs, not economy results. McCulloch and Pitts (1943) show every net corresponds to a propositional-logic expression and conversely a net can be built for any admissible expression; Kleene (1956) sharpens this into the theorem that exactly the regular events are representable in the state of a finite McCulloch-Pitts nerve net. Neither asks how few neurons and endbulbs (synapses) are needed to represent a given behavior; the constructions dedicate structure per sub-expression or state and are profligate with the one scarce resource, neurons. This is a resource bottleneck the sources themselves flag. Kleene notes that explaining memory by reverberating cycles is implausible partly because calculations on the amount of material stored would call for too many neurons, and stresses his theory assumes neurons never malfunction, which is unrealistic both for living neurons and for the corresponding units of a mechanical automaton. So the classical syntheses demand implausibly large and implicitly perfectly reliable hardware, yet a net of N neurons has up to 2^N distinguishable states, so local one-neuron-per-state encoding wastes almost all capacity. Because neurons, biological or the era's universal elements for automata, are the costly limited resource, net size limits how complex a representable behavior can be built. Craik's picture of the brain as a compact small-scale model of reality heightens the puzzle: real nervous systems are economical, but the theory offers no principle of economy. The gap is that there is no constructive theory for the minimal nerve net representing a given regular event, nor for trading neuron count against the unreliability the sources admit is unavoidable.
method: Turn the classical question of whether a nerve net exists for an event into the question of the smallest reliable net for it, by adding a resource-cost calculus on top of the McCulloch-Pitts and Kleene framework. First, define an explicit cost measure: neurons plus endbulbs/synapses, with loop (delay) elements counted separately since Kleene ties memory cost to cyclic structure, making economy a formal objective. Second, do a two-stage minimizing synthesis for a target regular event E: (a) state reduction, using Kleene's equivalence of regular events to collapse indistinguishable states via Myhill/Nerode-style right-congruence classes to the minimum number k of states any automaton for E requires, lower-bounding the memory needed; and (b) distributed encoding, where instead of one neuron per state the k states are encoded in a register of ceil(log2 k) neurons, exploiting the 2^N capacity, and the next-state and output logic is realized as acyclic McCulloch-Pitts sub-nets, invoking their theorem that any admissible propositional function is buildable and their result that alternative neurophysiological assumptions are interchangeable so the logic can be gate-minimized; the output is a provably correct net whose size scales with log(states) times logic complexity rather than linearly in states. Third, add a reliability budget: since Kleene concedes neurons err, extend minimization to a target error rate by inserting controlled redundancy (duplicated critical neurons and voting endbulbs) only where a failure would flip a state distinction, yielding a cost-versus-robustness frontier rather than assuming perfect neurons. Fourth, use incremental sample-driven growth to avoid ever building the profligate net: start compact and add a neuron only when an observed input string forces a new distinguishable state, in the spirit of Hebbian organization and Craik's incrementally refined internal model, so resources grow with demonstrated complexity rather than worst-case expression size. Fifth, evaluate by synthesizing nets for benchmark regular events (parity, bounded counters, pattern detectors, short-term reverberating memories) and comparing neuron and synapse counts against the direct McCulloch-Pitts and Kleene constructions and the information-theoretic lower bound, quantifying neuron savings and cost paid per unit of added reliability. This converts the sources' existence theorems into a constructive minimization method, exploits latent combinatorial capacity to shrink neuron counts from linear toward logarithmic in the number of states, and makes reliability a purchasable resource rather than a free assumption.

paper_title: A Tutorial on Hidden Markov Models and Selected Applications in Speech Recognition
motivation: Resource/usability bottleneck in deploying HMM recognizers to individual users. In this corpus the best accuracy comes from speaker-dependent whole-word or context-dependent HMMs (isolated-digit continuous-mixture HMMs, connected-word segmental k-means, multistyle training), but each needs a substantial per-user enrollment corpus (many tokens per word/style or minutes of labeled speech). Speaker-independent systems (SPHINX generalized triphones, VQ+HMM digit recognizers) avoid enrollment only by collecting large expensive multi-speaker databases and still trail speaker-dependent accuracy. Existing data-scarcity tools work inside one corpus: deleted/interpolated estimation (Jelinek-Mercer) and information-theoretic triphone clustering smooth sparse counts, and the KL-based probabilistic HMM distance quantifies similarity, but none cheaply transfers a trained model to a new speaker. The 1975 linguistic-statistical decoder conjectured bootstrapping a new speaker from the most similar known speaker but never operationalized it, and the Bahl/Jelinek substitution/insertion/deletion acoustic-channel formulation offers an unused, forward-backward-estimable mechanism. The gap: reach near-speaker-dependent accuracy from only seconds of new-speaker speech, without retraining thousands of state distributions or collecting a new large corpus.
method: Model each new speaker as a compact stochastic acoustic channel on top of an existing discrete-density (VQ) HMM system, so adaptation estimates a few shared parameters instead of every state distribution. (1) Base: a discrete HMM recognizer with VQ codebook size K and per-state pmfs b_j(k), trained speaker-independently; optionally a small library of speaker-dependent prototype model sets indexed by the KL-based probabilistic HMM distance. (2) Speaker channel: a single stochastic KxK matrix T with T(l,k)=Pr(speaker emits symbol k given reference emits l), giving adapted emissions b'_j(k)=sum_l b_j(l)T(l,k). Tying T across all states/words yields only O(K^2) parameters (reducible via low-rank or codebook-neighborhood tying); optional insertion/deletion channel arcs absorb rate differences. (3) Estimation: from a few seconds of transcribed adaptation speech, estimate T by a Baum-Welch/forward-backward EM that fixes topology, transitions, and reference emissions and updates only T; well-posed even with one or a few tokens. (4) Regularization: deleted interpolation between b'_j and b_j with weights fit on held-out enrollment frames, so near-zero data falls back to speaker-independent and adaptation strength grows with data. (5) Reference selection: use the probabilistic HMM distance to pick the nearest prototype speaker set before fitting T. (6) Evaluation: plot accuracy versus enrollment amount (1 vs 5 tokens per word / seconds) on isolated-digit and medium-vocabulary tasks against speaker-independent, full speaker-dependent retraining, and multistyle baselines; success is approaching speaker-dependent accuracy with an order of magnitude less new-speaker data and modest compute.

paper_title: Task-Level Robot Learning: Juggling a Tennis Ball More Accurately
motivation: Robotic hand/eye calibration—recovering the camera-to-gripper transform via either the AX=XB formulation (Shiu and Ahmad, 1987) or Tsai and Lenz's efficient decoupled method (1987/89)—underlies the vision-guided manipulation and fine-motion tasks pursued by the general hand-eye coordination framework (Liang et al., 1988) and rope handling (Inoue and Inaba, 1983). Tsai and Lenz show with explicit error formulas that calibration accuracy is dictated almost entirely by which robot calibration motions are chosen: the first-degree critical factors are the angle between interstation rotation axes (error proportional to 1/sin), the interstation rotation magnitude (error proportional to 1/angle), the camera-to-target distance, and the inter-station translation. Shiu and Ahmad give only a minimal admissibility condition (rotation axes must not be parallel). Yet the only guidance for choosing poses is a fixed, idealized star-drawing heuristic that rotates about uniformly distributed axes with the target directly overhead, plus the ad hoc advice to use redundant stations. This leaves three gaps. First, feasibility: the star pattern assumes free rotation about arbitrary axes and free target placement, ignoring joint limits, reachable and collision-free workspace, and the requirement that the target stay inside the camera field of view and focus range at every station, so the ideal geometry is often unreachable on a real arm. Second, non-adaptivity: the station set is fixed a priori, never exploits measured feature noise or intermediate estimate quality, and has no principled stopping rule despite each move costing real time. Third, no joint optimization: the heuristic tunes individual factors rather than directly optimizing the covariance of the full transform estimate. The framework paper aspires to dynamic adaptive calibration using the robot to supply points but never says how to choose them optimally. No method exists to automatically select a feasible, minimal set of calibration motions that provably optimizes accuracy under real constraints.
method: Cast calibration-motion selection as a constrained active experimental-design (optimal-search) problem that directly optimizes accuracy of the estimated hand-eye transform, solved greedily and adaptively. (1) Design objective: reuse Tsai and Lenz's error propagation to write, in closed form, the covariance of estimated rotation R_cg and translation T_cg as a function of a set of poses. The least-squares systems solving for rotation (interstation rotation-axis pairs) and translation yield a Fisher information matrix M whose entries depend on the critical factors (axis-pair angles, rotation magnitudes, target distance, inter-station translation) weighted by per-station feature-extraction and robot-positioning noise. This gives a cheap surrogate objective computable without images: A-optimality (trace of M inverse), D-optimality (determinant of M), or the min-singular-value or condition-number of the coefficient matrix that Tsai and Lenz flag as going singular. (2) Feasible pose set: candidate poses restricted by forward-kinematic reachability, joint limits, self-collision checks, and a visibility constraint that the target projects within the camera field of view and depth-of-focus. The star pattern projected onto this set is a warm start. (3) Greedy adaptive selection: seed with a minimal admissible pose pair obeying Shiu and Ahmad's non-parallel-axis condition; at each step search the feasible manifold for the pose maximizing marginal information gain or variance reduction (submodular-style greedy design), combining coarse sampling over reachable-visible poses with local gradient refinement of the surrogate. (4) Closed-loop adaptation and efficient stopping: after each executed move and image grab, update per-station noise estimates from observed feature residuals and re-optimize remaining poses (noise weights are data-driven, not uniform); stop when predicted, bootstrap-verified covariance falls below a task accuracy target, minimizing the number of moves (each move plus grab plus travel being the resource conserved), producing an accuracy-versus-number-of-motions trade-off curve. (5) Evaluation: using Tsai and Lenz's station-generation simulator and a real 6-DOF arm, compare accuracy-per-station of the optimized adaptive schedule against the fixed star-drawing heuristic, random feasible poses, and the star pattern truncated by infeasibility, measuring rotation and translation RMS error, moves to target accuracy, and robustness when workspace and visibility constraints exclude the ideal geometry. The method is estimator-agnostic, applying to both AX=XB and Tsai-Lenz solvers.

paper_title: Fuzzy Logic, Neural Networks, and Soft Computing
motivation: Data-driven neuro-fuzzy learners (ANFIS, Jang 1992; the neural-network-based fuzzy logic control/decision system, Lin and Lee 1991; NN-driven fuzzy reasoning, Nomura 1991; Takagi-Sugeno identification, 1985 and 1988) tune membership functions and rule consequents from finite, noisy data. Two robustness failures go unaddressed. First, overconfidence in uncovered regions: the ANFIS Layer-3 normalization forces firing strengths to sum to one, so outputs are equally confident even when total un-normalized rule support is essentially zero, i.e. when the model extrapolates beyond its training data. ANFIS notes it does NOT maintain epsilon-completeness during learning, so tuned membership functions drift and open coverage gaps that normalization then masks. Second, brittleness to noise: the squared-error objective overfits noisy data; ANFIS only speculatively mentions entropy weight-elimination and constrained epsilon-completeness. The stable adaptive fuzzy control line (Wang, Lyapunov-based) offers robustness only under bounded structural uncertainty and never quantifies data-coverage uncertainty or when a learned model is outside its evidential support. In the safety-relevant deployments driving this literature (automatic train operation, online nonlinear control, production planning) an overconfident wrong output in an uncovered or noisy region causes real failures. No prior work equips a data-driven fuzzy inference system to recognize when it is unreliable and behave conservatively.
method: Coverage-aware Robust Neuro-Fuzzy Inference (CR-NFIS): a training-plus-inference wrapper making ANFIS-style systems self-aware and fail-safe. (1) Expose coverage: keep the un-normalized firing strengths ANFIS discards at Layer 3 and define a per-input coverage measure c(x), the max or soft-sum of rule firings, near zero exactly when no rule applies, recovering an operational epsilon-completeness test the normalization hides. (2) Coverage-completeness regularizer: during hybrid training penalize any input whose max firing is below epsilon so membership functions cannot leave gaps, implementing the constrained-gradient epsilon-completeness ANFIS only sketched. (3) Robust fitting: replace squared error with a bounded Huber-type loss plus the entropy weight-elimination term, reducing overfitting and pruning redundant rules. (4) Two-part predictive uncertainty: epistemic uncertainty from coverage, plus aleatoric uncertainty from per-rule residual variance and local training density tracked via Takagi-Sugeno structure identification, combined into a predictive interval. (5) Calibration and guardrail: conformal-style thresholds on held-out data; when coverage is too low or the interval too wide, the system abstains and hands off to a conservative fallback: for control, a Lyapunov-stable adaptive fuzzy controller (Wang 1993) or validated default rule preserving closed-loop stability where the learned model is untrustworthy; for decision tasks, the expert rule base. The coverage signal can also drive active data collection and online rule addition to close gaps. Evaluate on the original ANFIS benchmarks (Mackey-Glass prediction, nonlinear function modeling, online identification in a control loop) with injected label noise and out-of-distribution inputs; metrics: error split by covered versus uncovered regions, calibration quality, reduction of high-confidence errors and failure rate under OOD and noise versus vanilla ANFIS, and maintained closed-loop stability when the guardrail engages. This robustification mitigates the overconfidence, coverage-gap, and noise-overfitting failure modes of learned fuzzy inference systems.

paper_title: A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets
motivation: CD-trained PoE and energy-based models in this corpus rely on contrastive divergence because the partition function is intractable, a reliability and risk gap. CD is a biased one-step estimator with undocumented failure modes and no diagnostic for a distorted energy landscape. The models emit only unnormalized scores, yet systems compare them for hard decisions such as ten-way digit log-probability comparison and a fixed Fields of Experts prior weight in denoising. Different unknown partition functions and biases make these comparisons brittle, miscalibrated, and prone to silent failure under noise mismatch or distribution shift in deployed pipelines like recognition, denoising, and embryo phenotyping.
method: A partition-function-free framework to audit and calibrate CD-trained energy-based and PoE models. A chain-length-sensitivity bias probe measures gradient drift and the energy gap between one-step and longer-chain samples to yield a reliability map without needing the partition function. Drift-regularized adaptive-anneal training raises chain length only where drift is high. Cross-model calibration with abstention corrects each unnormalized score using matched extended-chain samples to estimate a per-model offset, fits a calibration map, gates abstention on the drift signal, and sets the Fields of Experts prior weight from calibrated reliability. Evaluation covers Fields of Experts denoising under noise shift, digit-classification calibration under distribution shift, and synthetic Student-t and RBM models with near-exact likelihoods to confirm the drift probe tracks true error.

paper_title: Stable Function Approximation in Dynamic Programming
motivation: Solving continuous-state MDPs by dynamic programming requires discretizing the state space, and uniform discretization is defeated by the curse of dimensionality (Bellman 1959, 1961). Chow and Tsitsiklis's one-way multigrid algorithm (1991) gives provable accuracy-vs-computation bounds but refines the whole grid uniformly, wasting resolution where it does not matter. Moore's Variable Resolution DP (1991) and parti-game (1994) refine adaptively, but only where model-based trajectories travel, decoupled from the actual loss of the greedy policy, with no accuracy certificate or budget control. The theory to link error to loss exists but is used only for analysis: Singh and Yee (1994) bound greedy-policy loss by value-function sup-norm error times about 2/(1-gamma); Tsitsiklis and Van Roy (1994) and Gordon (1995) identify averaging approximators that keep DP a non-expansion. No work turns these bounds into an objective that decides where and how much to spend discretization resources. This matters because compute cost is dominated by the number of cells and backups, and placing them where they most reduce policy loss is the difference between feasible and intractable.
method: Cast adaptive multiresolution DP as a budget-constrained resource-allocation search that minimizes an upper bound on greedy-policy loss per unit of computation (Loss-Bounded Adaptive Resolution Allocation). Partition the state space with a trie of cells as in VRDP, each holding a non-expansion local approximator (multilinear or k-nearest-neighbor averager, per Gordon) so value iteration converges at every resolution; actions are discretized per cell and refined separately. Iterate coarse-to-fine with multigrid warm starts. First, solve value iteration on the current partition, prolonging the coarser solution as warm start. Second, score each cell by loss-reduction-per-cost: a local error indicator (Bellman residual or interpolation variation across the cell, which upper-bounds sup-norm error and via Singh-Yee bounds policy loss) times the discounted visitation weight of the cell under the current greedy policy (from model-based trajectories or asynchronous samples), divided by the extra cells a split creates. Third, allocate the next budget increment by greedy knapsack or priority-queue selection of highest-scoring splits, with optional beam look-ahead over jointly refined neighboring cells; refine actions instead of states where residuals come from action aliasing. Fourth, stop when the aggregated loss bound falls below target epsilon or the budget is exhausted, reporting the bound as a sub-optimality certificate. Provide a model-based variant using a learned forward model and a model-free variant embedding the same residual-driven allocation in asynchronous Q-learning. Evaluate on puck-on-a-hill, mountain-car, and cart-pole, plotting policy loss versus cells and backups against uniform grids, one-way multigrid, and trajectory-only VRDP, testing whether LB-ARA reaches a target loss with far fewer cells.

paper_title: Using Weight Decay to Optimize the Generalization Ability of a Perceptron
motivation: In the statistical-mechanics-of-learning literature, the dominant bottleneck to reaching a target generalization error is the scarce, costly labeled example: learning curves depend on alpha = P/N, where each example needs the teacher's answer. The review (Watkin, Rau, Biehl 1993) shows two partial remedies, each with its own resource cost. First, active selection cuts examples needed: query-by-committee (Seung, Opper, Sompolinsky) approaches about 1 bit per query, but requires maintaining and sampling a large committee of student vectors, and the review notes its selection time diverges as 1/epsilon squared and does not generalize easily; the probably optimal perpendicular-selection scheme's dynamics have not been analyzed. So sample efficiency comes at a steep compute and scalability price. Second, online learning (Kinouchi-Caticha modified Hebb) is cheap and needs no training-set storage, but on random examples is sample inefficient, and its optimal variants need knowledge of the question distribution. Separately, the standard cure for label noise and unrealizable rules, finite-temperature learning with cross-validation (the 1995 overfitting work; the continuous-output paper showing learning with errors can help), spends additional scarce labeled data on a validation hold-out and requires storing data and retraining at many temperatures. There is thus an open resource gap: no method is simultaneously sample efficient like active learning, storage-free and cheap like online learning, committee-free, and noise robust without sacrificing scarce data to validation. The optimal-perceptron (Opper et al.) and continuous-output analyses provide exact tools to design and predict such a method.
method: Propose and analytically characterize single-student online uncertainty-query learning (SOUL): a storage-free, committee-free active online algorithm for the perceptron, with closed-form statistical-mechanics learning curves. Three components. (1) Uncertainty query from a single student as a committee-free surrogate for query-by-committee: at each online step, rather than maintaining a committee, generate or select an input xi near the current student's own decision boundary, that is small margin, roughly perpendicular to J. A single student is the natural version-space center, so its boundary approximates the committee split, giving the informative near-one-bit query at O(N) cost instead of the diverging committee sampling. (2) Optimal online update for this query distribution: use a Hebb-like update that adds a modulated term W times xi times the teacher label, where the modulation W is derived as in Kinouchi-Caticha to maximize the expected decrease in generalization error per example, but recomputed in closed form for the uncertainty-query distribution, which concentrates at zero margin. (3) Self-regulated effective temperature replacing cross-validation: for noisy or unrealizable rules, anneal the update amplitude as an effective temperature; estimate the noise level online from the running rate at which fresh queries are mislabeled relative to the student's confident predictions, consuming no held-out data, and choose the annealing schedule the theory predicts minimizes asymptotic error, operationalizing the continuous-output finding that learning with errors can help. Analysis: derive coupled flow equations for the order parameters R (student-teacher overlap) and the student norm versus alpha under the uncertainty-query distribution, using the dynamical-averaging and replica machinery of the review and Opper et al.'s optimal-perceptron calculation; predict the learning curve in closed form and compare its decay rate to random online learning, query-by-committee, and perpendicular selection. Extend to sigmoid or continuous outputs and noisy teachers to map the regime where self-annealing matches finite-temperature-plus-cross-validation without spending examples on validation. Validation: teacher-student perceptron simulations with N from about 50 to 1000, realizable and noisy cases, measuring labeled examples to hit a target error, compute per query, and memory footprint, against query-by-committee, optimal online, and finite-temperature-plus-cross-validation baselines. Success criteria: match query-by-committee sample efficiency at online-learning compute and storage cost, and match cross-validation noise robustness using zero validation examples. This attacks the resource bottleneck by slashing the labeled-example budget via active selection while eliminating the committee compute cost, training-set storage, and validation-data cost, backed by predictive theory rather than trial-and-error tuning.

paper_title: Connectionist Learning Procedures
motivation: Resource-bottleneck gap: Among the learning procedures in this corpus, the stochastic Boltzmann machine (a-learning-algorithm-for-boltzmann-machines-1985; optimal-perceptual-inference-1983; learning-and-relearning-in-boltzmann-machines-1986) is uniquely attractive because its weight updates are purely LOCAL Hebbian/anti-Hebbian correlations, making it the natural fit for the analog/neuromorphic hardware envisioned in a-neuromorphic-vlsi-learning-system-1987 — unlike back-propagation (learning-internal-representations-by-back-propagating-errors-1986), which requires global, non-local error transport. Yet Boltzmann learning has essentially failed to scale: every weight update requires the network to reach thermal equilibrium (via slow simulated annealing, cf. optimization-by-simulated-annealing-1983; stochastic-relaxation-gibbs-distributions-1984) TWICE — once in the data-clamped positive phase and once in a free-running negative phase started from a random state — and this must be repeated for many patterns. This equilibration cost is the reason applications such as boltzmann-machines-for-speech-recognition-1986 remained small and modest in accuracy. The dominant and most wasteful component is the free-running negative phase: re-annealing to global equilibrium from scratch, per pattern, per update, discards all computation done a moment earlier and is the practical barrier to deploying local-learning networks at the scale of the speech and vision tasks represented in this corpus (phoneme-recognition-using-time-delay-neural-networks-1987; neocognitron-1982). The deterministic mean-field relaxation (a-mean-field-theory-learning-algorithm-for-neural-networks-1987) cheapens each settling step but still assumes settling to a full equilibrium in both phases. The corpus also contains a biological clue left unexploited computationally: the negative/"unlearning" phase is conjectured to correspond to an occasional, amortized off-line "sleep" process (the-function-of-dream-sleep-1983; unlearning-has-a-stabilizing-effect-in-collective-memories-1983), NOT a per-pattern re-equilibration. No work here turns that observation into a compute-saving training algorithm. The bottleneck is therefore compute/time and hardware-deployment friction, and it blocks the otherwise-ideal local learning rule from reaching useful scale.
method:
Propose "amortized-equilibrium local learning": a training procedure for Boltzmann-type networks that removes the per-pattern free-running anneal and instead pays the negative-phase cost once, spread thinly across the whole run. Three concrete components:
(1) Cheap positive phase. Clamp visible units to a data pattern and settle hidden units to a deterministic mean-field fixed point (a-mean-field-theory-learning-algorithm-1987) rather than by full stochastic annealing; collect clamped correlations <s_i s_j>+.
(2) Short-reverie negative estimate. Instead of re-annealing from a random state to global equilibrium, initialize the negative phase from the just-computed data-clamped configuration and run only k (e.g. 1-5) brief update steps to a nearby configuration; collect <s_i s_j>- from it. This "short reverie" measures the local gradient of the log-likelihood around the data rather than the global partition function, cutting settling steps per update by 1-2 orders of magnitude while keeping the update rule strictly local (Δw_ij ∝ <s_i s_j>+ − <s_i s_j>-).
(3) Persistent "dream" pool for the global correction. To avoid the bias of purely local reveries, maintain a small fixed pool of P free-running "fantasy" particles that are NOT reset between updates; each iteration advance every particle by only a few stochastic/mean-field steps and use their correlations as an additional, occasionally-applied negative ("unlearning") term. This operationalizes the dream-sleep/unlearning proposal (the-function-of-dream-sleep-1983; unlearning-has-a-stabilizing-effect-1983): equilibration is amortized across the entire training trajectory, so the pool tracks the model distribution as weights change slowly, giving a near-unbiased global negative signal at a tiny per-update cost. A temperature/annealing schedule (optimization-by-simulated-annealing-1983) is applied only inside the pool, not per pattern.
Experiments: reimplement the encoder, shifter, and small speech/phoneme benchmarks used by the Boltzmann and TDNN sources (boltzmann-machines-for-speech-recognition-1986; phoneme-recognition-using-time-delay-neural-networks-1987), and compare (a) standard two-phase Boltzmann learning, (b) mean-field learning, (c) the proposed short-reverie + persistent-pool scheme, and (d) back-propagation, measuring accuracy versus total settling steps (a hardware-neutral compute proxy), wall-clock, number of labeled patterns, and robustness of the local-only update. Success criteria: match Boltzmann/backprop accuracy at a small fraction of the settling-step budget, while retaining locality (so the rule maps directly onto the analog VLSI of a-neuromorphic-vlsi-learning-system-1987). Ablations over k, pool size P, and pool-refresh rate quantify the compute-versus-bias trade-off and identify the minimal "sleep" budget needed for stable learning.

paper_title: Structural Optimization Using Simulated Annealing
motivation: Stress-leveling shape optimizers (biological growth method, evolutionary structural optimization) assume uniform surface stress equals the optimum, yet the corpus shows this holds for torsional shafts (Li, matching Polya) but fails for constrained shoulder fillets (Sonmez), fracture objectives (Das), and multiple load cases. No causal theory explains when or why, and the heuristic parameters are set empirically. This gap matters for fatigue-critical design.
method: Cast biological-growth swelling and ESO removal as one boundary-evolution flow whose fixed point is uniform surface stress; derive the exact shape-derivative and KKT conditions for benchmark problems and prove when the uniform-stress state is or is not stationary; interpret the heuristic parameters as step size plus a target-stress multiplier; define a one-solve alignment indicator predicting validity and a gradient-projected correction; validate against rigorous optimizers on plate-with-hole, shoulder fillets, torsional shafts, fracture cutouts, and multiple-load problems from the corpus.

paper_title: Bayesian CART Model Search: Rejoinder
motivation: Bayesian MARS, MARS, GAM and CART assume homoscedastic noise; Bayesian MARS uses one global error variance across the whole domain, so predictive intervals are miscalibrated. Combination methods such as stacking, MLE-combining-CART and boosting optimize point or classification error, not predictive-uncertainty quality. Because real noise varies across inputs, these narrow assumptions leave room for a method that adapts both the mean and the noise structure and combines models by calibration.
method: Model the response as Normal with mean f(x) and variance v(x), where f and log v each have their own adaptive MARS basis expansion. Extend Bayesian MARS with Poisson priors on basis counts, and use reversible-jump MCMC with separate moves for the mean and variance expansions, marginalizing mean coefficients by weighted least squares and updating variance coefficients by Metropolis. Predict by posterior averaging for input-dependent densities. Combine heterogeneous learners by weights that maximize cross-validated predictive log-likelihood rather than squared error. Evaluate on heteroscedastic simulations and the MARS datasets using coverage, predictive log-likelihood and CRPS.

paper_title: Probability Inequalities for Sums of Bounded Random Variables
motivation: A puzzle drives these works. The Loeve review insists rigorous measure-theoretic foundations are practically necessary, warning that mathematically inexact arguments cause incorrect conclusions; yet it says practical problems are intentionally not discussed, so the rigor meant to protect analysts is divorced from the problems showing where it matters, while the classical Introduction to Mathematical Probability is concrete but inexact, and no one knows when rigor actually changes a conclusion versus when it is ceremonial.
method: Audit where measure-theoretic rigor changes an applied conclusion versus where heuristics suffice, over canonical tasks such as estimator consistency, central limit under dependence, ergodic time-averaging, martingale convergence, and spectral representation; for each write a heuristic derivation and a rigorous one, construct counterexamples and Monte Carlo tests where they differ, classify results as rigor-cosmetic, rigor-critical, or rigor-guarding, and deliver a graded-rigor checklist per problem class.

paper_title: A System for Induction of Oblique Decision Trees
motivation: Prior work reports conflicting, unexplained effects. Holte 1993 shows single-attribute rules match complex learners on most common datasets. Brodley and Utgoff 1994 show oblique multivariate splits generally beat univariate trees but by amounts that vary greatly and sometimes vanish. Schaffer 1993 argues pruning helps only because of the chosen benchmarks, a bias whose value depends on an unspecified domain match. OC1 1993 and linear-machine trees search hard for complex boundaries with domain-dependent payoff. The field has descriptive results but no causal theory of why the benefit of representational complexity and of overfitting avoidance changes sign and size across datasets. Without such an account, each reported win describes a benchmark rather than learning, method selection stays trial and error, and Schaffer's pessimism is unrefuted because we cannot say what makes a bias appropriate. This is the explanation gap the proposal targets.
method: Develop a mechanistic account predicting, from measurable dataset properties, the sign and size of two effects: the gain from univariate to oblique multivariate splits, and the gain from pruning. First define descriptors computed without training the learner: boundary obliqueness from local linear discriminants, concept dispersion as connected same-class regions in a nearest-neighbor graph, class overlap as a k-NN Bayes-error proxy, irrelevant-feature fraction, and sample density relative to boundary complexity. Second, run interventional synthetic experiments that vary one descriptor at a time while fixing others: rotate a linear boundary from axis-aligned toward diagonal, add label noise, add irrelevant dimensions, vary the number of class regions, and subsample for density. For each dataset train 1R, C4.5 pruned and unpruned, a linear-machine multivariate tree, and OC1, and record the two gains on held-out data. Third, regress each gain on the descriptors to obtain an interpretable law, testing hypotheses such as multivariate gain increasing with obliqueness and density but falling with noise and irrelevant features, and pruning gain increasing with noise and low density and vanishing for low-dispersion concepts. Fourth, validate on the UCI datasets used by Holte and by Brodley and Utgoff by predicting from descriptors which bias helps and comparing to measured accuracy, aiming to beat always-add-complexity and always-prune baselines and to reproduce the apparent contradiction between the two papers. The result is a causal explanation of when simple rules suffice versus when complex boundaries help, and a measurable version of Schaffer's bias-matching claim.

paper_title: Fuzzy Cellular Neural Networks: Theory
motivation: Fuzzy cellular neural networks (FCNNs) run global image-morphology operations, notably grey-scale reconstruction and Euclidean distance transformation, on locally connected, VLSI-friendly cell arrays that promise real-time processing. But these operations are inherently iterative: reconstruction repeats geodesic dilation until stability, and distance transform repeatedly applies small structuring elements. Since a single FCNN layer is purely local, information advances only one cell per settling time, so iteration count, latency, energy, and chip time scale linearly with the largest object diameter. On large or high-resolution images this linear depth dominates cost and cannot be cured by enlarging templates, because deployed chips fix the neighborhood radius and larger structuring elements cost quadratically more silicon and wiring. The global-stability result guarantees a unique equilibrium is reached but bounds no convergence time, which is the very resource limiting scalability and real-time deployment. How to keep results exact on cheap small-neighborhood hardware while paying sub-linear rather than linear iteration and energy cost is left open.
method: Propose a Hierarchical Multiresolution FCNN that uses only small-neighborhood additive min/max cells, so existing VLSI cell designs and stability theory transfer. Stack about log-N coarser-resolution FCNN layers into a pyramid. Add FCNN-implemented inter-level transfer templates: an erosion-based conservative down-projection of the mask, a dilation-based down-projection of the marker, and an up-projection that seeds a finer level with the coarser level's converged marker. Run a coarse-to-fine geodesic schedule: markers cross the whole image in a few coarse steps (each coarse cell spans many fine pixels, so one step covers a large geodesic distance), then each finer level performs only a few mask-constrained geodesic dilations to fix boundaries. Because reconstruction is the idempotent supremum of mask-constrained geodesic dilations, the fine-level constrained dilations remain exact regardless of coarse seeding; the pyramid only accelerates coverage of the true geodesic distance, cutting iterations from about diameter to about log-diameter plus local correction while preserving correctness. The same scheme instantiates grey-scale reconstruction and Euclidean distance transform. Extend the global-stability contraction argument to bound per-level and total settling iterations, yielding an explicit resource bound that enables analytic early stopping and per-image compute budgeting. Evaluate against single-scale FCNN on growing image sizes, measuring iteration count, settling time, estimated energy and hardware footprint at fixed radius, and fidelity to exact morphological ground truth.

paper_title: Freeman Code Based Online Handwritten Character Recognition for Malayalam Using Backpropagation Neural Networks
motivation: All six works report high accuracies (98.125% k-NN Malayalam, 91% VHLPA, 88.75% Kohonen, various 92-97% Indic and Arabic figures) but each is measured on its own private dataset, writer set, script, features, and preprocessing, so claims cannot be compared or audited on equal footing; writer-independent claims rest on tiny writer pools (Arabic uses only 4 writers and synthesizes data). Every paper names confusion among visually similar characters as the dominant error, yet only the Tamil work measures it (an LOOCV confusion matrix and enumerated confused pairs), entangled with a script-specific fix. The field lacks a shared way to measure where errors originate, attribute error to feature extractor versus classifier versus writer split, and test whether confusion structure is script-specific or general. Without such diagnostic evidence, accuracies cannot be validated, methods compared, or progress accumulated.
method: Build a unified confusion-centric diagnostic benchmark and ablation harness for handwritten character recognition of complex scripts. Define a common representation combining an online x,y,t trajectory and a rasterized offline view from the same samples so online and offline methods run on identical characters; assemble Malayalam, Tamil, and Arabic data with per-writer IDs for writer-disjoint splits. Under fixed shared preprocessing, plug in the six works feature extractors (chain-code histogram, context bitmap, direction and curvature, 2DPCA, directional matching, vertical-horizontal positional) and classifiers (k-NN, Kohonen SOM, scaled-conjugate-gradient net, template matching). For every feature, classifier, and script combination compute a confusion matrix under leave-one-writer-out cross-validation and derive four metrics: a confusion-set severity index, a component-attribution score from factorial ablation, a writer-generalization gap, and a cross-script confusion-transfer test against a geometric-similarity measure. Toggle synthetic-sample generation. Deliver a leaderboard, a per-class error atlas of confused-character clusters, and reusable metrics.

paper_title: Convexity, Classification, and Risk Bounds
motivation: Boosting is consistent only when regularized by early stopping, but choosing the stop time is a resource bottleneck: the theoretical rule stops far too early, while cross validation sacrifices scarce labeled data and re-runs the whole fit many times, and local Rademacher penalties that are computed fully in-sample have not been used to replace it.
method: Stop boosting at the iterate minimizing empirical loss plus an in-sample local Rademacher penalty equal to the L1 norm budget times a base-class Rademacher average estimated from randomly signed labels, needing no held-out data; prove an oracle bound and consistency and compare against cross validation on small datasets.

paper_title: Comparison of a New Hybrid Connectionist-SCHMM Approach with Other Hybrid Approaches for Speech Recognition
motivation: The hybrid ANN and HMM systems here rest on a vector-quantization bottleneck whose resolution is set globally and tuned to the wrong objective. The MLP-labeler paper says the codebook size is always a compromise and uses uniform hand-set choices. The LVQ-HMM paper picks a single global codebook size experimentally and notes speaker-independent tasks need more resolution and that LVQ raises frame accuracy but not word accuracy. The gap: quantization resources are allocated uniformly across phoneme classes and streams and tuned to frame-level criteria, leaving word error out of the loop. The SOM paper offers a topology-preserving prototype substrate with local split and merge operations, and the HMM tutorial offers embedded Viterbi training, but neither is used to decide where resolution should go. Because confusability is non-uniform, a fixed uniform budget wastes prototypes on easy regions and starves confusable ones, keeping frame gains from becoming word gains. Reallocating the same budget can improve accuracy without adding parameters.
method: Treat the codebook budget as a fixed resource allocated by search against held-out word error. Build a per-phoneme-class multi-stream prototype pool, SOM-initialized and LVQ2-refined, feeding an MLP fuzzy labeler and a discrete HMM trained by embedded Viterbi. Use SOM neighborhoods for cheap local split and merge moves, plus per-class budget shifts and phoneme-versus-subphoneme granularity moves. Guide allocation by a word-error sensitivity signal from decoder confusions and Viterbi backtraces: split prototypes in high-confusion regions and merge in low-utility regions, holding total count fixed. Screen many allocations by successive halving on small held-out subsets before promotion. For speaker independence, cluster speakers and run allocation per cluster so confusable regions gain resolution where cross-speaker variance is largest. Compare against fixed-uniform-codebook baselines at equal total prototype count, reporting word error, to test whether error-driven non-uniform allocation converts frame-level discrimination into word-level gains.

paper_title: Solving the Multiple Instance Problem with Axis-Parallel Rectangles
motivation: In these 3D QSAR works, models combine three separable choices. Representation includes field lattices in CoMFA, surface sampling in Compass, similarity matrices in Good and Richards, and shape descriptors in Hopfinger triazine DHFR analysis. Pose strategy includes manual rigid fit or field fit in CoMFA, adaptive dynamic reposing in Compass, and tangent distance linearization in Dietterich et al. Learner includes linear PLS, neural networks, and projection pursuit regression. The field asserts pose dominates. CoMFA calls the alignment rule its most important input yet leaves it to the chemist. Compass credits gains jointly to surface representation, nonlinear learning, and automated pose selection, but ablated on one dataset of 31 steroids. Comparisons confound all three factors and the dataset, so no one can attribute performance, know when automated pose selection helps, or pick a method for a new series. The gap is a controlled empirical map decomposing 3D QSAR accuracy into representation, pose handling, and learner components and relating them to dataset properties like flexibility, chemotype diversity, and size.
method: Build a modular benchmark and diagnostic protocol. Suite harmonizes datasets from these sources spanning difficulty. The 31 steroid set is rigid. The musk odorant sets are semi flexible. The triazine DHFR inhibitors are flexible. The multi chemotype 5HT1A set is diverse. Each dataset is annotated with flexibility such as rotatable bonds and conformer spread from Monte Carlo or distance geometry search, plus diversity, range, and size. A factorial component swap design follows the design of experiments philosophy from the biomedical multivariate source. A shared pipeline has swappable representation among field, surface, similarity matrix, and shape. It has swappable pose strategy among rigid fit, field fit, dynamic reposing, and tangent distance. It has swappable learner among PLS, projection pursuit, and neural net. Run the fractional factorial across datasets under one nested cross validation with shared conformer pools. Report cross validated q squared with confidence intervals. Variance decomposition gives each factor main effect and factor by dataset interactions. A learner independent pose sensitivity diagnostic perturbs alignment and conformer choice and traces accuracy degradation into a pose sensitivity surface. This tests whether automated pose selection truly flattens sensitivity. Outputs are empirical maps of which choice dominates per dataset property, a reusable implementation and datasets, and guidance predicting the best combination and needed pose search effort for a new series.

paper_title: Structural Optimization Using Simulated Annealing
motivation: Scope-mismatch gap. This corpus optimizes structural shape, topology, and composite layup under a narrow, idealized regime: single or few deterministic load cases, exactly known loads, rigid supports, nominal material properties, and geometry or stacking assumed realized exactly as designed. The shoulder-fillet work drives stress-concentration factors near one for a fixed nominal load; ESO, SA and GA works minimize peak stress for nominal loads; composite works optimize discrete ply angles for maximum buckling load assuming exact manufacture. Only the elastic-contact ESO paper considers multiplicity, and only as a few discrete load cases, not continuous uncertainty in loads, support compliance, boundary tolerances, or material scatter. Such optima are knife-edge peaks that degrade sharply under small realistic deviations (a few degrees of load-direction change, manufacturing tolerance on the boundary spline, ply-angle scatter, support flexibility), so a nominally better design can be worse in service, which is the failure mode these methods try to prevent. It is doubly problematic because the cheap engines used here (fixed-grid FEA, meshfree RKPM) give only approximate boundary stresses. The corpus already provides cheap repeated evaluation (surrogates) and robust metaheuristics, but uses them only to speed nominal optimization, leaving room to reuse them for robustness under realistic uncertainty.
method: A robustness-aware framework reusing the corpus metaheuristic plus cheap-analysis pipeline but replacing the nominal objective with a robust one over an explicit uncertainty set. Uncertainty parameters (load direction and magnitude intervals, support compliance, boundary spline key-point tolerances, and for composites ply-angle and material scatter) are attached to the existing design representations. Each candidate is scored by worst-case peak stress or worst-case buckling load, optionally with a mean-plus-k-standard-deviation term and a sensitivity penalty that flattens the optimum. To keep ensemble evaluation cheap, existing surrogates (lamination-parameter response surfaces, ANN, design of experiments) are extended to span the joint space of design and uncertainty parameters, so inner uncertainty sampling is nearly free and reusable, unlike per-instance surrogates; continuum shapes use fixed-grid or meshfree RKPM analysis that avoids remeshing across perturbations. Optimization is nested: a corpus-validated global metaheuristic (direct-search simulated annealing for fillets, shafts, 2D shapes; GA or ES for laminates and continua) in the outer loop over design variables, and an inner loop doing worst-case search or sampling over uncertainty via the surrogate, with occasional exact re-evaluation to correct and re-train it. Validation re-runs three canonical corpus problems (shoulder fillet, torsional shaft, composite buckling and stacking sequence), comparing nominal versus robust optima on nominal performance sacrificed, worst-case and variance under uncertainty, and optimum flatness, expecting robust optima to sacrifice little nominal performance while sharply reducing degradation and yielding landscapes easier for the metaheuristic to search.

paper_title: Shape Quantization and Recognition with Randomized Trees
motivation: Amit, Geman and Wilder reach about 0.7 percent digit error by inducing at each tree node an invariant geometric tag arrangement from a huge, partially ordered feature family. They make two fixed choices: at each node they score only a small uniformly random subset of candidate features on all node data, and they grow a fixed number of independent trees aggregated by uniform averaging. The subset size is both the compute knob and the diversity knob but is never tuned adaptively; scoring every candidate on full data wastes compute; doubling trees gives only marginal gains. Since ensemble gains depend on base-learner diversity (bagging; ECOC) and small-sample gain estimates are noisy (bias/variance dilemma), greedy split selection and uniform aggregation are fragile. No prior work turns this feature induction and ensemble building into a principled budget-aware search.
method: Recast ensemble construction as a compute-budget-constrained search, keeping the feature family, entropy criterion, and partial ordering fixed. First, node-level adaptive screening by racing and successive-halving: score candidate features first on a small subsample, drop statistically dominated ones via confidence bounds, refine survivors on more data; use the partial order as a prior by seeding gains from ancestors and pruning by monotone support bounds. Second, adaptive diversity control: track motif usage across trees and down-weight over-used tag and relation motifs when sampling candidates, with exploration strength set from out-of-bag inter-tree correlation. Third, global allocation: add trees greedily while marginal out-of-bag error reduction per compute exceeds a threshold, and weight trees by validated accuracy. Evaluate on NIST and USPS digits, plotting accuracy against training relation-checks and against number of trees, measuring inter-tree correlation and split-quality regret. Success is matching or beating 0.7 percent error at far lower compute while exposing a controllable accuracy-compute-diversity frontier; ablations isolate each component.

paper_title: Real-Time Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping with a Single Camera
motivation: Puzzle/contradiction at the heart of active-vision SLAM. The active-vision SLAM works (Davison and Murray 2002; the 2001 3D undulating-terrain system; the 2003 wearable single-camera system) all steer gaze by one greedy rule: measure the feature with the highest innovation covariance, since a predictable measurement conveys little information. Yet the same papers document that their dominant, potentially fatal failure mode is data-association mismatch, which is likely when robot and feature uncertainty grow and search regions become very large. So the innovation covariance the rule maximizes is exactly what sets search-ellipse size and hence the probability of a catastrophic mismatch, and a single mismatch can be fatal because there is no multiple-hypothesis machinery. The most informative measurement is simultaneously the most dangerous, and systems only get away with it while uncertainty stays small, crudely mitigated with large correlation patches. Nobody reconciles the two: information-greedy active systems ignore match reliability; Good Features to Track (1994) selects features for trackability but never asks whether a feature is distinctive within its predicted search region; and the efficiency line (Constant Time SLAM using postponement 2001; large-scale CML) cuts cost precisely by discarding the cross-covariance coupling active selection needs. Gap: an active measurement-selection strategy that treats information gain and data-association risk jointly.
method: Replace the pure highest-innovation-covariance rule with a risk-aware active gaze policy coupling expected information gain with probability of a correct match, using EKF coupling to shape uncertainty before risky measurements. First, a matchability prior: at feature initialization, add to the Good-Features texture score an appearance-ambiguity score by correlating each template against its local neighbourhood, capturing match-peak sharpness, second-peak ratio, and density of confusable locations. Second, per-step risk estimate: from the EKF compute each visible feature's innovation covariance giving search-region size and info score, and estimate probability of correct match as a decreasing function of search-region size times local ambiguity density. Third, a risk-aware utility: select the measurement maximizing expected information gain times probability of correct match minus expected mismatch damage, where damage scales with current global map and robot uncertainty; this avoids the large-ellipse-plus-ambiguous-patch trap that is both high-information and high-risk. Fourth, coupling-exploiting gaze sequencing: rather than one-shot grabbing a high-value high-risk feature, read cross-covariances already in the full EKF to find low-risk, well-localized features whose measurement most reduces the risky feature's predicted innovation covariance; measure those first to shrink its ellipse below a safe matchability threshold, then measure it, harvesting the same information at lower risk and justifying selective retention of coupling that constant-time methods discard. Fifth, a lazy multiple-hypothesis safety net: when a measurement must be attempted below the match-probability threshold, defer the state update and hold top candidate matches, resolved by the next one or two safe measurements. Evaluation: on the active stereo-head and wearable single-camera sequences, compare against the baseline rule on localization drift, mismatch and fatal-failure rate, re-fixation and loop-closure success on neglected then re-approached features, and per-step compute; the hypothesis is equal-or-better accuracy with far fewer fatal mismatches and longer error-free operation while keeping real-time near-constant-time updates.

paper_title: A Tutorial on Hidden Markov Models and Selected Applications in Speech Recognition
motivation:
Nearly all HMM-based speech recognizers of this era estimate parameters under an implicit "matched conditions" assumption: the statistics of the training data are taken to characterize the source at test time. Maximum-likelihood/Baum-Welch training (An introduction to the application of the theory of probabilistic functions of a Markov process...), maximum mutual information estimation (Maximum mutual information estimation of HMM parameters), and even the minimum-discrimination-information (MDI) approach of Ephraim, Dembo & Rabiner all fit a model to a single nominal set of measurements. In practice this assumption fails badly: performance "degrades dramatically as a talker's speech characteristics change" under workload/psychological stress, the Lombard effect in noise, or channel/speaker mismatch (Multistyle training for robust isolated word speech recognition; A speaker stress resistant HMM isolated word recognizer).

Two lines of work leave a clear gap. (1) The MDI approach usefully relaxes the assumption that the source is truly an HMM, but it is, if anything, anti-robust: given a model it selects the source distribution *closest* to the current model among those consistent with the measurements, and it uses a single nominal measurement set (a band-limited covariance). It therefore optimistically fits one nominal condition and offers no protection against condition mismatch. (2) Multistyle training makes a recognizer robust by pooling tokens recorded in several talking styles (normal, fast, clear, loud, question-pitch) and training with ordinary ML. This works, but it is purely heuristic: it requires actually collecting multi-style data, it optimizes only average (pooled) likelihood with no guarantee for unseen intermediate conditions, and it provides no theoretical account of *why* robustness is obtained or how to choose the styles.

The opportunity is to unify and generalize these: give robustness a principled, information-theoretic formulation that (a) works when test conditions differ from and are unknown at training time, (b) covers a whole family of operating conditions rather than one, and (c) can even build the required condition family by transforming nominal statistics when multi-condition recordings are unavailable.
method:
Robust minimax minimum-discrimination-information (RMDI) HMM training. We extend the Ephraim–Dembo–Rabiner MDI descent from fitting one nominal source to being robust against an explicit *uncertainty set* of source conditions, turning the estimation into a min–max (saddle-point) problem while reusing the existing forward–backward / Baum auxiliary-function machinery.

1. Uncertainty set over conditions. Represent each operating condition c (e.g., normal, loud/Lombard, noisy at SNR level k, stressed) by a set of measurement constraints — the band-limited covariance R^(c) already used in MDI. Constraints for extra conditions can be obtained three ways: measured from the few available tokens per style (as in multistyle training); *synthesized* from the nominal covariance by physically motivated transforms (add a noise-covariance term for additive noise, apply spectral tilt/gain and formant emphasis to emulate loud/clear/Lombard speech); or specified as *interval-valued* moments (each covariance entry allowed to lie in a range), which also absorbs sparse-data uncertainty. Define the uncertainty set U as the convex hull / union of the source PDs whose measurements are consistent with any of these constraint sets.

2. Robust objective. Instead of MDI's min_h min_{Q consistent with one measurement} D(Q‖P_h), estimate a single HMM by min_h max_{Q in U} D(Q‖P_h): minimize the worst-case cross-entropy between the model P_h and any source in the uncertainty family. Because the discrimination information D(Q‖P_h) is convex in Q, the inner maximum over the convex set U is attained at an extreme point, so the worst case reduces to the most adverse (e.g., noisiest/loudest) condition — giving a tractable, interpretable computation and a direct explanation of why worst-case-style training helps.

3. Alternating saddle-point descent. Iterate three steps, generalizing the two-step Csiszár–Tusnády alternation used by MDI: (i) Inner maximization — among the extreme measurement sets in U, and among the PDs consistent with each (via Lagrange multipliers on the covariance-band constraints, exactly as in MDI), find the Q maximizing D(Q‖P_h) for the current model; (ii) MDI projection of that worst-case Q; (iii) Baum-type re-estimation step that decreases the worst-case D(Q‖P_h) with respect to the HMM parameters using the standard forward–backward formulas. Initialize from the ML/Baum-Welch solution. Local convergence follows the same Luenberger/descent argument as MDI applied to the worst-case objective; per-iteration cost is that of MDI times the (small) number of extreme conditions.

4. Instantiation and evaluation. Use zero-mean Gaussian-AR state densities (as in the MDI and autoregressive-HMM work) so the method plugs directly into existing LPC/cepstral front-ends. Evaluate on clean digits plus the Lincoln stress-speech and TI multi-style databases and additive-noise mixtures, comparing RMDI against ML, MMI, plain MDI, and multistyle-ML training under matched, mismatched, and *unseen intermediate* conditions. Key metrics: worst-case error rate across conditions and error on conditions never seen (only interpolated within U).

This is a "relax/extend scope" contribution: it makes MDI/HMM estimation operate under the weaker, more realistic assumption that the test condition is unknown and differs from training, broadens scope from a single nominal source to a whole family of noisy/stressed/channel-varied conditions, and recovers multistyle training as the special case of averaging (rather than worst-casing) over a finite, hand-collected condition set — while additionally allowing the condition family to be generated by perturbing nominal statistics when robust data cannot be recorded.

paper_title: Kernelized Constrained Gaussian Fields and Harmonic Functions for Semi-supervised Learning
motivation: Graph-based SSL is very sensitive to graph construction, and prior studies report unexplained regularities: mutual-kNN gives smoother yet sometimes unstable error surfaces, Laplacian normalization helps some domains but not others, and effects reverse across domains with no explorable pattern. No prior work gives a causal account, and transductive stability theory was never linked to graph construction.
method: Derive a mechanistic theory linking graph construction to graph-SSL parameter-stability by combining transductive algorithmic stability with spectral perturbation of the Laplacian. For closed-form estimators (GFHF, LGC, LapRLS, RMGT), bound how predicted labels shift under a unit graph change via the Laplacian pseudo-inverse spectrum, cast as a stability coefficient driven by edge-addition rate, algebraic connectivity, and hub structure. Validate by correlating this coefficient with observed error-surface smoothness on the same benchmark and time-series datasets, explaining the cross-domain reversals and yielding a label-free graph-selection rule.

paper_title: Recognizing Action at a Distance
motivation: Exemplar-based pose recovery (Mori and Malik) transfers joint labels from stored views to a query via shape-context matching, needing no initialization and tolerating loose clothing. But it does not scale: covering pose, viewpoint and body shape makes the exemplar set explode, and each frame is matched against all exemplars with a costly correspondence plus spline alignment (quadratic to cubic per match, per Belongie et al.). K-medoids editing selects prototypes for classification, not pose-transfer accuracy, and is static. Temporal cues such as smoothness and gait period and phase from self-similarity (Cutler and Davis) are noted as useful but never used to prune search.
