No prior work jointly optimizes which exemplars to keep under a budget, how to search them sublinearly, and how to allocate matching effort across a video.
method: Treat exemplar pose recovery as three coupled optimization problems. One, coreset selection: greedily pick a budgeted exemplar subset that minimizes expected joint-localization error on validation poses, cast as submodular maximum coverage, for both whole-body and per-limb libraries so compositions still cover the pose manifold. Two, coarse-to-fine cascade retrieval: cheap global signatures such as coarse shape-context histograms or geometric-blur descriptors in a hierarchical tree screen out most exemplars, then full matching runs only on a shortlist, with stage thresholds tuned to minimize compute under a recall constraint, giving sublinear per-frame cost. Three, adaptive temporal search: keep top candidates per frame in a trellis and run spatio-temporal Viterbi search with velocity edges, estimate gait period and phase from self-similarity to phase-index the database and prune candidates, and allocate a per-clip matching budget across frames by spending more where candidate uncertainty is high. Add active growth: when residuals stay high, acquire a new exemplar in that pose region and rerun the greedy update. Evaluate on gait and everyday-movement clips, plotting accuracy versus exemplars matched per frame and wall-clock time against exhaustive matching and a K-medoids baseline.

paper_title: Adaptive Pattern Classification and Universal Recoding: II. Feedback, Expectation, Olfaction, Illusions
motivation: In this corpus, opposite-signed aftereffects have three separate explanations: Grossberg's slow-transmitter opponent rebound (fear-to-relief), Levine and Grossberg's shunting normalization and peak shift (tilt aftereffect), and Wilson's modifiable inhibitory synapses (spatial-frequency adaptation), where Wilson rejects fatigue because magnitude saturates while recovery lengthens with adaptation. No formal account links them, and none sees that Grossberg's bounded gate could itself reproduce Wilson's saturation-plus-lengthening-recovery signature. Affective rebounds, perceptual adaptation, and the CNV arousal literature thus stay disconnected despite sharing a tonic-arousal variable.
method: Define one operator, the Adaptation-Gated Shunting Opponent Field: shunting on-center off-surround opponent pairs over a feature continuum (color, orientation, frequency, or valence), each pathway multiplicatively gated by a slow bounded transmitter with accumulation-depletion kinetics and a shared tonic arousal input. Prove a theorem that input offset unmasks the differentially depleted gate, giving a transient opposite-signed rebound that instantiates afterimages, tilt and frequency aftereffects, and fear-to-relief as one event. Prove a bound: since transmitter is nonnegative, rebound magnitude saturates with adaptation duration while recovery time keeps lengthening, reproducing Wilson's data without synaptic learning. Corollary: rebound is an inverted-U of arousal, matching Grossberg's novelty inverted-U and predicting aftereffect strength tracks CNV amplitude. Taxonomy: distinguish gate-driven temporal contrast, normalization-driven spatial contrast, and synaptic modification by magnitude-versus-duration and recovery curves, arousal sensitivity, and interocular transfer.

paper_title: Introduction: The Challenge of Reinforcement Learning
motivation: Whitehead and Ballard showed that realistic (deictic/active) perception causes perceptual aliasing: many external states map to one internal state, destabilizing value learning. Their lion algorithm and Grefenstette's SAMUEL detect aliasing via return variance/overestimation and suppress high-variance states. But these detectors are valid only in deterministic worlds; the authors explicitly could not handle stochastic worlds, because there a truly Markov internal state also has return variance, so a variance test cannot separate aliasing from environmental stochasticity and wrongly suppresses good states. This matters because real embedded/robot domains (Mahadevan and Connell's box-pusher; the stochastic environments of the learning-automata survey) are stochastic and built on delayed-reward Q-learning defined for stochastic MDPs. Behavior decomposition and active perception empirically reduce aliasing but no source formalizes what aliasing contributes, why it (not stochasticity) hurts reactive policies, or gives a detector valid under noise.
method: A Formal Derivation separating hidden-state aliasing from environmental stochasticity. Model: MDP with external states, an aggregation map phi to internal states (many-to-one), memoryless policies over internal states, and at each internal state x with action a a visitation distribution mu over the external states mapped to x. Theorem 1 (decomposition): by the law of total variance, return variance given (x,a) equals the mu-average within-state return variance (sigma_env, intrinsic stochasticity) plus the mu-variance of the external expected return (sigma_alias, aliasing), splitting the lion's single inconsistency signal into two causes. Definition: x is harmfully aliased iff the greedy optimal action differs across the external states in mu's support, versus benign aliasing where only values differ. Theorem 2 (bound): the value loss of the best memoryless policy versus the optimal policy is bounded by an occupancy-weighted functional of the between-state dispersion of optimal action-values (aliasing) and is independent of sigma_env; corollary, stochasticity alone never forces reactive suboptimality, only sigma_alias does. Theorem 3 (non-identifiability): a deterministic-but-aliased world and a stochastic-but-consistent world can yield identical return-variance/overestimation profiles, so variance detectors (lion, SAMUEL) are correct only when sigma_env is zero, recovering the deterministic case and explaining the noise failure. Theorem 4 (identifiable signature): at a consistent internal state the TD error is a conditional martingale difference (zero mean given any observable history feature); at a harmfully aliased state some history feature yields non-zero conditional-mean TD error. Since stochasticity gives zero-mean unpredictable noise while aliasing gives history-predictable bias, this isolates sigma_alias even under noise. Detector: regress residual TD errors on history features and test for non-zero conditional mean. Corollary: a refinement/active-perception objective that selects perceptual actions or splits internal states to drive this statistic to zero provably shrinks the Theorem-2 bound; deictic attention and behavior decomposition are instances, and the lion rule is the vanishing-sigma_env limit. Validation: stochastic gridworlds and a stochastic box-pushing/block task with tunable aliasing and noise, showing variance detectors suppress consistent states as noise rises, the TD-predictability statistic localizes only harmful aliasing, and statistic-guided refinement recovers near-optimal reactive policies where lion/SAMUEL fail.

paper_title: Slice Sampling
motivation: The provided literature is a family of MCMC methods whose shared selling point is moving efficiently through a target rather than diffusing slowly: overrelaxation for Gaussian fields (1981; 1990), ordered overrelaxation (1998), Hybrid/guided Monte Carlo (1987; 1991; 1994), non-reversible samplers (2000), auxiliary-variable and slice samplers (1996; 2002; 1999), adaptive-rejection and black-box samplers (ARS 1992; ARMS 1995/1997; random-direction interior-point 1998), and general Metropolis/Gibbs machinery (1953; 1970; 1990; WinBUGS 2000; annealed importance sampling 2001). The central claim of most of these works, that they suppress random walks or explore ballistically rather than diffusively (the non-reversible-sampler paper defines diffusive precisely as needing time about T^2 to travel distance T), is asserted with method-specific, target-specific, incommensurable evidence: acceptance rates, eigenvalue bounds on toy chains, or the integrated autocorrelation time of one hand-picked scalar function (spatial statistics 1993; Metropolis/Gaussian-proposals 1992). There is no shared, cost-normalized instrument to observe and measure, on a given problem, whether a sampler is diffusive or random-walk-suppressed, and no benchmark on which such different algorithms can be compared fairly. This is an evidence gap: claims of random-walk suppression and of black-box automaticity cannot be audited, replicated, or accumulated across papers, and practitioners (e.g., WinBUGS users) cannot diagnose when a nominally efficient sampler has silently degenerated into a slow random walk on their model. This matters because the practical value of every method here rests on exactly the property that is currently not portably measurable.
method: Build a diagnostic and benchmark framework that makes "random-walk suppression" measurable and comparable across samplers. Core diagnostic: the cost-normalized displacement-scaling exponent. Run a sampler to stationarity, project onto a decorrelating coordinate (known/estimated target covariance, default the slowest-mixing direction from lag-covariance), and fit mean-squared displacement MSD(w) proportional to w^alpha, where w is work billed in a common currency of density/gradient evaluations (so HMC leapfrog steps, slice step-out/shrinkage, and ARS rejections are charged fairly). alpha near 1 = diffusive random walk; alpha near 2 = ballistic suppressed exploration. Report alpha, per-cost diffusion constant, and a suppression ratio versus a reference random-scan Gibbs/random-walk-Metropolis chain on the same target and budget. Benchmark suite with controlled geometry from these papers: Gaussians with tunable condition number/correlation (1981;1990), the witch's-hat and exponential slice-sampler targets, hierarchical funnel models (overrelaxation example; WinBUGS), lattice/Ising image models, and multimodal/heavy-tailed targets motivating annealed importance sampling; known geometry gives ground-truth scaling. Tuning audit: sweep each method's knobs (proposal scale, slice width, leapfrog step size/length, overrelaxation parameters) and report the full distribution of alpha and cost-normalized effective sample size, not a best case, as an auditable tuning-robustness profile quantifying how "black-box" each method is. Validate the instrument on solvable cases: the non-reversible 1-D walk (known T vs T^2 travel) and Gaussians under overrelaxation with closed-form speedups, confirming measured alpha recovers theory. Deliverable: release suite, reference sampler implementations, and scoring protocol so new samplers plug in, yielding an accumulable cross-paper evidence base and a per-model diagnostic to detect diffusive degeneration in real inference.

paper_title: Regularization and Variable Selection via the Elastic Net
motivation: Sparse gene-selection methods that dominate high-dimensional cancer classification (lasso, LARS, SCAD, SVM recursive feature elimination, nearest shrunken centroids, penalized logistic regression) optimize prediction accuracy and output one signature of a few genes. These signatures are brittle and non-reproducible, a reliability and safety risk for clinical diagnostics and biological discovery. Breiman shows unstable selection changes drastically under small data changes and needs perturb-and-average, but averaging destroys sparsity. The microarray regression paper notes correlated genes create many equally good models, so the chosen gene within a group is arbitrary and flips under resampling or preprocessing; gene harvesting relies on one brittle clustering. SAM controls false-discovery only for single-gene tests, not signatures. No method gives a sparse signature with a calibrated per-gene reliability score and a guarantee on spurious selections, so signatures fail to replicate and mislead interpretation and treatment.
method: Stability-controlled signature selection over many resampled half-samples with correlated-module aggregation and permutation-calibrated false-stability control, yielding a reproducible sparse gene list plus a bagged classifier with calibrated probabilities, evaluated on leukemia, SRBCT and breast-cancer data against lasso, SVM-RFE and shrunken centroids for accuracy and signature overlap.

paper_title: Increased Rates of Convergence Through Learning Rate Adaptation
motivation: Additive-gradient learners here (LMS, perceptron in Linear function neurons, multilayer backpropagation) work on continuous noisy nonlinear problems but scale poorly with irrelevant inputs; Hampson and Volper show perceptron learning grows linearly with irrelevant features. Littlestone WINNOW gets logarithmic dependence via multiplicative updates but assumes Boolean inputs, one threshold unit, positive weights, known margin, and no noise, leaving noise and unknown margin open. Attribute-efficient learning is thus unavailable for realistic continuous, noisy, unknown-margin, multilayer settings dominated by irrelevant features.
method: Extend WINNOW multiplicative updates to continuous, noisy, unknown-margin, multilayer settings. Exponentiated LMS scales weights by exp of minus eta times the squared-error gradient with renormalization on real inputs and targets so irrelevant inputs decay geometrically not linearly; positive and negative weight pairs give signed weights; clip gradients, anneal eta, and floor weights for robustness without knowing the margin; apply the exponentiated update through backpropagation for hidden layers. Test on irrelevant-feature and disjunction tasks with real inputs, noise, and sparse filters versus LMS, second-order LMS, and backprop, expecting logarithmic scaling preserved under noise.

paper_title: A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets
motivation: The corpus clusters around energy-based vision models trained by contrastive divergence (CD): products of experts and binary/rate-coded RBMs, Student-t/sparse-overcomplete/topographic energy models, exponential family harmoniums, and the Field of Experts image prior, plus an isolated analysis of CD bias. Two gaps remain. First, every model uses a truncated, sampler-dependent CD gradient, but each paper fixes its own recipe and reports one-off qualitative results with mutually untested claims (PoE stresses unbiased gradients need equilibrium sampling; FoE claims insensitivity to CD step count with a 1-step HMC sampler). No controlled cross-model study maps how CD design axes (steps k, sampler, expert nonlinearity, overcompleteness) jointly shape gradient bias, emergent filters, and downstream utility. Second, these EBMs are used both as generative priors judged by denoising/inpainting and as classifiers ranked by intractable unnormalized log-probability scores, yet nobody checks whether CD-trained energy is a trustworthy quality proxy or whether good filters imply good scores. Practitioners trust recipes and energy scores on faith, while strong discriminative baselines in the same corpus (LeNet, invariant SVM, shape contexts) show reliable evaluation is feasible. This leaves room for a systematic empirical map converting folk practice into measurement.
method: Build a unified diagnostic benchmark mapping CD-trained energy-based vision models while holding data and evaluation fixed and sweeping training choices. Testbed: natural image patches (FoE, sparse overcomplete, topographic Student-t) and labeled handwritten digits (PoE, RBM), which supply labels and strong baselines. Re-implement canonical models in one codebase: binary/rate-coded RBM-PoE, product of Student-t with and without topographic pooling, sparse linear-energy overcomplete model, and a Field-of-Experts MRF; add PCA/Sanger and projection pursuit as linear reference feature learners. Sweep axes: CD steps k in 1,3,10 plus persistent chains; sampler (Gibbs vs Langevin/HMC); expert nonlinearity; overcompleteness ratio, with matched budgets and repeated seeds. Diagnostics: (i) CD gradient bias by estimating a near-unbiased reference gradient via long-run/many-chain sampling and annealed-importance partition-function estimates where feasible, recording angular/magnitude discrepancy of CD-k, extending the toy CD analysis to real vision EBMs; (ii) filter structure via localization, orientation/frequency tuning, response kurtosis/sparsity, topographic organization, and redundancy versus PCA and projection-pursuit references; (iii) generative utility via denoising/inpainting performance vs design axes; (iv) discriminative utility via both the unnormalized per-class log-prob scoring scheme and linear read-out from features, benchmarked against LeNet, invariant SVM, and shape contexts; (v) score reliability by testing whether unnormalized energy consistently ranks held-out real vs corrupted/generated images and correlates with reference-likelihood proxies. Deliverables: phase-diagram-style maps linking each design choice to each diagnostic with significance across seeds, direct tests of untested claims (FoE step-insensitivity; filters-imply-good-scores), identification of regimes where short-run CD bias is benign vs harmful for generation vs classification, and a reusable benchmark with evidence-based recipes for CD settings, samplers, and expert families.

paper_title: Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers
motivation:
The sources pioneered two paradigms of machine intelligence that both rest, silently, on the same unexamined assumption. (1) Connectionist/self-organizing learners: Rosenblatt's perceptron explicitly derives its "probability of correct generalization" (Pg) from physical connectivity parameters, and states that generalization is above chance only in a "differentiated environment" where the machine's similarity structure (sensory/A-unit overlap) correlates with the environment's classes — "in such an [ideal, undifferentiated] environment, no basis for generalization exists." Farley & Clark's self-organizing systems and Rochester et al.'s cell-assembly simulations similarly let generalization emerge from connectivity, and note the assemblies "do not yet act just as the theory requires." (2) Symbolic heuristic search: Shannon's chess program relies on an evaluation function whose principles "are only generalizations from empirical evidence... only have a kind of statistical validity," and "any chess principle can be contradicted by particular positions."

In every case, the machine's success depends on a prior choice of WHICH of the infinitely many hypotheses consistent with the evidence it projects onto novel inputs — its similarity metric or its feature basis — yet each work takes that choice as given and never asks where it comes from or what it forbids. Goodman's Fact, Fiction and Forecast (1954), among these very sources, poses exactly this as the "new riddle of induction": generalization is impossible without a prior selection of projectible predicates, since the same evidence supports incompatible forecasts (grue). But the AI works and Goodman's philosophy were never connected, and no source offers a formal, unified account — spanning connectionist and symbolic machines — of where the indispensable inductive bias resides, why it must be there, and what it cannot do. This gap matters because the very claims that these systems "learn," "generalize," or "know chess principles" are meaningful only relative to such a bias; making it explicit explains the acknowledged defeasibility of heuristics, the collapse of perceptron generalization in undifferentiated environments, and the stated ceiling of "statistical separability" for higher-order abstraction.
method:
Develop a formal theory of "machine projectibility" that recasts the shared, unexamined bias of these systems as an instance of Goodman's new riddle of induction, and derive its consequences as theorems.

(1) Formal model. Define a forecasting machine M = (X, Y, F, e) that maps finite evidence e (observed input–output or position–value pairs) to a total prediction function on the instance space X. Define M's inductive bias as the equivalence/similarity structure Π_M it imposes on X: x ~ x' when the machine is architecturally constrained to assign them related outputs. Instantiate Π_M for each paradigm: for the perceptron, the map from stimuli to A-unit activation patterns (statistical separability); for self-organizing systems, Farley–Clark's class C and its transform decomposition; for cell assemblies, the co-activation partition induced by the connectivity graph; for chess, the level sets of the evaluation function f(P)=Σ w_i g_i(P), whose feature set {g_i} is the projectible-predicate basis.

(2) Representation theorem (what a machine can project). Prove that the set of hypotheses M can converge to from finite evidence is exactly the hypotheses measurable with respect to the σ-algebra generated by Π_M (unions of Π_M-cells). Corollary: a predicate is M-projectible iff it does not cut across Π_M-cells; "grue"-type predicates are non-projectible precisely when they split cells. This formally identifies Goodman's projectible predicates with the machine's architectural/feature partition and identifies Rosenblatt's "ideal environment, no basis for generalization" with Π_M degenerating to the trivial partition.

(3) Conservation / no-free-lunch theorem (why bias is necessary). Prove that, averaged uniformly over all environments consistent with any finite evidence, expected out-of-sample accuracy of any M equals chance; hence above-chance generalization implies a non-uniform prior, and that prior is exactly Π_M. This derives Rosenblatt's empirical Pg condition (Pci2 < Pa < Pci1) as the special case "Π_M correlates with the environment's true class partition," and derives Shannon's "only statistical validity / contradicted by particular positions" as the misalignment residual between the evaluation function's level sets and true game-theoretic value — turning two 1950s empirical observations into corollaries of one bound, and instantiating Goodman's "no projection without entrenchment" in the machine setting.

(4) Taxonomy of entrenchment (a conceptual distinction). Classify how the required bias is installed: (a) structural entrenchment — bias emergent from connectivity, tunable only through physical parameters (Rosenblatt's six), opaque and justifiable only by environmental match; (b) symbolic/heuristic entrenchment — bias explicitly encoded as designer-chosen features/weights, interpretable but defeasible; (c) dynamical/self-organizing entrenchment — a time-varying Π_M(t) that reorganizes (cell-assembly growth and fractionation). Show all three are the same formal object — a prior over partitions of X — differing only in mechanism, and map Goodman's linguistic "entrenchment by past use" as a fourth instance. Derive that a machine can enlarge its projectible class only by changing Π_M itself (not by more data), formally explaining Rosenblatt's stated limit that statistical separability alone cannot yield higher-order abstraction.

(5) Falsifiable consequences. From the theory define an alignment index A(Π_M, environment) and prove it upper-bounds achievable Pg and lower-bounds evaluation-function error; propose re-deriving/re-simulating the classic perceptron and cell-assembly experiments to confirm that measured generalization tracks A, and testing that any modification improving generalization on one environment must, by the conservation theorem, degrade it on the complementary class — a direct, checkable prediction unifying the connectionist and symbolic sources under one derivation.

paper_title: Learning Motor Primitives for Robotics
motivation: Across this literature, DMP-based policy search (PoWER, Reward-Weighted Regression, Natural/Vanilla policy gradients) repeatedly succeeds on tasks generic RL cannot touch, culminating in real-robot skills like Ball-in-a-Cup. Embedded in these successes is a load-bearing empirical fact the field states but never explains: how exploration noise is structured in time dominates outcomes. The canonical account is that per-timestep, state-independent white Gaussian exploration is too fragile for real systems, while temporally-correlated, state-dependent exploration learns fast and safely. Yet the justification is qualitative hand-waving: the system acts as a low-pass filter and accumulation can drive the robot far from seen states. There is no mechanistic or quantitative theory explaining WHY exploration structure so strongly determines learning speed, the variance/bias of the policy-search update, and physical safety, and no principled rule for choosing the exploration correlation timescale. This is an explanation gap: exploration design is currently folk-knowledge and per-task tuning. It matters because this fragility silently caps sample efficiency and safety of essentially every DMP-based robot-learning method in these papers, and a mechanistic account would convert a heuristic into a predictive, transferable design principle.
method: Develop and validate a mechanistic theory of why exploration temporal structure governs DMP policy search. First, model the DMP transformation system as a linear time-varying second-order filter driven by a forcing term equal to the perturbed shape parameters times the phase-localized, decaying basis functions of the canonical system. Treating exploration noise as a stochastic process with a tunable temporal-correlation timescale tau_c and state-dependence, propagate it analytically through this filter to obtain closed-form expressions for the induced trajectory-deviation covariance, the covariance of the episodic return estimate, and the variance and bias of the PoWER and policy-gradient updates as functions of tau_c, the DMP time constants, and basis width. Second, derive a credit-assignment signal-to-noise ratio: the fraction of return variation attributable to reproducible parameter-space perturbations versus high-frequency noise the low-pass dynamics wash out. The theory should predict that white noise drives this ratio to zero while maximizing jerk and torque cost, explaining fragility, and that an optimal correlation timescale exists matched to the plant and DMP bandwidth; it should also explain why parameter-coupled state-dependent noise automatically tapers as the phase-localized bases decay near the goal, giving both better credit and inherent safety. Third, instantiate an exploration-coherence family that continuously interpolates from per-timestep white noise to fully parameter-coupled state-dependent noise, sweeping tau_c. Fourth, test predictions on the benchmarks in these papers (the ten-parameter minimum-motor-command primitive, underactuated swing-up, and Ball-in-a-Cup) plus simulations: measure learning curves, empirical update variance, achieved signal-to-noise ratio, and mechanical strain versus tau_c, checking for the predicted optimum and the white-noise failure mode. Fifth, deliver a design rule that sets exploration correlation from estimated plant bandwidth and basis width, plus an online scheme that estimates the signal-to-noise ratio to adapt the exploration meta-parameters. Success is a quantitative theory whose predicted optimal exploration structure matches measured learning speed and safety across tasks.

paper_title: The Upstart Algorithm: A Method for Constructing and Training Feedforward Neural Networks
motivation: Growth algorithms like tiling, the Gallant tower and pyramid, and the Nadal growth algorithm add layers whose master unit is a perceptron-trained linear discriminant such as pocket, Minover, or the thermal perceptron. Two things are asserted but unexplained. Mechanistic gap: the tiling theorem guarantees only a drop of at least one error per layer, yet Mezard and Nadal report that the master-unit error and the number of internal representations decay approximately linearly with layer index at a problem-dependent slope, and say explicitly they have no interpretation for these linear behaviours; they guess the slope measures complexity but never explain it or its dependence on data and per-unit rule. Generalization gap: the good generalization of small grown nets is attributed only to a general belief about a phase-space volume ratio, never tracing the causal chain from greedy layerwise error minimization to network size to test accuracy. This matters because growth algorithms are attractive precisely because structure emerges, so explaining the growth dynamics would test whether the complexity slope is real and turn the phase-space belief into a measurable predictor.
method: Explain why error and representation counts decay linearly with a problem- and rule-dependent slope, and whether this predicts generalization. Phenomenology reproduces the decay on tunable tasks: Monte-Carlo Ising domain-wall patterns with varied length, training size and difficulty; random Boolean functions; parity. Record per-layer error, representation count, master-unit margin distribution, final size and held-out accuracy, while swapping the per-unit rule among pocket, Minover and thermal, and the scheme among tiling, tower and growth, to separate geometry from margin effects. Theory models a layer as separating current prototypes weighted by pattern-volume with one hyperplane, so the reduction equals the largest volume-weighted misclassified subset a single discriminant can cut; via perceptron statistical mechanics, using Gardner capacity and the rule-induced margin distribution, derive the expected per-layer reduction from representation geometry, effective dimension and margin, find when it is constant giving linear decay, and obtain an estimable slope, then extend to representation counts. Test predicted slope and total size across difficulty, size, scheme and rule, checking that higher-margin rules shift them as predicted. Finally test whether a steep clean slope with large margins signals hyperplanes aligning with true regularities rather than memorization, predicting smaller nets and better accuracy, correlating slope and margins with generalization, comparing to the phase-space argument, and contrasting with fixed-architecture backpropagation.

paper_title: Short Term Load Forecasting Using Artificial Neural Network
motivation: The prior works span the main STLF families: feed-forward ANNs, recurrent/functional-link ANNs, adaptive modular ANN ensembles, fuzzy rule bases, and expert systems. All claim accurate or robust results, yet the field cannot compare them because each is evaluated in isolation. Datasets differ, input sets differ, and metrics differ. Robustness and portability are asserted anecdotally rather than measured. This is an evidence gap: there is no shared benchmark, common protocol, or condition-stratified measurement to observe which approach works, under which conditions, and how well models transfer across utilities.
method: Build an open, reproducible STLF benchmark. Harmonize multi-utility load series into a common schema of hourly load, weather, holiday flags, and price. Fix horizons, rolling splits, and a unified metric panel. Report metrics on condition-stratified slices: normal days, holidays, rapid weather change, price spikes, seasonal transitions. Re-implement the method families under identical inputs with input ablations to isolate the value of price and holiday features. Run leave-one-utility-out tests to measure portability. Publish datasets, code, and a leaderboard so future methods accumulate comparable evidence.

paper_title: Regularization and Variable Selection via the Elastic Net
motivation: Evidence gap on the reliability of gene signatures. The sources document many methods for selecting predictive genes from high dimensional microarray data: the lasso, least-angle-regression, SCAD nonconcave penalties, bridge penalties, penalized logistic regression, gene groups, shrunken centroids, SVM recursive feature elimination, gene harvesting and shaving, and foundational cancer signatures. All are validated almost exclusively by predictive accuracy, yet the identity of the selected gene set is never systematically measured, audited, or compared across methods. This matters because Breiman's instability paper shows selection procedures are unstable and that instability inflates predictive loss, and because the regression-approach and gene-harvesting work invokes the Rashomon effect: with correlated genes many distinct gene sets predict comparably well, so reporting one signature falsely implies a unique answer. The field lacks a shared instrument to observe how reproducible a signature is, to score per-gene reliability, to distinguish a stable core gene from an interchangeable correlated stand-in, and to benchmark methods on stability rather than accuracy. Breiman measured and stabilized instability via perturb-and-average, but only for prediction error, never for the identity of selected features, which is the opening this idea fills.
method: Build a resampling-based diagnostic and benchmark framework, Selection Stability Profiling, to measure, compare, and audit the reproducibility of gene signatures across selection methods. First, a perturbation engine generates many perturbed datasets following Breiman's stabilization idea and the perturbation catalogue in the regression-approach paper by bootstrapping and subsampling cases and optionally varying defensible preprocessing. Second, path-indexed selection runs each method such as lasso, LARS, SCAD, bridge, penalized logistic regression, shrunken centroids, SVM-RFE, and gene harvesting on every perturbed dataset across its complexity parameter so all methods are compared at matched signature sizes. Third, for each gene and each complexity level estimate the selection probability, summarize signature reproducibility by expected Jaccard overlap between signatures from two independent perturbations, and use the per-gene selection probability as a reliability score. Fourth, a correlation-aware audit of Rashomon multiplicity clusters genes into correlated modules and decomposes instability into module-level stability versus within-module gene-level stability, labeling each selected gene as core or interchangeable stand-in with a confidence score. Fifth, a joint benchmark places every method on a stability-accuracy frontier, Breiman predictive loss versus signature reproducibility, on the shared datasets in the sources. Sixth, a stabilized ensemble aggregates selection probabilities over perturbations to output a ranked reliability-scored signature and tests whether it improves cross-study reproducibility and predictive loss over single-run methods. Validation recovers known simulation truth with planted signals plus correlated decoys, confirms the diagnostic flags methods Breiman's theory predicts unstable, and checks that stability rankings transfer to held-out cohorts.

paper_title: Thumbs Up or Thumbs Down? Semantic Orientation Applied to Unsupervised Classification of Reviews
motivation: Association-based word-meaning methods in these works estimate orientation as point quantities and threshold them into nominal labels. Church and Hanks note that estimating the variance of their association ratio is out of scope and instead use an arbitrary count threshold. Turney's PMI-IR reports a single PMI value with no uncertainty. Hatzivassiloglou and McKeown collapse a log-linear conjunction model to a binary positive or negative label. The gradability study shows orientation is intrinsically graded, yet pipelines still emit categorical labels. Frank and Hall show class order carries information but assume a calibrated classifier untied to association statistics. Thus direction, intensity, and reliability are conflated, with no single probabilistic object yielding all three, and no principled neutral or uncertain rule. This matters for subjectivity detection, opinion tracking, and hostile-message recognition, which act on low-count words where a point PMI is dominated by sampling noise and where graded intensity is exactly the discarded signal.
method: A formal derivation unifying mutual-information association, orientation labeling, gradability, and ordinal classification under one log-odds-ratio model. Model: fix a positive paradigm set and a negative set; for a word build the two-by-two count table over word presence by paradigm polarity using windowed or web-hit co-occurrence, treated as multinomial under a saturated log-linear model. Define orientation as the interaction log-odds-ratio of that table. Theorem one: this orientation equals the sum of PMI to positive paradigms minus the sum of PMI to negative paradigms up to constants, so Turney's SO is its maximum-likelihood estimate, the association ratio is a single term, and the Hatzivassiloglou label is its sign; prior estimators are projections of one parameter. Theorem two: by the delta method its variance is the sum of reciprocal cell counts, giving a confidence interval and a sample-complexity bound on the counts needed for a significant sign, answering the open variance question raised by Church and Hanks. Taxonomy: separate direction, intensity, and reliability, with gradability entering as a covariate scaling expected intensity. Ordinal step: partition the orientation line into ordered classes; under the Gaussian approximation the nested exceedance probabilities are Normal cumulative functions, so the Frank and Hall recursion gives calibrated ordinal posteriors, and the neutral class is where the interval contains zero. Theorem three: under absolute ordinal loss the optimal label is the class holding the posterior median, monotone in the estimate, with a neutral band that widens as variance grows. Evaluation: estimate from corpora and web counts; validate sign against the General Inquirer, intensity against human adjective ratings, reliability via interval coverage, and show lower ordinal loss than binary baselines on low-count words.

paper_title: Fast Exact Multiplication by the Hessian
motivation: Perturbation-based learning is the workhorse for on-chip training in analog VLSI neural networks because it avoids the prohibitive hardware cost of backpropagation bidirectional and derivative circuitry. Weight perturbation (Jabri and Flower 1991), node perturbation (Madaline Rule III), summed weight neuron perturbation, and stochastic error-descent (Cauwenberghs 1993) all estimate the gradient from finite differences of the measured error E, physically measuring a tiny error change on noisy, offset-prone, limited-precision, drifting analog hardware. This is a serious, under-examined reliability gap. The gradient estimate has an intrinsic bias-variance tension set by the perturbation amplitude p: a small p, needed to keep finite-difference bias (proportional to local curvature) small, makes the measured change comparable to the hardware noise floor, quantization step, and A/D sampling error, so estimate variance explodes and the update direction becomes unreliable; a large p yields a systematically biased descent direction. The weight-perturbation paper treats p as one fixed ad hoc constant (0.001), demonstrates robustness to noise only anecdotally on a tiny XOR, and attributes divergent final solutions to the perturbation strength, a reproducibility red flag. Worse, capacitor-stored weights leak and are periodically refreshed, so the optimum drifts, turning training into a nonstationary tracking problem whose excess error (misadjustment, per Widrow LMS analysis) compounds with measurement noise. No prior work here sets the perturbation amplitude in a principled noise-aware way, detects when a weight update is dominated by noise, or bounds combined noise-plus-drift error. Since analog VLSI is exactly where exact gradients cannot be computed, these failure modes (unreliable updates, run-to-run irreproducibility, drift-induced divergence) directly limit the trustworthiness of on-chip learning.
method: Develop a curvature- and noise-aware perturbation-learning framework that preserves the cheap analog-VLSI hardware model (only forward relaxations and error reads, no backprop circuitry) but makes each update statistically reliable. Step one, a noise-bias model and optimal per-weight perturbation: model each error read as the true finite-difference term plus additive noise of variance sigma-squared plus an offset; for central differences the gradient-estimate mean squared error is a bias-squared term of order (half times diagonal curvature H_ii times p_i) squared plus a variance term of order two sigma-squared over p_i-squared, and minimizing over p_i gives an adaptive per-weight amplitude proportional to the fourth root of sigma-squared over H_ii-squared, turning perturbation strength from a fragile global constant into a principled locally set quantity. Step two, on-chip estimation reusing existing measurements: estimate H_ii cheaply from the three evaluations already taken for the central difference via the second difference of E at plus p, minus p, and center divided by p-squared (connecting to Becker-LeCun and Fahlman diagonal-Hessian and Optimal Brain Damage approximations, but obtained by perturbation not backprop), and estimate sigma from the variance of repeated identical reads, both using only forward passes. Step three, a reliability gate against brittle updates: for each weight compute an online signal-to-noise ratio equal to the magnitude of the gradient estimate divided by its noise standard deviation, and if below a threshold either average K repeated perturbation reads (variance falls as one over K) until the gradient clears the noise floor or freeze that weight this step, optionally aggregating via sign or majority-vote updates for extra noise immunity, giving per-weight confidence in every update and refusing noise-driven ones. Step four, a drift-aware learning-rate schedule: treat capacitor leakage and refresh as a moving optimum and adopt the LMS misadjustment decomposition, where total excess error equals gradient-noise misadjustment (growing with learning rate) plus lag or tracking error (growing when the rate is too small relative to drift), and choose update cadence and per-weight gain to minimize the sum, giving a schedule stable under a specified drift rate. Step five, evaluation for reliability not just accuracy: build a hardware-in-the-loop simulator injecting realistic analog noise, DC offsets, quantization, and refresh drift, and compare fixed-amplitude weight, node, and summed perturbation against the adaptive scheme on final accuracy on a realistic task (for example the ICEG classification from the weight-perturbation paper) beyond toy XOR, run-to-run variance of the final solution as a reproducibility measure, fraction of runs that diverge or stall as a failure rate, and measured excess MSE or misadjustment versus the drift-aware bound. Success means substantially lower variance and failure rate at equal or better accuracy and hardware cost, quantifying the reliability gained by making perturbation learning noise- and curvature-aware.

paper_title: Monte Carlo Sampling Methods Using Markov Chains and Their Applications
motivation: Metropolis Monte Carlo studies here report error as if samples were independent (one over root-N) and judge convergence only by comparing two chains, which fails near critical points where correlation times diverge.
method: Estimate error from the variance of the mean equal to the zero-frequency spectral density over sample count, giving an autocorrelation time and effective sample size, using a self-consistent Blackman-Tukey window validated on the Ising lattice.

paper_title: Fast Exact Multiplication by the Hessian
motivation: Perturbation-based model-free learning rules — weight perturbation and node perturbation (Jabri and Flower 1991), summed-weight neuron perturbation, and the simultaneous-perturbation stochastic error-descent rule — estimate gradients from scalar error measurements, avoiding the bidirectional and derivative hardware that backprop needs. Empirically they match backprop accuracy on XOR and ICEG and tolerate analog noise, yet the papers report unexplained puzzles: convergence speed depends on perturbation strength, recurrent nets converge to different solutions, and training succeeds despite noise. There is no causal account of why these methods have the convergence rate, residual steady-state error, and generalization they do, or how these depend on perturbation size, noise, number of weights, and error-surface curvature. Widrow's LMS theory (1979) explains the analogous linear case via misadjustment from gradient noise, tied to eigenvalue disparity and weight count; and Hessian-spectrum work (second-order error-surface properties, online Hessian-eigenvector learning-rate maximization, exact and order-n Hessian-vector products, effective number of parameters) shows curvature governs learning time and generalization in nonlinear nets. No one has joined these to explain perturbative learning, which is the missing mechanistic account this proposal targets.
method: Build and validate a misadjustment theory for nonlinear perturbative learning. First, derive the bias and variance of each rule's gradient estimate as functions of perturbation size and measurement-noise variance. Bias is governed by curvature (forward difference scales with the size times the Hessian, central difference with the size squared), while variance scales inversely with the size squared and grows with the number of weights for simultaneous-perturbation schemes. Second, model learning near a minimum as stochastic approximation on a locally quadratic surface, and decompose the weight-error recursion along the Hessian eigenvectors to obtain a closed-form steady-state excess error, a nonlinear analogue of Widrow's misadjustment, expressed through learning rate, perturbation size, noise, and the eigenvalue spectrum. The theory predicts an optimal perturbation size trading bias against noise, a penalty proportional to the number of weights for simultaneous versus per-weight perturbation, and convergence time set by the ratio of largest to smallest eigenvalue. Third, extend the analysis to recurrent networks to explain why perturbative training and recurrent backprop reach different final solutions. Fourth, validate on XOR and an ICEG-like task by measuring the true Hessian spectrum with exact and order-n Hessian-vector methods, injecting controlled analog-like noise, sweeping perturbation size and learning rate, and comparing measured against predicted convergence rate, excess error, optimal perturbation size, and weight-count scaling, while relating generalization to the effective number of parameters. Finally, turn the theory into an eigenvalue-spectrum-informed adaptive schedule for perturbation size and learning rate that minimizes misadjustment, giving a principled design rule for analog on-chip learning.

paper_title: Decoupled Extended Kalman Filter Training of Feedforward Layered Networks
motivation: Around 1989-1991 several fast alternatives to backpropagation appeared for training feedforward networks: global Extended Kalman filtering, the neuron-local Multiple Extended Kalman Algorithm (MEKA), and Marquardt-Levenberg adaptive least-squares training (Kollias and Anastassiou). Each claims better convergence and solution quality, but the evidence is fragmentary and non-comparable: MEKA uses two benchmark problems, the adaptive least-squares work uses XOR and image halftoning, and each uses different architectures, initializations, stopping rules, and error definitions. These methods are judged almost exclusively by how fast and how low they drive the training least-squares error. Yet Kohonen, Barna and Chrisley's benchmarking study shows that for genuinely statistical problems the least-square criterion may be a poor proxy, and the meaningful yardstick is proximity to the decision-theoretic Bayes-optimal error and generalization, which none of the fast-training papers measure. Moreover, the settings where fast second-order training matters most, nonlinear dynamic-system identification and control (Narendra and Parthasarathy) and real sensor-image classification (the microCT bone-thresholding classifier of Feldkamp et al.), are never used to test these training algorithms. This is an evidence gap: the field has no common, decision-theoretically grounded way to observe, compare, and accumulate evidence about what these Kalman/second-order training algorithms actually buy, i.e., whether faster training-error convergence yields better statistical accuracy and generalization, merely reflects overfitting of a least-squares surrogate, or is an artifact of a particular task, seed, or architecture.
method: Build a reproducible benchmarking-and-diagnosis framework that separates optimization behavior from statistical quality across a common set of training algorithms. First, a common protocol: implement, with identical architectures, initializations, data splits, and matched compute budgets, standard backpropagation, global Extended Kalman training, neuron-local MEKA, and the adaptive least-squares Marquardt-Levenberg method, so cross-algorithm claims become auditable. Second, a three-tier task suite with known or external ground truth: Tier A, Bayes-referenced statistical classification with analytically specified class densities and controllable overlap and dimensionality following Kohonen et al., so Bayes-optimal error is computable; Tier B, nonlinear dynamic-system identification using the plant models from Narendra and Parthasarathy, giving an exact reference for multi-step prediction error and stability; Tier C, the real microCT bone grayscale-thresholding classification task. Third, a metric battery decoupling the conflated quantities: for each algorithm-task-seed report optimization dynamics (flops and epochs to fixed training-error milestones, plus wall-clock and memory versus network size, probing global-EKF quadratic storage against MEKA's locality claim); statistical suboptimality (gap between held-out error and the Tier-A Bayes limit or Tier-B true-system error); generalization gap; and robustness (variance across many seeds and across small networks and datasets, the regime MEKA claims). Fourth, a central diagnostic: track along each trajectory the joint evolution of training least-squares error and test error or distance to Bayes, testing whether fast second-order trainers reach lower training error yet plateau further from the Bayes boundary or overfit sooner; also test MEKA's local-minima claim by measuring dispersion and Bayes-gap of converged solutions across seeds on nonconvex, disjoint-class tasks. Fifth, output an evidence ledger: per-task tables with confidence intervals, significance tests for pairwise comparisons, and cost-versus-accuracy Pareto curves, turning scattered superiority claims into a standardized, extensible record. The framework is feasible with the exact models and tasks in the provided papers and gives the field a shared, decision-theoretically anchored instrument to measure and accumulate evidence about fast network-training algorithms.

paper_title: Q-Learning
motivation: Barto and Singh's "On the Computational Economics of Reinforcement Learning" (1990) explicitly poses, but only empirically probes on a single small Markov chain, the question: given a fixed amount of computation per control action, should it be spent on cheap direct (model-free) updates (Watkins Q-learning, Sutton TD) or on expensive indirect model-estimation-plus-DP? They conclude a direct method augmented with indirect techniques (Dyna) is promising but leave the allocation open and context-dependent. Sutton's Dyna (1990) operationalizes this by interleaving real experience with k hypothetical model backups, and Barto/Bradtke/Singh real-time asynchronous DP does selective backups during control. Yet in Dyna the number of planning backups k is a hand-set hyperparameter and the planning state x is simply picked arbitrarily, and real-time DP does not say which backups are worth their cost. None of these works treats a unit of computation itself as a decision to be optimized: there is no formal objective, no marginal-value quantity, and no bound tying the amount and targeting of computation to learning progress. Kushner and Clark stochastic-approximation theory certifies asymptotic convergence of the direct updates but is silent about finite per-step compute budgeting; Bellman DP gives exact backups but assumes a full model and unlimited sweeps. The gap is a principled theory of which backups (direct, model, or simulated) to perform under a fixed compute budget, and a derivation of when indirect computation is worth its cost. It matters because it is the missing analytical foundation for the observed direct-vs-indirect and Dyna trade-offs, and it converts arbitrary hyperparameters (k, planning-state choice) into quantities derived from the agent's own uncertainty.
method: Deliver a formal-derivation contribution: a value-of-computation theory for budget-constrained reinforcement learning, comprising a taxonomy, an objective, and bounds. (1) Taxonomy of elementary computational operations: formalize every learning act as an operation o with cost c(o): a direct backup using one real transition (Q/TD update), a model-estimation update refining transition/reward estimates, and a simulated planning backup at an agent-chosen (s,a) using the current model. This makes the direct/indirect distinction (Barto and Singh) and the real/hypothetical distinction (Dyna) two orthogonal axes: source of sample vs whether a model is updated, giving a clean 2x2 conceptual map. (2) Meta-level objective: define the agent epistemic state K = value estimates Q, model estimates Phat and Rhat, and counts N. Cast one control step as choosing a multiset of operations O with total cost at most B (the Barto and Singh per-action budget) to maximize expected reduction in policy suboptimality J(K)=norm(V* minus V of pi(K)); maximize the sum of DeltaJ(o)/c(o) subject to total cost at most B. This is a formal knapsack over computations. (3) Marginal-value theorem: prove that for a Bellman backup at (s,a) the immediate reduction of the max-norm value error equals the current Bellman residual Delta(s,a)=abs(r + gamma E V(s') minus Q(s,a)), and the reduction in policy suboptimality is upper-bounded by a discounted-reachability-weighted sum of residuals, sum over x of rho_gamma(x) times Delta(x), where rho_gamma propagates residuals backward along transitions with factor gamma. Corollary: the compute-optimal targeting rule assigns each candidate backup priority equal to expected residual times downstream reachability, turning Dyna arbitrary pick-a-state and fixed k into a derived, uncertainty-driven allocation, and giving real-time DP a formal selection criterion. (4) Direct-vs-indirect crossover bound formalizing Barto and Singh empirically: model a simulated backup value as the exact-backup value degraded by model error epsilon(s,a) (a function of N(s,a)) and non-stationarity drift delta. Derive a closed-form threshold: indirect (model plus planning) allocation dominates direct allocation iff the per-unit-cost residual reduction through planning, discounted by model error, exceeds that of a direct update, yielding an explicit budget/stationarity boundary B*(gamma, epsilon, delta) predicting when planning pays off. This analytically recovers their finding that under tight budgets direct-plus-light-indirect beats fully indirect DP. (5) Convergence/regret guarantee: treat the direct stochastic updates with Kushner-Clark stochastic-approximation (ODE) conditions to guarantee asymptotic correctness of the model-free component, and use Bellman contraction for the planning component; then prove the residual-priority, budget-constrained allocation attains a cumulative-suboptimality (regret) bound no worse than, and generically strictly better than, both pure direct Q-learning (all budget to direct backups) and uniform Dyna (fixed random k), as a function of B, gamma, model error, and reachability. Feasibility/validation: instantiate on the deterministic gridworld navigation task used in Dyna and on the finite Markov chain of Barto and Singh, comparing the derived allocation against fixed-k Dyna, pure Q-learning, and full indirect DP to confirm the predicted crossover B* and the regret ordering. The contribution is primarily the formal model, marginal-value theorem, crossover bound, and convergence result; experiments merely corroborate the derivation.

paper_title: Teaching and Learning Logic in a Virtual Learning Environment
motivation: Continuance/EDT models (Chiu et al.) treat e-learning performance generically; math e-learning (Bringslid, CAS) shows tools that do the math for the learner raise satisfaction but may replace the cognition that yields learning. No prior work formalizes when satisfaction diverges from learning, though institutions judge math platforms by retention and satisfaction.
method: Formal derivation: split perceived performance into usability, substitutive value (system does the math), and generative value (system scaffolds the learner's own work). Model continuance as increasing in all three but learning gain as decreasing in substitutive value; prove a misalignment theorem (a satisfaction trap) giving the weight condition where satisfaction rises while learning falls; derive a learning-constrained continuance objective yielding a scaffolding-fade schedule, plus a feature taxonomy and SEM-testable instrument.

paper_title: Reinforcement learning of dialogue strategies with hierarchical abstract machines
motivation: RL dialogue-management policies are trained against user simulators because real corpora are too small to explore the state and action space (survey; hybrid RL/supervised on COMMUNICATOR; HMM simulation). Simulator families include n-grams, Levin-style, HMM and IOHMM networks, and Bayesian models. The evidence gap is that the field has no standardized, trustworthy way to measure whether a simulator is good enough that policies learned against it will transfer to reality. Direct accuracy metrics (HMM-distance dialogue similarity, precision-recall, perplexity, speech-act statistics) and indirect utility metrics (learned-policy quality) are reported in isolation, with no evidence that any cheap accuracy metric predicts downstream policy quality. The survey documents that the near-universal practice of training and testing a policy on the same simulator is misleading, and that learned policies systematically exploit simulator deficiencies (e.g., requesting all slots in one turn because no simulator models user cooperativeness or the growth of misunderstandings with simultaneous requests). Such exploits are detected only anecdotally and after the fact, and human user studies (as in NJFun) are too expensive and require a working system, so developers cannot audit a simulator beforehand. Without principled ways to observe, benchmark, diagnose, and compare simulator-induced artifacts, reported RL-dialogue gains have uncertain validity and evidence cannot accumulate.
method: Create a reusable diagnostic benchmark and audit protocol for user simulators on the DARPA COMMUNICATOR corpus and its user/Information-State annotations. Step 1, simulator suite: train a graded family (bigram/n-gram, Levin-style, HMM, IOHMM) plus one hand-crafted simulator whose behavioral dimensions (cooperativeness, patience, expertise, and an error/misunderstanding rate that scales with the number of simultaneous requests) are individually tunable, giving controllable ground truth about what each statistical simulator omits. Step 2, cross-simulator policy-transfer matrix: with a single fixed RL setup (using reduced/hierarchical HAM- and MAXQ-style state-action machinery for tractability) learn one policy per simulator, then evaluate every policy against every simulator and against held-out real dialogues via the corpus-restricted, function-approximation off-policy evaluation from the hybrid RL/supervised method; the off-diagonal generalization gap (self-model score minus cross-model/real-data score) becomes a standardized trustworthiness statistic. Step 3, exploitation probes: for a policy trained on a simulator, apply targeted counterfactual perturbations to the hand-crafted knobs and define a per-dimension exploitability score as the reward drop when only that dimension is made realistic, localizing exactly which deficiency the policy exploits (e.g., fill-all-slots-at-once), complemented by behavioral fingerprints (actions-per-turn, grounding-vs-goal ratio, dialogue length) compared to real dialogues. Step 4, predictive validity: correlate, across the suite, each simulator's cheap accuracy metrics with the utility-based transfer and exploitability scores to establish which accuracy metrics actually forecast policy robustness. Step 5, public protocol: release corpus splits, simulator implementations, the transfer-matrix computation, and the exploitation-probe battery with a fixed reporting template so simulator-quality evidence can be compared and accumulated, and RL gains certified as robust rather than self-model artifacts.

paper_title: Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers
motivation:
Two families of "thinking machines" appear in these works, and both hide an unexamined reliability/brittleness problem.

(1) Probabilistic, self-organizing learners. Rosenblatt's perceptron is built on random connections between projection and association units; the enterprise, as he notes citing Ashby and von Neumann, is whether "an imperfect neural network, containing many random connections, can be made to perform reliably." Yet Rosenblatt concedes failure modes: the sum-discriminating and beta-systems "amplify small statistical differences, causing an unreliable performance." Farley & Clark's self-organizing system is "initially randomly organized" and reorganizes differently every run. The cell-assembly simulations found reliability depended on scale (diffuse reverberation "fairly reliable" in a 63-neuron net but "quite erratic" in a 21-neuron net) and that "even slight differences rapidly grow to be large differences" — behavior is chaotic and irreproducible. So the competence of these machines is an accident of random wiring, is not reproducible, and offers no signal about whether any single output can be trusted.

(2) Deterministic heuristic search. Shannon's chess program concedes its static evaluation f(P) is "not perfect" and that "the only errors will be due to deficiencies of the program." The machine plays confidently on top of an evaluation that is systematically wrong in sharp positions, with no internal awareness of when its move rests on an untrustworthy evaluation.

The shared gap is a Failure/Risk gap: none of these systems can (a) estimate the reliability of an individual decision at run time, or (b) guarantee reproducibility across random initializations. Von Neumann's "synthesis of reliable organisms from unreliable components," cited by Rosenblatt, is never turned into an operational per-decision reliability signal. This matters because any deployment (recognition, control, game play) requires knowing when to trust an output and when to defer.
method:
Propose a reliability-through-redundancy framework that turns von Neumann's "reliable from unreliable components" principle into a concrete, per-decision reliability meter, evaluated in the same digital-computer simulations these papers already use.

Part A — Reliability meter for random-wired learners (perceptron / self-organizing nets). Instantiate a population of N replicas differing only in random organization (different random projection-to-association wirings and reinforcement seeds), each trained on the same discrimination task. For each stimulus, compute a reliability score equal to the agreement/vote-margin across replicas. Calibrate this score against actual error rate to show low agreement predicts likely error. Convert a single unreliable machine into a trustworthy one by thresholding: the population answers when agreement is high and abstains/defers when low, yielding an explicit error-vs-abstention tradeoff curve. Separately, quantify reproducibility by measuring variance of learned competence across random wirings and how variance and abstention shrink as functions of population size N and network size — directly testing the cell-assembly claim that reliability grows with scale (21 vs 63 units).

Part B — Transfer to heuristic search (chess). Replace Shannon's single fixed evaluation f(P) with a population of evaluators over the same features (mobility, material, pawn structure) whose coefficients are perturbed and/or learned by a self-organizing rule. Use disagreement among evaluators at a position as an evaluation-reliability estimate. Drive Shannon's selective "type B" search adaptively: deepen/expand only at nodes where disagreement is high (evaluation untrustworthy) and prune where evaluators agree, spending scarce computation where static evaluation is least reliable. If disagreement stays high after deepening, flag the position as unreliable (defer/abstain) rather than committing to a confident blunder.

Evaluation. (i) Perceptron: agreement-vs-error calibration, error-abstention curves, reproducibility variance vs N. (ii) Chess: number of shallow-move blunders overturned by disagreement-triggered deepening, and search-node budget vs a fixed-depth type-A baseline at matched strength. The framework addresses the gap by making both paradigms self-aware of their own unreliability, reproducible in aggregate despite random components, and able to trade a small abstention rate for large gains in trustworthiness.

paper_title: Robust wide-baseline stereo from maximally stable extremal regions
motivation: Local-feature papers each fuse a specific detector and descriptor and evaluate on their own data with their own criterion, so it is unknown which component drives matching success and how robustness transfers across nuisances.
method: Create a controlled benchmark with ground-truth transformations spanning scale, rotation, affine slant, resolution, illumination, and blur; wrap corpus detectors and descriptors in a common interface; and measure detector repeatability, isolated descriptor distinctiveness, and full-pipeline matching to map which combination works where.

paper_title: A Note on Split Selection Bias in Classification Trees
motivation: Tree induction suffers linked pathologies: selection bias toward high-arity variables, overfitting, and oversearching, all from keeping a maximum score from exhaustive search; permutation correction is trustworthy but costly and no prior work treats search effort as an allocable resource.
method: Cast node splitting as budget-constrained best-arm identification with permutation-adjusted maximally selected statistics, adaptive racing of permutation budget across attributes, search-calibrated stopping, and global compute allocation by decision uncertainty.

paper_title: Computational principles of movement neuroscience
motivation: Across this literature the central explanatory construct is that the CNS builds internal models by combining "building blocks" or basis functions. Yet the field has no direct, dense way to observe and measure the shape of these basis functions, and the indirect evidence is contradictory. Behavioral force-field studies infer that adaptation builds a local map from visited states (position, velocity) to forces (Gandolfo/Mussa-Ivaldi field approximation; Conditt et al.), and function-approximation accounts argue these local elements have SMALL domains of influence. In tension, spinal convergent force fields and muscle synergies (Bizzi; Tresch, Saltiel & Bizzi) describe motor primitives with LARGE domains, and population coding (Georgopoulos; Sanger; Todorov) describes yet another basis, broad cosine directional tuning. The modular-features review explicitly flags this unresolved small-vs-large discrepancy. Compounding this, the coordinate frame of the behavioral basis (intrinsic joint/muscle vs. extrinsic hand space) is asserted differently across studies; MOSAIC posits discrete switching modules whereas field-approximation posits a smoothly blended continuum; and composition/decomposition work (Flanagan & Kawato) assumes but has not densely verified linear superposition. These debates persist for a methodological reason: studies probe generalization at only a handful of locations, directions, or speeds with idiosyncratic metrics, so the generalization function has never been reconstructed densely over state space, and behavioral estimates have never been placed on a common footing with physiological primitives. The field thus lacks the evidence needed to adjudicate competing internal-model theories or to test whether behaviorally inferred basis functions correspond to physiologically observed primitives.
method: We propose generalization tomography: a protocol plus model-comparison benchmark that reconstructs the full basis function of a freshly learned internal model densely over state space and scores competing theories on it. (1) Localized training: using a planar robotic manipulandum, subjects adapt to a perturbation localized in state space, with forces applied only when the hand state falls in a narrow region (specific position, narrow band of directions, narrow speed range), approximating a point source in the position-velocity space the internal model is claimed to map. (2) Dense probe read-out: interleave frequent refresher training trials with randomly placed probe trials on which the perturbation is withheld or the hand is constrained to a straight channel, so the laterally expressed compensatory force directly reads out the internal model output at the probed state, applying the corpus aftereffect logic as a systematic sampling grid rather than at one point. Probes tile a grid over hand positions, movement directions (0-360 deg), and several speeds, yielding f(position, velocity) = expressed compensatory force: the empirical receptive field of the learned element. (3) Coordinate-frame test: train at one arm configuration and probe at another to reconstruct the field in both extrinsic hand and intrinsic joint/muscle coordinates, quantifying which frame makes the basis compact and invariant. (4) Superposition test: train two separated localized perturbations and test whether the combined field equals the sum of the individually measured fields, quantifying the linearity assumed by composition/decomposition accounts. (5) Modular-vs-continuous test: attach distinct contextual cues to two adjacent perturbations and probe the transition zone for abrupt switching (MOSAIC responsibility) vs. smooth blending (continuous basis). (6) Benchmark and adjudication: cast each theory as a quantitative predictor of the reconstructed field (a small Gaussian/radial-basis local map, a broad spinal-primitive-style field, a cosine-tuned population-vector directional profile) and score by cross-validated prediction error on held-out probe states, estimating basis width, coordinate frame, directional tuning shape, and additivity. Because it produces a standardized, sharable dataset with common metrics across environments (dynamic force fields vs. kinematic visuomotor rotations) and effectors, it lets labs accumulate comparable evidence and enables the first quantitative comparison between behaviorally reconstructed basis functions and physiologically measured primitives, resolving the small-vs-large, intrinsic-vs-extrinsic, and modular-vs-continuous debates that current sparse probing cannot settle.

paper_title: Recognizing Human Actions: A Local SVM Approach
motivation: Puzzle. To recognize actions from video, a strong representation is a set of local space-time features (Laptev-Lindeberg space-time interest points with velocity adaptation), giving a bag of descriptors per clip. Comparing two bags means matching descriptors, which the kernel recipe (Wallraven, Caputo, Graf) turns into a video similarity via a sum-of-max over local Mercer kernels, reported to beat plain matching inside an SVM. But SVM and statistical-learning-theory guarantees require positive-definite (Mercer) kernels. Contradiction: the kernel recipe claims its max-matching kernel is Mercer, yet a sum of pairwise maxima of PSD kernels is not in general PSD, and Belongie et al warn many vision similarities are indefinite. The one provably-PSD set kernel here (Wolf-Shashua kernel principal angles) is valid only by collapsing a set into a linear subspace, discarding the matching structure that makes local features powerful. So the faithful, high-performing matching kernel is likely invalid, while the valid kernel abandons matching. No one has measured whether the space-time matching kernel is actually indefinite on action data, nor whether that indefiniteness is a defect to repair or a discriminative signal to exploit.
method: Treat the matching kernel indefiniteness head-on, repurposing indefinite-Nystrom machinery from segmentation to whole videos. Encode each clip as velocity-adapted space-time interest-point descriptors. Compute the clip-level Gram matrix W with the kernel-recipe max matching kernel and eigendecompose it, reporting negative-eigenvalue mass as a direct test of the disputed Mercer claim. Rather than discarding matching or naively PSD-repairing W, adapt Belongie indefinite-Nystrom: sample m clips, form block A, apply the modified orthogonalization tolerating indefinite A, extend to all clips, yielding a Krein-space pseudo-Euclidean embedding preserving the kernel sign structure. Then run normalized-cut partitioning (valid with indefinite W) for unsupervised action discovery and a Krein-space SVM respecting positive and negative eigenvalue directions for classification. Ablate on identical features: raw indefinite kernel with standard SVM, PSD-repaired variants, the Krein embedding, and the PSD principal-angle kernel. If keeping negative-eigenvalue directions wins, indefiniteness is informative; if PSD repair matches it, the structure is noise, resolving the puzzle.

paper_title: The Recognition of Human Movement Using Temporal Templates
motivation: Prior human-motion recognizers force every input into a fixed known class and never signal when they are unreliable. Model-based 3D tracking is admitted to be non-robust under noise and occlusion, while the view-based alternatives (temporal templates, optical-flow features, phase-space constraints, HMMs) assume clean segmentation and a static camera, are viewpoint-dependent, and always emit a best-match label with no calibrated confidence and no reject option. Deployed in interactive spaces used by thousands of untrained users (ALIVE, KidsRoom), such overconfident misclassification silently drives wrong agent behavior. No prior work lets these systems detect novel gestures, unsupported viewpoints, or corrupted input and abstain.
method: Add self-monitoring to view-based recognition via three reliability signals. One, per-class per-view generative familiarity scores (reconstruction residual against stored template, flow, and phase-space models) that flag inputs far from every known model even when one class is nominally closest. Two, cross-representation disagreement, extending the multi-representation HMM state-membership fusion of Learning Visual Behavior to output channel agreement as an uncertainty measure. Three, input-quality and view-consistency monitors from background-subtraction stability, optical-flow residual, and best-fitting aspect. A fusion and rejection module outputs a calibrated posterior over known classes plus an explicit abstain outcome. Evaluate calibration, open-set rejection of unseen gestures and off-model viewpoints, robustness under degraded segmentation, and reduced false agent triggers in an interactive closed loop.

paper_title: A System for Induction of Oblique Decision Trees
motivation: Comprehensibility is asserted as the primary advantage of decision-tree and rule learners and is the goal of much machinery in these papers: pruning to reduce size (Quinlan; Mingers pruning comparison), feature selection to minimize features per test to increase understandability (Brodley and Utgoff, Multivariate decision trees), and the simplicity-first agenda (Holte, Very simple classification rules). Yet there is no validated way to measure it. Mingers states that the understandability of a tree is difficult to quantify or measure and must be weighed informally against size and accuracy, and that trees are difficult to understand and therefore to validate. As a stopgap everyone uses proxies: static complexity (leaves, nodes, depth) and Holte's dynamic complexity (average attributes tested per classification). These proxies are never calibrated against human understanding and are not comparable across representations. A univariate threshold node, a many-attribute weighted oblique split (OC1, linear-machine and perceptron trees), a symbolic rule, and a nearest-hyperrectangle exemplar impose very different cognitive loads, yet each counts as one node. Thus the central claim that oblique trees are more concise and that conciseness buys comprehensibility cannot be audited. Randomized inducers such as OC1 add unmeasured run-to-run structural instability. The evidence gap is a measurement gap: there is no observable, cross-representation, human-validated metric or shared benchmark for comprehensibility, so smaller-equals-more-understandable claims remain untested.
method: Build a representation-agnostic, human-calibrated framework and benchmark for classifier comprehensibility. First, define a parameterized interpretation-cost model decomposing any learned classifier into three additive parts: structural cost from nodes or rules and depth; per-test cost as a function of how many attributes a test references, operation type such as threshold versus weighted linear sum versus distance, symbolic or numeric type, and coefficient precision in bits; and inference cost equal to the expected number of attribute look-ups and operations to classify an instance from the data distribution. This generalizes Holte's static and dynamic complexity but adds per-node weights so an oblique node is not counted equal to a univariate one, exposing a few free weights like the relative cost of a many-attribute split versus a single threshold. Second, calibrate these weights with controlled human-subject experiments where participants execute models to classify held-out instances and answer comprehension probes such as which attribute most affects a decision and how the prediction changes when an attribute increases, while recording time and error. Use synthetic domains with known concepts so difficulty is controllable, then fit the weights by regressing human time and error on the model components. Third, assemble an open benchmark running representative inducers spanning these papers, including C4.5 univariate, OC1 randomized oblique, linear-machine and perceptron trees, 1R, and a nearest-hyperrectangle learner, on a fixed suite of UCI datasets, reporting each on the calibrated comprehensibility metric alongside accuracy to produce an accuracy-comprehensibility Pareto frontier that replaces raw size as the reporting standard. Fourth, add two diagnostics: an obliqueness-dividend measure quantifying how much of an oblique tree's node-count reduction survives once per-node cost is charged, and a stability audit that reruns randomized inducers across seeds and bootstraps to report variance in structure and comprehensibility.
