Deliverables are the validated metric, the human-calibration dataset, and a reusable benchmark harness.

paper_title: Boosting the Performance of Weightless Neural Networks by using a Post-processing Transformation of the Output Scores
motivation: n-tuple RAM classifiers train one-shot but cost classes times two-to-the-n bits per table, blocking many-class and on-device use; the 1999 free leave-one-out Bayes theory improved only accuracy, not memory.
method: Hash tuple addresses into few buckets to shrink memory, refit MAP borders via free leave-one-out to cancel collision bias, and greedily size memory by LOO sensitivity; test on NIST characters.

paper_title: Structural Optimization Using Simulated Annealing
motivation: Shape optimizers in these papers assume a fully stressed, uniform-stress boundary is optimal, yet report it fails under geometric constraints and multiple loads, with no theory saying when it holds.
method: Derive KKT stationarity for minimum-volume shape design with stress and geometric constraints, proving uniform boundary stress is optimal only for a single unconstrained load, generalizing to a multiplier-weighted stress envelope otherwise, and using it to guide ESO, biological-growth, and metaheuristic search.

paper_title: Varying Naïve Bayes Models with Applications to Classification of Chinese Text Documents
motivation: Two-stage functional classification (PACE FPC scores then a large-margin classifier such as SVM, robust truncated-hinge SVM, DWD, LUM) lacks any way to measure how much test error stems from representation degradation (sparse, irregular, noisy sampling) versus intrinsic class overlap. The only such measure, Wu and Liu's modified Bayes error, is an oracle needing the true model, so it cannot be computed on real data or used to audit or benchmark methods. PACE also yields a per-subject score reliability (conditional variance) that is discarded, so no diagnostic reveals which predictions are driven by reconstruction noise, and there is no benchmark of hard versus soft functional classifiers as reliability degrades.
method: Retain PACE conditional posterior variances as per-subject score reliabilities. Replace the oracle modified Bayes error with a computable proxy by sampling M score vectors per subject from the PACE posterior, retraining any margin classifier across draws, and reporting error inflation plus a per-subject label-stability reliability score. Decompose error into intrinsic overlap, FPC-truncation, and representation-uncertainty parts, and plot error versus sampling density by subsampling dense cohorts to benchmark methods across regimes. Build reliability-weighted classifiers via subject weights (weighted-DWD) and an errors-in-variables correction, fit under hard (SVM, RSVM, DWD) and soft (LUM, logistic) losses to compare them as reliability degrades. Validate against the oracle in known-model simulations and apply to a real sparse longitudinal dataset.

paper_title: Forecasting of Electric Peak Load Using ANN-Cascaded, ANN-NARX and GPR Techniques
motivation: Load forecasting in these sources uses a diverse toolbox: multiple linear regression, exponential smoothing, ARMAX (via gradient search, EP, or PSO), NARMAX, ANNs trained by back-propagation, SCG, GA, PSO, and sine-cosine, genetic-fuzzy-neural hybrids, expert systems, robust statistical estimators, and an ad hoc joint-of-adaptive-predictors ensemble. Yet nearly every paper just swaps optimizer or model class and measures MAPE, leaving two blind spots. First, multi-horizon structure is treated informally. Every method forecasts several steps ahead via one of two strategies, made explicit only in the joint-predictors paper: recursive Iterative-Simulation (feeding predictions back, the implicit mode of exponential smoothing, ARMAX, iterated ANNs) versus direct Always-Real-Inputs (a separate predictor per horizon). That paper builds an intermediate six-predictor ensemble purely empirically, noting only that recursion risks that each new step increases forecasting error. No source formally characterizes how error propagates across horizons, when recursive beats direct, or how heterogeneous predictors should be combined per horizon. Second, uncertainty is neglected: point forecasts dominate; the Gaussian Processes reference offers principled predictive distributions and the robust-methods paper offers robust residual autocovariance estimators, but neither is used to calibrate multi-horizon uncertainty or to combine competing predictors. The gap: no unifying formal model explains the recursive-versus-direct-versus-hybrid tradeoff by horizon, prescribes optimal combination of the heterogeneous predictors already studied, and yields calibrated intervals. This matters because unit commitment, dispatch, and planning need both the best per-horizon forecast and its risk.
method: Develop a formal error-propagation theory of multi-horizon load forecasting and derive an optimal, uncertainty-aware combination rule, reframing the empirical joint-of-predictors ensemble as a suboptimal special case. Step 1, common formalism: cast every predictor (MLR, exponential smoothing, ARMAX, NARMAX, ANN variants) as a one-step map y at t+1 equals f of z at t plus innovation e, in a shared NARMAX state-space form, where z collects past loads, exogenous variables (temperature, humidity, calendar) and delay vectors as in the joint-predictors model, and e has variance sigma-squared and bias b. Define the recursive operator (f composed h times, feeding estimates back) and the direct operator (mapping real inputs at time t to load at time t plus h). Step 2, error-propagation theorem: assuming local Lipschitz continuity of f with constant L, prove and solve a recursion for the recursive h-step MSE whose variance term accumulates as sigma-squared times the sum over k of L to the power 2k, which is geometric for L below one, polynomial for L near one, and explosive for L above one, plus a compounding bias term; for the direct strategy bound the h-step MSE by an approximation gap A of h plus estimation variance that scales with model capacity over a fixed sample. This yields closed-form horizon-indexed bias-variance expressions for both strategies. Step 3, crossover-horizon theorem: prove existence of a crossover horizon h-star, expressed through L, sigma-squared, b, and A, such that recursion has lower MSE below h-star and the direct strategy is lower above it, giving a principled justification for hybrid ensembles and a rule for choosing, per horizon, which strategy and model instances to include. Step 4, optimal horizon-aware combination: treat the M predictors errors at horizon h as a zero-mean, bias-corrected vector with covariance Sigma-h; minimizing ensemble MSE under a convexity constraint yields closed-form weights proportional to the inverse of Sigma-h times the ones vector, suitably normalized, a Markowitz-type solution. Prove this dominates any single predictor and any equal-weight or fixed ensemble (recovering the joint-predictors scheme when Sigma-h equals the identity), with the ensemble variance directly giving predictive intervals. Step 5, estimation and calibration: estimate Sigma-h nonparametrically from validation residuals as a function of horizon and regime (temperature, day-type) with a Gaussian process, using the GP reference, giving smooth data-driven covariances and calibrated distributions; robustify Sigma-h against outliers via the residual-autocovariance and M-estimators from the robust-methods paper; derive a bound relating interval-coverage error to the estimation error of Sigma-h, making calibration a provable target. Step 6, instantiation and validation: build the predictor pool from the sources (PSO-ARMAX, NARMAX, ANN-GA, ANN-PSO, ANN-SCA, exponential smoothing, MLR), apply the crossover rule and optimal weights per horizon, and evaluate on the datasets in these papers (for example Taipower and Sharjah SEWA) against each single method and the ad hoc six-predictor ensemble, reporting point accuracy (MAPE) and probabilistic accuracy (coverage and pinball loss). The theorems predict, and the experiments test, that horizon-dependent switching plus covariance-optimal weighting beats all constituents and that GP-robust Sigma-h estimates yield calibrated intervals.

paper_title: Kernelized Constrained Gaussian Fields and Harmonic Functions for Semi-supervised Learning
motivation: Graph based semi supervised learning methods are compared mostly by experiments and lack a formal theory explaining when the class mass prior constraint actually helps classification here.
method: We unify the methods into one constrained Laplacian objective and derive a transductive stability bound that trades variance reduction against prior misspecification to predict behavior.

paper_title: Neocognitron: A Self-Organizing Neural Network Model for a Mechanism of Visual Pattern Recognition
motivation: The neocognitron self-organizes by winner-take-all reinforcement but is brittle: plane counts are hand-fixed (24 planes failed on ten patterns) and success depends critically on parameter values and presentation order. No prior work treats capacity, parameters, and exposure schedule as quantities to discover automatically.
method: Recast self-organization as unsupervised search over capacity, parameters, and scheduling. Grow S-planes on demand when a feature is not matched above a novelty threshold, and merge/prune redundant planes. Tune the few per-layer parameters greedily bottom-up via coordinate search. Score configurations by a label-free objective of pattern separability plus jitter-invariance minus a plane-count penalty. Adaptively schedule which stimulus to present next by targeting the most ambiguous top-layer response. Validate on the paper's digit protocol against the fixed-24-plane baseline.

paper_title: Feature-Rich Part-of-Speech Tagging with a Cyclic Dependency Network
motivation: MEMMs cause label bias and cascaded pipeline errors while CRFs train expensively, and dependency networks enable cheap local conditionals so a unified toolkit is needed.
method: A toolkit making POS and chunk labels a cyclic dependency network of maxent classifiers decoded by Gibbs sampling to remove bias and cascaded errors without a partition function.

paper_title: The Recognition of Human Movement Using Temporal Templates
motivation: Model-based sensing of humans is repeatedly formulated as recovering a high-degree-of-freedom articulated kinematic chain per frame. Rehg & Kanade track self-occluding hands frame-to-frame; Goncalves et al. estimate a 4-DOF arm recursively; and Gavrila & Davis explicitly note that with ~22 DOF per person "straight-on" pose search is daunting and self-occlusion makes matching brittle. Their remedy is a *fixed, heuristic* search-space decomposition (search the torso/head first, then limbs) driven by a generic constant-acceleration predictor. In parallel, a whole cluster of recognition works observes something the trackers never exploit: humans use only a *small subspace* of the space of motions permitted by their DOFs (movement/activity/action; learning-visual-behavior), these motions are strongly temporally structured (HMM action models; phase-space constraints), and they are viewpoint-dependent. Crucially, these action/gesture models are used only *downstream*, to classify motion after tracking has already paid the full high-dimensional search cost. Nobody uses the learned, low-dimensional, temporally-structured action priors to actually *drive and budget the pose search itself*, nor to decide which of several cameras/regions to evaluate. This gap matters because tracking — not recognition — is the expensive, error-prone, initialization-hungry bottleneck, and the recognition literature already proves the effective search space is far smaller and more predictable than the raw DOF count implies.
method: Propose an action-conditioned adaptive-search framework that fuses recognition priors into articulated pose optimization and allocates a fixed per-frame compute budget to maximize expected reduction in pose/action uncertainty. (1) Offline, learn a library of action models, each stored as a low-dimensional manifold plus temporal dynamics in joint-angle space (e.g., PCA/spline of trajectories from labeled sequences, or HMM states as in learning-visual-behavior) together with view-dependent edge/appearance templates and, via the kinematic model, precomputed self-occlusion/visibility orderings à la Rehg-Kanade. (2) Online, maintain a posterior belief over active action hypotheses and their phase. For each surviving hypothesis, restrict the pose search to that action's low-dimensional subspace and predict the next pose from its learned dynamics rather than generic extrapolation — this collapses effective dimensionality and sharpens the chamfer-matching landscape into the "wide, pronounced maxima" Gavrila desires. (3) Replace fixed hierarchical decomposition with an information-gain scheduler (greedy/bandit): given the budget, iteratively spend model-projection/matching evaluations on the (hypothesis × body part × camera view × pose sample) expected to most reduce joint pose+action posterior entropy, prune hypotheses whose likelihood collapses, and refine survivors coarse-to-fine. (4) Active view/region selection: use each action model to predict which camera(s) and image windows best disambiguate the current ambiguity (self-occlusion, viewpoint dependence), evaluating expensive chamfer matching only where it pays off and skipping predicted-occluded parts. (5) Close the loop: pose updates re-weight the action posterior, which retightens the next search, giving joint tracking-and-recognition; when no action explains the data (likelihood floor), fall back to Gavrila-style generic decomposition and flag the segment for learning a new action model. (6) Evaluate on monocular and multiview sequences, measuring tracking accuracy and number of pose evaluations against fixed-decomposition and straight-on baselines, robustness under heavy self-occlusion, and recognition accuracy obtained essentially for free as a byproduct.

paper_title: Statistical Behavior and Consistency of Classification Methods Based on Convex Risk Minimization
motivation: Consistency theory for stagewise boosting is confined to binary classification, exact greedy steps, and a priori regularization schedules, whereas deployed methods are multiclass, use approximate weak learners, and are tuned by cross-validation.
method: Extend the regularized greedy-boosting consistency framework to multiclass classification with approximate weak learners and data-driven stopping via a leave-one-out cross-validation bound, proving a multiclass calibration inequality and universal consistency with rates.

paper_title: Real-Time Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping with a Single Camera
motivation: Active-vision EKF-SLAM (Davison and Murray 2002; wearable active vision 2003) chooses where to look with an uncertainty-maximizing criterion (VS): fixate the feature whose predicted position is most uncertain, since it is most informative about pose. But the 2002 paper reports the dominant failure mode is data association: as uncertainty grows, search ellipses become large (about 100 px versus a normal 10-20 px), similar-looking regions get matched incorrectly, gating fails, and with no multiple-hypothesis framework a single mismatch is fatal. The key unaddressed issue is that information gain and mismatch risk are positively correlated: the highest-uncertainty feature is both the most informative and the most dangerous, yet VS ignores risk. This makes drift correction and loop closure fragile, because re-observing an old neglected persistent landmark (which anchors the global frame and enables long-term localization, made affordable by constant-time/submap methods, Knight 2001) is exactly the reobservation with the largest ellipse and highest mismatch probability, and worst in the erratic wearable case. Good Features to Track (Shi and Tomasi 1994) provides appearance-distinctiveness monitoring but keeps it decoupled from the SLAM uncertainty and gaze decision. No work here plans gaze to make high-value high-risk reobservations safe, leaving room for a policy that trades information gain against data-association risk and sequences measurements to enable safe loop closure.
method: Replace the greedy information-maximizing gaze policy with a risk-aware decision-theoretic gaze scheduler built on existing infrastructure such as the coupled covariance, predicted search ellipses, active head, and saved patches. First, for each reachable feature compute both an expected information gain from the existing VS criterion and a mismatch probability estimated from predicted ellipse area, local ambiguity from nearby similar features and clutter projecting into the region, a Shi-Tomasi-style appearance-distinctiveness score updated for appearance drift, and the expected-visibility term Davison already uses. Second, select the fixation that maximizes expected information gain penalized by the mismatch probability weighted by the cost of fusing a wrong match, which down-weights the risky high-uncertainty features the current criterion greedily picks. Third, for safe loop closure, when a high-value old landmark has mismatch probability above a safety threshold, plan a short sequence of lower-risk intermediate fixations whose predicted filter updates, estimated via Davison's simulated-prediction lookahead, shrink the target ellipse below threshold, then reobserve, turning loop closure into a planned robustness maneuver. Fourth, before fusing a risky reobservation, validate with a lightweight joint-compatibility test over a small co-visible set, fusing only if unambiguous and otherwise deferring, which removes the single-fatal-mismatch mode. Fifth, bound intermediate fixations and hypotheses per step to fit the constant-time budget. Evaluate on active-head and wearable sequences against the greedy VS baseline on loop-closure success rate, catastrophic-mismatch rate, drift after revisits, and per-step computation.

paper_title: A Resource-Allocating Network for Function Interpolation
motivation: Explanation gap: the hybrid RBF training method of Moody and Darken places unit centers by unsupervised k-means (Lloyd 1957; MacQueen 1967), sets widths by P-nearest-neighbor heuristics, and fits output weights by LMS. It matches or beats backpropagation on the logistic map, Mackey-Glass prediction, and phoneme classification while being far faster, yet there is no account of why it works. K-means is blind to the target, minimizing an input-space quantization distortion and allocating centers by input density (Lloyd's density-to-the-one-third law), regardless of where the target function varies. No theory links this unsupervised, density-driven objective to the supervised approximation error, nor says when it fails. Poggio and Girosi's regularization/HyperBF theory grounds RBF networks as generalized splines only when centers equal all data points, treating fewer movable centers as an empirical heuristic; Lloyd and MacQueen explain only where centers land, not approximation error. This leaves a bridging explanation missing, which matters because center count, placement, and widths are all chosen heuristically.
method: Develop and test a mechanistic bridge between k-means quantization and RBF approximation error. Step 1: using the regularization view (target smooth under a stabilizer P penalizing curvature), expand the network expected squared error per Voronoi cell to derive an upper bound equal to the integral over inputs of density times a target-complexity weight w times squared distance to the nearest center, where w reflects local target curvature. Standard k-means is the special case w equals one, so it is optimal only when target complexity is uniform or co-varies with input density; this is a testable proportionality condition explaining the observed successes. Step 2: predict a failure regime where high curvature sits in low-density regions, an optimal center density proportional to (density times w) to the power one over (d plus two) generalizing Lloyd's law, and how mis-set widths trade bias for variance. Step 3: on the papers' own benchmarks (logistic map, Mackey-Glass, phonemes), build controlled density-curvature mismatches by reweighting inputs and warping targets, and check that the gap between hybrid-RBF error and an all-centers reference tracks the predicted weighted distortion. Step 4: derive a curvature-weighted k-means that minimizes the weighted distortion, estimating w online from LMS residual magnitude, and confirm it restores accuracy exactly in the predicted failure regime but not elsewhere, closing the causal loop.

paper_title: Parametric shape recognition using a probabilistic inverse theory
motivation: Prior works fit parametric volumetric models to range data (superquadrics, geons, implicit polynomials), attach a confidence measure to each fit, and use it to recognize objects and plan the next view. Each confidence signal (covariance ellipsoid, belief density, Mahalanobis distance, chi-squared misfit statistic) is validated only in its own paper, yet the papers admit degeneracies, misfit statistics fooled by slow residual growth, and reliance on Gaussian approximations. The open gap is calibration: whether these signals predict true error and whether they fire when the model family itself is wrong. No source offers a shared benchmark or cross-method map of when they are trustworthy versus misleading, which matters because the active-vision loop trusts them to decide when to keep looking, accept a recognition, or switch models.
method: Build a benchmark of range-image views of part-based objects with full ground truth, varying viewpoint, partial coverage, noise, and a model-family mismatch axis where the true shape lies inside versus outside each representation. Instrument the standard estimators and their self-reported confidence signals. For each condition record both true error and reported confidence, then produce calibration diagrams, over/under-confidence and sharpness metrics, ROC and detection-latency curves for misfit detection along the mismatch axis, and reliability heatmaps exposing overconfident degeneracies and fooled misfit statistics. Run the uncertainty-minimizing next-best-view loop to test whether reducing reported uncertainty reduces true error. Deliver the benchmark, protocol, maps, and a taxonomy of failure regimes with guidance on which signal to trust and when to switch models.

paper_title: Slice Sampling
motivation: Annealed importance sampling (AIS) and its relatives are a workhorse for sampling multimodal posteriors and for estimating normalizing constants and marginal likelihoods needed in Bayesian model comparison. Yet AIS efficiency hinges on three hand-set choices: the annealing schedule, the number of intermediate distributions, and the MCMC effort and transition tuning spent at each temperature. In Neal's AIS paper these are chosen after experimentation, and the efficiency analysis derives the optimal number of distributions only under unrealistic assumptions of equally spaced inverse temperatures and transitions that draw independently from each intermediate distribution, while admitting that in practice one should use cheaper, non-equilibrating transitions and more, unequally spaced distributions. The paper identifies but does not solve a coupled design problem: interpolation variance from too few or badly placed distributions trades off against equilibration variance from too few MCMC steps per distribution under a fixed compute budget. The corpus supplies the ingredients but never connects them to schedule design: ordered overrelaxation and slice and auxiliary-variable transitions suppress the random walks that make transitions slow to equilibrate, and black-box sampling and delayed-rejection work articulate the goal of removing hand-tuning. No prior work turns AIS's own weight-variance diagnostic into an objective optimized by jointly and adaptively designing the schedule and allocating MCMC effort. This matters because a poor schedule can inflate estimator variance and marginal-likelihood error by orders of magnitude, and practitioners currently rediscover good schedules by trial and error for every new model.
method: Propose ALLOCATE-AIS, an adaptive budget-constrained optimizer that automatically designs the annealed importance sampling schedule and distributes computation to minimize estimator variance per unit CPU time. The inefficiency is modeled as a sum over schedule segments of two competing terms: an interpolation term proportional to the squared inverse-temperature gap times a local variance density g of the log density ratio, and an equilibration term proportional to a mixing factor h divided by the number of MCMC steps used at that segment, all under a fixed total cost budget. Step one, pilot estimation: run several short parallel AIS chains on a coarse geometric schedule; because AIS already visits every intermediate distribution, estimate g directly from those samples and estimate h from the integrated autocorrelation time of the energy statistic. Step two, schedule optimization by adaptive design and search: place the inverse-temperature points so that the cumulative thermodynamic length, the integral of the square root of g, is divided into equal increments, which equalizes per-segment interpolation variance; implement by greedy bisection that inserts points where the estimated segment variance is largest and removes negligible ones. Step three, effort allocation as resource allocation: given the schedule, minimize total variance under the budget with a Lagrangian rule that sets the number of steps per segment proportional to the square root of the product of the local mixing factor and per-step cost, spending more effort where mixing is slow, and choose the total number of distributions by minimizing the modeled cost. Step four, transition tuning: at each temperature use low-random-walk transitions from the corpus, namely ordered overrelaxation when conditional CDFs are available, otherwise slice sampling or hybrid Monte Carlo, and tune each transition parameter such as the overrelaxation strength, slice width, or leapfrog step size by a cheap local search minimizing temperature-local autocorrelation. Step five, adaptive iteration and validity: alternate estimation and re-optimization for a few rounds while monitoring the empirical weight-variance diagnostic; treat this whole phase as warm-up, then freeze the schedule, effort allocation, and transition parameters and run the final production AIS with the frozen design so that unbiasedness for expectations and normalizing constants is preserved. Evaluate against fixed geometric and linear schedules with uniform effort on the paper's own testbeds, including multimodal and witch's-hat targets and a Bayesian marginal-likelihood computation, reporting effective sample size and normalizing-constant error per CPU second. This converts AIS's ad hoc, hand-tuned choices into a principled optimization that places distributions by an estimated thermodynamic-length metric instead of assuming equal spacing, explicitly balances interpolation against equilibration variance under a budget, and exploits random-walk-suppressing transitions to make each segment cheaper.

paper_title: Regularization and Variable Selection via the Elastic Net
motivation: Breiman's instability paper says unstable selection procedures pay a large predictive loss, while ridge is stable. Yet microarray classification papers (Golub, SVM-RFE, penalized logistic regression, shrunken centroids, gene shaving) achieve similar stable accuracy but produce highly non-reproducible gene lists. The LARS discussants note greedy/L1 methods arbitrarily pick one gene from a correlated block. No work explains why unstable supports coexist with stable accuracy, what data property governs each, and why L2 is stable while L1/greedy is not. This explanation gap matters because irreproducible signatures undermine biological interpretation.
method: Distinguish support instability from function instability and predict each from data covariance. Build a latent-factor model where signal lives in K correlated gene modules. Show analytically that as within-module correlation grows the active set becomes non-identifiable (arbitrary representative) while the fitted function converges to the signal subspace, so support instability tracks within-module condition number and eigen-gaps whereas function instability tracks subspace error. This reconciles Breiman (near-orthogonal predictors) with microarrays. Measure both via bootstrap perturbation: Jaccard overlap of gene sets vs prediction agreement, using lasso/LARS, SVM-RFE, PLR, shrunken centroids on Golub, breast cancer, and prostate data, and test that covariance metrics predict instability. Finally, cluster genes into modules, select at module level and bag (or add L2 to L1) to yield reproducible module signatures without accuracy loss.

paper_title: The Nonstochastic Multiarmed Bandit Problem
motivation: The provided literature splits into two traditions that never fully meet. The multiplicative-weights / expert-advice tradition (Littlestone-Warmuth weighted majority; Freund-Schapire; Cesa-Bianchi et al. How to use expert advice; Hannan/Blackwell) delivers explicit finite-time O(sqrt(T log n)) bounds but only for EXTERNAL regret, whose equilibrium content is limited to zero-sum game value and coarse correlated equilibrium. The learning-to-equilibrium tradition (Foster-Vohra calibrated learning and no-internal-regret; Hart-Mas-Colell regret-matching; the Foster-Vohra survey) reaches the richer target of CORRELATED equilibrium, but proves it via Blackwell approachability, so its guarantees are asymptotic and almost-sure only: empirical play converges to the SET of correlated equilibria, with no finite-time rate and no characterization of which equilibrium is selected. Two gaps follow: there is no unifying formal object organizing the regret notions (external, internal, swap, calibration) and their equilibrium counterparts into one ordered structure with a quantitative regret-to-equilibrium-distance theorem; and the fast explicit rates for external regret have never been transferred to the internal/swap regret needed for correlated equilibrium. Closing these gaps would give the first finite-time guarantees for learning correlated equilibrium and a principled account of equilibrium selection, unifying the traditions these sources represent.
method: A formal theory, the Phi-regret lattice and Regret-Equilibrium Correspondence, in four derivational steps using only machinery in the sources. STEP 1 ontology: index a regret notion by a submonoid Phi of the transformation monoid of maps phi from action set A to A, and define Phi-regret as the max over phi in Phi of the summed gain from replacing each played action a_t by phi(a_t). Order notions by inclusion of generators and prove it is a lattice whose bottom (constant maps) is external regret, top (all maps) is swap regret, with internal regret and a calibration class as intermediate points, so weighted-majority, Hart-Mas-Colell, and Foster-Vohra calibration all sit in one structure; monotonicity theorem: Phi subset Phi' implies Phi-regret at most Phi'-regret. STEP 2 correspondence theorem: define a Phi-correlated equilibrium as a joint distribution with expected deviation gain at most zero for every player i and phi in Phi_i, giving a polytope CE(Phi) recovering coarse correlated equilibrium at the bottom and Aumann correlated equilibrium at the top; prove a two-sided bound: if every player time-averaged Phi-regret is at most eps_T then distance from empirical play to CE(Phi) is at most c times eps_T in a maximum-deviation-gap semimetric, and conversely distance eps forces some averaged regret at least c' times eps, turning the asymptotic set-convergence of Foster-Vohra and Hart-Mas-Colell into an explicit approximation identity governed by the regret rate. STEP 3 constructive lifting: reduce any external-regret minimizer with bound B(T) to a Phi-regret minimizer by running one copy per generator phi with weights w_t(phi) and defining the play distribution p_t as the fixed point of the induced stochastic operator M_t equal to the sum over phi of w_t(phi) times P_phi, where P_phi is the 0/1 transition matrix of phi, so p_t is the stationary distribution p_t = p_t M_t; derive that Phi-regret is bounded by the summed component external regrets, so multiplicative weights gives Phi-regret O(sqrt(T log|A|)) times the number of generators, and with Step 2 the first explicit O(1/sqrt(T)) finite-time rate to CE(Phi) including full correlated equilibrium, replacing rate-free approachability and showing regret-matching switch probabilities are exactly this fixed point. STEP 4 selection: since the multiplicative-weights lift is driven by the entropic log-partition potential underlying the Freund-Schapire proof, derive that among limit points in CE(Phi) the dynamics approaches the maximum-entropy potential-minimizing element, a closed-form selection criterion absent from approachability procedures, and match the Cesa-Bianchi et al. sqrt(T) lower bound for rate-optimality at every lattice level. Feasibility: all ingredients come from the sources, derivations are self-contained algebra and convex geometry, the reduction is simulable on small games, and an extension replaces full-information payoffs with bandit feedback (Robbins; Lai-Robbins; Gittins) via importance-weighted estimators to obtain correlated-equilibrium rates under partial monitoring.

paper_title: BoosTexter: A Boosting-based System for Text Categorization
motivation:
Two research communities represented in these sources select the textual features that drive a classifier using very different, disconnected principles. The applied text/speech-classification line — automatic indexing (AIR/PHYS; "Towards automatic indexing"), "How may I help you?" call routing, "Automatic acquisition of salient grammar fragments," and statistical text-categorization evaluations — acquires features (terms, phrase fragments) by ranking them with an information-theoretic *salience/association* score (roughly, how strongly the presence of a fragment shifts the class posterior away from the prior) and then combining detections by ad-hoc means (thresholded pattern matching, a downstream neural net, or per-category feature counts). The learning-theory line — AdaBoost ("A decision-theoretic generalization…"), confidence-rated / abstaining predictions, "Using and combining predictors that specialize," "Boosting the margin," and output codes — instead selects each feature (weak hypothesis) by *greedy loss reduction* (minimizing the exponential-loss factor Z at a reweighted distribution) and combines them by a provably good confidence-weighted vote with margin and abstention guarantees.

Nobody has formally related these two selection criteria, even though they are applied to the very same objects: sparse, mostly-absent lexical features over short noisy texts. This matters for three reasons the sources leave open. (i) Salience-based acquisition has no generalization guarantee and, being computed once against the prior, greedily picks mutually redundant fragments; boosting has guarantees and diversifies via reweighting but is never connected to the salience heuristics practitioners actually trust. (ii) Text/speech features are naturally *abstaining* specialists (a fragment says nothing about documents that do not contain it), yet salience methods treat absence heuristically and standard boosting analyses assume always-awake hypotheses; the specialist-abstention framework exists in isolation and has not been fused with confidence-rated boosting for feature acquisition. (iii) Without a formal account, the field cannot say when a heuristic salience ranking is safe versus provably suboptimal. A derivation that shows exactly how salience relates to loss-optimal feature selection would let indexing/call-routing systems keep their interpretable salience machinery while inheriting boosting's diversification and provable bounds.
method:
Contribution is a formal model plus theorems that place salience-based feature acquisition and confidence-rated boosting inside one family, expose where they agree and diverge, and yield a corrected, provably bounded acquisition procedure for sparse text features.

1) Abstaining-fragment weak hypothesis. Model each lexical/phrase feature w as a specialist weak hypothesis h_w that emits a confidence a_w on documents containing w and abstains (outputs 0) otherwise, unifying the confidence-rated weak learner with the "predictors that specialize" abstention setting. For a weighting D over labeled examples (y∈{−1,+1}) define W+ , W− (weight of positives/negatives containing w) and W0 (abstained weight, W0+W++W−=1).

2) Exact per-fragment loss reduction. Derive the boosting objective Z(w)=W0+W+e^{−a}+W−e^{a}; minimize over a to get the optimal confidence a_w=½ln(W+/W−) and Z*(w)=W0+2√(W+W−). Hence the one-round loss reduction is ΔZ(w)=(√W+ −√W−)², so the loss-optimal fragment maximizes a squared-Hellinger (Matusita) affinity between the class distribution given w and its balance point, weighted by fragment weight.

3) Salience–loss equivalence theorem. At the first round (D = data distribution) rewrite ΔZ(w)=p(w)·(√p(+|w) −√p(−|w))², and show this is the *frequency-weighted Hellinger member* of a general family of f-divergence salience functionals p(w)·D_f(P(·|w)‖prior). Prove that the classic mutual-information/KL salience used for grammar-fragment and index-term acquisition is the KL member of the same family. Theorem: greedy salience selection equals first-round boosting-optimal selection to leading order (the two f-divergences agree to second order for weak/rare fragments), but strictly diverges for strongly discriminative fragments, with a closed-form gap bounding the loss suboptimality of KL-salience. This is the ontology/conceptual distinction: salience = a single-shot f-divergence against the prior; boosting = the Hellinger member iterated against a *reweighted* distribution.

4) Redundancy explanation and correction. Show formally that because salience is computed once against the prior, two highly correlated fragments both score high, whereas the reweighting D_t (which after selecting w down-weights the examples w already explains) provably drives ΔZ_{t}(w') of a redundant w' toward zero. Define "reweighted salience" acquisition: iterate selecting argmax_w p_t(w)(√p_t(+|w) −√p_t(−|w))² under D_t, assign a_w=½ln(W+/W−), and combine detections by the confidence-weighted abstaining vote.

5) Guarantees. Compose the multiplicative product ∏_t Z*(w_t) into a training-error/ranking bound for the abstaining ensemble by importing the specialist-abstention loss bound and the margin-distribution generalization bound; extend to multiple call types/categories via one-vs-rest and error-correcting output codes, giving a per-code Z-product bound. This produces the first formal statement of when interpretable salience feature acquisition is loss-optimal, a quantified penalty when it is not, and a drop-in corrected algorithm with margin and abstention guarantees—validated on the Reuters categorization and HMIHY-style call-type tasks described in the sources by comparing salience-ranked versus reweighted-salience feature sets under the derived bounds.

paper_title: Solving the Multiple Instance Problem with Axis-Parallel Rectangles
motivation: 3D-QSAR shape-based methods select each ligand bioactive pose and present it as design guidance, yet are judged only by activity accuracy. The field cannot measure whether chosen poses are physically correct, so it cannot audit or accumulate evidence about when pose-level guidance is trustworthy.
method: Create a benchmark scoring pose-recovery and field fidelity separately from activity accuracy, using co-crystal ground-truth poses and a synthetic pseudo-receptor. Report pose RMSD and field overlap beside cross-validated r2 for Compass, CoMFA and MSA, and plot activity-versus-pose dissociation curves.

paper_title: Neural network credit scoring models
motivation: The credit-scoring and financial-distress papers here are dominated by empirical bake-offs comparing global classifiers (LDA, logistic regression, recursive partitioning, k-NN, neural and neuro-fuzzy nets). They repeatedly find only marginal, statistically fragile accuracy differences, consistent with the flat-maximum effect, reject-inference, and combining-classifiers concerns in Hand's classification-rule work, and with the cost-of-misclassification framing in Reichert et al. and the recursive-partitioning Bayesian expected-cost paper. Three gaps remain. First, no theory predicts WHEN a more flexible or modular model reduces expected decision COST rather than raw error; Type I versus Type II cost asymmetry is acknowledged but decoupled from model comparison. Second, powerful local and modular tools exist in the corpus (adaptive mixtures of local experts by Jacobs et al., locally tuned RBF units by Moody and Darken, self-organizing maps, Fuzzy ART, adaptive-metric k-NN) but nothing characterizes the population conditions of heterogeneity and boundary density under which localization pays off. Third, classifier comparison via Dietterich's tests uses overall error, the statistic most contaminated by the flat-maximum effect. A unifying formal account tying cost asymmetry, reject-inference selection bias, and the local-versus-global choice to one decomposable notion of decision regret would explain the near-ties and make model selection a principled, estimable decision.
method: A formal-derivation contribution: a cost-regret model, an exact decomposition, two theorems, and an estimable diagnostic. Setup: applicants have covariates x, class in good or bad, posterior p of x equal to probability bad given x, and costs c12 (accept a bad) and c21 (reject a good); the cost-optimal Bayes rule accepts when p of x is below t-star, where t-star equals c21 over (c21 plus c12), recovering the Reichert and RPA cost-weighted rule. A scorecard s with threshold t-s induces its own decision. Step 1 defines regret R of s as expected cost of the s-decision minus cost of the p-decision; only threshold disagreements contribute, each contributing (c12 plus c21) times absolute value of (p of x minus t-star), so regret is a boundary-distance-weighted probability of confident disagreement and only confident disagreements are costly. Step 2, Theorem 1, the Flat-Maximum Bound: for two ordering-monotone approximations of p that agree wherever p is farther than delta from t-star, the gap in their regrets is at most (c12 plus c21) times probability p lies within delta of t-star times delta; proof confines disagreements to the margin band. Corollary: when the band carries little mass, as in typical credit data, all reasonable models lie within an explicit epsilon, formally deriving the observed near-ties. Step 3 is an exact additive decomposition of regret into R-bias, R-local, and R-select, each a difference of Step-1 regrets between nested oracles: R-bias is misspecification of the best single global boundary, R-local is regret removed by allowing region-specific boundaries, R-select is regret from estimating s on the reject-inference-truncated accepted-only sample. Step 4, Theorem 2, the Localization Gap: defining heterogeneity H as the mass-weighted divergence between global and region-local optimal boundaries measured only inside the margin band, a mixture of local experts with partition-aligned gating reduces regret by a lower bound increasing in both H and boundary-band mass; outside the band Theorem 1 makes localization irrelevant, inside it savings scale with local slope mismatch times local mass. This yields an explicit cost-aware value of localization: local models (mixtures of experts, RBF-, SOM-, or Fuzzy-ART-gated experts, adaptive-metric k-NN) beat global ones only when heterogeneity concentrates in the boundary band, which moves with the cost ratio through t-star. Step 5 bounds R-select by (c12 plus c21) times the mass of the historically rejected region intersecting the current margin band, showing selection bias only hurts where past rejections overlap today's boundary and directing where reject-inference data should be collected. Step 6 is operationalization and validation on the corpus datasets: (a) estimate p of x with a flexible reference model, plug the cost ratio into t-star, and Monte-Carlo-estimate each regret component as a pre-deployment diagnostic of whether to invest in a local model and where to gather reject data; (b) derive a boundary-band-restricted cost-weighted comparison statistic and insert it into Dietterich's resampling test, gaining power by removing confident-agreement noise; (c) re-analyze the credit-union, k-NN, distress, and thrift-failure datasets to verify Theorem 1 predicts the near-ties, Theorem 2 predicts which datasets yield genuine gains from mixture-of-experts, RBF, or adaptive-metric models, and the new test resolves ties overall-error tests miss.

paper_title: Query by Committee
motivation: Boundary querying (asking the perceptron's most uncertain input) is called the most efficient training rule, yet gains are puzzlingly small and inconsistent, and it ignores uncertainty orthogonal to the estimate, unlike Fedorov optimal design.
method: Treat active learning as optimal experimental design: parametrize queries by margin and orthogonal exploration, use replica order-parameter dynamics to optimize the query schedule minimizing generalization error, benchmarking greedy boundary queries against a Fedorov D-optimal criterion.

paper_title: Neocognitron: A Self-Organizing Neural Network Model for a Mechanism of Visual Pattern Recognition
motivation: The self-organizing hierarchical models here (Rosenblatt's series-coupled perceptron, Fukushima's cognitron, and the neocognitron) justify their architecture by claiming their self-organized units resemble neurons from the visual neurophysiology papers: orientation-selective, increasingly position-invariant simple, complex, and hypercomplex cells (Hubel and Wiesel) and complex-feature, position and size invariant grandmother-like units of inferotemporal cortex (Gross et al. 1972; Sato et al. 1980). The neocognitron explicitly maps S-cells to simple and hypercomplex cells and C-cells to complex cells. Yet evidence for these claims is purely qualitative, resting on inspecting a few trained weight maps. There is no shared quantitative protocol that probes artificial and biological units with the same stimuli and scores them with the same metrics, no benchmark stimulus battery drawn from the physiology experiments, and no standardized measurement of how tuning properties progress layer-by-layer. So the field cannot observe or audit whether unsupervised self-organization genuinely reproduces neurophysiological tuning statistics, cannot validate the biological rationale motivating these architectures, and cannot compare model variants on common evidence. This is an evidence gap: we lack instrumentation to measure and accumulate comparable evidence for the biological-fidelity claims on which the modeling program rests.
method: Build a neurophysiology-in-silico benchmark and diagnostic that applies the classic single-unit probing protocols uniformly to the artificial units of these models and scores correspondence with reported physiology. First, a curated stimulus battery reconstructs as digital input patterns the stimuli described in the physiology sources: oriented slits, bars, and edges swept over orientation, position, length, width, and contrast (Hubel and Wiesel protocol), stationary versus moving variants, plus complex object silhouettes as used for IT recordings; each class is parameterized so the same sweep can drive any layer. Second, standardized metrics are computed identically for every unit at every stage: orientation tuning curve and half-width bandwidth, orientation-selectivity index, position-invariance index, size-invariance index, stationary-versus-moving preference, and a feature-complexity score. This converts static weight maps into physiology-comparable tuning profiles. Third, a layer-wise fidelity comparison runs the battery on each model after self-organization to produce per-stage metric distributions and compares them to quantitative summaries extracted from the physiology papers, yielding per-stage correspondence scores and an invariance-growth curve across the hierarchy to test the claimed simple-to-complex-to-IT progression. Fourth, as a diagnostic, sweep architectural and training knobs (lateral-inhibition efficacy, plane-wise competition, number of stages, supervised perceptron layers versus unsupervised cognitron rule, and training-set composition) and measure how each changes correspondence scores and the invariance-growth curve. All models are fully specified and directly simulatable on the input arrays they were designed for, and the probing stimuli and target tuning descriptions are given in the sources, so no external data are needed. Deliverables are the reusable stimulus battery, metric definitions, and per-model per-layer fidelity reports.

paper_title: An Analysis of Temporal-Difference Learning with Function Approximation
motivation: The resource bottleneck for applying TD learning to control of large congested queueing systems is the simulation and sample cost of getting trustworthy value estimates, not the learning rule. Exact lookup-table representation costs O(n) storage and is infeasible at scale (Gordon; feature-based and soft-state-aggregation work), yet function approximation is fragile and can diverge (Bertsekas' counterexample). Value estimation by simulation is dominated by transients: Stamoulis and Tsitsiklis prove a congested GI/G/1 queue's settling time scales like N0/(mu-lambda), blowing up near capacity, and Konstantopoulos and Baccelli show a cut-off phenomenon where the process stays far from stationarity for a long transient then abruptly converges. So TD and Monte-Carlo estimates carry large transient bias for a long burn-in and need enormous numbers of simulated events, precisely in heavy traffic where control matters most. Existing improvements are load-agnostic: replacing eligibility traces (Singh and Sutton) and asynchronous stochastic-approximation step sizes (Tsitsiklis) improve generic efficiency but ignore the known transient structure of queues, and no work links settling-time and cut-off theory to the RL sampling budget. This leaves room to slash simulation cost using the queue's transient theory and its cheap fluid approximation.
method: Propose fluid-guided, settling-time-aware TD (FG-TD) for policy evaluation and control in congested queueing systems, minimizing simulated events for a target accuracy. Representation and warm start: use a stable averager or linear feature architecture whose convergence follows from Gordon's contraction-mapping analysis plus Tsitsiklis' asynchronous stochastic-approximation results, with basis functions from the queue's fluid model; since the fluid model tracks transient dynamics, compute the fluid value function analytically and use it as a feature and initial weight so TD only learns the small stochastic residual, removing the large expensive-to-learn component. Settling-time-aware budgeting: use the bound tau(N0) approx N0/(mu-lambda) to set an adaptive per-trajectory burn-in that discards transient-biased samples, and detect the cut-off online with a cheap quasi-stationarity statistic such as running occupancy versus its fluid-predicted stationary value; after a trajectory passes cut-off, terminate or restart it, allocating the event budget across initial states in proportion to predicted relaxation time. Load-adaptive traces and step sizes: tie lambda and step sizes to load, using lambda toward 1 with replacing traces near heavy traffic to reduce bootstrap bias, and asynchronous step sizes matched to uneven per-state visitation. Analysis: bound total error as fluid error plus residual-TD error and prove convergence via averager contraction plus asynchronous SA. Evaluation: on a GI/G/1 queue and a small network, sweep load toward 1 and measure simulated events needed to reach target accuracy and control performance versus vanilla TD(lambda) and fluid-only control. Hypothesis: FG-TD simulation cost grows far more slowly as load approaches 1.

paper_title: A Recurrent Network That Learns to Pronounce English Text
motivation: Elman's starting-small result (1993) and the SRN work Finding Structure in Time (1990) established a striking phenomenon: a recurrent net trained on the full grammar fails, yet the same net succeeds when its effective memory window is reset early on then annealed upward, or paradoxically when early data are made noisier. Elman explains this only qualitatively via four informal properties of gradient descent: small-sample non-representativeness, early plasticity versus late ossification from sigmoid saturation, inescapable local minima, and a Catch-22 in which long-range structure cannot be learned without first acquiring the primitive representations that short-range regularities supply. Three gaps remain. First, no formal criterion predicts when starting small helps versus hurts; Elman notes some problems require starting big but gives no distinguishing principle. Second, his asserted equivalence between opposite manipulations, restricting early memory versus injecting early noise, is a mere curiosity with no explanation of why both work. Third, window restriction, the SRN implicit representation of time, and the NETtalk text-to-phoneme alignment problem are all about learning dependencies at different temporal distances yet are treated as unrelated. A formal theory of curriculum benefit keyed to a task dependency-distance structure would turn Elman's post-hoc narrative into a predictive, testable account and unify these sequence-learning results.
method: Develop a formal derivational account of memory-annealed starting-small curriculum learning in recurrent predictors, organized around a task dependency spectrum. Formal object: for a stationary source define incremental predictive information at lag d, S(d), as the conditional mutual information between the target and the symbol at distance d given all closer symbols; a task is characterized by the profile of S(d). Define a nesting relation in which the sufficient statistic exploiting lag d factorizes through the statistics at shorter lags, formalizing Elman's Catch-22 that long-range structure is conditionally identifiable only given resolved short-range representations. Gradient decomposition and bound: model SRN backprop-through-time learning so the loss gradient decomposes into per-lag terms equal to a true signal plus interference arising when shorter-lag parameters are not yet near solution; derive a Gradient Signal-to-Interference Ratio as a function of effective memory window w and training time, and prove windowing acts as a projection zeroing components at lags beyond w. Theorem of curriculum benefit: under nesting plus strongly-informative short lags there exists an increasing window schedule whose expected loss trajectory stochastically dominates full-window training and raises the probability of entering the global-error basin; under an anti-nested spectrum with informative mass at large lags independent of short-lag structure the inequality reverses, giving a start-big regime and supplying the missing when-helps-versus-hurts criterion. Duality theorem: show the memory-window operator, Elman's periodic context reset, and early input-noise injection are two operators on the same effective dependency spectrum seen by the gradient, window truncation hard-thresholding S(d) above w while noise injection low-pass attenuates long-lag gradient variance, and derive conditions under which they induce the same ordering of basin-entry probabilities, explaining why both worse initial data and less initial memory work. Taxonomy: derive a three-class taxonomy, decomposable-nested where curriculum helps, separable independent-lag where it is neutral, and anti-nested long-range-only where it hurts, recovering Elman's two regimes as special cases, and apply it to SRN agreement-across-embeddings versus flat prediction and to NETtalk text-to-phoneme whose spectrum is dominated by short grapheme windows with sparse long-range items such as silent-e and stress, reframing the alignment problem as lag identification. Validation: instantiate on Elman's SRN prediction tasks and a NETtalk-style corpus with word-frequency staging from the Teacher's Word Book, estimate S(d) empirically, and measure ratio trajectories and basin-entry rates under window-annealing versus noise-injection versus full training to test the inequalities and the duality prediction.

paper_title: The General Regression Neural Network - Rediscovered
motivation: GRNN, the Parzen-window mapping network, and equivalent RBF and fuzzy systems give consistent, one-pass, instantly trained nonlinear estimators useful for system identification and control (GRNN matched a Narendra benchmark with about 1000 samples versus 100,000 backprop iterations). Two weaknesses persist in the sources: first, they store one kernel per sample so networks grow unbounded, with only ad hoc clustering to reduce size; second, they use a single global smoothing parameter tuned by hand. Specht (1971) notes the optimum should vary with location and density, that no analytic formula exists, and only a known-density closed form is available. The mapping-network paper gives only asymptotic conditions on a scalar width, and the RBF and fuzzy equivalence paper notes the shared tunable structure but no principled tuning. For dynamic identification, lagged regressors differ in relevance and are visited non-uniformly, so isotropic global bandwidth and uniform storage misestimate sparse regions and waste capacity. This leaves room for a data-driven optimization making these networks compact and adaptive.
method: An adaptive builder co-optimizes centers, bandwidths, and sampling using GRNN's closed-form leave-one-out (LOO) error, which needs no refit since dropping a sample just removes its kernel. First, greedy center screening admits a sample only if it lowers aggregate LOO error beyond a threshold, giving a bounded accuracy-driven subset instead of ad hoc clustering. Second, replace the scalar bandwidth with a per-dimension relevance-weighted vector that down-weights weak lagged regressors, optimized by minimizing LOO error via coordinate and gradient descent inside a coarse global search such as multi-start or simulated annealing; scale local bandwidth by the estimator's own denominator, a local density measure, so kernels widen where data are sparse. Third, active experiment design exploits instant retraining: predictive uncertainty in sparse regions picks the next excitation input to drive the plant into least-covered regressor regions, maximizing information per sample. The RBF and fuzzy equivalence lets the same search tune RBF and fuzzy widths, with rules seeding centers. Evaluate on Narendra-type identification benchmarks and the control example, comparing error versus network size and sample count against fixed-bandwidth GRNN and the backpropagation fuzzy system.

paper_title: Learning Distributed Representations of Concepts Using Linear Relational Embedding
motivation:
Across the provided works, several architectures are claimed to learn distributed representations that internalize symbolic/compositional structure: Elman's simple recurrent networks and the second-order RNNs induce hidden-state codes for finite-state-grammar states and word categories; Pollack's RAAM builds fixed-width codes for recursive trees and case-frame propositions; and LSA/SVD produces vectors said to encode semantic relations. The central promissory claim of this whole line of work is that the GEOMETRY of the learned space mirrors an abstract, symbolic structure (grammar states, constituent hierarchies, semantic neighborhoods) — and, by extension, that it generalizes systematically (the very property Fodor & Pylyshyn challenged connectionism on, as Pollack notes).

Yet the EVIDENCE for this claim is almost entirely qualitative and non-comparable. Elman and Pollack both inspect hierarchical-clustering dendrograms — Pollack's tree figures are even "manually clustered by phrase type"; LSA relies on eyeballed cosine similarities and MDS/PCA projections. Elman explicitly warns that clustering "loses the temporal relationship between states" and calls for "more systematic analysis using better-defined tasks." There is currently no principled, quantitative, architecture-independent instrument that answers: how faithfully does a learned representation's geometry reflect a KNOWN ground-truth symbolic structure? Because each paper uses a bespoke, subjective visualization, results cannot be compared across models, cannot separate genuine structural induction from memorization, and cannot accumulate into cumulative evidence about systematicity. The field lacks a way to observe, measure, benchmark, and compare structural fidelity. Notably, Kruskal's nonmetric MDS already provides exactly the missing ingredient — a dimensionless "stress" measuring how well a configuration's distances satisfy an ordinal hypothesis about dissimilarities — but it has never been repurposed as a fidelity yardstick against symbolic ground truth for learned representations.
method:
Build a Structural-Fidelity Benchmark: a controlled, ground-truth-anchored instrument for measuring and comparing how well any distributed representation encodes a known symbolic structure.

(1) Synthetic domains with known symbolic ground truth, each defining an ordinal ("nonmetric") dissimilarity hypothesis over probe items:
  - Finite-state grammar sequences (as in Elman and the second-order RNN work): ground truth = the automaton state that generated each prefix; target dissimilarity = a Myhill-Nerode-style state-distinguishing distance (states are close iff they license similar continuations).
  - Recursive structures (as in RAAM): ground truth = tree-edit / shared-constituent distance among trees and case-frame propositions.
  - Semantic relations (as in LSA): ground truth = geodesic distance in a hand-built concept/relation graph used to synthesize a corpus.

(2) Train each learner (SRN, RAAM, LSA/SVD; using fast optimizers such as scaled conjugate gradient where applicable) on each domain and extract representation vectors for the probe items; compute a representation dissimilarity matrix (cosine and Euclidean).

(3) Core metric — Structural Fidelity via Kruskal stress: perform monotone regression of representation distances onto the ground-truth structural dissimilarities and report the residual stress. Low stress = the geometry faithfully preserves the ordinal structure implied by the symbols; stress becomes a single, dimensionless, cross-architecture score (with Kruskal's interpretive bands: <2.5% excellent … >20% poor). This converts today's dendrogram-eyeballing into a reproducible number and, critically, makes SRN, RAAM, and LSA directly comparable on the same yardstick.

(4) Generalization/systematicity audit: split probes into training-observed vs. held-out novel structures (unseen sequences, novel trees/propositions built from known parts, unseen word-context pairs). The fidelity gap between the two directly quantifies whether structure was genuinely induced or merely memorized — operationalizing Pollack's generalization question and the systematicity debate.

(5) Discrete-continuous cross-check: in the grammar domains, also extract an explicit automaton (per the second-order RNN method) and test stress of the representation geometry against the extracted-state partition, linking continuous fidelity to discrete symbol recovery.

(6) Capacity and trajectory diagnostics: report fidelity as a function of hidden-unit count (testing Elman/Servan-Schreiber's claim that minimal networks align hidden states with grammar nodes), and, to address Elman's "lost trajectory" concern, extend the ordinal hypothesis to include temporal succession relations so that stress also measures faithfulness of state-transition geometry.

The deliverable is an open benchmark plus the stress-based fidelity/generalization metrics, giving the field its first common, quantitative way to observe, benchmark, and accumulate evidence on whether learned distributed representations really encode the symbolic structure they are claimed to.

paper_title: Improving Generalization with Active Learning
motivation: Two theories of learning speed in these sources are unreconciled. Distribution-free VC/PAC theory (Blumer et al.; Baum and Haussler; Valiant) gives worst-case error decaying only as a power law d/m and ignores queries. The query line (Seung-Opper-Sompolinsky Query by committee; MacKay Information-based objective functions) shows actively chosen queries drive error down exponentially via asymptotically finite information gain, each maximal-disagreement query bisecting the version space at about one bit. Cohn and Tesauro find even passive average-case generalization is sometimes exponential yet cannot find the spectral gap prior theories predicted. Gaps: the exponential-vs-power-law dichotomy is derived only for toy models under realizability, flat prior, and Gibbs training, with no distribution-dependent measure predicting the regime and no bridge to VC dimension; Mitchell Generalization as search supplies the version-space object but never quantifies it information-theoretically. MacKay warns his criteria assume the hypothesis space is correct, their main weakness, and no theory describes degradation under noise, though Haussler decision-theoretic PAC gives the agnostic framework. Eisenberg-Rivest show queries sometimes barely help, so a principled boundary between queries-help-exponentially and queries-barely-help is missing. This matters for expensive-label active learning, where practitioners lack an invariant saying whether committee querying pays off.
method: A formal derivation unifying version-space search, query-by-committee information gain, and VC capacity via one distribution-dependent invariant. Model: class H of VC dimension d, distribution D, posterior uniform on the version space V of hypotheses consistent with the P labels seen. Define entropy as log volume of V and query information as binary entropy H2(p_x), p_x the fraction of V labeling x positive. Invariant, the bisection index gamma: inf over reachable V of sup over x in support of D of min(p_x, 1 minus p_x); it certifies some query splits V into parts each of measure at least gamma. Master theorem: error bounded by a function of initial entropy minus accumulated expected information gain. Passive sampling: expected gain tends to zero, recovering error of order d/P. Active committee: if gamma positive, disagreement queries yield per-query information at least H2(gamma), so error bounded by exp(minus c H2(gamma) P); exponential learnability holds iff gamma bounded from zero, with label complexity of order (d over H2(gamma)) log(1/eps), interpolating d/eps and the QBC regime. Cohn-Tesauro puzzle: prove exponential average-case decay needs only information-rate positivity, strictly weaker than a spectral gap, and show the former can hold while the latter fails. Agnostic robustness: replace exact V by an eps-version space of near-optimal hypotheses under Haussler loss, re-derive split probabilities, and prove an effective index gamma_eff equal to gamma minus g(eta) at noise level eta, with a threshold beyond which the exponential term collapses to the power law. Taxonomy and validation: classify problems by gamma and gamma_eff into exponentially query-learnable, query-indifferent (recovering Eisenberg-Rivest), and noise-fragile; validate on perceptron-learning-a-perceptron and Cohn-Tesauro functions by estimating gamma from committee disagreement and checking the crossover from exp(minus cP) to d/P as noise increases.

paper_title: The CMA Evolution Strategy: A Comparing Review
motivation: Distribution-based continuous EAs (CMA-ES, IDEA/EDAs, continuous PBIL) sample candidates from a learned distribution and update it from selected individuals. The sources show internal constants can be set robustly, since the completely-derandomized CMA-ES paper states its covariance and step-size constants are not meant to be in the user's choice and the comparative review fixes them at defaults, so the decisive free knob is the resource-level configuration: population size lambda, plus initial step size sigma0 and the distribution learning rate the PBIL papers show control exploration versus exploitation. Yet this knob is critical and set by brute force: the multimodal CMA-ES study shows success rate is sigmoidal in lambda, expected running time as evaluations over success probability has an interior optimum, and the optimizing lambda varies by more than an order of magnitude across functions and dimensions. The authors find optimal lambda only by manual scans and propose only a blind schedule of restarting while multiplying lambda by three, which wastes budget on too-small lambda, never brackets the interior optimum, and ignores sigma0 and learning-rate effects. No principled online method allocates the evaluation budget across resource configurations to minimize expected running time, leaving room for a self-tuning, parameter-free variant.
method: ERT-Racing is an online resource-allocation wrapper, an optimization and search meta-strategy, for any distribution-based continuous EA that searches resource-level parameters to minimize expected running time, replacing manual lambda scans and blind geometric restarts. It maintains a geometric ladder of population sizes, optionally crossed with sigma0 and learning-rate multipliers, and each configuration is an independently restartable arm. It defines descending intermediate targets below the running global best and logs, per arm, the evaluations to first reach each target. Per configuration it estimates success probability and mean evaluations-to-hit, forms ERT as their ratio, and extrapolates across targets. The search core interleaves arms and periodically applies successive halving: rank configs by projected ERT, kill the worst fraction, and reinvest freed budget as fresh restarts of the best configs. Because ERT versus lambda is bathtub-shaped, it brackets the minimum by extending the ladder at edges and refining interior neighbors. Restart and failure triggers reuse the source stopping rules such as covariance condition-number blow-up, TolX, and stagnation. Evaluation: on the study eight multimodal functions and dimensions, compare total ERT against oracle best fixed lambda, the times-three successive-increase restart, and default lambda; test generality on a Gaussian EDA and continuous PBIL by tuning sample size and learning rate identically.

paper_title: Neural network method for solving convex programming problem with linear inequality constraints
motivation: The five prior works are recurrent neural-network solvers for optimization (bound-constrained QP, extended LP, linear-convex programming with inequality constraints, semi-infinite multiobjective), each with convergence or stability proofs and a few bespoke examples. Clear EVIDENCE GAP: there is no common way to observe, measure, benchmark, audit, or accumulate evidence on how these solvers actually behave. Guarantees are asymptotic and theoretical; the QP paper itself notes an earlier exponential-convergence proof was shown to be flawed, so claims need empirical auditing. Real non-idealities (noise, roundoff, inaccurate weights, discrete-time integration) threaten stability but are patched with ad hoc preconditioning and never measured comparably. Cross-paper superiority claims rest on incompatible tiny examples with different metrics, so they cannot be compared or reproduced. The field cannot tell which design converges faster, stays feasible, tolerates finite precision, or beats classical solvers in which regimes, which matters because these networks target hardware and analog real-time deployment where precision, noise, and discretization dominate.
method: Build a standardized open testbed that turns theorem-only claims of these neural optimizers into measurable, comparable evidence. A parameterized instance generator covers all problem classes in the sources with controllable size, condition number, degeneracy, active-set structure, and optima multiplicity, plus independently computed ground-truth solutions. A unified ODE-integration harness instantiates each paper's governing dynamics identically and runs them under systematically varied non-idealities: integration step size, fixed-point precision, additive weight perturbations, and swept random initializations. Diagnostic metrics operationalize each theoretical property: empirical convergence rate versus the paper's own derived bound, time-to-tolerance, running trajectory feasibility-violation to audit the feasible-only claim, accuracy versus ground truth, robustness indices under noise and precision, basin-of-attraction estimates from many starts, and a stability margin from the trajectory Jacobian. A comparison protocol pits all networks against each other and against classical baselines such as simplex and interior-point for head-to-head evidence on contested claims. An auditing layer statistically tests whether observed behavior matches each stated guarantee, flagging reproducible counter-evidence that would have caught the earlier flawed proof. A versioned leaderboard accumulates results per problem class and non-ideality regime so future designs plug in on identical footing. This closes the evidence gap by supplying the missing means to observe, measure, benchmark, audit, and accumulate comparable evidence, replacing one-off examples and unverified asymptotic claims with reproducible, regime-resolved characterization.

paper_title: The CMA Evolution Strategy: A Comparing Review
motivation: Kern et al. 2004 show evolution strategies with explicit scale control (1/5-rule, self-adaptation, CSA, CMA) beat EDAs (IDEA, MBOA, continuous PBIL, which re-estimate variance from selected samples) by orders of magnitude, and note that efficient overall-variance estimation is an open issue for EDAs. But those whole-algorithm comparisons confound distribution model, replacement rule, and scale control, and ran only at dimension ten. The downward bias of maximum-likelihood variance under selection has never been empirically mapped against selection ratio, dimension, and landscape, nor against progress-rate-optimal scale dynamics. This leaves room for a controlled component-level empirical map of scale control.
method:
Build an empirical map isolating the scale-control module. Use one template with identical Gaussian sampling, mean update, and truncation selection, swapping only the scale-control rule among ML re-estimation, PBIL relaxation, 1/5-rule, self-adaptation, CSA, and CMA path, each with isotropic and full-covariance variants. Test on a diagnostic suite with known ideal scale behavior: sphere, linear and boundary functions, ridge, scaled ellipsoid axis-parallel and rotated, and Rastrigin. Measure per-generation scale-change bias versus predicted selection-induced contraction, scale-tracking error versus the sphere progress-rate optimum, premature-convergence and stagnation rates, and scaling from dimension two to one hundred. Produce a phase-diagram map over mechanism and regime that attributes premature convergence versus stagnation, separates contributions of scale control, covariance, and cumulation, and yields a reusable scale-dynamics diagnostic.
