paper_title: Markov Games as a Framework for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
motivation: Schwartz's R-learning (1993) argues continuing tasks should be judged by undiscounted average reward rather than a hand-tuned discounted return, learning model-free via a gain estimate rho and differential action-values. But it is strictly risk-neutral, assumes unichain (a single gain), and is only heuristically robust in the multichain case. Risk is treated only under other assumptions: Consideration of risk in reinforcement learning (1994) adds risk sensitivity within discounted Q-learning, and Stochastic dynamic programming (1981) obtains cautious control only via model-based DP. Gap: no model-free, undiscounted, risk-sensitive control method exists. Yet the motivating domains (financial trading and process control named in Tesauro 1992, and navigation) are undiscounted and highly stochastic, so variance and worst-case outcomes matter, not just expectation. R-learning is also fragile under noise: exploration biases rho and high variance slows convergence. The opportunity is to relax R-learning's risk-neutrality and unichain assumption so undiscounted RL works in noisy, risk-conscious, multichain regimes.
method: Extend R-learning into a risk-sensitive undiscounted method (Risk-R-learning) under weaker assumptions. Objective: instead of maximizing expected gain rho, maximize a risk-adjusted gain via two variants. Variant a, mean-variance: rho minus beta times the long-run variance of the average-adjusted reward, beta a risk-aversion knob. Variant b, worst-case: extend Heger's discounted minimax operator to the undiscounted regime by replacing the expectation in R-learning's average-adjusted recurrence with a min over observed successors. Updates: keep rho and differential values sigma(s,a) updated by sigma equals r minus rho plus max sigma of next state; add a differential second-moment estimator M(s,a) from the squared average-adjusted TD error. Improve policy by maximizing sigma(s,a) minus beta times M(s,a) (variant a) or the worst-case differential value (variant b); beta zero recovers R-learning and discounted Q-learning stays a special case. Robustness: restrict rho and M updates to on-policy greedy transitions to avoid exploration bias; replace scalar rho with a state-indexed rho(s) bootstrapped along transitions for multichain problems. Evaluation: Schwartz's value-disambiguation and double-loop domains with added reward noise and a multichain variant; measure long-run average, variance, and worst-case outcomes; trace the mean-variance frontier over beta and show it dominates risk-neutral R-learning, discounted risk-sensitive Q-learning tuned over discount factors, and plain Q-learning, with faster convergence under noise.

paper_title: Robot Juggling: Implementation of Memory-Based Learning
motivation: Explanation gap: in juggling learning-control, task-level learning (Aboaf, Atkeson) converges fast for some tasks, memory-based inverse-model control (Moore) gets stuck in unrepairable inaccuracy pockets, and Schaal-Atkeson show one task admits open-loop-stable strategies (focusing hits, energy dissipation, wedge geometry) versus neutrally-stable diverging ones. No work explains why learning speed and reliability vary so much across strategies for the same task. These works either fit error surfaces while ignoring physics, or analyze physics while only conjecturing a link to learnability. A mechanistic account is missing.
method: Model one task cycle as a Poincare return map parameterized by the per-cycle command and fixed strategy parameters (hit acceleration, wedge angle, reset gain), and the learner as locally-weighted regression with Moore reliability. Compose them into one iterated map whose Jacobian spectral radius factorizes into open-loop contraction times learner-gain times command sensitivity, defining a learnability index; predict stuck pockets where command Jacobians are singular or the map expands out of the basin. Validate on paddle juggling, ball-in-wedge, and devil sticking by measuring eigenvalues and basins via perturbations and correlating with learning curves, then causally sweep hit-acceleration to drive the eigenvalue through 1 and expose a learning phase transition. Deliver a two-stage recipe: pick strategy parameters maximizing the index, then learn the command model in the contractive regime.

paper_title: Beyond Bags of Features: Spatial Pyramid Matching for Recognizing Natural Scene Categories
motivation: Recognition systems in this corpus hard-assign each local descriptor to one codeword in a fixed k-means visual vocabulary (Bayesian hierarchical scene model, pLSA and LDA scene models, pLSA object discovery, boosting over quantized SIFTs, texton-histogram kernels). This hard quantization is a brittleness none addresses: descriptors near Voronoi boundaries are assigned unstably, so small changes from noise, illumination, scale or viewpoint flip assignments and perturb histograms; results are highly sensitive to vocabulary size k with no uncertainty; and codewords are treated as equally trustworthy despite many arising from clutter. Signature+EMD avoids a shared vocabulary but uses hard per-image clustering, is costly, and lacks reliability weighting. The corpus shows no soft assignment. Robustifying the representation against these failure modes is an unfilled gap.
method: Replace hard vector quantization with a robust front end feeding existing histogram-intersection and pyramid-match SVMs: soft density-calibrated assignment spreads each descriptor over codewords via a Gaussian kernel with per-codeword bandwidth from local density; ambiguity gating downweights high-entropy or far descriptors to suppress clutter; per-codeword reliability weights are learned from perturbation stability and mutual information with labels, generalizing tf-idf; and vocabulary-size marginalization combines histograms across sizes. Evaluate via robustness degradation curves versus noise, illumination/scale change, occlusion, and k, against hard-assignment BoW, signatures+EMD, and pyramid match, seeking flatter curves and lower k-sensitivity at comparable clean accuracy with per-component ablations.

paper_title: The CMA Evolution Strategy: A Comparing Review
motivation: Continuous distribution-learning evolutionary algorithms have split into two families that each solve half the problem. The Estimation-of-Distribution / PBIL family (IDEA, MBOA, continuous PBIL, Gaussian-network EDAs) offers flexible probabilistic models — independent Gaussians, factorizations/Gaussian networks, kernels/histograms, mixtures — that capture rich variable structure, but they re-estimate the whole distribution from the current selected population every generation and use no internal, generation-varying state. The Evolution-Strategy family (CSA-ES, CMA-ES) is restricted to a single Gaussian but carries powerful history machinery: evolution-path cumulation and an explicit, separately-controlled overall step size. The comparative review by Kern et al. (2004) makes the consequences explicit: only the ESs work efficiently at small population sizes because only they use explicit control of the overall distribution variance, and efficient estimation of overall variance is an open issue in IDEA and MBOA. IDEA's variance shrinks to zero even on a linear function (premature convergence); MBOA changes variance too slowly. Conversely CMA-ES fails when no single global quadratic topology points to the optimum, exactly where structured/mixture EDA models could help. Yet no work grafts ES cumulation and decoupled step-size control onto flexible EDA models: the review's own unifying table gives cumulation and explicit variance control only to the ES rows, leaving IDEA/MBOA with no internal-state parameters, and the EDA papers (Bosman & Thierens' IDEA, Sebag & Ducoulombier's continuous PBIL, Yuan & Gallagher's PBIL extensions, Larranaga's EDA review) treat model estimation and variance handling as one entangled step. The optimality of cumulative path-length control is itself questioned (the qualms work), yet there is no common platform to swap adaptation mechanisms while holding the model fixed. This entanglement blocks the field from answering how much performance comes from model structure versus history/variance-control mechanism, and from building hybrids combining EDA structure learning with ES small-population efficiency and premature-convergence resistance.
method: Build a modular optimization platform (an open, benchmarked software artifact) that operationalizes the review's unifying formulation by physically decoupling a distribution-learning EA into three interchangeable plug-in components with fixed interfaces, so any model can be composed with any adaptation mechanism. Component 1, the Model plug-in, implements sample(state) and estimate(selected_pop, prior_model, state), returning only the shape of the search distribution (mean direction and a scale-free/normalized covariance or factorization). Ship implementations covering the sources: independent Gaussians (UMDAc/PBIL), full covariance (EMNA/CMA shape), Gaussian network/factorization with selectable dependency structure (IDEA), Gaussian kernels and histograms (MBOA, histogram-PBIL), and Gaussian mixtures via clustering. Component 2, the Adaptation plug-in, is the reusable core contribution: a component owning the generation-varying internal state (evolution paths p_sigma and p_c, damping d, learning rates c_sigma, c_c, c_cov) that modulates the model between generations. It provides an explicit overall step-size sigma controlled independently of model estimation (cumulative step-size adaptation) and a mean/scale cumulation path injecting historical information the current selected sample lacks. Crucially it operates on the abstract (mean, normalized-shape) output of ANY model plug-in, so ES-style cumulation and decoupled variance control attach to a Gaussian-network or mixture EDA for the first time. Alternative policies (no-history rebuild, elitism, 1/5-rule, CSA, and non-cumulative variance-control alternatives motivated by the qualms critique) are drop-in siblings. Component 3 is a Selection/replacement plug-in (truncation, elitist, restricted-tournament), plus a diagnostics harness logging overall distribution variance per generation to detect premature convergence. Deliverables and validation: (i) reproduce all five reviewed algorithms as pure configurations and recover the review's behavior on its own test suite (unimodal/multimodal by separable/non-separable by scaled/rotated: ellipsoid, tablet, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin), establishing correctness; (ii) use efficient incremental covariance updates from the CMA-ES time-complexity work so full-covariance and network models stay tractable; (iii) run a full factorial ablation crossing every model with every adaptation mechanism to quantify, on equal footing, the separate contributions of model structure and history/variance control; (iv) instantiate and evaluate the concrete new hybrid the gap demands, a Gaussian-network/mixture EDA whose overall scale and mean are governed by ES-style cumulation and decoupled step-size control, testing whether it eliminates IDEA's variance collapse on linear/unimodal functions, restores small-population efficiency, and retains structured/multimodal search where single-Gaussian CMA-ES fails. Success criteria: linear-function variance no longer collapses; small-population performance approaches CMA-ES on unimodal functions; structured models plus cumulation beat both CMA-ES and vanilla EDAs on non-separable multimodal functions, with diagnostics attributing gains to the adaptation-versus-model axis.

paper_title: Neural network method for solving convex programming problem with linear inequality constraints
motivation: All five sources study neurodynamic optimizers: recurrent neural networks as continuous-time ODE systems whose equilibria solve QP (1993), LP (1996), extended LP and L1 (1997), convex inequality programs (2013), and semi-infinite multiobjective programs (2011). Each asserts, for one network in isolation, global convergence, exponential stability, projection-based feasibility, no tuning, and preconditioned robustness, but only via proofs or tiny examples. No shared benchmark compares them, so it is unknown how convergence-rate bounds match practice, whether robustness and no-tuning claims survive ill-conditioning and degeneracy, and how projection feasibility holds under finite precision and ODE discretization.
method: Build a benchmark comparing these neurodynamic optimizers. Reimplement each as its ODE in a shared harness with selectable integrators, quantization, and noise. Generate parametric instances varying dimension, condition number, constraint tightness, and degeneracy, with matched reformulations (LP, L1) and standard-solver ground truth. Measure time-to-optimality, feasibility-violation trajectories (projection vs penalty), accuracy, fitted convergence rate vs analytic bounds, preconditioner and gain sensitivity, and robustness over step size, bit-width, and noise. Produce heatmaps, scaling curves, and per-class rankings, and release the suite as a reusable diagnostic map of neurodynamic solvers.

paper_title: Forecasting of Electric Peak Load Using ANN-Cascaded, ANN-NARX and GPR Techniques
motivation: Across the 13 works, load forecasting advances as isolated new-method-beats-old-method claims (multiple linear regression, exponential smoothing, robust SARIMA, PSO-ARMAX, expert systems, and ANNs trained by back-propagation or GA/PSO/sine-cosine, with Gaussian Processes and NARMAX as reference toolkits). Each is validated on a different utility, horizon and dataset with a single pooled error number and no shared protocol, which hides where and when methods fail. The robust-methods paper shows breaks and heteroscedasticity hurt classical models, and the regression paper reports season-dependent MAPE, yet the ANN and metaheuristic papers report only pooled errors and never quantify regime-specific degradation, never audit calibrated uncertainty (only point forecasts, though a GP reference exists), and conflate multi-step error growth with regime effects. The field lacks any way to observe, benchmark, diagnose and accumulate comparable evidence on which method works under which operating condition, so method selection is guesswork and reported gains may be artifacts of easy test periods.
method: Build a regime-stratified diagnostic benchmark and evidence-accumulation protocol. First, automatically annotate every timestep of a load series with operating-condition regimes: calendar (weekday/weekend/holiday/transition), weather-anomaly (large residuals after a temperature/humidity regression), structural breaks and outliers (via the robust ratio-of-medians and minimum-Hellinger-distance detectors from the robust-methods paper), heteroscedastic-volatility windows, and high-growth nonstationary segments. Second, reimplement the corpus method families (MLR, double-seasonal exponential smoothing, robust SARIMA, ARMAX, ANN back-propagation, ANN trained by GA/PSO/SCA, genetic-fuzzy-neural, and a Gaussian-Process baseline) in one harness with identical features, splits and horizons, separating iterative-simulation from always-real-inputs multi-step evaluation. Third, replace pooled MAPE with error conditioned per regime plus a break-versus-normal degradation ratio and horizon-resolved error growth. Fourth, audit uncertainty by wrapping each point method with split-conformal prediction intervals and using the GP posterior as a calibration reference, scoring coverage and sharpness per regime. Fifth, distill standardized per-method capability cards and test a regime-conditioned switching ensemble as a falsifiable hypothesis that condition-aware selection beats any single method.

paper_title: Teaching and Learning Logic in a Virtual Learning Environment
motivation: Testing parsing with a concise motivation. The field lacks shared ways to observe, measure, benchmark, and accumulate comparable evidence about whether interactive and CAS-based online mathematics learning actually improves learning; existing distance and e-learning studies (Zirkle 2003) are descriptive single-course case studies with poor validity, confound medium with pedagogy, and never link satisfaction measures (Chiu 2005) to measured learning outcomes.
method: Build a shared benchmarking protocol and cross-institution observatory that isolates media from method, measures tool-available versus tool-withheld learning to separate doing from learning, logs interaction traces, links usability and value surveys to learning gains, and pools standardized effect sizes in a public repository for cumulative comparison.

paper_title: An Empirical Study of Smoothing Techniques for Language Modeling
motivation: N-gram estimators in this collection all emit a single point probability fed to noisy-channel decoders (Katz 1987; IBM 1984; spelling correction Kernighan/Church/Gale 1990; PP-attachment; parsing). But sparse-data estimates are brittle: add-one/ELE is worse than none (Estimation procedures 1990; What's wrong with adding one? 1994) and naive Good-Turing can be wildly inaccurate (Good-Turing without tears 1995). Reliability is wildly heterogeneous — an estimate from one observation versus thousands — yet all are emitted identically, so a decoder can be confidently wrong on the low-count contexts that dominate errors. Methods are tuned only by aggregate perplexity, which hides these tail failures, and methods that do compute uncertainty (the Dirichlet posterior of the hierarchical model 1995; Church-Gale Good-Turing variance) discard it instead of exposing it to the decision. This is a failure/risk gap: uncalibrated point estimates feed high-stakes decisions with no reliability signal or guardrail.
method: Build risk-aware n-gram estimation. (1) For each context derive a posterior over its conditional distribution using the analytic Dirichlet posterior of the hierarchical model, or alternatively the Church-Gale Good-Turing r* variance, giving a point estimate plus a credible interval per n-gram. (2) Calibrate these intervals against reality via deleted/held-out estimation (Jelinek-Mercer 1980): compare predicted variance to observed held-out squared error and rescale, binned by count-of-counts, until intervals reach nominal coverage. (3) Decode risk-adjustedly: rather than plugging point estimates into the noisy-channel product, integrate the score over the posterior or use a pessimistic lower-confidence bound so uncertain estimates shrink harder toward the Katz back-off distribution, and blend MLE, Good-Turing, back-off, and Dirichlet estimators per context by inverse-variance weights instead of one global choice. (4) Abstain: when an interval is too wide, back off further or flag the decision low-confidence. (5) Evaluate on the Kernighan/Church/Gale spelling corrector and bigram estimation, reporting not just average accuracy and perplexity but worst-case error on low-count contexts, catastrophic-error rate, and interval coverage. Hypothesis: matched on average perplexity, the risk-aware model cuts catastrophic downstream errors and is well-calibrated, showing that calibrating uncertainty, not minimizing mean perplexity, makes sparse-data language modeling reliable.

paper_title: Dynamical Movement Primitives: Learning Attractor Models for Motor Behaviors
motivation: DMPs dominate robot motor-skill learning, but their forcing term uses a fixed number of Gaussian basis functions spread uniformly over phase with the same budget per degree of freedom, wasting kernels on smooth regions, under-resolving sharp features, and inflating the reinforcement-learning parameter search space that Peters and Schaal call the core scaling barrier; Ude et al. flag choosing basis-function number and placement as open. No prior work allocates DMP basis resources by both demonstration complexity and reward sensitivity, motivating an optimization method treating basis functions as a scarce resource.
method: Resource-Adaptive DMPs, a two-level search-and-allocation wrapper around DMPs and PI2 policy-gradient refinement. Level 1 greedily selects a sparse kernel subset from a dense candidate pool by orthogonal-least-squares, adding kernels that most reduce imitation error until a fidelity criterion. Level 2 probes each parameter reward sensitivity with finite-difference perturbations reusing Fisher information, prunes low-sensitivity kernels, and scales exploration-noise variance by sensitivity. An adaptive loop splits kernels at high reward-pressure phases, merges redundant ones, and re-screens. Evaluate versus fixed uniform-N DMPs on imitation error, RL sample efficiency, generalization, and kernel count.

paper_title: An Empirical Comparison of Supervised Learning Algorithms
motivation: Prior calibration methods learn a fixed map from classifier score to class probability on a calibration set and apply it unchanged, baking in that set base rate and assuming deployment is stationary, identical to calibration, balanced, and data-rich.
method: Decoupled shift-robust calibration separates a base-rate-invariant monotone score-to-likelihood-ratio term from an explicit prior term, estimated at deployment from unlabeled target scores via confirmatory EM, then recomposed into posteriors.

paper_title: Bayesian inference for time-varying applications: Particle-based Gaussian process approaches
motivation: Many online and adaptive Gaussian process methods such as KRLS-T with a forgetting factor, sparse online Gaussian processes, online FITC and PITC, GP-BayesFilters, Gaussian process dynamical models, and mixtures of Gaussian process experts claim to track non-stationary data and emit predictive uncertainty. Yet the field lacks any way to observe, measure, benchmark, or diagnose whether that uncertainty stays calibrated under drift. Evaluation is dominated by point error such as normalized mean square error. Calibration of predictive intervals during and after concept drift is never audited, and forgetting rates are hand-tuned without evidence about resulting over-confidence or under-confidence.
method: Create a streaming calibration audit for online Gaussian process methods under drift. Compute a per-step probability integral transform of one-step-ahead predictions, then track windowed uniformity, interval coverage, and proper scores such as log predictive density and continuous ranked probability score, producing drift-localized calibration curves that separate over-confidence from under-confidence. Benchmark on synthetic generators with known drift such as change points, gradual drift, heteroscedastic noise shifts, and warping, plus real source data such as traffic flow and inertial attitude dynamics, comparing KRLS-T variants, sparse online Gaussian processes, online FITC and PITC, GP-BayesFilters, and mixtures of Gaussian process experts. Finally close the loop by using running coverage as feedback to adapt the forgetting rate, comparing fixed versus calibration-driven adaptation.

paper_title: A Resource-Allocating Network for Function Interpolation
motivation: RBF and locally-tuned networks were introduced as fast alternatives to backpropagation, but the sources give disconnected recipes. Broomhead-Lowe and Powell interpolate with one center per data point; Moody-Darken place centers by unsupervised k-means grounded in Lloyd and MacQueen quantization, set widths by ad hoc P-nearest-neighbor rules, and fit output weights by LMS; Poggio-Girosi use regularization and HyperBF networks with movable centers and adaptive metrics. A key unquantified gap: k-means minimizes input-space quantization error, ignoring the target, so centers cluster where inputs are dense rather than where the target is complex. No work maps when cheap task-agnostic recipes suffice versus when supervised center-moving is worth its cost.
method: Build a benchmark and empirical map of the RBF design space. The task suite dissociates input density from target complexity via a tunable mismatch, plus canonical tasks such as logistic-map prediction, chaotic time-series prediction, and ECG-style classification. Sweep center placement (interpolation, random, Lloyd k-means, MacQueen online, target-aware residual-weighted), number of centers, width rule, response normalization, distance metric, and training regime. Measure held-out error, training cost, effective locality, hyperparameter sensitivity, and a placement-mismatch diagnostic correlating center density with local target complexity. Produce phase-diagram maps over mismatch, dimensionality, and center count showing which strategy wins where, plus the measured generalization gap between unsupervised and task-aware placement.

paper_title: Reinforcement learning of dialogue strategies with hierarchical abstract machines
motivation: RL of dialogue policies almost always relies on a statistical user simulator trained from a corpus (the user-simulation survey; NJFun; multi-goal reduced state-action RL; hierarchical RL/HAM/HMDP). Two sources make a key limitation explicit but leave it unresolved. The survey (Schatzmann et al.) shows via cross-model evaluation that a policy learned against a poor simulator can look excellent on that same simulator yet collapse on a better one, and that even good policies often win only by exploiting simulator deficiencies (e.g. requesting all unfilled slots in one turn because simulators do not model cooperativeness or the growth of misunderstandings with simultaneous requests). The hybrid RL/SL paper (Henderson et al.) states directly that simulator accuracy and learned policy quality are dependent, and that finding simulator metrics predictive of final policy quality is an open problem. The direct simulator-quality metrics that exist (precision/recall, perplexity, dialogue length/style statistics, and the HMM/KL similarity of Cuayahuitl et al.) are validated only as measures of simulator realism, never as predictors of the utility, robustness, or naturalness of policies trained against them. There is thus no systematic map linking simulator design choices, cheap direct simulator metrics, and the downstream behavior and cross-simulator robustness of learned policies, nor any diagnostic for detecting when a policy merely exploits a simulator artifact.
method: Build an empirical benchmark and diagnostic suite on the annotated COMMUNICATOR corpus (reusing the user-action and Information-State annotations from the hybrid RL/SL work). Vary three axes. (1) Simulator battery: simulators of graded fidelity (bigram/n-gram, standard HMM, Input HMM, Input-Output HMM following Cuayahuitl et al.) crossed with explicit deficiency knobs toggling user cooperativeness and an error/misunderstanding model whose rate scales with the number of simultaneous system requests. (2) Policy battery: a handcrafted state-transition baseline (CSLU/COMMUNICATOR style), flat RL (NJFun-style), the hybrid RL/SL policy, and a hierarchical/reduced state-action policy (multi-goal RL grounded in HAM/HMDP), each trained against each simulator with identical setups. (3) Evaluation: run the full cross-model matrix (every policy tested against every simulator, plus held-out human data and handcrafted references), reporting utility (filled/grounded slots with a length penalty) and behavioral statistics. Define three diagnostic instruments: (a) a Simulator-Exploitation Index equal to the utility drop when a policy moves from its training simulator to the ensemble of other simulators/human data; (b) behavioral-signature profiling that measures emitted policy statistics (mean simultaneous slot requests, confirmation ratio, initiative, dialogue length) and attributes pathologies to specific simulator deficiencies by comparing policies trained with vs. without each knob; and (c) a predictiveness analysis correlating each cheap direct simulator metric (precision/recall, perplexity, HMM/KL similarity, cooperativeness statistic) with the cross-model utility and robustness of policies trained on that simulator. The deliverable is a reusable empirical map and diagnostic protocol identifying which simulator dimensions cause which policy behaviors, which policy architectures are most susceptible to exploitation, and a minimal validated set of simulator metrics predictive of policy transfer.

paper_title: Neural Networks and Principal Component Analysis: Learning from Examples Without Local Minima
motivation: Bourlard-Kamp prove linear autoencoders equal PCA and the hidden nonlinearity is useless; Oja and Linsker show Hebbian nets recover principal components; yet Elman-Zipser and Cottrell claim rich nonlinear features only qualitatively. Evidence gap: no shared way to measure how much of a network's representation exceeds the PCA optimum or to attribute gains to nonlinearity.
method: A Linear-Explainability Audit comparing hidden activations to the top-p PCA reference via principal-angle subspace alignment, canonical correlation, and a nonlinear-gain metric measuring task performance beyond the aligned linear subspace, plus per-unit PCA-explained versus novel labels, tested on autoencoders, speech nets, Hebbian nets, and a weight-decay teacher-student control.

paper_title: A Simple Neural Network Generating an Interactive Memory
motivation:
The provided works converge on one question from different directions but never join them empirically. Barlow's program in Sensory Communication argues that sensory systems transform messages to reduce redundancy and expose the structure of the world. Minsky's Computation and the Pattern Recognition volume establish that classification is fundamentally geometric: what a perceptron-like machine can separate depends on the arrangement of patterns as points in a space, and Sommerville's Geometry of N-Dimensions supplies the formal yardstick for that space. The Uncertain Nervous System and Neural Theory and Modeling insist that this space is noisy, so any category boundary must be wide enough to survive noise. Most suggestively, Mayr's Animal Species and Evolution defines a natural category (a species) not by a difference but by a "gap" — a region of discontinuity that surrounds a cluster of forms in multidimensional character space, an objective, nonarbitrary criterion for category membership.

The gap in the literature is that these ideas have never been unified into a measurement. Everyone assumes that "redundancy reduction" or "feature detection" makes patterns more separable, and everyone assumes natural perceptual categories correspond to something real in the world, but no one has empirically mapped whether the discontinuity structure — the gaps — that defines natural categories in the world is preserved, enhanced, or created by successive transformations of the sensory message, nor measured this with a single geometric yardstick that ties Mayr's gap concept to Minsky's separability and Barlow's coding. This matters because it would convert the vague slogan "carving nature at its joints" into a testable claim: that good sensory coding is coding that widens, relative to neural noise, the gaps between the categories an organism must tell apart.
method:
Build a systematic empirical map — a benchmark, a diagnostic toolkit, and a comparative study — of how the gap-structure of natural categories changes across stages of sensory transformation, using high-dimensional geometry as the common measuring stick.

(1) Corpus. Assemble stimulus sets with ground-truth natural categories sampled densely enough to reveal both within- and between-category structure: e.g., visual object/animal forms, speech sounds, and, where possible, stimulus sets tied to the discrimination problems different species actually face (importing Mayr's comparative, ecological framing).

(2) Representation ladder. For each stimulus, compute a sequence of representations approximating successive stages of processing envisioned by Barlow: a raw receptor-like encoding, a redundancy-reduced/decorrelated encoding, and a feature-detector encoding. Each stage places every stimulus as a point in an n-dimensional space.

(3) Geometric diagnostics (the core instrument). Adapting Sommerville's n-dimensional geometry and Mayr's gap criterion, define and compute for every pair/family of categories: intrinsic dimensionality; a "discontinuity index" = width of the empty gap between category clusters normalized by within-category scatter (an operationalization of Mayr's species gap); and a Minsky-style separability score = the fraction of category distinctions realizable by a single linear (perceptron) boundary versus requiring higher-order boundaries.

(4) Noise scaling. Following The Uncertain Nervous System, inject graded noise and measure how the discontinuity index and separability degrade — yielding, for each stage, the noise level at which each natural category boundary collapses. This makes "gap width relative to noise" the central reliability metric.

(5) Mapping and alignment tests. Chart, across modalities and species-relevant stimulus sets, how much each transformation stage opens gaps and raises linear separability — producing an empirical map of where redundancy reduction actually "carves at the joints" versus where it does not. Finally, compare the geometric boundaries against known behavioral/perceptual category boundaries to test the alignment hypothesis: that perceived categories fall precisely where the coded representation, at ecologically relevant noise levels, exhibits maximal gaps and linear separability.

The deliverable is an open benchmark plus the gap/separability/noise diagnostic suite and the resulting comparative map. This directly addresses the gap by turning the shared but untested assumptions of these works into quantitative, reproducible measurements linking world-structure, neural-representation geometry, and perceptual categories.

paper_title: Volterra Signal Modelling Using Lagrange Programming Neural Networks
motivation: The provided works are methods for identifying quadratic second-order Volterra systems, but they leave a critical evidence gap: there is no principled way to observe whether an identified quadratic model is correct, nor to compare competing methods on common ground. Kim and Powers use bispectra with input and output; Mathews orthogonalization and the adaptive 2-D Volterra work assume a Gaussian input or a reference signal; the blind Volterra LPNN work is output-only, relating kernels to second- and third-order moments under a white-Gaussian-input assumption. Each is evaluated on its own simulation, so evidence about accuracy, robustness to non-Gaussianity, and noise cannot be accumulated. The blind case has no observable ground truth: the LPNN solver only guarantees a Kuhn-Tucker equilibrium, equations are tractable only for special structures, and nothing tells the user whether recovered kernels are true, ambiguous, spurious solver equilibria, or invalid due to a broken Gaussian assumption. Since true input and kernels are unavailable in practice, the field lacks any diagnostic to validate a blindly identified model, which matters because these models feed equalization, nonlinearity compensation, and image features where mis-identification silently degrades results.
method: Build Moment-Consistency Auditing, a framework that turns model forward statistics into observable evidence of correctness plus a shared benchmark. First, a forward moment simulator using the derived second-order relations (autocorrelation and third-order moment sequence in kernels a, b and variance beta), extended to a held-out higher-order statistic not used in fitting, such as fourth-order cumulant slices, giving disjoint fit and audit maps. Second, out-of-sample cross-validation: predict the audit statistics from recovered kernels and compare to the same statistics estimated from observed output; small discrepancy is evidence of correctness, large discrepancy flags failure and, by which slices break, discriminates undermodeling, non-Gaussian input, or solver error, yielding an audit signal even when blind. Third, identifiability diagnostics: compute the Jacobian of the moment map at the solution, using its condition number and null space to expose unidentifiable directions and sign, scale, and permutation ambiguities as a per-solution certificate. Fourth, a solver audit: instrument LPNN-type solvers with their own stability apparatus, checking Kuhn-Tucker and local-convexity Hessian conditions to separate true minima from spurious equilibria, running many initializations to map solution multiplicity. Fifth, a benchmark of ground-truth 1-D and 2-D quadratic Volterra systems, sweeping input from Gaussian to non-Gaussian and varying SNR, reporting normalized kernel error, transfer-function error, and held-out moment-discrepancy score so blind and input-output methods compare head-to-head. It reuses the Gaussian-moment factorization and known-system validation already in the sources, now shared and quantitative, making correctness observable and comparable from statistics alone.

paper_title: Three New Probabilistic Models for Dependency Parsing: An Exploration
motivation: Every parsing and tagging model here (Collins's lexical-dependency parser, Magerman's SPATTER decision-tree parser, stochastic lexicalized TAG, the PCFG methods, and the robust HMM tagger) is a point predictor that emits one best analysis and treats it as uniformly trustworthy. This creates a Failure/Risk gap where models fail silently. Evidence: (1) The HMM tagging paper notes unknown-word rates rival or exceed error rates and that extending dictionary coverage per domain is neither practical nor economical, yet unknown words get one suffix heuristic with no per-token reliability. (2) Collins's parser is plagued by sparse data and must back off from head-word dependencies to POS-only estimates, but never characterizes how much less reliable a backed-off decision is, so a near-guess attachment looks identical to a well-estimated one. (3) Magerman attributes the movement away from parsing-based approaches to poor performance on ambiguous large-vocabulary text and tests SPATTER across domains reporting only aggregate accuracy, never which individual decisions to trust under domain shift. Because none expose calibrated per-decision reliability, downstream consumers cannot separate a confident-correct constituent from an overconfident-wrong one, nor detect out-of-domain or rare-word inputs, which limits adoption of statistical parsers.
method: Build a reliability-aware wrapper that turns these probabilistic parsers/taggers into self-diagnosing, selectively-abstaining systems without changing the underlying model, by exploiting latent uncertainty signals they currently discard. (1) Instrument the backoff/interpolation chain: for each local decision (POS tag, head-word dependency, rule expansion, TAG combination) record backoff depth (which level of the Jelinek-Mercer/Collins/HMM-suffix chain carried the mass, from full lexical pair to POS-only to open-class default), lexical flags (unknown or rare words), the entropy and top-1/top-2 margin of the local distribution, and training support counts. (2) Cross-model disagreement: run complementary base models on the same input (Collins-style lexical dependency, SPATTER-style decision-tree history, plain PCFG, optionally link-grammar/SLTAG) and record per-span agreement, an error signal no single model sees about itself. (3) Calibration meta-model: on held-out treebank data label each local decision correct/incorrect against gold and fit a lightweight calibrator (logistic regression or small decision tree) mapping these features to P(correct); aggregate to constituent and sentence confidence. (4) Selective output: given a threshold, output only high-confidence structure and abstain elsewhere, degrading gracefully to partial parses instead of an overconfident full parse, trading coverage for precision; scores can also drive reliability-weighted model combination. (5) Evaluation: train on WSJ Penn Treebank, test in-domain and cross-domain on IBM computer manuals and Brown, the domain-shift and unknown-word conditions the sources flag. Report calibration via reliability diagrams, risk-coverage curves showing abstention concentrates errors and precision rises as low-confidence decisions are withheld, and an ablation isolating backoff-depth vs. unknown-word flags vs. cross-model disagreement. Success means the parser reliably knows when it does not know on out-of-domain, rare-word inputs where point-prediction parsers fail silently.

paper_title: Feature-Rich Part-of-Speech Tagging with a Cyclic Dependency Network
motivation: Maximum entropy taggers use rich features but their directed conditional Markov structure suffers label bias and observation bias which reduce tagging accuracy in practice today
method: Build a cyclic bidirectional dependency network tagger whose maximum entropy conditionals depend on both neighboring tags and rich features and are trained cheaply and locally

paper_title: Kernelized Constrained Gaussian Fields and Harmonic Functions for Semi-supervised Learning
motivation: Graph-based semi-supervised learning (SSL) methods dominate transductive classification when data lie on a manifold, but the studies here reveal an evidence gap about reliability: performance is heavily influenced by graph construction and hyperparameters, with no evident explorable pattern for practitioners. The influence-of-graph-construction, time-series, and constrained-LGC/RMGTHOR papers document this only descriptively via best-case error and qualitative error surfaces, and note that labels are too scarce for cross-validation and that method rankings flip with hyperparameters, harming reproducibility. The field lacks label-free, quantitative instruments to observe, measure, and predict how good and how stable a configuration is before use, and lacks a standard way to accumulate comparable reliability evidence across datasets and methods. Related pieces are disconnected: transductive stability theory targets labeled regression; Nystrom and Geometric-Harmonics tools were built for scaling not auditing; and the Demsar methodology has not been used to validate label-free selection criteria.
method: Develop Graph-SSL Audit, a label-free diagnostic-and-benchmark framework measuring and predicting the transductive reliability of any algorithm-by-graph-by-hyperparameter configuration without labeled validation. Three unsupervised indicators from the closed-form solution: (1) perturbation-stability, perturbing graph construction (subsample nodes/edges, jitter k and bandwidth, swap Laplacian normalization), re-solving cheaply via Nystrom/Geometric-Harmonics extension, and measuring prediction churn on unlabeled nodes; (2) reflexive self-consistency, a transductive leave-one-labeled-out proxy hiding each scarce labeled node and predicting it from the remaining solution; (3) solution regularity, the normalized Dirichlet energy of the soft-label field on the Laplacian. Combine them into one audit score to rank and flag configurations. Validate on the benchmark datasets and grids already used in these papers by correlating indicators with true error, testing whether audit-selected configurations approach oracle best-case error and beat defaults like k=20 with RBF, and aggregating across datasets with the Demsar methodology. Deliverables: an open configuration-reliability benchmark and validated label-free audit metrics.

paper_title: Factorial Hidden Markov Models
motivation: The sources span exactly-trainable HMMs and richer componential stochastic sequence models (Boltzmann chains, sigmoid belief networks, mean-field networks, structured variational methods, and the free-energy/MDL view). These richer models train on approximate objectives, not exact likelihood. Evidence Gap: there is no shared instrument to measure how much the approximation costs, and no common benchmark placing exact HMMs and approximate models on equal footing, so we cannot tell whether reported gains come from richer structure or looser bounds.
method: Build a diagnostic benchmark measuring the approximation gap of structured sequence models, calibrated against the exact HMM. Use shared data such as Baldi protein families, temporally distorted strings, and synthetic factorial sources with known ground truth. Fit a model ladder at equal parameter budgets: exact HMM, factorial Boltzmann-chain models, and belief-net sequence models, each trained via mean field, structured variational inference on tractable substructures, and Gibbs sampling. Compute the free-energy gap as the training bound minus true likelihood, which is exact for the HMM and estimated via annealed importance sampling that bridges from the tractable substructure for intractable models. Add a structure-versus-slack decomposition on known-truth sources, an inference-adequacy score, and an MDL description-length readout. Calibrate the estimators on the exact-likelihood HMM rung, then propagate up the ladder, reporting per-model gaps and downstream accuracy.

paper_title: An Experimental Comparison of Three Methods for Constructing Ensembles of Decision Trees: Bagging, Boosting, and Randomization
motivation: Ensembles top empirical comparisons (Caruana; Bauer and Kohavi) but cost N times more compute, storage, and inference latency than a single model, such as forests of 1024 trees. Practice uses large fixed-size ensembles regardless of dataset. Ali and Pazzani show benefit varies from sevenfold error reduction to near zero, driven by cheaply measurable factors: gain-tie frequency, correlated errors, irrelevant attributes, and class noise. Breiman shows only unstable learners benefit. These works are post-hoc and never yield an a-priori tool to decide if an ensemble is worth its cost or how big it must be. Practitioners thus waste resources where a single model suffices and under-size where big gains exist. Gap: no method uses cheap diagnostics to set a per-dataset compute budget.
method: Build an ensemble-profitability predictor. Cheap diagnostics: from one base model plus a small pilot ensemble on a subsample, extract gain-tie frequency, pilot correlated-error rate on out-of-bag data, an instability estimate, and irrelevant-attribute and noise descriptors. Meta-model: over UCI datasets from Ali and Pazzani plus Caruana and Bauer-Kohavi suites and several base learners, fit a regressor from diagnostics to predicted error ratio and a marginal-gain-versus-size curve. Budget policy: given a compute or latency budget, decide whether to ensemble and choose the smallest size whose predicted marginal gain clears a threshold, stopping early at plateau; for boosting couple with pruning. Validate compute, memory, and latency saved versus accuracy retained using Dietterich five-by-two cross-validation tests. Goal: match full-ensemble accuracy on high-benefit domains yet collapse to near single-model cost elsewhere.

paper_title: Simplifying Neural Networks by Soft Weight-Sharing
motivation: Complexity-control criteria for neural forecasting (AIC, MDL, Bayesian evidence, weight-elimination, optimal brain damage, relevance pruning) were each validated in isolation; no controlled study maps which one generalizes best versus noise, record length, and dynamical dimension, nor whether the best forecaster recovers the true dynamics.
method: Benchmark all these criteria on synthetic systems with known invariants (threshold-AR limit cycles, logistic, Henon, Mackey-Glass) plus sunspots and lynx, holding architecture fixed and varying only the regularizer, scoring out-of-sample error, selected complexity, and recovered invariants (correlation dimension, Lyapunov exponent, nonlinearity), to map the best method per data regime and test whether the best forecaster is the best dynamics-recoverer.

paper_title: Quantitative Performance Metrics for Mobile Robots Navigation
motivation: Reactive obstacle-avoidance methods dominate the collection (potential fields, VFH, DWA, elastic bands, ORM, Nearness Diagram). Each is justified by the brittleness of its predecessors, and failure modes recur: Potential Field Methods and Their Inherent Limitations lists trap/local-minima cyclic behavior, inability to pass closely spaced obstacles, and oscillations in narrow corridors, while ND targets the same troublesome scenarios. This is a Failure/Risk gap: every reactive planner fails silently in geometry-dependent situations, and none is universally safe. Planners lack self-awareness: recovery such as the Virtual Obstacle concept only reacts after the robot is already trapped, so safety-critical deployment is unreliable. Evaluation is inconsistent and non-reproducible: the Evaluation of Navigation paper, MoVeMA benchmarks, PerMIS Performance Metrics, and the SIG on Good Experimental Methodology all note missing consensus metrics, reliance on path length and time, and no protocol quantifying how often a method fails or how near collision it comes. The prior works leave open a reproducible characterization of failure probability and an online mechanism that anticipates a planner's own imminent failure.
method: Build a reliability framework with two coupled parts: a reproducible failure-mode benchmark and an online failure-anticipation monitor. A scenario generator parametrically synthesizes the canonical troublesome scenarios from the sources (U-traps, narrow corridors, closely spaced gaps, dense clutter, moving obstacles) with interpretable difficulty knobs (gap width versus robot diameter, trap depth, clutter density, obstacle speed), seed-controlled for reproducibility, and scores runs with existing metrics (security/proximity, path length and time, smoothness) plus a primary failure-probability metric with confidence intervals. Data collection runs a portfolio of planners (potential field, VFH, DWA, ND) over thousands of scenarios, logging at each control period the local scan and ND-style situation descriptors (nearness gaps, free-region geometry, goal bearing, velocity) plus the outcome seconds ahead. A calibrated failure predictor maps the current descriptor plus active planner to probability of imminent failure with an uncertainty estimate, using the ND situation taxonomy as an interpretable feature space. A runtime monitor runs the predictor alongside the executing planner to raise anticipatory alerts before traps or oscillations, switch among the planner portfolio per-situation when predicted risk is high, and proactively trigger recovery such as virtual obstacle insertion instead of waiting until stuck. Evaluation reports the full outcome distribution (failure probability, minimum-clearance margins, predictor calibration and lead-time) on the released benchmark, turning brittle silently-failing navigators into self-monitoring systems with quantified anticipatory reliability.

paper_title: Learning in feedforward layered networks: the tiling algorithm
motivation:
Two very different quantitative "explanations" of good learning have emerged from these works, but the field has no common empirical way to observe, measure, and compare them against how real learning algorithms actually behave. (1) Carnevali & Patarnello's exhaustive thermodynamical analysis of Boolean learning networks argues that generalization is a consequence of the second law: among all zero-error networks, training preferentially lands on the function P that is implemented by the largest number of networks H(P), so problem "complexity" is precisely measurable as an entropy decrease ΔS = log2(N/H(P)). (2) Krauth & Mézard's optimal-stability learning proposes an entirely geometric quality measure — the margin/stability Δ — as the predictor of large basins (their proxy for robustness/generalization), computed by linear programming for an individual solution.

Crucially, both leave an evidence gap. Carnevali & Patarnello can only compute H(P)/ΔS by full enumeration of tiny networks and explicitly note it would be "extremely interesting" to estimate complexity without exhaustive analysis; their entropic story also assumes the training dynamics (T→0 simulated annealing) sample zero-error configurations in proportion to H(P). But the actual algorithms in this literature — the perceptron/optimal-stability rule (Krauth–Mézard), error backpropagation (Rumelhart et al.), and choice-of-internal-representations / activating-neurons algorithms — are NOT uniform samplers; each has its own inductive bias, yet all of them are reported and compared only by final training error or a single anecdotal generalization result (e.g., the 8-bit adder, NETtalk). No one has measured, on a common footing, WHICH solution among the many zero-error solutions each algorithm selects, whether that selection tracks the high-entropy (high-H(P)) functions that the thermodynamic theory says drive generalization, whether it tracks high margin Δ, and how the entropy-based and margin-based measures relate to each other and to true out-of-sample error. Without such a measurement/benchmark framework we cannot audit an algorithm's inductive bias, validate the competing generalization theories, or accumulate comparable evidence across algorithms.
method:
Build a reproducible measurement-and-benchmark framework that characterizes each learning algorithm by the distribution over implemented functions it induces, and grounds that distribution against the two theoretical quality measures already in the literature (entropy ΔS and margin Δ).

Step 1 — Ground-truth solution census. On small architectures where enumeration is tractable (Boolean gate networks of the Carnevali–Patarnello type with N_I≈4–6, and small threshold/perceptron networks), exhaustively (or via dense sampling) compute the "function-volume" histogram H(P) for every realizable function P, and hence its complexity ΔS = log2(N/H(P)). This is the reference prior the second-law argument predicts training should follow.

Step 2 — Algorithm "sampling fingerprints." For a fixed architecture and a partial training set S of size N_E, run each candidate learning algorithm many times under randomized initial conditions and example orderings: (a) simulated annealing (Carnevali reference), (b) perceptron/optimal-stability LP rule (Krauth–Mézard), (c) backpropagation on the matched soft architecture, (d) choice-of-internal-representations / learning-by-activating-neurons rules. For each run that reaches zero training error, record the actual global function P' it implements. This yields an empirical distribution Q_alg(P') — the algorithm's inductive-bias fingerprint.

Step 3 — Diagnostic metrics. Define and report: (i) fingerprint divergence D(Q_alg || H) between the algorithm's function distribution and the entropic prior H(P), plus the correlation between an algorithm's probability of selecting a function and that function's H(P) — this measures how "uniform/thermodynamic" the algorithm is; (ii) for each produced solution, its margin Δ (via the Krauth–Mézard LP) and its complexity ΔS, so we can test empirically whether high-margin solutions coincide with high-entropy functions; (iii) true generalization error Ē over all inputs, regressed against both ΔS and Δ to determine which measure — entropic volume or geometric margin — is the better predictor, and whether they add independent information.

Step 4 — Learning-curve audit. Sweep N_E to produce learning curves of generalization probability per algorithm, overlaid on the theoretical entropic curve implied by H(P). Deviations quantify where an algorithm's bias helps or hurts relative to the uniform-sampling ideal (e.g., does margin-maximization over-select simple functions and generalize better than annealing, or does it distort the entropic prior and generalize worse?).

Step 5 — Toward a scalable estimator. Using the enumerable cases as calibration, test cheap surrogates for H(P)/ΔS that avoid full enumeration (e.g., Monte Carlo estimation of the zero-error configuration volume around a found solution, and local margin as a proxy), evaluating how well each surrogate reproduces the ground-truth complexity ranking. This directly addresses the open call for estimating complexity without exhaustive analysis and provides a portable audit tool for larger networks.

The framework turns single-number reporting (final error, or one anecdotal generalization result) into a systematic, comparable body of evidence: it lets researchers observe where in function/solution space an algorithm lands, benchmark algorithms against each other and against the entropic ideal, adjudicate the entropy-vs-margin debate empirically, and diagnose an algorithm's inductive bias.

paper_title: Reinforcement Learning for RoboCup Soccer Keepaway
motivation: Keepaway comparisons reduce to one scalar hold-time, so the field cannot audit value-function fidelity, measure generalization, or detect negative transfer.
method: Use simulator rollouts from frozen states to build an oracle probe set of true option values, then score learners on value fidelity, decision regret, generalization, and transfer error.

paper_title: Neural network method for solving convex programming problem with linear inequality constraints
motivation: Prior works each build a separate analog recurrent neural network circuit for one optimization class, such as bound constrained quadratic programs, linear programs, extended linear programs, convex programs with inequality constraints, and semi infinite multiobjective programs. Each requires a bespoke circuit and physically accurate analog weights, and the diagonal preconditioner is fixed at design time. This is a resource bottleneck: high fabrication and calibration cost, sensitivity to weight inaccuracy and noise, and no ability to reconfigure one device across problem types, even though all these solvers share the same underlying projection dynamics.
method: Build one reconfigurable multiplier free recurrent network optimization fabric that instantiates all five problem classes by programming rather than refabrication, plus a runtime self calibrating preconditioner. Rewrite the classes in one shared projection form so each source network is a special case selected by which linear blocks are active and which projection attaches to each neuron. A shared programmable crossbar implements the constraint operator and its transpose, with an optional second crossbar for the quadratic matrix, using multiplier free summers and integrators. Switchable projection blocks cover box, sign, and inequality constraints, and a digital front end reduces semi infinite multiobjective problems to loadable rows via discretization and scalarization. The self calibrating preconditioner models realized weights as ideal weights times bounded error and uses a slow outer loop to set diagonal gains online, reducing condition number and cancelling drift while preserving convergence. Evaluate in simulation across all classes, measuring component and energy cost versus five separate networks, latency versus digital solvers, and accuracy under injected weight error with and without self calibration.

paper_title: Robot Learning using Learning Classifier Systems Approach
motivation: LCSs were meant to model cognitive emergence and latent learning, but are judged only by reward-based steps-to-goal, an evidence gap: no mechanism-agnostic way to measure whether a system built a transferable world-model versus a reactive policy.
method: A Latent-Learning Diagnostic Benchmark: explore reward-free, then introduce reward and measure the learning-speed advantage over controls, plus model-fidelity, representation, and memory-encoding audits against ground truth, applied uniformly to ZCS, XCS, ACS2, MACS, ATNoSFERES-II.

paper_title: Teaching and Learning Logic in a Virtual Learning Environment
motivation:
A contradiction runs across these sources on mathematics e-learning. On one side, the interactive-web-mathematics literature (Bringslid, "Mathematical e-learning using interactive mathematics on the Web"; the WALTM assessment work) assumes that giving learners a powerful web "advanced calculator" — one-click MathML/CAS symbolic solving, animated step-by-step reveals, instant graphing — will "improve understanding" and "reverse bad trends." On the other side, the CAS reflection paper poses exactly the unresolved worry embedded in its title: are such tools "Assistance for Doing or Learning Mathematics?" — offloading the cognitive work that produces conceptual understanding. Crossing this with the e-learning continuance literature (Chiu et al.) sharpens the paradox: continued use (and thus program survival against isolation/dropout risk flagged in the CTE review) is driven by perceived usability, quality, and value, where value is "the utility based on what is received versus what is given." A tool that instantly delivers answers with minimal effort maximizes perceived usability/value → satisfaction → continuance. 

The puzzle is therefore a tradeoff nobody has reconciled: the very affordances that make interactive math tools satisfying and "sticky" (low effort, fast correct answers) are precisely those that let students avoid the productive struggle that builds conceptual understanding — so the most-continued tools may produce the least learning, while tools that demand effortful learning raise perceived cost, depress satisfaction/value, and risk abandonment. The continuance literature treats perceived value as monotonically good and never measures learning depth; the math-e-learning literature assumes tool engagement equals understanding and never measures the satisfaction–learning divergence; the CAS paper names the doing-vs-learning tension but offers no design or continuance-aware resolution. This leaves open whether a "satisfaction–learning gap" actually exists in interactive math e-learning, and whether a system can be designed to sustain continuance while shifting learners from "doing" to "learning."
method:
Build and empirically test an interactive web-mathematics module (MathML rendering + a CAS engine as in the webMathematica-style "Calc" tools, plus animations and embedded web assessment) equipped with an "assistance dial": a continuous control over how much the system does for the learner, from a full solver mode (instant symbolic answer + revealed steps) to a scaffolded mode (faded worked examples → completion problems → independent solving with targeted feedback).

Study 1 — establish the contradiction. Run a controlled comparison on the same engineering-mathematics content across three fixed conditions: (a) high-assistance solver, (b) low-assistance/effortful, (c) a baseline static resource. For every participant measure, in parallel, (i) the decomposed-EDT continuance constructs from Chiu et al. — perceived usability, quality, value, satisfaction, disconfirmation, and continuance intention (survey + behavioral proxies: session length, return visits, one-click-solve frequency), and (ii) learning via a pre/post/delayed battery separating procedural fluency from conceptual understanding and near/far transfer. The hypothesis is a dissociation: solver mode maximizes value/satisfaction/continuance but yields mainly procedural gains, whereas effortful mode yields conceptual/transfer gains but depresses perceived value and continuance — quantifying the satisfaction–learning gap.

Study 2 — resolve it with adaptive "productive friction." Add a controller that, per problem, sets the assistance level from two live signals: formative conceptual-assessment performance and continuance-risk indicators (disengagement, drop in perceived value from brief in-task prompts). It fades assistance as competence grows but re-injects support when disengagement rises, and it reframes perceived value toward learning value (progress/mastery feedback rather than answer delivery). Because the CTE review finds instructor/peer interaction is positively tied to learning and buffers isolation, the controller triggers lightweight human/peer interaction precisely when it raises friction, protecting continuance. Randomly compare adaptive productive-friction against the two fixed modes on the same dual outcomes (EDT continuance constructs and conceptual/transfer learning).

The design directly addresses the gap: it operationalizes and tests the doing-vs-learning tension using the exact continuance constructs the field assumes are benign, and it tests whether adaptively trading momentary usability/value for productive struggle — while reframing value and adding interaction — can decouple the tradeoff, sustaining continuance while producing genuine conceptual learning. Feasibility is high: the tool components (MathML, CAS solving, web assessment), the validated EDT instrument, and standard pre/post/transfer math assessments all already exist in the cited works and can be integrated into one instrumented platform.

paper_title: Robust wide-baseline stereo from maximally stable extremal regions
motivation: Resource bottleneck in organizing growing image collections. A recurring goal is to take an unordered set of widely-separated views and group them into scene clusters and recover relative viewpoints (Schaffalitzky and Zisserman 2002). The machinery is powerful but expensive: affine-covariant region detection, viewpoint-invariant descriptors (Schmid and Mohr 1997; Tuytelaars and Van Gool 1999), and multi-view geometric verification. Even the linear-in-N pipeline reports about 400,000 features and 42 minutes of inter-image hashing on a 46-image set, holding hundreds of thousands of descriptors in memory. All these methods are batch: they assume a fixed collection, extract every region from every image, index everything, and match. Real collections grow continuously, so adding one photo forces re-extraction, re-indexing, and re-clustering of the entire set, prohibitive on commodity hardware, with the index growing unboundedly as near-duplicate views accumulate. This deployment friction is the gap these works leave open.
method: An incremental, memory-bounded framework that turns batch wide-baseline multi-view organization into an online, per-image-amortized operation. (1) Budgeted feature extraction: detect scale-invariant interest points via cheap Laplacian scale selection, rank by distinctiveness, and compute expensive affine-covariant neighbourhoods plus MSER-like watershed regions only for the top-B points, then affine-invariant descriptors; B caps cost and footprint. (2) Incremental locality-sensitive-hash index whose buckets hold posting lists of image-feature ids; inserting an image is O(B) with no rebuild. (3) Sublinear retrieval: hash new descriptors and accumulate bucket-collision votes per existing image for a top-k shortlist, avoiding all-pairs comparison. (4) Budgeted verification: robust epipolar or homography estimation only against the k shortlisted images, reusing cached descriptors, adding edges to a persistent scene graph. (5) Online maintenance via union-find clustering as edges arrive, re-estimating viewpoints only within affected clusters. (6) Memory governance: a global index-size cap with redundancy pruning that keeps canonical representative descriptors per cluster, making index growth sublinear for repeatedly-photographed scenes. Evaluation on landmark sets and growing web-query streams measures per-image update time and peak memory versus batch recomputation, plus clustering and viewpoint accuracy, with ablations over B, k, and pruning cap.

paper_title: A New Extension of the Kalman Filter to Nonlinear Systems
motivation: Prior works give many separate nonlinear filters for range and bearing tracking, but each compares only a few filters on one scenario with non comparable metrics and only qualitative notions of nonlinearity, so no map ties measurable problem descriptors to filter accuracy and statistical consistency.
method: Build an empirical filter selection atlas via Monte Carlo over dimensionless descriptors of measurement and dynamic nonlinearity, running all corpus filters on canonical tracking problems and scoring bias, error, divergence, cost, and the normalized estimation error squared consistency statistic to map where each filter stays consistent.

paper_title: Probability Inequalities for Sums of Bounded Random Variables
motivation: Loeve's Probability Theory surveys classical limit theorems (LLN, law of the iterated logarithm, central limit problem, martingale and ergodic convergence, second-order and Markov processes) purely as asymptotic statements; the review notes rate results (large deviations) are excluded while applied time-series work needs them. EVIDENCE GAP: there is no common, reproducible instrument to observe, measure, benchmark, and audit how faithfully finite samples realize each limit, or how fidelity degrades along the independence-to-dependence axis. Comparable, accumulable finite-sample evidence across dependence regimes is missing.
method: Build a convergence-fidelity benchmark. Provide generators along Loeve's dependence axis (independent sums, martingales, stationary/ergodic and second-order processes, Markov/stable-law processes) with knobs for tail index, memory, and moments. For each, form the theorem's normalized quantity, take its empirical characteristic function, and compare to the predicted limiting characteristic function via a scale-invariant integrated distance, yielding one fidelity score. Vary n and dependence to chart convergence-rate and breakdown curves, compare theorems on this shared metric, validate against Berry-Esseen rates in the independent case, then extend to dependent regimes lacking bounds, accumulating a versioned evidence base.

paper_title: Snakes: Active Contour Models
motivation:
A large fraction of the provided works are really about one recurring problem in early vision: how to "fill the gaps" — interpolating a smooth contour or surface between sparse, locally-detected evidence under generic smoothness/continuity constraints. Ullman's "Filling the gaps" derives subjective-contour shape from isotropy + smoothness + minimum-curvature + locality and realizes it as a biarc/cubic-spline-like network; Terzopoulos' "Regularization of inverse visual problems involving discontinuities" argues that global quadratic smoothness fails at discontinuities and proposes controlled-continuity stabilizers; Zucker/Hummel/Rosenfeld's relaxation labeling enhances smooth curves by local orientation compatibilities; Witkin's scale-space filtering manages the scale at which such descriptions are computed; Kanizsa's "Subjective contours" and "Shape encoding and subjective contours" supply the human phenomenology (including corners, virtual lines, multi-inducer triangles) that any such model must reproduce; and even the disparity-gradient limit is a smoothness/continuity bound governing when the system fuses vs. breaks.

The gap: each of these models/constraints was proposed and "validated" only on a handful of hand-picked demonstration figures, in its own formalism, and largely in isolation. There is no common, quantitative benchmark that (a) parameterizes the space of gap-filling problems, (b) runs the competing constraint formulations on identical inputs, and (c) systematically maps where they agree with one another and with measured human contour shapes. Crucially, the single most contested issue across the sources — how interpolation should behave at discontinuities/corners (Terzopoulos' entire motivation; Ullman's explicit caveat about "special cases of filled-in corners") — has never been tested comparatively. This matters because these smoothness priors still underlie modern reconstruction/regularization, yet we lack an empirical account of which prior matches perception in which geometric regime. The listed works therefore leave clear room for a systematic empirical mapping.
method:
Build "GapAtlas," a benchmark and empirical map of contour-completion constraints in early vision, as an empirical-mapping contribution.

1) Parametric stimulus atlas. Generate a controlled dataset of gap-filling problems defined by interpretable geometric factors: two (and later N) inducer edges specified by gap length, orientation difference, lateral offset, inducer curvature, and a discontinuity flag (aligned-smooth vs. corner/kink), plus classical multi-inducer configurations (Kanizsa triangle, virtual-line dot triads) reconstructed from the "Subjective contours" and "Shape encoding" sources. Each cell of the factor grid yields many instances, giving dense coverage of the problem space rather than isolated demos.

2) Ground truth. Curate human-perceived contour shapes as targets: digitize the shapes documented/traced in the subjective-contour sources, and specify a lightweight tracing protocol (participants draw the perceived contour) to obtain shape distributions for a representative subset. Store ground truth as a curve plus its curvature profile.

3) Unified model bank. Reimplement the competing constraints behind a common interface (same inputs = inducer endpoints/tangents; same output = a sampled interpolated curve): (i) Ullman's minimum-curvature biarc network; (ii) cubic-spline interpolation; (iii) Terzopoulos controlled-continuity variational splines with an explicit continuity-control parameter for discontinuities; (iv) Zucker–Hummel–Rosenfeld relaxation-labeling curve enhancement seeded from the inducers; (v) a scale-space-smoothing baseline (Witkin) that varies the observation scale. Expose each model's key knob (e.g., smoothness order, continuity control, relaxation compatibility, scale).

4) Diagnostics. Define shape-agreement metrics between any two curves: area-between-curves, curvature-profile L2 error, tangent-continuity error at inducers, and a corner-preservation index (does the model reproduce a perceived kink vs. round it off). Add robustness probes: sensitivity to inducer position/orientation noise and to gap size.

5) Empirical maps. Produce (a) per-model error heatmaps over the geometric factor grid against human ground truth; (b) pairwise model-vs-model divergence maps showing where formalisms that are "equivalent in spirit" actually disagree; (c) regime-boundary maps identifying, e.g., the orientation-difference / gap-length region where minimum-curvature biarcs match perception vs. where controlled-continuity is required; and (d) a discontinuity stress test isolating corner stimuli, quantifying how continuity order and discontinuity control explain match-to-human. Summarize into a taxonomy of failure modes (over-smoothing corners, curvature overshoot at large gaps, instability under noise) and report which single constraint, or which combination, best predicts human subjective-contour shape across the atlas.

6) Deliverable. Release the parametric stimulus generator, human-traced ground truth, common-interface model bank, metric suite, and the resulting empirical maps, providing the first systematic comparative measurement of gap-filling constraints and an actionable map of where each prior is perceptually valid.

paper_title: Reinforcement Learning in the Multi-Robot Domain
motivation: No shared benchmark or mechanism-attribution method exists to compare or validate the claim that behavior-based decomposition speeds robot reinforcement learning.
method: Build BehaviorBench, a controlled benchmark with a shared scoring metric, mechanism-attribution ablations, and a validated pre-training decomposition-quality diagnostic.

paper_title: Improving Generalization with Active Learning
motivation: Evidence Gap: early-1990s active/query-learning methods (Query by Committee, MacKay, Hwang, Cohn-Tesauro) each cover one setting, so there is no shared way to measure and compare per-query information gain and generalization, or audit failures under noise and model misspecification.
method: Build a measurement framework: define observables (per-query information gain, version-space reduction, error-versus-queries, committee-disagreement entropy calibrated to true error) and benchmark random, Hwang, QBC, and MacKay strategies across complexity, realizability, and noise axes.

paper_title: A Trainable System for Object Detection
motivation: Prior human-detection works each use one cue and evaluate on private data with incompatible metrics, so cues cannot be compared or their failure conditions mapped.
method: Build a common benchmark with per-instance nuisance labels, run one detector per cue family, unify metrics, and map where each cue dominates and how cues complement each other.

paper_title: Learning the parts of objects by non-negative matrix factorization
motivation: Learning sparse parts based image codes is bottlenecked by cost because eigenfaces gives dense holistic codes ICA is expensive to train and matrix factorization is slow and memory heavy so none scale cheaply or enroll new classes from few samples at large scale
method: Learn a non negative parts dictionary and sparse codes with cheap multiplicative EM updates trained online in mini batches so memory stays independent of dataset size and new classes enroll from one image on a frozen dictionary using nearest neighbor
